sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: asymptoticSpaceComplexity

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines asymptotic space complexity as: The limiting behavior of the use of memory space of an algorithm when the size of the problem goes to infinity. This is usually denoted in big-O notation .

nodes.label: asymptotic time complexity

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: asymptoticTimeComplexity

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines asymptotic time complexity as: The limiting behavior of the execution time of an algorithm when the size of the problem goes to infinity. This is usually denoted in big-O notation .

nodes.label: augmenting path

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: augmentngpth

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines augmenting path as: A path with alternating free and matched edges that begins and ends with free vertices . Used to augment (improve or increase) a matching or flow .

nodes.label: average-case cost

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: averageCaseCost

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines average-case cost as: The sum of costs of an algorithm over all possible inputs divided by the number of possible inputs.

nodes.label: average case

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: averagecase

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines average case as: Having to do with the mathematical average of all cases.

nodes.label: axiomatic semantics

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: axiomaticSemantics

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines axiomatic semantics as: Defining the behavior of an abstract data type with axioms.

nodes.label: bag

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bag

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bag as: An unordered collection of values that may have duplicates. Formal Definition: A bag has a single query function, numberIn(v, B), which tells how many copies of an element are in the bag, and two modifier functions, add(v, B) and remove(v, B). These may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a bag numberIn(v, new()) = 0 numberIn(v, add(v, B)) = 1 + numberIn(v, B) numberIn(v, add(u, B)) = numberIn(v, B) if v ≠ u remove(v, new()) = new() remove(v, add(v, B)) = B remove(v, add(u, B)) = add(u, remove(v, B)) if v ≠ u where B is a bag and u and v are elements. The predicate isEmpty(B) may be defined with the following additional axioms. isEmpty(new()) = true isEmpty(add(v, B)) = false Also known as multi-set.

nodes.label: balanced two-way merge sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: balanc2wayms

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines balanced two-way merge sort as: A balanced k-way merge sort that sorts a data stream using repeated merges. It distributes the input into two streams by repeatedly reading a block of input that fits in memory, a run , sorting it, then writing it to the next stream. It then repeatedly merges the two streams and puts each merged run into one of two output streams until there is a single sorted output.

nodes.label: balance

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: balance

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines balance as: The (weight) balance of a tree is the number of leaves of the left subtree of a tree, denoted |T l |, divided by the total number of leaves of the tree. Formally, ρ(T) = |T l |/|T|. Also known as root balance.

nodes.label: balanced binary search tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: balancedbist

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines balanced binary search tree as: A binary search tree that is balanced .

nodes.label: balanced quicksort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: balancedqsrt

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines balanced quicksort as: A variant of quicksort which attempts to choose a pivot likely to represent the middle of the values to be sorted.

nodes.label: balanced tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: balancedtree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines balanced tree as: A tree where no leaf is much farther away from the root than any other leaf. Different balancing schemes allow different definitions of "much farther" and different amounts of work to keep them balanced.

nodes.label: balanced k-way merge sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: balanckwayms

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines balanced k-way merge sort as: A merge sort that sorts a data stream using repeated merges. It distributes the input into k streams by repeatedly reading a block of input that fits in memory, called a run , sorting it, then writing it to the next stream. It then repeatedly merges the k streams and puts each merged run into one of j output streams until there is a single sorted output.

nodes.label: balanced merge sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: balancmrgsrt

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines balanced merge sort as: A k-way merge sort in which the number of input and output data streams is the same. See balanced k-way merge sort .

nodes.label: BANG file

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bangfile

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines BANG file as: A balanced and nested grid (BANG) file is a point access method that divides space into a nonperiodic grid. Each spatial dimension is divided by a linear hash . Cells may intersect, and points may be distributed between them.

nodes.label: Baum Welch algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: baumWelch

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Baum Welch algorithm as: An algorithm to find hidden Markov model parameters A, B, and Π with the maximum likelihood of generating the given symbol sequence in the observation vector.

nodes.label: BB(α) tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bbalphatree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines BB(α) tree as: A binary tree where the balance of every subtree, ρ(T'), is bounded by α ≤ ρ(T') ≤ 1-α. Also known as weight-balanced tree.

nodes.label: BBP algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bbp

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines BBP algorithm as: Compute the nth hexadecimal digit of π efficiently, without having to compute preceding digits.

nodes.label: BDD

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bdd

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines BDD as: A binary lattice data structure that succinctly represents a truth table by collapsing redundant nodes and eliminating unnecessary nodes.

nodes.label: BD-tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bdtree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines BD-tree as: A binary tree that organizes multidimensional points by splitting off regular subintervals.

nodes.label: best case

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bestcase

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines best case as: (1) The situation or input for which an algorithm or data structure takes the least time or resources. (2) Having to do with this situation or input.

nodes.label: best-case cost

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bestcasecost

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines best-case cost as: The minimum cost to process an input sequence. Also known as optimal cost.

nodes.label: best-first search

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bestfirst

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines best-first search as: A state-space search algorithm that considers the estimated best partial solution next. This is typically implemented with a priority queue .

nodes.label: biconnected component

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: biconnectedComponent

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines biconnected component as: A maximal subset of edges of a connected graph such that the corresponding induced subgraph cannot be disconnected by deleting any vertex .

nodes.label: biconnected graph

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: biconnectedGraph

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines biconnected graph as: A connected graph that is not broken into disconnected pieces by deleting any single vertex (and incident edges ).

nodes.label: bidirectional bubble sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bidirectionalBubbleSort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bidirectional bubble sort as: A variant of bubble sort that compares each adjacent pair of items in a list in turn, swapping them if necessary, and alternately passes through the list from the beginning to the end then from the end to the beginning. It stops when a pass does no swaps. Also known as cocktail shaker sort, shaker sort, double-direction bubble sort.

nodes.label: binary priority queue

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binaryPriorityQueue

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines binary priority queue as: A priority queue implemented with a binary tree having the following restrictions: The key of a node is greater than keys of its children , i.e., it has the heap property . If the right subtree is not empty, the left subtree is not empty. If there are both left and right children, the left child's key is greater than the right child's key.

nodes.label: binary relation

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binaryRelation

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines binary relation as: A relation between exactly two items at a time, such as "greater than" (>), "not equal to" (≠), "proper subset of" (⊂), or "is connected to" (has an edge to) for vertices of a graph .

nodes.label: binary function

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binaryfunc

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines binary function as: A function with two arguments.

nodes.label: binary insertion sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binaryinsort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines binary insertion sort as: Insertion sort in which the proper location for the next item is found with a binary search .

nodes.label: bingo sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bingosort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bingo sort as: A variant of selection sort that orders items by first finding the least value, then repeatedly moving all items with that value to their final location and find the least value for the next pass. This is more efficient than selection sort if there are many duplicate values.

nodes.label: bin packing problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binpacking

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bin packing problem as: Determine how to put the most objects in the least number of fixed space bins. More formally, find a partition and assignment of a set of objects such that a constraint is satisfied or an objective function is minimized (or maximized). There are many variants, such as, 3D, 2D, linear, pack by volume, pack by weight, minimize volume, maximize value, fixed shape objects, etc.

nodes.label: bipartite matching

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bipartmatch

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bipartite matching as: (1) A perfect matching between vertices of a bipartite graph , that is, a subgraph that pairs every vertex with exactly one other vertex. (2) The problem of finding such a matching. Also known as maximum bipartite matching.

nodes.label: bit vector

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bitVector

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bit vector as: An array of bits.

nodes.label: blind sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: blindSort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines blind sort as: A specialized sort algorithm that first builds a blind trie , then traverse the tree left to right.

nodes.label: blind trie

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: blindTrie

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines blind trie as: A specialized Patricia tree whose internal nodes store only an integer, k, which is the length of the common prefix of the strings in the children . Equivalently, the strings first differ in the (k+1) st character.

nodes.label: block

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: block

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines block as: (1) A number of items which are handled together for efficiency. (2) A sequence of don't care symbols.

nodes.label: block addressing index

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: blockAddressingIndex

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines block addressing index as: An inverted index that includes the block , or general location, within texts, in addition to the text in which the word appears.

nodes.label: blocking flow

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: blockingflow

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines blocking flow as: A flow function in which any directed path from the source to the sink contains a saturated edge .

nodes.label: Bloom filter

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bloomFilter

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Bloom filter as: A data structure with a probabilistic algorithm to quickly test membership in a large set using multiple hash functions into a single array of bits.

nodes.label: blossom

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: blossom

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines blossom as: An odd length cycle which appears during a matching algorithm on general graphs .

nodes.label: bogosort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bogosort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bogosort as: A terribly inefficient sort algorithm that repeatedly generates a random permutation of the items until the items are in order.

nodes.label: boolean

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: boolean

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines boolean as: (1) In computer science, entities having just two values: 1 or 0, true or false, on or off, etc. along with the operations and , or , and not . (2) In mathematics, entities from an algebra equivalent to intersection , union , and complement over subsets of a given set .

nodes.label: boolean expression

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: booleanexpr

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines boolean expression as: An expression consisting solely of boolean variables and values and boolean operations, such as and , or , not , implies , etc.

nodes.label: boolean function

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: booleanfnctn

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines boolean function as: A function whose range is {0, 1}. It can be understood to evaluate the truth or falsity of each element of its domain .

nodes.label: border

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: border

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines border as: A string v which is both a prefix and a suffix of another string u. String v is the border of u if it is the longest proper border of u.

nodes.label: Boruvka's algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: boruvkasAlgorithm

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Boruvka's algorithm as: Compute a minimum spanning tree .

nodes.label: bottleneck traveling salesman

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bottleneckTravelingSales

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bottleneck traveling salesman as: Find a tour where no edge is more costly than some (bottleneck) amount.

nodes.label: boundary-based representation

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: boundarybasd

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines boundary-based representation as: A representation of a region that is based on its boundary.

nodes.label: bounded queue

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: boundedqueue

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bounded queue as: A queue limited to a fixed number of items.

nodes.label: bounded stack

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: boundedstack

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bounded stack as: A stack limited to a fixed number of items.

nodes.label: Boyer-Moore-Horspool

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: boyerMooreHorspool

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Boyer-Moore-Horspool as: A string matching algorithm that compares characters from the end of the pattern to its beginning. When characters don't match, searching jumps to the next matching position in the pattern. Also known as Horspool.

nodes.label: bozo sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bozoSort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bozo sort as: A terribly inefficient sort algorithm that randomly swaps items until they are in order.

nodes.label: BPP

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bpp

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines BPP as: The class of languages for which a membership computation by a probabilistic Turing machine halts in polynomial time with the right answer (accept or reject) at least 2/3 of the time. "BPP" means " B ounded error P robability in P olynomial" time. Also known as bounded error probability in polynomial time.

nodes.label: Bradford's law

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bradfordsLaw

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Bradford's law as: Journals in a field can be divided into three parts, each with about one-third of all articles: 1) a core of a few journals, 2) a second zone, with more journals, and 3) a third zone, with the bulk of journals. The number of journals is 1:n:n².

nodes.label: Bresenham's algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bresenham

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Bresenham's algorithm as: An efficient algorithm to render a line with pixels. The long dimension is incremented for each pixel, and the fractional slope is accumulated.

nodes.label: bridge

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bridge

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bridge as: An edge of a connected graph whose removal would make the graph unconnected.

nodes.label: British Museum technique

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: britishMuseum

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines British Museum technique as: Find a solution by checking all possibilities one by one, beginning with the smallest. This is a conceptual, not a practical, technique where the number of possibilities are enormous.

nodes.label: brute force string search with mismatches

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bruteForceStrSrchwMismatch

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines brute force string search with mismatches as: Beginning with the (leftmost) position in a string and trying each position in turn, find the number of characters for which the pattern and the substring beginning at that position don't match (the Hamming distance ). Return the first position with k or fewer mismatches.

nodes.label: brute force string search

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bruteForceStringSearch

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines brute force string search as: Find a string in another string or body of text by trying each position one at a time. There are many far faster string matching algorithms. Also known as naive string search.

nodes.label: brute force

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bruteforce

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines brute force as: An algorithm that inefficiently solves a problem, often by trying every one of a wide range of possible solutions.

nodes.label: BSP-tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bsptree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines BSP-tree as: A binary space partitioning (BSP) tree is a binary tree for multidimensional points where successive levels are split by arbitrary hyperplanes.

nodes.label: B*-tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bstartree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines B*-tree as: A B-tree in which nodes are kept 2/3 full by redistributing keys to fill two child nodes, then splitting them into three nodes.

nodes.label: bucket

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bucket

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bucket as: An area of storage where items with a common property are stored. Typically tree data structures and sort algorithms use many buckets, one for each group of items. Usually buckets are kept on disk.

nodes.label: bucket trie

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bucketTrie

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bucket trie as: A variant of a trie in which leaf nodes are buckets which hold up to k strings. Usually implies fixed sized buckets.

nodes.label: bucketing method

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bucketmeth

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bucketing method as: Data organization methods that decompose the space from which spatial data is drawn into regions called buckets. Some conditions for the choice of region boundaries include the number of objects that they contain or on their spatial layout (e.g. minimizing overlap or coverage).

nodes.label: buddy system

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: buddysystem

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines buddy system as: A memory allocation strategy which recursively divides allocatable blocks of memory into pairs of adjacent equal-sized blocks called "buddies".

nodes.label: buddy tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: buddytree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines buddy tree as: A point access method which splits multidimensional space in different dimensions at each level. It also keeps a minimum bounding box of points accessible by each node.

nodes.label: build-heap

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: buildHeap

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines build-heap as: Convert an array into a heap by executing heapify progressively closer to the root . For an array of n nodes, this takes O(n) time under the comparison model.

nodes.label: Burrows-Wheeler transform

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: burrowsWheelerTransform

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Burrows-Wheeler transform as: Permute a string . Repeated substrings lead to repeated characters in the permuted string, which is easier to compress. Knowing which character was last in the original string, the original can be reconstructed from the rearranged string. Also known as BWT.

nodes.label: busy beaver

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: busyBeaver

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines busy beaver as: (1) A Turing machine with a small number of states that halts when started with a blank tape, but writes a huge number of non-blanks or takes a huge number of steps. (2) The problem of finding the maximum number of non-blanks written or steps taken for any Turing machines with a given number of states and symbols.

nodes.label: BV-tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bvtree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines BV-tree as: A conceptual idea which generalizes B-trees to multiple dimensions. BV-trees are not balanced, and searching may require backtracking .

nodes.label: Byzantine generals

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: byzantine

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Byzantine generals as: The problem of reaching a consensus among distributed units if some of them give misleading answers. To be memorable, the problem is couched in terms of generals deciding on a common plan of attack. Some traitorous generals may lie about whether they will support a particular plan and what other generals told them. Exchanging only messages, what decision making algorithm should the generals use to reach a consensus? What percentage of liars can the algorithm tolerate and still correctly determine a consensus?

nodes.label: cactus stack

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cactusstack

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cactus stack as: A variant of stack in which one other cactus stack may be attached to the top. An attached stack is called a "branch." When a branch becomes empty, it is removed. Pop is not allowed if there is a branch. A branch is only accessible through the original reference; it is not accessible through the stack. Formal Definition: The operations new to this variant of stack, branch(S, T) and notch(v), may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. top(branch(S, T)) = top(S) notch(new()) = false notch(push(v, S)) = false notch(branch(S, T)) = true Also known as saguaro stack.

nodes.label: Calculus of Communicating Systems

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: calcucommsys

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Calculus of Communicating Systems as: Robin Milner's algebraic theory to formalize the notion of concurrent computation. Commonly known as CCS.

nodes.label: calendar queue

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: calendarQueue

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines calendar queue as: A fast priority queue implementation having N buckets each with width w, or covering w time. An item with priority p more than current goes in bucket (p/w)%N. Choose N and w to have few items in each bucket. Keep items sorted within buckets. Double or halve N and change w if the number of items grows or shrinks a lot.

nodes.label: candidate consistency testing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: candidate

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines candidate consistency testing as: The stage of two-dimensional matching where a candidate occurrence of the pattern is checked against the "witness" table.

nodes.label: candidate verification

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: candidateVerification

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines candidate verification as: The stage of two-dimensional matching where candidate occurrences of the pattern are actually tested.

nodes.label: canonical complexity class

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: canonical

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines canonical complexity class as: One of the classes defined by logarithmic , polynomial , and exponential bounds on time and space, for deterministic and nondeterministic machines. These classify most of the important computational problems.

nodes.label: capacitated facility location

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: capacifacloc

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines capacitated facility location as: Given a set of demand points, a distance function, and a parameter p, find a set of p supply object (points, lines, segments, etc.) which minimizes some distance objective function and no supply supports too many demand points.

nodes.label: capacity

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: capacity

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines capacity as: The maximum flow that may be sent through an edge or a vertex .

nodes.label: capacity constraint

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: capacitycstr

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines capacity constraint as: The property that the flow on every edge of a flow network is no more than the edge's capacity . More formally, for all edges e, f(e) ≤ u(e), where f(e) is the flow on e and u(e) is its capacity.

nodes.label: Caverphone

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: caverphone

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Caverphone as: An algorithm to code English names phonetically.

nodes.label: CCS

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: ccs

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines CCS as: Robin Milner's algebraic theory to formalize the notion of concurrent computation. An acronym for Calculus of Communicating Systems.

nodes.label: cell probe model

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cellProbeModel

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cell probe model as: A model of computation where the cost of a computation is measured by the total number of memory accesses to a random access memory with ⌈log n⌉ bits cell size. All other computations are not counted and are considered to be free.

nodes.label: cell tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: celltree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cell tree as: A spatial access method where successive levels are split by arbitrary hyperplanes. Concave objects are decomposed into convex pieces. Each convex piece is indexed in every cell which it overlaps.

nodes.label: cellular automaton

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cellulartmtn

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cellular automaton as: Usually a two-dimensional organization of simple finite state machines whose next state depends on their own state and the states of their eight closest neighbors. In general the machines may be arranged in meshes of higher or lower dimension, have larger neighborhoods, or be arbitrarily complex processors.

nodes.label: centroid

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: centroid

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines centroid as: The center of gravity or center of mass of an object.

nodes.label: certificate

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: certificate

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines certificate as: (1) Extra information so the correctness of an answer to a decision problem can be quickly checked. (2) For any graph property P and graph G, a certificate for G is a graph G' such that G has property P if and only if G' has the property.

nodes.label: chain

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: chain

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines chain as: A set with a total order .

nodes.label: chaining

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: chaining

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines chaining as: A class of collision resolution schemes in which linked lists handle collisions in a hash table . The two main subclasses are separate chaining , where lists are outside the table, and coalesced chaining , where the lists are within the table.

nodes.label: child

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: child

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines child as: A node of a tree referred to by a parent node. See the figure at tree . Every node, except the root , is the child of some parent.

nodes.label: Chinese postman problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: chinesePostman

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Chinese postman problem as: Find a minimum length closed walk that traverses each edge at least once. Finding an optimal solution in a graph with both directed and undirected edges is NP-complete .

nodes.label: Chinese remainder theorem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: chineseRmndr

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Chinese remainder theorem as: An integer n can be solved uniquely mod LCM(A(i)) , given modulii (n mod A(i)), A(i) > 0 for i=1..k, k > 0. In other words, given the remainders an integer gets when it's divided by an arbitrary set of divisors, you can uniquely determine the integer's remainder when it is divided by the least common multiple of those divisors.

nodes.label: Christofides algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: christofides

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Christofides algorithm as: (1) A heuristic algorithm to find a near-optimal solution to the traveling salesman problem. Step 1: find a minimum spanning tree T. Step 2: find a perfect matching M among vertices with odd degree . Step 3: combine the edges of M and T to make a multigraph G. Step 4: find an Euler cycle in G. Step 5: Turn the Euler cycle into a Hamiltonian cycle by skipping vertices already seen. (2) An algorithm to find the chromatic number of a graph.

nodes.label: chromatic number

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: chromatcnmbr

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines chromatic number as: The minimum number of colors needed to color the vertices of a graph such that no two adjacent vertices have the same color.

nodes.label: chromatic index

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: chromaticndx

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines chromatic index as: The minimum number of colors needed to color the edges of a graph .

nodes.label: circuit

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: circuit

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines circuit as: (1) An acyclic network of inputs, logic gates, and outputs. Contrasted with a Turing machine , it has no memory. (2) A cycle in a graph .

nodes.label: circuit complexity

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: circuitComplexity

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines circuit complexity as: The study of the size, depth, and other attributes of circuits that decide specified languages or compute specified functions.

nodes.label: clique

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: clique

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines clique as: A set of vertices in an undirected graph in which there is an edge between every pair of vertices. In other words, a subgraph that is complete .

nodes.label: clique problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cliqueproblm

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines clique problem as: Find the largest clique in an undirected graph .

nodes.label: clustering

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: clustering

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines clustering as: The tendency for entries in a hash table using open addressing to be stored together, even when the table has ample empty space to spread them out.

nodes.label: clustering free

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: clusteringFree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines clustering free as: When a collision resolution scheme spreads out entries in a hash table .

nodes.label: coalesced chaining

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: coalescedChaining

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines coalesced chaining as: A scheme in which linked lists within the hash table handle collisions . An item that collides is put in the next empty place in the array and added to the end of a list embedded in the array items. Any open addressing method to compute possible new positions may be used to find the "next" empty place.

nodes.label: coarsening

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: coarsening

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines coarsening as: To alter a problem, typically restricting it to a less complex feasible region or objective function , so that the resulting problem can be efficiently solved, usually by dynamic programming .

nodes.label: codeword

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: codeword

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines codeword as: Sequence of bits of a code corresponding to a symbol.

nodes.label: coding tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: codingTree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines coding tree as: A full binary tree that represents a coding, such as produced by Huffman coding . Each leaf is an encoded symbol. The path from the root to a leaf is its codeword.

nodes.label: collective recursion

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: collectiveRecursion

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines collective recursion as: A special form of tail recursion , where the results are produced during the recursive calls and nothing is returned. The recursion may be optimized away by executing the call in the current stack frame, rather than creating a new stack frame, or by deallocating the entire recursion stack at once rather than a little at each return.

nodes.label: collision

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: collision

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines collision as: When two or more items should be kept in the same location, especially in hash tables , that is, when two or more different keys hash to the same value.

nodes.label: collision resolution scheme

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: collisionres

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines collision resolution scheme as: A way of handling collisions , that is, when two or more items should be kept in the same location, especially in a hash table . The general ways are keeping subsequent items within the table and computing possible locations ( open addressing ), keeping lists for items that collide ( chaining ), or keeping one special overflow area.

nodes.label: combination

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: combination

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines combination as: Choose m of n elements, where m ≤ n.

nodes.label: Communicating Sequential Processes

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: communseqpro

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Communicating Sequential Processes as: C. A. R. Hoare's algebraic theory to formalize the notion of concurrent computation. Commonly known as CSP.

nodes.label: commutative

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: commutative

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines commutative as: A function where f(A, B) = f(B, A).

nodes.label: compact DAWG

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: compactDAWG

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines compact DAWG as: A directed acyclic word graph (DAWG) representing the suffixes of a given string in which each edge is labeled with the longest possible string. The strings along a path from the root to a node are the substring which the node represents.

nodes.label: compact data structure

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: compactDataStruct

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines compact data structure as: A data structure that needs far less space and allows efficient access without decompression.

nodes.label: compact trie

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: compactTrie

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines compact trie as: A trie in which nonbranching subtrees leading to leaf nodes are cut off.

nodes.label: competitive analysis

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: competitiveAnalysis

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines competitive analysis as: An analysis in which the performance of an on-line algorithm is compared to the best that could have been achieved if all the inputs had been known in advance.

nodes.label: competitive ratio

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: competitivrt

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines competitive ratio as: The worst case of the ratio between the cost incurred by an on-line algorithm and the best-case cost .

nodes.label: complement

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: complement

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines complement as: (1) Of a boolean , 0 if 1, or 1 if 0. See not . (2) Of a set A, a set having all the members which are in the universe , but not in A.

nodes.label: complete binary tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: completeBinaryTree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines complete binary tree as: A binary tree in which every level (depth), except possibly the deepest, is completely filled. At depth n, the height of the tree, all nodes must be as far left as possible.

nodes.label: complete tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: completetree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines complete tree as: A tree in which every level , except possibly the deepest, is entirely filled. At depth n, the height of the tree, all nodes are as far left as possible.

nodes.label: complexity

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: complexity

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines complexity as: The intrinsic minimum amount of resources, for instance, memory, time, messages, etc., needed to solve a problem or execute an algorithm .

nodes.label: complexity class

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: complexityClass

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines complexity class as: Any of a set of computational problems with the same bounds ( Θ(n) ) on time and space, for deterministic and nondeterministic machines.

nodes.label: compound algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: compoundAlgorithm

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines compound algorithm as: An algorithm in which one or more of the computable steps is a call to execute another algorithm.

nodes.label: computable

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: computable

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines computable as: A function that can be computed by an algorithm --- equivalently, by a Turing machine .

nodes.label: concurrent data structure

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: concurrentDataStructure

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines concurrent data structure as: A data structure designed to work correctly while being accessed by many asynchronous threads. The two main types are blocking and nonblocking.

nodes.label: concurrent read, concurrent write

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: concurrentReadConWrt

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines concurrent read, concurrent write as: A parallel memory model in which multiple processors can read simultaneously from a single memory location, and multiple processors can write simultaneously to a single memory location. Also known as CRCW.

nodes.label: concurrent read, exclusive write

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: concurrentReadExcluWrt

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines concurrent read, exclusive write as: A parallel memory model in which multiple processors can read simultaneously from a single memory location, but only one processor can write to any one memory location at one time. Also known as CREW.

nodes.label: concurrent flow

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: concurrntflw

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines concurrent flow as: A multi-commodity flow in which the same fraction of the demand of each commodity is satisfied.

nodes.label: confluently persistent data structure

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: confluentlyPersistData

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines confluently persistent data structure as: A fully persistent data structure that allows meld or merge operations to combine two different versions.

nodes.label: conjunction

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: conjunction

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines conjunction as: The boolean and function.

nodes.label: connected components

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: connectedComponents

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines connected components as: The set of maximally connected components of an undirected graph .

nodes.label: constant function

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: constantfunc

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines constant function as: A function that always gives the same value.

nodes.label: Cook reduction

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cookreductin

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Cook reduction as: A reduction computed by a deterministic polynomial time oracle Turing machine .

nodes.label: Cook's theorem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cookstheorem

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Cook's theorem as: The language SAT of satisfiable Boolean formulas is NP-complete .

nodes.label: CORDIC

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cordic

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines CORDIC as: Compute trigonometric functions by iterative complex rotations. The advantage is that all computations can be done with addition, subtraction, and binary shifts.

nodes.label: covering

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: covering

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines covering as: Given a finite collection of subsets of a finite ground set, to find an optimal subcollection whose union covers the ground set.

nodes.label: critical path problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: criticalPath

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines critical path problem as: Find the longest path from any source to any sinks in a directed acyclic graph which has weights, or numeric values, on vertices .

nodes.label: CSP

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: csp

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines CSP as: C. A. R. Hoare's algebraic theory to formalize the notion of concurrent computation. An acronym for Communicating Sequential Processes.

nodes.label: CTL

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: ctl

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines CTL as: A propositional, branching-time temporal logic for which formulas can be checked in linear time. An acronym for Computation Tree Logic.

nodes.label: cut

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cut

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cut as: A nonempty, proper subset of vertices of a graph .

nodes.label: cutting stock problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cuttingStock

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cutting stock problem as: Find the best arrangement of shapes on rectangles to minimize waste or the number of rectangles. This is a two-dimensional variant of the bin packing problem . It is NP-complete .

nodes.label: cutting plane

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cuttingplane

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cutting plane as: A valid inequality for an integer polyhedron that separates the polyhedron from a given point outside it.

nodes.label: cut vertex

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cutvertex

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cut vertex as: A vertex whose deletion along with incident edges results in a graph with more components than the original graph. Also known as articulation point.

nodes.label: cyclic redundancy check

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cyclicRedundancyCheck

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cyclic redundancy check as: (1) A method to detect and correct errors by adding bits derived from a block or string of bits to the block. (2) An algorithm to compute bits characteristic of a block based on the algebra of polynomials over the integers, modulo 2. (3) The characteristic bits of a block. Also known as CRC.

nodes.label: D-adjacent

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dadjacent

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines D-adjacent as: An entry reachable for a (d-1)-extremal entry through a unit vertical, horizontal, or diagonal-mismatch step.

nodes.label: DAG shortest paths

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dagShortPath

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines DAG shortest paths as: Solve the single-source shortest-path problem in a weighted directed acyclic graph by 1) doing a topological sort on the vertices by edge so vertices with no incoming edges are first and vertices with only incoming edges are last, 2) assign an infinite distance to every vertex (dist(v)=∞) and a zero distance to the source, and 3) for each vertex v in sorted order, for each outgoing edge e(v,u), if dist(v) + weight(e) < dist(u), set dist(u)=dist(v) + weight(e) and the predecessor of u to v.

nodes.label: decidable language

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: decidableLanguage

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines decidable language as: A language for which membership can be decided by an algorithm that halts on all inputs in a finite number of steps --- equivalently, can be recognized by a Turing machine that halts for all inputs. Also known as recursive language, totally decidable language.

nodes.label: decidable problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: decidableProblem

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines decidable problem as: A decision problem that can be solved by an algorithm that halts on all inputs in a finite number of steps. The associated language is called a decidable language . Also known as totally decidable problem, algorithmically solvable, recursively solvable.

nodes.label: decision problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: decisionProblem

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines decision problem as: A problem with a "yes" or "no" answer. Equivalently, a function whose range is two values, such as {0,1}.

nodes.label: decomposable searching problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: decomposable

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines decomposable searching problem as: A searching problem for which one can decompose the searched domain into subsets, find answers from these subsets, and combine these answers to form the solution to the original problem. More formally a problem with a query Q is decomposable given if there exists an efficiently computable associative and commutative binary operator @ satisfying the condition: Q(x, A ∪ B) = @(Q(x,A),Q(x,B)).

nodes.label: degree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: degree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines degree as: (1) Of a vertex , the number of edges connected to it. (2) Of a graph , the maximum degree of any vertex. (3) Of a tree node , the number of child nodes it has.

nodes.label: dense graph

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: densegraph

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines dense graph as: A graph in which the number of edges is close to the possible number of edges.

nodes.label: depoissonization

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: depoissonization

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines depoissonization as: To interpret a solution to a poisson model in the original model after poissonization .

nodes.label: depth

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: depth

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines depth as: Of a node , the distance from the node to the root of the tree . Formal Definition: The depth of the root is 0. The depth of a node is one plus the depth of its parent .

nodes.label: derangement

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: derangement

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines derangement as: A permutation of elements, where no element is in its original position.

nodes.label: descendant

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: descendant

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines descendant as: A child of a node in a tree , any of the children of the children, etc.

nodes.label: deterministic finite automata string search

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: determFinitAutSrch

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines deterministic finite automata string search as: A string matching algorithm which builds a deterministic finite state machine to recognize the search string. The machine is then run at each location in turn. If the machine accepts, that is a match.

nodes.label: deterministic finite tree automaton

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: determFinitTreeAutom

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines deterministic finite tree automaton as: A deterministic finite state machine that accepts finitary trees rather than just strings . The tree nodes are marked with the letters of the alphabet of the automaton, and the transition function encodes the next states for each branch of the tree. The acceptance condition is modified accordingly. Also known as DFTA.

nodes.label: deterministic tree automaton

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: determTreeAutom

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines deterministic tree automaton as: A deterministic finite state machine that accepts infinite trees rather than just strings . The tree nodes are marked with the letters of the alphabet of the automaton, and the transition function encodes the next states for each branch of the tree. The expressive power of such automata varies depending on the acceptance conditions of the trees.

nodes.label: deterministic

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: deterministc

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines deterministic as: Permitting at most one next move at any step in a computation.

nodes.label: deterministic algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: deterministicAlgorithm

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines deterministic algorithm as: An algorithm whose behavior can be completely predicted from the input.

nodes.label: Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: deutschJozsaAlgo

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm as: A quantum algorithm to determine whether a function is constant or balanced, that is, returns 1 for half the domain and 0 for the other half. For a function taking n input qubits, first, do Hadamards on n 0's, forming all possible inputs, and a single 1, which will be the answer qubit. Next, run the function once; this exclusive or 's the result with the answer qubit. Finally, do Hadamards on the n inputs again, and measure the answer qubit. If it is 0, the function is constant, otherwise the function is balanced.

nodes.label: diagonalization

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: diagonaliztn

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines diagonalization as: A proof technique for showing that a given language does not belong to a given complexity class, used in many separation theorems .

nodes.label: diameter

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: diameter

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines diameter as: The maximum of the distances between all possible pairs of vertices of a graph .

nodes.label: dichotomic search

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dichotomicSearch

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines dichotomic search as: Search by selecting between two distinct alternatives (dichotomies) at each step.

nodes.label: dictionary

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dictionary

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines dictionary as: An abstract data type storing items, or values. A value is accessed by an associated key . Basic operations are new, insert, find and delete. Formal Definition: The operations new(), insert(k, v, D), and find(k, D) may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a dictionary find(k, insert(k, v, D)) = v find(k, insert(j, v, D)) = find(k, D) if k ≠ j where k and j are keys, v is a value, and D is a dictionary. The modifier function delete(k, D) may be defined as follows. delete(k, new()) = new() delete(k, insert(k, v, D)) = delete(k, D) delete(k, insert(j, v, D)) = insert(j, v, delete(k, D)) if k ≠ j If we want find to be a total function , we could define find(k, new()) using a special value: fail . This only changes the return type of find. find(k, new()) = fail Also known as association list, map, property list.

nodes.label: difference

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: difference

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines difference as: The difference of set A minus set B is a set having all the members which are in A, but not in B.

nodes.label: digital search tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: digitalSearchTree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines digital search tree as: A trie which stores the strings in internal nodes , so there is no need for extra leaf nodes to store the strings.

nodes.label: digital tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: digitaltree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines digital tree as: A tree for storing strings in which nodes are organized by substrings common to two or more strings.

nodes.label: diminishing increment sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: diminishingIncSort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines diminishing increment sort as: An in-place sort algorithm that repeatedly reorders different, small subsets of the input until the entire array is ordered. On each pass it handles i sets of n/i items, where n is the total number of items. Each set is every i th item, e.g. set 1 is item 1, 1+i, 1+2i, etc., set 2 is item 2, 2+i, etc. On each succeeding pass, the increment or gap, i, is reduced until it is 1 for the last pass.

nodes.label: dining philosophers

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: diningphilos

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines dining philosophers as: Suppose a number of philosophers surround a dining table. Adjacent philosophers share one fork. They spend time thinking or trying to eat. A philosopher must have both the fork on the left and the fork on the right to eat. Clearly adjacent philosophers cannot eat at the same time. The problem is to find an algorithm for taking forks that prevents deadlock, starvation, etc.

nodes.label: direct chaining

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: directChaining

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines direct chaining as: A collision resolution scheme in which the hash table is an array of links to lists . Each list holds all the items with the same hash value.

nodes.label: directed acyclic word graph

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: directedAcyclicWordGraph

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines directed acyclic word graph as: (1) A directed acyclic graph representing the suffixes of a given string in which each edge is labeled with a character. The characters along a path from the root to a node are the substring which the node represents. (2) A finite state machine that recognizes a set of words. Also known as DAWG.

nodes.label: discrete interval encoding tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: discretintrv

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines discrete interval encoding tree as: A binary search tree that stores consecutive values as intervals. Also known as diet.

nodes.label: discrete p-center

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: discretpcntr

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines discrete p-center as: A facility location problem in which the supply points must be a subset of demand points.

nodes.label: disjoint set

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: disjointset

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines disjoint set as: A set whose members do not overlap, are not duplicated, etc.

nodes.label: disjunction

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: disjunction

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines disjunction as: The boolean or function.

nodes.label: distribution sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: distributionSort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines distribution sort as: Any sort algorithm where items are distributed from the input to multiple intermediate structures, which are then gathered and placed on the output.

nodes.label: distributional complexity

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: distributionalComplex

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines distributional complexity as: The expected running time of the best possible deterministic algorithm over the worst possible probability distribution on the inputs.

nodes.label: distributive partitioning sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: distributivePartitioningSort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines distributive partitioning sort as: Step 1: find the median key . Step 2: distribute the n items into n/2 buckets linearly covering the interval from the minimum to the median and n/2 buckets linearly covering the interval from the median to the maximum. Step 3: compact the buckets, removing empty buckets. Recursively start again at step 1 for any bucket with multiple items. Linked lists are used to avoid moving items until a final phase and to avoid bucket overflows.

nodes.label: divide and marriage before conquest

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dividemarrig

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines divide and marriage before conquest as: A variant of divide and conquer in which subproblems created in the "divide" step are merged before the "conquer" step.

nodes.label: domain

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: domain

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines domain as: (1) The inputs for which a function or relation is defined. For instance, 0 is not in the domain of reciprocal (1/x). (2) The possible values of a variable.

nodes.label: don't care

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dontcare

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines don't care as: A special symbol which matches any other symbol of a given alphabet .

nodes.label: Doomsday rule

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: doomsday

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Doomsday rule as: An algorithm to find the day of the week for any date. It is simple enough to memorize and do mentally.

nodes.label: double metaphone

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: doubleMetaphone

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines double metaphone as: An algorithm to code English words (and foreign words often heard in the United States) phonetically by reducing them to a combination of 12 consonant sounds. It returns two codes if a word has two plausible pronunciations, such as a foreign word. This reduces matching problems from wrong spelling.

nodes.label: double-ended priority queue

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: doubleendpq

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines double-ended priority queue as: A priority queue which simultaneously keeps track of the maximum and minimum keys , and supports operations efficiently on either extreme (minimum or maximum).

nodes.label: dual

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dual

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines dual as: The dual of a planar graph , G, is a graph with a vertex for each region in G and an edge between vertices for each pair of adjacent regions. The new edge crosses the edge in G which is the boundary between the adjacent regions.

nodes.label: dual-pivot quicksort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dualPivotQuicksort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines dual-pivot quicksort as: Pick two elements from the array to be sorted (the pivots), partition the remaining elements into (i) those less than the lesser pivot, (ii) those between the pivots, and (iii) those greater than the greater pivot, and recursively sort these partitions.

nodes.label: dynamic

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dynamic

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines dynamic as: When the problem domain may change, e.g., there may be insertions and deletions.

nodes.label: dynamic hashing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dynamicHashing

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines dynamic hashing as: A hash table that grows to handle more items. The associated hash function must change as the table grows. Some schemes may shrink the table to save space when items are deleted.

nodes.label: dynamic array

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dynamicarray

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines dynamic array as: An array whose size may change over time. Items are not only added or removed, but memory used changes, too.

nodes.label: dynamization transformation

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dynamization

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines dynamization transformation as: A data structuring technique that can make a static data structure dynamic . In so doing, the performance of the dynamic structure will exhibit certain space-time tradeoffs.

nodes.label: easy split, hard merge

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: easySplitHardMerge

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines easy split, hard merge as: A recursive algorithm, especially a sort algorithm, where dividing (splitting) into smaller problems is quick or simple and combining (merging) the solutions is time consuming or complex.

nodes.label: edge connectivity

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: edgeConnectivity

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines edge connectivity as: (1) The smallest number of edges whose deletion will cause a connected graph to not be connected. (2) For a pair of vertices s and t in a graph, the smallest number of edges whose deletion will separate s from t.

nodes.label: edge coloring

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: edgecoloring

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines edge coloring as: An assignment of colors (or any distinct marks) to the edges of a graph . A coloring is a proper coloring if no two adjacent edges have the same color.

nodes.label: edge crossing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: edgecrossing

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines edge crossing as: Two different edges cross in a graph drawing if their geometric representations intersect. The number of crossings in a graph drawing is the number of pairs of edges which cross.

nodes.label: edit operation

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: editoperation

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines edit operation as: On a string , the operation of deletion, insertion, or substitution performed on a single symbol. On a tree , the deletion of a node v followed by the reassignment of all children of v to the node of which v was formerly a child , the insertion of a new node followed by the reassignment of some arcs departing from the parent of the new node, or the substitution of the label of one of the nodes with another label. Each edit operation may have an associated nonnegative real number representing its cost.

nodes.label: edit script

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: editscript

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines edit script as: A sequence of viable edit operations on a string or tree .

nodes.label: efficiency

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: efficiency

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines efficiency as: The resources an algorithm used to find an answer. It is usually measured in terms of the theoretical computations, such as comparisons or data moves, the memory used, the number of messages passed, the number of disk accesses, etc.

nodes.label: 8 queens

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: eightqueens

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines 8 queens as: Place eight chess queens on an 8 × 8 board such that no queen can attack another. Efficiently find all possible placements.

nodes.label: elastic-bucket trie

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: elasticBucketTrie

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines elastic-bucket trie as: A variant of a bucket trie in which each leaf node for n strings is a bucket allocated to hold exactly n strings.

nodes.label: element uniqueness

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: elementnqnss

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines element uniqueness as: The problem of determining if there are duplicates in a set of numbers.

nodes.label: end-of-string

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: endofstring

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines end-of-string as: A special character indicating the end of a string .

nodes.label: Euclidean Steiner tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: euclidSteinerTree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Euclidean Steiner tree as: A tree of minimum Euclidean distance connecting a set of points, called terminals , in the plane. This tree may include points other than the terminals, which are called Steiner points .

nodes.label: Euclidean traveling salesman problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: euclidntrvls

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Euclidean traveling salesman problem as: Find a path of minimum Euclidean distance between points in a plane which includes each point exactly once and returns to its starting point.

nodes.label: Euler cycle

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: eulercycle

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Euler cycle as: A path through a graph which starts and ends at the same vertex and includes every edge exactly once. Also known as Eulerian path, Königsberg bridges problem.

nodes.label: Eulerian graph

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: euleriangrph

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Eulerian graph as: A graph that has an Euler cycle .

nodes.label: EXCELL

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: excell

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines EXCELL as: A point access method using a dynamic multidimensional array .

nodes.label: exclusive read, concurrent write

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: exclusiveReadConWrt

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines exclusive read, concurrent write as: A parallel memory model in which only one processor can read from any one memory location at one time, but multiple processors can write simultaneously to a single memory location. Also known as ERCW.

nodes.label: exclusive read, exclusive write

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: exclusiveReadExcluWrt

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines exclusive read, exclusive write as: A parallel memory model in which only one processor can read from any one memory location at one time, and only one processor can write to any one memory location at one time. Also known as EREW.

nodes.label: existential state

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: existentlstt

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines existential state as: A state in a nondeterministic Turing machine from which the machine accepts if any move leads to acceptance.

nodes.label: extended Euclid's algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: extendEuclid

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines extended Euclid's algorithm as: An algorithm to find the greatest common divisor , g , of two positive integers, a and b , and coefficients, h and j , such that g = ha + jb .

nodes.label: extended binary tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: extendedBinaryTree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines extended binary tree as: A binary tree with special nodes replacing every null subtree. Every regular node has two children , and every special node has no children.

nodes.label: extendible hashing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: extendibleHashing

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines extendible hashing as: A hash table in which the hash function is the last few bits of the key and the table refers to buckets . Table entries with the same final bits may use the same bucket. If a bucket overflows, it splits, and if only one entry referred to it, the table doubles in size. If a bucket is emptied by deletion, entries using it are changed to refer to an adjoining bucket, and the table may be halved.

nodes.label: extended k-d tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: extendkdtree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines extended k-d tree as: A spatial access method where successive levels are split along different dimensions into nonoverlapping cells. Objects are indexed in all cells they intersect.

nodes.label: external memory algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: externalMemoryAlgo

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines external memory algorithm as: An algorithm that is efficient when accessing most of the data is very slow, such as, on disk.

nodes.label: external memory data structure

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: externalMemoryDataStr

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines external memory data structure as: A data structure that is efficient even when accessing most of the data is very slow, such as, on a disk.

nodes.label: external quicksort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: externalQuicksort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines external quicksort as: Read the M/2 first and last elements into a buffer (the buffer acts like the pivot in quicksort ), and sort them. Read the next element from the beginning or end to balance writing. If the next element is less than the least of the buffer, write it to available space at the beginning. If greater than the greatest, write it to the end. Otherwise write the greatest or least of the buffer, and put the next element in the buffer. Keep the maximum lower and minimum upper keys written to avoid resorting middle elements that are in order. When done, write the buffer. Recursively sort the smaller partition, and loop to sort the remaining partition.

nodes.label: external index

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: externalindx

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines external index as: An auxiliary data structure added to a main data structure to improve operations, such as a search on a secondary key .

nodes.label: external merge

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: externalmerg

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines external merge as: To combine multiple sorted data streams into a single sorted stream using external storage.

nodes.label: extremal

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: extremal

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines extremal as: Some of the entries of the auxiliary array used in a string matching algorithm. An entry is d-extremal if it is the deepest entry on its diagonal to be given value d.

nodes.label: extreme point

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: extremepoint

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines extreme point as: A corner point of a polyhedron . More formally, a point which cannot be expressed as a convex combination of other points in the polyhedron.

nodes.label: facility location

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: facilityloc

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines facility location as: Given a set of demand points, a distance function, and a parameter p, find a set of p supply objects (points, lines, segments, etc.) which minimizes some distance objective function . The function may be the maximum distance between any demand point and the nearest supply, so no demand point is too far from a supply, or the sum of distances to the nearest supply.

nodes.label: fathoming

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fathoming

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines fathoming as: Pruning a search tree .

nodes.label: feasible region

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: feasibleregn

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines feasible region as: The set of all possible solutions of an optimization problem .

nodes.label: feasible solution

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: feasiblesltn

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines feasible solution as: Any element of the feasible region of an optimization problem .

nodes.label: feedback edge set

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: feedbackEdgeSet

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines feedback edge set as: The smallest set of edges whose deletion results in an acyclic graph .

nodes.label: feedback vertex set

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: feedbackVertexSet

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines feedback vertex set as: The smallest set of vertices whose deletion results in an acyclic graph .

nodes.label: Fibonacci tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fibonacciTree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Fibonacci tree as: A variant of a binary tree where a tree of order n (n>1) has a left subtree of order n-1 and a right subtree of order n-2. An order 0 Fibonacci tree has no nodes , and an order 1 tree has 1 node.

nodes.label: Find

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: find

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Find as: An algorithm to select the k th smallest element of an array and partition the array around it. First, partition around the value of the k th element. If the split is not at element k, move the upper or lower boundary and partition again.

nodes.label: finitary tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: finitarytree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines finitary tree as: A tree with a finite number of children at every node .

nodes.label: first-in, first-out

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: firstinfrstt

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines first-in, first-out as: A policy that items are processed in order of arrival. A queue implements this.

nodes.label: fixed-grid method

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fixedgrdmthd

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines fixed-grid method as: Space decomposition into rectangular cells by overlaying a grid on it.If the cells are congruent (i.e.,of the same width, height, etc.), then the grid is said to be uniform.

nodes.label: flow

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: flow

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines flow as: A measure of the maximum weight along paths in a weighted, directed graph .

nodes.label: flow conservation

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: flowconsrvtn

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines flow conservation as: The property that no vertex , except the source and sink , of a flow network creates or stores flow. More formally, the incoming flow is the same as the outgoing flow, or, the net flow is 0.

nodes.label: flow function

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: flowfunction

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines flow function as: An assignment of flow values to the edges of a flow network that satisfies flow conservation , skew symmetry , and capacity constraints . Also known as network flow.

nodes.label: flow network

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: flownetwork

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines flow network as: A weighted , directed graph with two specially marked nodes, the source s and the sink t, and a capacity function that maps edges to positive real numbers, u: E |→ ℜ + .

nodes.label: Floyd-Warshall algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: floydWarshall
