nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Floyd-Warshall algorithm as: An algorithm to solve the all pairs shortest path problem in a weighted, directed graph by multiplying an adjacency-matrix representation of the graph multiple times. The edges may have negative weights, but no negative weight cycles . The time complexity is Θ (V³) .

nodes.label: Ford-Fulkerson method

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fordFulkerson

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Ford-Fulkerson method as: Given a flow function and its corresponding residual graph (a maximum-flow problem ), select a path from the source to the sink along which the flow can be increased and increase the flow. Repeat until there are no such paths.

nodes.label: forest

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: forest

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines forest as: A collection of one or more trees . Formal Definition: An undirected , acyclic graph .

nodes.label: forest editing problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: forestedit

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines forest editing problem as: The problem of finding an edit script of minimum cost which transforms a given forest into another given forest.

nodes.label: formal methods

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: formalmethod

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines formal methods as: A group of analytical approaches having mathematically precise foundation which can serve as a framework or adjunct for human engineering and design skills and experience.

nodes.label: formal verification

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: formalverf

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines formal verification as: Establishing properties of hardware or software designs using logic, rather than (just) testing or informal arguments. This involves formal specification of the requirement, formal modeling of the implementation, and precise rules of inference to prove, say, that the implementation satisfies the specification.

nodes.label: forward index

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: forwardIndex

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines forward index as: An index into a set of texts . This is usually created as the first step to making an inverted index .

nodes.label: fractional solution

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fractional

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines fractional solution as: Typically, a solution to a relaxation of an optimization problem .

nodes.label: fractional knapsack problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fractionalKnapsack

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines fractional knapsack problem as: Given materials of different values per unit volume and maximum amounts, find the most valuable mix of materials which fit in a knapsack of fixed volume. Since we may take pieces (fractions) of materials, a greedy algorithm finds the optimum. Take as much as possible of the material that is most valuable per unit volume. If there is still room, take as much as possible of the next most valuable material. Continue until the knapsack is full. Also known as continuous knapsack problem.

nodes.label: free edge

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: freeedge

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines free edge as: An edge which is not in a matching .

nodes.label: free tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: freetree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines free tree as: A connected , acyclic , undirected graph .

nodes.label: free vertex

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: freevertex

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines free vertex as: A vertex not on a matched edge in a matching , or, one which has not been matched.

nodes.label: frequency count heuristic

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: frequencyCountHueristic

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines frequency count heuristic as: A heuristic that keeps the elements of a list ordered by number of times each element is the target of a search .

nodes.label: full binary tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fullBinaryTree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines full binary tree as: A binary tree in which each node has exactly zero or two children . Also known as proper binary tree.

nodes.label: full inverted index

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fullInvertedIndex

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines full inverted index as: An inverted index that includes the exact location within texts, in addition to the text in which the word appears.

nodes.label: fully persistent data structure

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fullyPersistData

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines fully persistent data structure as: A persistent data structure that allows updates to all versions, previous and latest.

nodes.label: fully dynamic graph problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fullydynamic

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines fully dynamic graph problem as: Problem where the update operations include unrestricted insertions and deletions of edges .

nodes.label: fully polynomial approximation scheme

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fullypolynml

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines fully polynomial approximation scheme as: A set of algorithms {A ε | ε > 0}, where each A ε is a 1+ε- approximation algorithm bounded by a polynomial in the length of the input and 1/ε.

nodes.label: function

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: function

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines function as: (1) A computation which takes some arguments or inputs and yields an output. Any particular input yields the same output every time. More formally, a mapping from each element in the domain to an element in the range . (2) A subroutine which returns a value.

nodes.label: GBD-tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: gbdtree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines GBD-tree as: A generalized BD-tree , hence the name, which stores spatially extended objects as a hierarchy of minimum bounding boxes . It is a balanced multiway tree which serves as a spatial access method .

nodes.label: geometric optimization problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: geometricopt

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines geometric optimization problem as: An optimization problem induced by a collection of geometric objects.

nodes.label: global optimum

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: globalOptimum

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines global optimum as: The best possible solution to a problem.

nodes.label: graph partition

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: graphPartition

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines graph partition as: Partition the vertices while keeping the cost of spanning edges low.

nodes.label: graph concentration

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: graphconcen

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines graph concentration as: Contracting a graph by removing a subset of the vertices .

nodes.label: graph drawing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: graphdrawing

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines graph drawing as: The problem of representing a graph in a plane "neatly," for instance with a minimum number of edge crossings .

nodes.label: graph isomorphism

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: graphisomrph

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines graph isomorphism as: Determine if two graphs are isomorphic .

nodes.label: greatest common divisor

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: greatestCommonDivisor

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines greatest common divisor as: (1) The greatest integer which is a divisor of given positive integers. For instance, GCD(30, 42) = 6. (2) An algorithm to find the same. Also known as GCD, highest common factor.

nodes.label: greedy heuristic

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: greedyHeuristic

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines greedy heuristic as: Solve an optimization problem by finding locally optimal solutions .

nodes.label: grid drawing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: griddrawing

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines grid drawing as: A graph drawing in which each vertex is represented by a point with integer coordinates.

nodes.label: grid file

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: gridfile

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines grid file as: A point access method which splits space into a nonperiodic grid. Each spatial dimension is divided by a linear hash . Small sets of points are referred to by one or more cells of the grid.

nodes.label: halting problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: haltingProblem

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines halting problem as: Is there an algorithm to determine whether any arbitrary program halts? Turing proved the answer is, no. Since many questions can be recast to this problem, we can conclude that some programs are absolutely impossible, although heuristic or partial solutions are possible.

nodes.label: Hamiltonian cycle

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hamiltonianCycle

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Hamiltonian cycle as: A path through a graph that starts and ends at the same vertex and includes every other vertex exactly once. Also known as tour.

nodes.label: Hamiltonian path

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hamiltonianPath

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Hamiltonian path as: A simple path through a graph that includes every vertex in the graph.

nodes.label: hard split, easy merge

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hardSplitEasyMerge

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hard split, easy merge as: A recursive algorithm, especially a sort algorithm, where dividing (splitting) into smaller problems is time consuming or complex and combining (merging) the solutions is quick or trivial.

nodes.label: hashbelt

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hashbelt

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hashbelt as: Use a short list or array of hash tables to implement a hash table with aging to expire items. To expire items, add a new table at the head of the list and drop the oldest table, along with its contents. To find an item, search all the tables.

nodes.label: hash heap

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hashheap

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hash heap as: An efficient implementation of a priority queue . The linear hash function monotonically maps keys to buckets , and each bucket is a heap .

nodes.label: hash table delete

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hashtabdelet

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hash table delete as: If the hash table uses chaining , use the chaining data structure delete. If it uses open addressing , mark the item "deleted" for future reuse.

nodes.label: Hausdorff distance

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hausdorffdst

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Hausdorff distance as: A measure of the resemblance of two (fixed) sets of geometric points P and Q, defined as H(P,Q)=max{max a∈ P min b∈ Q d(a,b), max a∈ Q min b∈ P d(a,b)} where d(·,·) is the distance metric, usually the Euclidean distance .

nodes.label: hB-tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hbtree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hB-tree as: A point access method which uses k-d trees to organize the space, but partitions as excluded intervals, like the BANG file . Searching is like in a k-d-B-tree .

nodes.label: head

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: head

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines head as: The first item of a list .

nodes.label: heapify

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: heapify

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines heapify as: Rearrange a heap to maintain the heap property , that is, the key of the root node is more extreme (greater or less) than or equal to the keys of its children . If the root node's key is not more extreme, swap it with the most extreme child key, then recursively heapify that child's subtree. The child subtrees must be heaps to start.

nodes.label: heap property

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: heapproperty

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines heap property as: Each node in a tree has a key which is more extreme (greater or less) than or equal to the key of its parent .

nodes.label: height

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: height

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines height as: The maximum distance of any node from the root . If a tree has only one node (the root), the height is zero. The height of an empty tree is not defined.

nodes.label: height-balanced binary search tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: heightBalancedBinSrchTree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines height-balanced binary search tree as: A height-balanced tree which is also a binary search tree . It supports membership, insert, and delete operations in time logarithmic in the number of nodes in the tree.

nodes.label: height-balanced tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: heightBalancedTree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines height-balanced tree as: A tree whose subtrees differ in height by no more than one and the subtrees are height-balanced, too. An empty tree is height-balanced.

nodes.label: heuristic

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: heuristic

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines heuristic as: An algorithm that usually, but not always, works or that gives nearly the right answer.

nodes.label: histogram sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: histogramSort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines histogram sort as: An efficient 3-pass refinement of a bucket sort algorithm. The first pass counts the number of items for each bucket in an auxiliary array , and then makes a running total so each auxiliary entry is the number of preceding items. The second pass puts each item in its proper bucket according to the auxiliary entry for the key of that item. The last pass sorts each bucket. Also known as interpolation sort.

nodes.label: homeomorphic

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: homeomorphic

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines homeomorphic as: Two graphs are homeomorphic if they can be made isomorphic by inserting new vertices of degree 2 into edges .

nodes.label: horizontal visibility map

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: horizontalVisMap

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines horizontal visibility map as: A partition of the plane into regions by drawing a horizontal straight line through each vertex p of a planar straight-line graph until it intersects an edge e of the graph or extends to infinity. The edge e is said to be horizontally visible from p.

nodes.label: hsadelta

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hsadelta

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hsadelta as: An algorithm to produce a sequence of insert and copy commands (an edit script ) which creates a new version file from a reference file. To begin, hash every block of the reference file and store every hash in a hash value array . Build a suffix array and three other data structures for quick access. Beginning at the first location in the version file, hash a block and look for the longest match in the reference file. Upon a match, encode an insert back to the previous match and a copy of the match. If no match, look at the next location. At the end, encode an insert for remaining unmatched characters.

nodes.label: hybrid algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hybridAlgorithm

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hybrid algorithm as: Any algorithm composed of simpler algorithms.

nodes.label: hyperedge

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hyperedge

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hyperedge as: A connection between any number of vertices of a hypergraph . Formal Definition: A hyperedge is a set of vertices of a hypergraph.

nodes.label: ideal random shuffle

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: idealRandomShuffle

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ideal random shuffle as: A permutation algorithm, or shuffle, that has exactly the same chance of producing any permutation.

nodes.label: ideal merge

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: idealmerge

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ideal merge as: Merge n sorted streams into one output stream. To begin the streams are sorted by the value of the head element of each. Then the head of the first stream, which is the least since the streams were sorted, is removed and written to the output. That stream is inserted back into the list of streams according to its new head. Taking the head of the first stream and reinserting that stream is repeated until all elements have been processed. Using linear search to insert a stream into the list, the execution time is Θ(M N) where M is the total number of elements. Keeping the streams in a heap , the execution time is Θ(M log N) .

nodes.label: implication

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: implication

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines implication as: The boolean implies function.

nodes.label: implies

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: implies

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines implies as: Implication: 0 → 0 = 1, 0 → 1 = 1, 1 → 0 = 0, 1 → 1 = 1.

nodes.label: incompressible string

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: incompressbl

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines incompressible string as: A string whose Kolmogorov complexity equals its length, so that it has no shorter encodings.

nodes.label: in-degree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: indegree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines in-degree as: The number of edges coming into a vertex in a directed graph .

nodes.label: independent set

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: independentSet

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines independent set as: A set of vertices in a graph such that for any pair of vertices, there is no edge between them.

nodes.label: index file

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: indexfile

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines index file as: A file which stores keys and an index into another file. The index file may have additional structure, e.g., be a B-tree .

nodes.label: information theoretic bound

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: information

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines information theoretic bound as: lower bounds on the execution of a computation based on the rate at which information can be accumulated.

nodes.label: in-order traversal

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: inorderTraversal

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines in-order traversal as: Process all nodes of a tree by recursively processing the left subtree, then processing the root , and finally the right subtree. Also known as symmetric traversal.

nodes.label: integer polyhedron

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: integer

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines integer polyhedron as: A polyhedron , all of whose extreme points are integer valued.

nodes.label: integer linear program

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: integerliner

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines integer linear program as: A linear program with additional constraints that all of the variables must take on integer values. Solving such problems is NP-hard .

nodes.label: integer multi-commodity flow

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: integermulti

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines integer multi-commodity flow as: A multi-commodity flow in which the flow of each commodity through each edge must take an integer value. The term is also used to capture the multi-commodity flow problem in which each demand is routed along a single path.

nodes.label: interactive proof system

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: interactvprf

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines interactive proof system as: A protocol in which one or more provers try to convince another party, called the verifier, that the prover(s) possess certain true knowledge, such as the membership of a string x in a given language , often with the goal of revealing no further details about this knowledge. The prover(s) and verifier are formally defined as probabilistic Turing machines with special "interaction tapes" for exchanging messages.

nodes.label: interior-based representation

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: interiorbasd

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines interior-based representation as: A representation of a region that is based on its interior (i.e., the cells that compose it).

nodes.label: internal node

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: internalnode

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines internal node as: A node of a tree that has one or more child nodes, equivalently, one that is not a leaf . Also known as nonterminal node.

nodes.label: interpolation-sequential search

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: interpsequen

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines interpolation-sequential search as: An approximate location is interpolated from the first and last items of a sorted array , then a linear search finds the actual location.

nodes.label: intersection

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: intersection

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines intersection as: The intersection of two sets is a set having those members which are in both sets.

nodes.label: intractable

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: intractable

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines intractable as: A problem for which no algorithm can exist which computes all instances of it in polynomial time .

nodes.label: introspective sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: introspectiveSort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines introspective sort as: A variant of quicksort which switches to heapsort for pathological inputs, that is, when execution time is becoming quadratic. Also known as introsort.

nodes.label: inverse suffix array

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: inverseSuffixArray

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines inverse suffix array as: For each position in a string , the inverse suffix array has its index in the string's suffix array . Formal Definition: Given a suffix array, sa, and the corresponding inverse suffix array, isa, isa[i] = j iff sa[j] = i.

nodes.label: inversion list

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: inversionList

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines inversion list as: A set of non-overlapping numeric ranges, stored in an array in increasing order. Items in odd indexes begin ranges, and items in even indexes are the first number after the ends. Use a form of binary search to determine if a number is in any of the ranges. If the search ends on an odd index (a beginning), the number is in the set. If the search ends on an even index (a just-after-end) or outside the array, it is not in the set.

nodes.label: inverted file index

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: invertedFileIndex

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines inverted file index as: An inverted index that only indicates the text in which a word appears, not where the word appears within the text.

nodes.label: inverted index

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: invertedIndex

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines inverted index as: An index into a set of texts of the words in the texts. The index is accessed by some search method. Each index entry gives the word and a list of texts, possibly with locations within the text, where the word occurs.

nodes.label: invertible Bloom lookup table

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: invertibleBloomTable

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines invertible Bloom lookup table as: Algorithms and an array of cells to store key/value pairs. Each cell has a count of how many pairs are mapped to the cell, the sum of the keys mapped to it, and the sum of the values mapped to it. Using k hash functions , each pair is mapped to T[h 1 (k)], T[h 2 (k)], ..., T[h k (k)]. Also known as IBLT.

nodes.label: irreflexive

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: irreflexive

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines irreflexive as: A binary relation R for which there is no element a such that a R a.

nodes.label: isomorphic

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: isomorphic

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines isomorphic as: Two graphs are isomorphic if there is a one-to-one correspondence between their vertices and there is an edge between two vertices of one graph if and only if there is an edge between the two corresponding vertices in the other graph.

nodes.label: J sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: j_sort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines J sort as: An in-place sort algorithm that uses strand sort to sort fewer than about 40 items and shuffle sort to sort more.

nodes.label: Jaro-Winkler

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: jaroWinkler

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Jaro-Winkler as: A measure of similarity between two strings . The Jaro measure is the weighted sum of percentage of matched characters from each file and transposed characters. Winkler increased this measure for matching initial characters, then rescaled it by a piecewise function, whose intervals and weights depend on the type of string (first name, last name, street, etc.).

nodes.label: jelly-fish

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: jellyfish

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines jelly-fish as: A theoretical data structure for n items. It starts with a balanced binary search tree of about √(n) nodes. The leaf nodes lead to "tentacles" or linked lists , each of about √(n) nodes.

nodes.label: Johnson-Trotter

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: johnsonTrotter

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Johnson-Trotter as: Generate permutations by swapping one adjacent pair of elements at a time. Also known as Steinhaus-Johnson-Trotter, Trotter-Johnson.

nodes.label: Johnson's algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: johnsonsAlgorithm

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Johnson's algorithm as: An algorithm to solve the all pairs shortest path problem in a sparse weighted, directed graph . First, it adds a new node with zero weight edges from it to all other nodes, and runs the Bellman-Ford algorithm to check for negative weight cycles and find h(v), the least weight of a path from the new node to node v. Next it reweights the edges using the nodes' h(v) values. Finally for each node, it runs Dijkstra's algorithm and stores the computed least weight to other nodes, reweighted using the nodes' h(v) values, as the final weight. The time complexity is O(V²log V + VE) .

nodes.label: k²-tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: k2tree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k²-tree as: A compact representation of a sparse directed graph . It requires 1 to 3 bits per edge. Many access functions, like successor(s), predecessor(s), and range (all links from a range of vertices to another range of vertices), have very efficient implementations.

nodes.label: Karnaugh map

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: karnaughmap

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Karnaugh map as: A method for minimizing a boolean expression , usually aided by a rectangular map of the value of the expression for all possible input values. Input values are arranged in a Gray code . Maximal rectangular groups that cover the inputs where the expression is true give a minimum implementation. Also known as Veitch diagram, KV diagram.

nodes.label: Karp-Rabin

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: karpRabin

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Karp-Rabin as: A string matching algorithm that compares string's hash values, rather than the strings themselves. For efficiency, the hash value of the next position in the text is easily computed from the hash value of the current position. Also known as Rabin-Karp.

nodes.label: Karp reduction

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: karpreductin

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Karp reduction as: A reduction given by a polynomial time computable transformation function.

nodes.label: k-ary Huffman coding

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: karyHuffman

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-ary Huffman coding as: A minimal variable-length coding based on the frequency of each character. Similar to a Huffman coding , but joins k trees into a k-ary tree at each step, and uses k symbols for each level.

nodes.label: k-ary tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: karyTree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-ary tree as: A tree with no more than k children for each node . Also known as k-way tree.

nodes.label: k-ary heap

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: karyheap

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-ary heap as: A complete tree where every node has a key more extreme (greater or less) than the key of its parent . Each node has k or fewer children .

nodes.label: k-coloring

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kcoloring

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-coloring as: 1) The assignment of k colors (or any distinct marks) to the vertices of a graph . 2) The assignment of k colors to the edges of a graph . A coloring is a proper coloring if no two adjacent vertices or edges have the same color.

nodes.label: k-connected graph

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kconnectedGraph

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-connected graph as: A connected graph such that deleting any k-1 vertices (and incident edges ) results in a graph that is still connected.

nodes.label: k-d-B-tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kdbtree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-d-B-tree as: A data structure which splits multidimensional spaces like an adaptive k-d tree , but balances the resulting tree like a B-tree .

nodes.label: k-dimensional

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kdimensional

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-dimensional as: (1) Dealing with or restricted to a space where location can be completely described with exactly k orthogonal axes. (2) Dealing with a space of any number of dimensions.

nodes.label: K-dominant match

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kdominant

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines K-dominant match as: A match [i,j] having rank k and such that for any other pair [i',j'] of rank k either i'>i and j'≤ j or i' ≤ i and j'>j.

nodes.label: k-d tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kdtree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-d tree as: A multidimensional search tree for points in k dimensional space. Levels of the tree are split along successive dimensions at the points.

nodes.label: key

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: key

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines key as: The part of a group of data by which it is sorted, indexed, cross referenced, etc.

nodes.label: knight's tour

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: knightstour

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines knight's tour as: A series of moves of a chess knight that visits all squares on the board exactly once.

nodes.label: Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: knuthMorrisPratt

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm as: A string matching algorithm that turns the search string into a finite state machine , then runs the machine with the string to be searched as the input string. Execution time is O(m+n) , where m is the length of the search string, and n is the length of the string to be searched. Also known as KMP.

nodes.label: Kolmogorov complexity

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kolmogorov

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Kolmogorov complexity as: The minimum number of bits into which a string can be compressed without losing information. This is defined with respect to a fixed, but universal decompression scheme, given by a universal Turing machine .

nodes.label: Kripke structure

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kripkeStruct

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Kripke structure as: A nondeterministic finite state machine whose states are labeled with boolean variables, which are the evaluations of expressions in that state. It may be extended with fairness constraints.

nodes.label: k-way merge sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kwayMergeSort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-way merge sort as: A merge sort that sorts a data stream using repeated merges. It distributes the input into k streams by repeatedly reading a block of input that fits in memory, called a run , sorting it, then writing it to the next stream. It merges runs from the k streams into an output stream. It then repeatedly distributes the runs in the output stream to the k streams and merges them until there is a single sorted output. Also known as p-way merge sort.

nodes.label: k-way merge

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kwaymerge

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-way merge as: Combine k sorted data streams into a single sorted stream.

nodes.label: labeled graph

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: labeledgraph

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines labeled graph as: A graph which has labels associated with each edge or each vertex .

nodes.label: language

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: language

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines language as: A set of strings over some fixed alphabet . A characterization of inputs which may or may not be solved by algorithms . Also known as formal language.

nodes.label: Las Vegas algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: lasVegas

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Las Vegas algorithm as: A randomized algorithm that always produces correct results, with the only variation from one run to another being its running time.

nodes.label: last-in, first-out

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: lastfirstout

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines last-in, first-out as: A policy that the most recently arrived item is processed first. A stack implements this.

nodes.label: lattice

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: lattice

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines lattice as: A point lattice generated by taking integer linear combinations of a set of basis vectors.

nodes.label: LCFS hashing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: lcfsHashing

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines LCFS hashing as: In case of collision , move the existing item to another position, dictated by the open addressing scheme used.

nodes.label: least common multiple

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: leastCommonMultiple

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines least common multiple as: The least integer which is a multiple of given integers. For instance, LCM(6, 10) = 30. Also known as LCM.

nodes.label: leftist tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: leftisttree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines leftist tree as: A priority queue implemented with a variant of a binary tree . Every node has a count which is the distance to the nearest leaf . In addition to the heap property , leftist trees are kept so the right descendant of each node has the shorter distance to a leaf.

nodes.label: left rotation

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: leftrotation

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines left rotation as: (1) In a binary search tree , pushing a node N down and to the left to balance the tree. N's right child replaces N, and the right child's left child becomes N's right child. (2) In an array , moving all items to the next lower location. The first item is moved to the last location, which is now vacant. (3) In a list , removing the head and inserting it at the tail . Also known as rotate left.

nodes.label: omega

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: letterOmega

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines omega as: The Greek letter written as ω (see ω(n) ) or Ω (see Ω(n) ).

nodes.label: level

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: level

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines level as: (1) All the nodes of a tree with the same depth . (2) Of a node, the depth.

nodes.label: level-order traversal

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: levelOrderTraversal

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines level-order traversal as: Process all nodes of a tree by depth : first the root , then the children of the root, etc. Equivalent to a breadth-first search from the root.

nodes.label: lexicographical order

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: lexicgrphcl

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines lexicographical order as: Alphabetical or "dictionary" order.

nodes.label: linear hash

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linearhash

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines linear hash as: A numeric function that maintains the order of input keys while changing their spacing. Formal Definition: A hash function f for keys in S such that k1, k2 ∈ S ∧ k1 > k2 → f(k1) > f(k2). Also known as order-preserving hash.

nodes.label: linear quadtree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linearquadtr

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines linear quadtree as: A quadtree implemented as a single array of nodes .

nodes.label: link

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: link

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines link as: A reference, pointer, or access handle to another part of the data structure. Often, a memory address.

nodes.label: linked data signature

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linkedDataSignature

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines linked data signature as: A digital signature, and information to verify it, for linked data. Also known as LDS.

nodes.label: list contraction

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: listcontrctn

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines list contraction as: Contracting a list by removing some of the items.

nodes.label: little-o notation

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: littleOnotation

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines little-o notation as: A theoretical measure of the execution of an algorithm , usually the time or memory needed, given the problem size n, which is usually the number of items. Informally, saying some equation f(n) = o(g(n)) means f(n) becomes insignificant relative to g(n) as n approaches infinity. The notation is read, "f of n is little oh of g of n". Formal Definition: f(n) = o(g(n)) means for all c > 0 there exists some k > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) < cg(n) for all n ≥ k. The value of k must not depend on n, but may depend on c.

nodes.label: load factor

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: loadfactor

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines load factor as: The number of elements in a hash table divided by the number of slots. Usually written α (alpha).

nodes.label: local alignment

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: localalgnmnt

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines local alignment as: The detection of local similarities among two or more strings .

nodes.label: locality-sensitive hashing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: localitySensitiveHashing

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines locality-sensitive hashing as: A probabilistic algorithm to quickly find points in a high dimensional space near a query point. Preprocessing: put every point in multiple hash tables . Each table has its own locality-sensitive hash function and uses buckets (or chaining ) since many collisions are expected. The hash functions come from a family of functions. Finding: look up the query point in each hash table, and compute the distance from the query point of every point in the bucket.

nodes.label: local optimum

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: localoptimum

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines local optimum as: A solution to a problem that is better than all other solutions that are slightly different, but worse than the global optimum .

nodes.label: logarithmic

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: logarithmic

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines logarithmic as: (1) Any function that is a constant times the logarithm of the argument: f(x)=c log x. (2) In complexity theory, when the measure of computation, m(n) (usually execution time or memory space), is bounded by a logarithmic function of the problem size, n. More formally m(n) = O(log n) . (3) Sometimes imprecisely used to mean polylogarithmic .

nodes.label: longest common subsequence

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: longestCommonSubsequence

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines longest common subsequence as: The problem of finding a maximum length (or maximum weight) subsequence of two or more strings . Also known as heaviest common subsequence.

nodes.label: longest common substring

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: longestCommonSubstring

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines longest common substring as: Find the longest substring of two or more strings .

nodes.label: lower triangular matrix

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: lowerTriangularMatrix

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines lower triangular matrix as: A matrix that is only defined at (i,j) when i ≥ j.

nodes.label: lower bound

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: lowerbound

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines lower bound as: A function or growth rate below which solving a problem is impossible.

nodes.label: lowest common ancestor

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: lowestcommon

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines lowest common ancestor as: The deepest node in a tree that is an ancestor of two given leaves .

nodes.label: l-reduction

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: lreduction

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines l-reduction as: A Karp reduction that preserves approximation properties of optimization problems .

nodes.label: lucky sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: luckySort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines lucky sort as: The best possible sort algorithm: it is so lucky that the input is already sorted, and it need do nothing!

nodes.label: Malhotra-Kumar-Maheshwari blocking flow

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: malhotraKumr

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Malhotra-Kumar-Maheshwari blocking flow as: Given a flow function and its corresponding residual graph (a maximum-flow problem ), select a vertex with the least throughput and greedily push the maximum flow from it to the sink . This is repeated until all vertices are deleted.

nodes.label: Manhattan distance

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: manhattanDistance

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Manhattan distance as: The distance between two points measured along axes at right angles. In a plane with p 1 at (x 1 , y 1 ) and p 2 at (x 2 , y 2 ), it is |x 1 - x 2 | + |y 1 - y 2 |.

nodes.label: many-one reduction

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: manyonerdctn

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines many-one reduction as: A reduction that maps an instance of one problem into an equivalent instance of another problem.

nodes.label: Markov chain

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: markovchain

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Markov chain as: A finite state machine with probabilities for each transition, that is, a probability that the next state is s j given that the current state is s i .

nodes.label: Master theorem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: mastertheorm

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Master theorem as: A theorem giving a solution in asymptotic terms for recurrence relations of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) where a ≥ 1 and b > 1 are constants and n/b means either ⌊ n/b⌋ or ⌈ n/b⌉.

nodes.label: matched edge

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: matchededge

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines matched edge as: An edge which is in a matching .

nodes.label: matched vertex

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: matchedvertx

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines matched vertex as: A vertex on an matched edge in a matching , or, one which has been matched.

nodes.label: matching

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: matching

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines matching as: (1) A subgraph in which every vertex has a degree at most one. In other words, no two edges share a common vertex. (2) The problem of finding such a subgraph.

nodes.label: matrix

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: matrix

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines matrix as: A two-dimensional array. By convention, the first index is the row, and the second index is the column.

nodes.label: matrix-chain multiplication problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: matrxchnmltp

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines matrix-chain multiplication problem as: Given a sequence of matrices such that any matrix may be multiplied by the previous matrix, find the best association such that the result is obtained with the minimum number of arithmetic operations. One may use dynamic programming to find the best association.

nodes.label: max-heap property

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: maxheapprop

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines max-heap property as: Each node in a tree has a key which is less than or equal to the key of its parent .

nodes.label: maximal independent set

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: maximalIndependentSet

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines maximal independent set as: A set of vertices in a graph such that for any pair of vertices, there is no edge between them and such that no more vertices can be added and it still be an independent set .

nodes.label: maximally connected component

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: maximallyConnectedComponent

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines maximally connected component as: A connected subgraph of a graph to which no vertex can be added and it still be connected. Formal Definition: Given a graph G=(V, E), a subgraph S=(V', E') is a maximally connected component if S is connected , and for all vertices u such that u∈ V and u∉ V' there is no vertex v∈ V' for which (u, v)∈ E.

nodes.label: maximum-flow problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: maximumflow

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines maximum-flow problem as: The problem of finding the maximum flow between any two vertices of a directed graph . Also known as network flow problem.

nodes.label: Mealy machine

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: mealyMachine

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Mealy machine as: A finite state machine which produces an output for each transition .

nodes.label: mean

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: mean

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines mean as: The (arithmetic) mean of some values is the sum of all values divided by the number of values.

nodes.label: median

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: median

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines median as: The value that has an equal number of values greater and less than it. For an even number of values, it is the mean of the two middle values.

nodes.label: meld

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: meld

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines meld as: Joining several data structures with particular properties into one large data structure having those properties. For instance, some priority queue implementations support the operation of joining two priority queues into a larger one.

nodes.label: metaheuristic

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: metaheuristic

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines metaheuristic as: (1) A high-level algorithmic framework or approach that can be specialized to solve optimization problems . (2) A high-level strategy that guides other heuristics in a search for feasible solutions .

nodes.label: metaphone

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: metaphone

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines metaphone as: An algorithm to code English words phonetically by reducing them to 16 consonant sounds. A better variant is double metaphone .

nodes.label: midrange

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: midrange

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines midrange as: The sum of the minimum and maximum values, divided by two.

nodes.label: min-heap property

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: minheapprop

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines min-heap property as: Each node in a tree has a key which is greater than or equal to the key of its parent .

nodes.label: minimal perfect hashing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: minimalPerfectHash

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines minimal perfect hashing as: A perfect hashing function that maps each different key to a distinct integer and has the same number of possible integers as keys. Formal Definition: A function f is a minimal perfect hash function for a set of keys K iff ∀ j, k ∈ K f(j) = f(k) → j = k and the range of f(k) is 1… |K|.

nodes.label: minimax

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: minimax

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines minimax as: Generate all nodes in a game tree. Score each leaf node with its utility value. Score each minimizing node with the smallest of its children's scores, and maximizing node with the largest of its children's scores.

nodes.label: minimum bounding box

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: minimumBoundingBox

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines minimum bounding box as: The smallest rectangle completely enclosing a set of points. Also known as MBB.

nodes.label: minimum cut

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: minimumcut

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines minimum cut as: The smallest set of edges in an undirected graph which separate two distinct vertices . That is, every path between them includes some member of the set.

nodes.label: minimum vertex cut

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: minvertexcut

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines minimum vertex cut as: The smallest set of vertices in an undirected graph which separate two distinct vertices. That is, every path between them passes through some member of the cut .

nodes.label: mixed integer linear program

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: mixedinteger

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines mixed integer linear program as: A linear program with additional constraints that some of the variables must take on integer values. Solving such problems is NP-hard .

nodes.label: mode

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: mode

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines mode as: The value that occurs most often. If no value is repeated, there is no mode. If more than one value occurs with the same greatest frequency, each value is a mode.

nodes.label: model of computation

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: modelOfComputation

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines model of computation as: A formal, abstract definition of a computer. Using a model one can more easily analyze the intrinsic execution time or memory space of an algorithm while ignoring many implementation issues. There are many models of computation which differ in computing power (that is, some models can perform computations impossible for other models) and the cost of various operations.

nodes.label: model checking

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: modelcheckng

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines model checking as: Efficiently deciding whether a temporal logic formula is satisfied in a finite state machine model.

nodes.label: MODIFIND

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: modifind

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines MODIFIND as: Select the k th smallest element of an array and partition the array around it. Partition around the value of the k th element. If the partition boundary is not at k, repeat in the partition that includes k.

nodes.label: monotonically decreasing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: monotonicallyDecreasing

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines monotonically decreasing as: A function from a partially ordered domain to a partially ordered range such that x ≤ y implies f(x) ≥ f(y).

nodes.label: monotonically increasing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: monotonicallyIncreasing

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines monotonically increasing as: A function from a partially ordered domain to a partially ordered range such that x ≤ y implies f(x) ≤ f(y).

nodes.label: monotone priority queue

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: monotonprioq

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines monotone priority queue as: A priority queue in which a key being inserted is never higher in priority than a previously deleted node.

nodes.label: Monte Carlo algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: monteCarlo

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Monte Carlo algorithm as: A randomized algorithm that may produce incorrect results, but with bounded error probability.

nodes.label: Moore machine

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: mooreMachine

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Moore machine as: A finite state machine that produces an output for each state .

nodes.label: move-to-front heuristic

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: movefront

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines move-to-front heuristic as: A heuristic that moves the target of a search to the head of a list so it is found faster next time.

nodes.label: move-to-root heuristic

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: movetoroot

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines move-to-root heuristic as: A heuristic that moves the target of a search to the root of the search tree so it is found faster next time.

nodes.label: multi suffix tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: multiSuffixTree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines multi suffix tree as: A suffix tree extended to multiple strings by concatenating the strings .

nodes.label: multi-commodity flow

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: multicommdty

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines multi-commodity flow as: A maximum-flow problem involving multiple commodities, in which each commodity has an associated demand and source - sink pairs.

nodes.label: multigraph

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: multigraph

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines multigraph as: A graph whose edges are unordered pairs of vertices , and the same pair of vertices can be connected by multiple edges. Formal Definition: Same as graph, but E is a bag of edges, not a set .

nodes.label: multikey Quicksort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: multikeyQuicksort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines multikey Quicksort as: Pick an element from the array (the pivot). Consider the first character (key) of the string (multikey). Partition the remaining elements into three sets: those whose corresponding character is less than, equal to, and greater than the pivot's character. Recursively sort the "less than" and "greater than" partitions on the same character. Recursively sort the "equal to" partition by the next character (key). Also known as three-way radix quicksort.

nodes.label: multilayer grid file

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: multilaygrd

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines multilayer grid file as: A spatial access method which is two or more simultaneous grid files . Objects reside in the first grid file where it doesn't have to be split across hyperplanes.

nodes.label: multiprefix

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: multiprefix

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines multiprefix as: A generalization of scan in which the partial sums are grouped by keys .

nodes.label: multiprocessor model

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: multiprocssr

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines multiprocessor model as: A model of parallel computation based on a set of communicating sequential processors.

nodes.label: multiway decision

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: multiwayDecision

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines multiway decision as: A decision which has more than two results. For instance, testing if a < b yields two results, but some languages allow a test to return a < b, a=b, or a > b in one operation.

nodes.label: multiway merge

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: multiwayMerge

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines multiway merge as: Combine more than two sorted data streams into a single sorted stream.

nodes.label: multiway tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: multiwaytree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines multiway tree as: A tree with any number of children for each node .

nodes.label: Munkres' assignment algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: munkresAssignment

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Munkres' assignment algorithm as: Solve the assignment problem in polynomial time by marking and unmarking entries and covering and uncovering rows and columns. Also known as Hungarian algorithm.

nodes.label: NP-complete language

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nPcompltlngg

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines NP-complete language as: A language in NP such that every language in NP can be reduced to it in polynomial time .

nodes.label: nand

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nand

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines nand as: Negated conjunction: 0 NAND 0 = 1, 0 NAND 1 = 1, 1 NAND 0 = 1, 1 NAND 1 = 0.

nodes.label: n-ary function

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: naryfunc

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines n-ary function as: (1) A function with exactly n arguments. (2) A function which takes any number of arguments, or a variable number of arguments.

nodes.label: nearest neighbor

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nearestNeighbor

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines nearest neighbor as: Find the point (rectangle, line, etc.) that is closest to another point.

nodes.label: negation

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: negation

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines negation as: The negation of 0 is 1; the negation of 1 is 0.

nodes.label: next state

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nextstate

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines next state as: The state immediately following the current state, defined by the transition function of a finite state machine and the input.

nodes.label: NIST

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nist

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines NIST as: The United States National Institute of Standards and Technology.

nodes.label: node

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: node

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines node as: (1) A unit of reference in a data structure. Also called a vertex in graphs and trees . (2) A collection of information which must be kept at a single memory location.

nodes.label: nonbalanced merge sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nonbalncmsrt

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines nonbalanced merge sort as: A k-way merge sort in which the number of input and output data streams is different for any particular pass. Typically P input streams are merged and distributed to T output streams on one pass followed by a merge of the T inputs and distribution to P outputs.

nodes.label: nondeterministic algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nondetermAlgo

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines nondeterministic algorithm as: A conceptual algorithm with more than one allowed step at certain times and which always takes the right or best step. It is not random, as in randomized algorithm , or indeterminate. Rather it has the supercomputational characteristic of choosing the optimal behavior.

nodes.label: nondeterministic finite tree automaton

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nondetermFiniteTreeAutom

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines nondeterministic finite tree automaton as: A nondeterministic finite state machine that accepts finitary trees rather than just strings . The tree nodes are marked with the letters of the alphabet of the automaton, and the transition function encodes the next states for each branch of the tree. The acceptance condition is modified accordingly. Also known as NFTA.

nodes.label: nondeterministic tree automaton

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nondetermTreeAutom

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines nondeterministic tree automaton as: A nondeterministic finite state machine that accepts infinite trees rather than just strings . The tree nodes are marked with the letters of the alphabet of the automaton, and the transition function encodes the next states for each branch of the tree. The expressive power of such automata varies depending on the acceptance conditions of the trees.

nodes.label: nondeterministic

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nondeterministic

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines nondeterministic as: Permitting more than one choice of next move at some step in a computation.

nodes.label: nor

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nor

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines nor as: Negated disjunction: 0 NOR 0 = 1, 0 NOR 1 = 0, 1 NOR 0 = 0, 1 NOR 1 = 0.

nodes.label: not

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: not

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines not as: Negation: NOT 0 = 1, NOT 1 = 0. Also known as complement .

nodes.label: NP

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: np

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines NP as: The complexity class of decision problems for which answers can be checked by an algorithm whose run time is polynomial in the size of the input. Note that this doesn't require or imply that an answer can be found quickly, only that any claimed solution can be verified quickly. "NP" is the class that a N ondeterministic Turing machine accepts in P olynomial time. Also known as nondeterministic polynomial time.

nodes.label: NP-hard

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nphard

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines NP-hard as: The complexity class of decision problems that are intrinsically harder than those that can be solved by a nondeterministic Turing machine in polynomial time . When a decision version of a combinatorial optimization problem is proved to belong to the class of NP-complete problems, then the optimization version is NP-hard.

nodes.label: n queens

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nqueens

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines n queens as: Place n chess queens on an n × n board such that no queen can attack another. Efficiently find all possible placements.

nodes.label: null tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nulltree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines null tree as: (1) A tree which is empty. (2) A tree whose leaf nodes all have a null value.

nodes.label: NYSIIS

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nysiis

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines NYSIIS as: Convert a name to a phonetic coding of up to six characters.

nodes.label: objective function

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: objective

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines objective function as: A function associated with an optimization problem which determines how good a solution is, for instance, the total cost of edges in a solution to a traveling salesman problem.

nodes.label: oblivious algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: obliviousAlgorithm

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines oblivious algorithm as: An algorithm whose behavior, by design, is independent of some property that influences a typical algorithm for the same problem.

nodes.label: occurrence

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: occurrence

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines occurrence as: A string v occurs in a string u if v is a substring of u.

nodes.label: octree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: octree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines octree as: A tree to index three dimensions. Each node has either eight children or no children.

nodes.label: off-line algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: offline

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines off-line algorithm as: An algorithm which is given the entire sequence of inputs in advance.

nodes.label: offset

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: offset

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines offset as: The distance from the beginning of a string to the end of a segment in that string.

nodes.label: ω

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: omega

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ω as: A theoretical measure of the execution of an algorithm , usually the time or memory needed, given the problem size n, which is usually the number of items. Informally, saying some equation f(n) = ω (g(n)) means g(n) becomes insignificant relative to f(n) as n goes to infinity. Formal Definition: f(n) = ω (g(n)) means that for any positive constant c, there exists a constant k, such that 0 ≤ cg(n) < f(n) for all n ≥ k. The value of k must not depend on n, but may depend on c.

nodes.label: omicron

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: omicron

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines omicron as: The Greek letter written as "o" (see little-o notation ) or "O" (see big-O notation ).

nodes.label: 1-based indexing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: oneBasedIndexing

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines 1-based indexing as: Indexing (an array ) beginning with 1.

nodes.label: one-dimensional

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: onedimensnal

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines one-dimensional as: Dealing with or restricted to a line. An organization where location can be completely described with exactly one axis.

nodes.label: on-line algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: online

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines on-line algorithm as: An algorithm that must process each input in turn, without detailed knowledge of future inputs.

nodes.label: optimal triangulation problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: optimTriangulation

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines optimal triangulation problem as: Find the triangulation with the greatest overall minimum angle. There is an incremental algorithm that takes O(n log n) time.

nodes.label: optimal

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: optimal

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines optimal as: (1) A solution to an optimization problem which has the minimum (or maximum) value of the objective function . (2) The time, space, resource, etc. complexity of an algorithm which matches the best known lower bound of a problem.

nodes.label: optimal mismatch

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: optimalMismatch

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines optimal mismatch as: A string matching algorithm that compares the rarest character first. When a character doesn't match, the next character in the text beyond the search string determines where the next possible match begins.

nodes.label: optimal polyphase merge sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: optimalPolyphaseMergeSort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines optimal polyphase merge sort as: An external sort algorithm that uses optimal polyphase merges .

nodes.label: optimal solution

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: optimalsoltn

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines optimal solution as: A solution to an optimization problem which minimizes (or maximizes) the objective function .

nodes.label: optimal value

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: optimalvalue

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines optimal value as: The minimum (or maximum) value of the objective function over the feasible region of an optimization problem .

nodes.label: optimization problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: optimization

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines optimization problem as: A computational problem in which the object is to find the best of all possible solutions. More formally, find a solution in the feasible region which has the minimum (or maximum) value of the objective function .

nodes.label: optimal polyphase merge

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: optimpolymrg

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines optimal polyphase merge as: A polyphase merge which seeks to minimize the number of merge passes by allocating output runs of each pass to the various output files. Since polyphase merging must have a different number of runs in each file to be efficient, one seeks the optimal way of selecting how many runs go into each output file. A series of kth order Fibonacci numbers is one way to select the number of runs.

nodes.label: or

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: or

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines or as: Disjunction: 0 OR 0 = 0, 0 OR 1 = 1, 1 OR 0 = 1, 1 OR 1 = 1. Also known as inclusive or.

nodes.label: oracle Turing machine

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: oracleTur

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines oracle Turing machine as: A Turing machine with an extra oracle tape and three extra states q ? , q y , q n . When the machine enters q ? , control goes to state q y if the oracle tape content is in the oracle set ; otherwise control goes to state q n .

nodes.label: oracle set

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: oracleset

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines oracle set as: A predetermined set of tapes used by an oracle Turing machine to make decisions otherwise not feasibled.

nodes.label: oracle tape

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: oracletape

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines oracle tape as: An extra tape used by an oracle Turing machine to make decisions otherwise not feasible.

nodes.label: order

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: order

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines order as: (1) The height of a tree . (2) The number of children of the root of a binomial tree . (3) The maximum number of children of nodes in a B-tree . (4) The number of data streams, usually denoted ω, in a multiway merge .

nodes.label: order-preserving minimal perfect hashing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: orderPreservMinPerfectHash

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines order-preserving minimal perfect hashing as: A minimal perfect hashing function for keys in S such that if k1, k2 ∈ S and k1 > k2, then f(k1) > f(k2).

nodes.label: order-preserving Huffman coding

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: orderPreservingHuffmanCoding

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines order-preserving Huffman coding as: A variable-length character coding based on the frequency of each character. The algorithm is similar to Huffman coding , but the trees are kept in the same order as the characters. Two adjacent trees with the least combined frequency are joined as subtrees of a new root. As with Huffman coding, that new tree is assigned the sum of the subtrees' frequencies. Repeat until all characters are in one tree.

nodes.label: ordered linked list

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: orderedLinkedList

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ordered linked list as: A linked list whose items are kept in some order.

nodes.label: ordered array

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: orderedarry

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ordered array as: An array whose items have some order. Usually, it means a sorted array , but may mean not fully ordered, for example, all values less than the median are in the first half.

nodes.label: ordered tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: orderedtree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ordered tree as: A tree where the children of every node are ordered, that is, there is a first child, second child, third child, etc.

nodes.label: orthogonal drawing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: orthogonalDrawing

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines orthogonal drawing as: A graph drawing in which each edge is represented by a polyline, each segment of which is parallel to a coordinate axis.

nodes.label: orthogonal lists

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: orthogonalLists

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines orthogonal lists as: Lists that share items, but are structurally independent.

nodes.label: orthogonally convex rectilinear polygon

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: orthogoncnvx

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines orthogonally convex rectilinear polygon as: A rectilinear polygon P in which every horizontal or vertical segment connecting two points in P lies totally within P.

nodes.label: oscillating merge sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: oscillatingMergeSort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines oscillating merge sort as: Given n tape drives, one input and n-1 work drives, distribute a portion of the input to n-2 tapes, then merge them onto the final tape reading the n-2 backward. Repeat until n-2 (backward) merged runs have been created, at which time they are merged. Continue building up powers of n-2 batches until done.

nodes.label: out-degree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: outdegree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines out-degree as: The number of edges going out of a vertex in a directed graph .

nodes.label: P

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: p

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines P as: The complexity class of languages that can be accepted by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time .

nodes.label: packing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: packing

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines packing as: Given a finite collection of subsets of a finite ground set, to find an optimal subcollection that are pairwise disjoint.

nodes.label: padding argument

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: paddingrgmnt

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines padding argument as: A method for transferring results about one complexity bound to another complexity bound, by padding extra dummy characters onto the inputs of the machines involved.

nodes.label: pagoda

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: pagoda

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines pagoda as: A priority queue implemented with a variant of a binary tree . The root points to its children, as in a binary tree. Every other node points back to its parent and down to its leftmost (if it is a right child ) or rightmost (if it is a left child) descendant leaf . The basic operation is merge or meld , which maintains the heap property . An element is inserted by merging it as a singleton. The root is removed by merging its right and left children. Merging is bottom-up, merging the leftmost edge of one with the rightmost edge of the other.

nodes.label: parallel computation thesis

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: parallel

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines parallel computation thesis as: Sequential space is a polynomial of parallel time.

nodes.label: parallel random-access machine

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: parallelRandomAccessMachine

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines parallel random-access machine as: A shared memory model of computation , where typically the processors all execute the same instruction synchronously, and access to any memory location occurs in unit time. Also known as PRAM.

nodes.label: parent

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: parent

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines parent as: Of a node : the tree node conceptually above or closer to the root than the node and which has a link to the node. See the figure at tree .

nodes.label: partial function

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: partialfunct

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines partial function as: A function which is not defined for some inputs of the right type, that is, for some of a domain . For instance, division is a partial function since division by 0 is undefined (on the Reals).
