nodes.label: partially decidable problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: partiallyDecidableProb

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines partially decidable problem as: One whose associated language is a recursively enumerable language . Equivalently, there exists an algorithm that halts and outputs 1 for every instance having a "yes" answer, but for instances having a "no" answer is allowed either not to halt or to halt and output 0.

nodes.label: partially dynamic graph problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: partiallyDynamicGraph

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines partially dynamic graph problem as: Problem where the update operations include either edge insertions (incremental) or deletions (decremental).

nodes.label: partially persistent data structure

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: partiallyPersistData

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines partially persistent data structure as: A persistent data structure that allows updates to the latest version only.

nodes.label: partial order

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: partialorder

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines partial order as: An order defined for some, but not necessarily all, pairs of items. For instance, the sets {a, b} and {a, c, d} are subsets of {a, b, c, d}, but neither is a subset of the other. So "subset of" is a partial order on sets. Formal Definition: A partial order is a binary relation that is reflexive , transitive , and antisymmetric .

nodes.label: partial recursive function

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: partialrcrsv

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines partial recursive function as: A function computed by a Turing machine that need not halt for all inputs.

nodes.label: passive data structure

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: passiveDataStruc

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines passive data structure as: A data structure that is only changed by external threads or processes, in contrast to an active data structure .

nodes.label: path system problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: pathsystem

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines path system problem as: For a path system P=(x,R,S,T), where S⊆ X, T ⊆ X, and R⊆ X × X × X, the problem of whether there is an admissible vertex in S. A vertex is admissible if and only if x∈ T, or there exists admissible y, z ∈ X such that (x,y,z) ∈ R.

nodes.label: pattern

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: pattern

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines pattern as: A finite number of strings that are searched for in texts .

nodes.label: pattern element

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: patternelmnt

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines pattern element as: A positive (negative) pattern element is a "partial wild card" presented as a subset of the alphabet Σ, with the symbols in the subset specifying which symbols of Σ are matched (mismatched) by the pattern element.

nodes.label: Pearson's hash

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: pearsonshash

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Pearson's hash as: A hash function that uses an auxiliary array, but no shift or exclusive-or ( xor ) operations.

nodes.label: perfect binary tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: perfectBinaryTree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines perfect binary tree as: A binary tree with all leaf nodes at the same depth . All internal nodes have degree 2.

nodes.label: perfect shuffle

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: perfectShuffle

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines perfect shuffle as: Split a list of elements (or deck of cards) exactly in half then precisely interleave the two halves.

nodes.label: perfect matching

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: perfectmatch

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines perfect matching as: A matching , or subset of edges without common vertices , of a connected graph that touches all vertices exactly once. A graph with an odd number of vertices is allowed one unmatched vertex.

nodes.label: performance guarantee

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: performance

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines performance guarantee as: An expression of the most the result of an approximation algorithm may depart from the optimal solution .

nodes.label: permutation

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: permutation

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines permutation as: A rearrangement of elements, where none are lost, added, or changed. The Fisher-Yates shuffle randomly permutes elements. Also known as shuffle.

nodes.label: permutation sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: permutationSort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines permutation sort as: A terribly inefficient sort algorithm that generates each permutation of the items until the items are in order.

nodes.label: persistent data structure

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: persistentDataStructure

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines persistent data structure as: A data structure that preserves its old versions, that is, previous versions may be queried in addition to the latest version.

nodes.label: phonetic coding

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: phoneticCoding

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines phonetic coding as: Code a string based on how it is pronounced.

nodes.label: pigeonhole sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: pigeonholeSort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines pigeonhole sort as: A 2-pass sort algorithm that is efficient when the range of keys is approximately equal to the number of items. The first pass allocates an array of buckets , one bucket for each possible key value, then moves each item to its key's bucket. The second pass goes over the bucket array moving each item to the next place in the destination.

nodes.label: pile

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: pile

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines pile as: An ordered deque , that is, items may only be added to or removed from the head or the tail . An item is added to the head if it is smaller than the current head. An item is added to the tail if it is greater than the current tail. Items are never inserted into the middle, rather, an additional pile may be created.

nodes.label: pipelined divide and conquer

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: pipelineddvd

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines pipelined divide and conquer as: A divide and conquer paradigm in which partial results from recursive calls can be used before the calls complete. The technique is often useful for reducing the depth of an algorithm .

nodes.label: planar graph

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: planargraph

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines planar graph as: A graph that can be drawn in the plane with no crossing edges .

nodes.label: planarization

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: planarization

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines planarization as: The process of transforming a graph into a planar graph . More formally, the transformation involves either removing edges (planarization by edge removal), or replacing pairs of nonincident edges by 4-starts (planarization by adding crossing vertices ). In both cases, the aim of planarization is minimize the number of edge removals or replacements.

nodes.label: planar straight-line graph

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: planarstrght

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines planar straight-line graph as: A graph that can be embedded in the plane without crossings in which every edge in the graph is a straight line segment. It is sometimes referred to as planar subdivision or map.

nodes.label: PLOP-hashing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: plophashing

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines PLOP-hashing as: Piecewise linear order-preserving (PLOP) hashing is a spatial access method which splits space into a nonperiodic grid. Each spatial dimension is divided by nodes of a binary tree . Object are stored in the grid cell of their centroid .

nodes.label: point access method

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: pointAccessMethod

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines point access method as: A data structure and associated algorithms primarily to search for points defined in multidimensional space. Also known as PAM.

nodes.label: pointer jumping

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: pointerJumping

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines pointer jumping as: In a linked structure, replacing a pointer with the pointer it points to. Used for various algorithms on lists and trees . Also known as recursive doubling, shortcutting.

nodes.label: pointer machine

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: pointermachn

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines pointer machine as: A model of computation whose memory consists of an unbounded collection of registers, or records, connected by pointers. Each register may contain an arbitrary amount of additional information. No arithmetic is allowed to compute the address of a register. The only way to access a register is by following pointers.

nodes.label: poissonization

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: poissonizatn

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines poissonization as: To replace a deterministic input by poisson process, changing the model into a poisson model. A solution to the poisson model must be interpreted in the original model.

nodes.label: polychotomy

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: polychotomy

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines polychotomy as: Division into many distinct classifications.

nodes.label: polynomial approximation scheme

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: polynomaprox

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines polynomial approximation scheme as: A set of algorithms {A ε | ε > 0}, where each A ε is a (1+ε)-approximation algorithm and the execution time is bounded by a polynomial in the length of the input. The execution time may depend on the choice of ε. Sometimes referred to more precisely as polynomial-time approximation scheme. Also known as PTAS.

nodes.label: polynomial hierarchy

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: polynomhier

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines polynomial hierarchy as: The classes of languages accepted by k- alternating Turing machines , over all k≥ 0 and with initial state existential or universal. The bottom level (k=0) is the class P . The next level (k=1) comprises NP and co- NP .

nodes.label: polynomial-time reduction

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: polynomtredc

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines polynomial-time reduction as: A transformation of one problem into another which is computable in polynomial time .

nodes.label: polyphase merge

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: polyphmerge

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines polyphase merge as: A nonbalanced k-way merge which reduces the number of output files needed by reusing the emptied input file or device as one of the output devices. This is most efficient if the number of output runs in each output file is different.

nodes.label: polyphase merge sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: polyphmrgsrt

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines polyphase merge sort as: A merge sort algorithm that reduces the number of intermediate files needed by reusing emptied files.

nodes.label: polytope

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: polytope

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines polytope as: A closed, bounded N-dimensional figure whose faces are hyperplanes. Informally, a multidimensional solid with flat sides. A generalization of polyhedron.

nodes.label: poset

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: poset

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines poset as: A set the elements of which are subject to a partial order . Also known as partially ordered set.

nodes.label: postman's sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: postmansort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines postman's sort as: A highly engineered variant of top-down radix sort where attributes of the key are described so the algorithm can allocate buckets and distribute efficiently.

nodes.label: postorder traversal

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: postorderTraversal

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines postorder traversal as: Process all nodes of a tree by recursively processing all subtrees, then finally processing the root . Also known as postfix traversal.

nodes.label: Post's correspondence problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: postsCorrespondProb

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Post's correspondence problem as: Given a set of pairs of strings , find a sequence of pairs such that the concatenation of all first members of the pairs is the same string as the concatenation of all second members. This is an undecidable problem . Also known as PCP.

nodes.label: potential function

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: potentialfnc

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines potential function as: A measure of a data structure whose change after an operation corresponds to the time cost of the operation.

nodes.label: predicate

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: predicate

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines predicate as: A function that returns true or false. Conceptually it tests for a condition.

nodes.label: prefix

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: prefix

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines prefix as: The beginning characters of a string . More formally a string v∈Σ * is a prefix of a string u∈Σ * if u=vu' for some string u'∈Σ * .

nodes.label: prefix code

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: prefixcode

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines prefix code as: Set of words such that no word of the set is a prefix of another word in the set. A prefix code may be represented by a coding tree .

nodes.label: preorder traversal

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: preorderTraversal

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines preorder traversal as: Process all nodes of a tree by processing the root , then recursively processing all subtrees. Also known as prefix traversal.

nodes.label: primary clustering

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: primaryClustering

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines primary clustering as: The tendency for some collision resolution schemes to create long runs of filled slots near the hash function position of keys .

nodes.label: primitive algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: primitiveAlgorithm

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines primitive algorithm as: An algorithm in which all the computable steps are basic operations.

nodes.label: primitive recursive

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: primitiveRecursive

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines primitive recursive as: A total function that can be written using only nested conditional (if-then-else) statements and fixed iteration (for) loops.

nodes.label: principle of optimality

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: principle

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines principle of optimality as: In some optimization problems , components of a globally optimal solution are themselves globally optimal.

nodes.label: prisoner's dilemma

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: prisonersDilemma

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines prisoner's dilemma as: Two prisoners are questioned separately about a crime they committed. Each may give evidence against the other or may say nothing. If both say nothing, they get a minor reprimand and go free because of lack of evidence. If one gives evidence and the other says nothing, the first goes free and the second is severely punished. If both give evidence, both are severely punished. The overall (globally) best strategy is for both to say nothing. However not knowing (or trusting) what the other will do, each prisoner's (locally) best strategy is to give evidence, which is the worst possible outcome. In general, a situation where local optimization leads to the worst possible outcome globally.

nodes.label: probabilistically checkable proof

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: probabilisticallyCheckableProof

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines probabilistically checkable proof as: An interactive proof system in which provers follow a fixed strategy, that is, one not affected by any messages from the verifier. The prover's strategy for a given instance x of a decision problem can be represented by a finite oracle language B x , which constitutes a proof of the correct answer for x.

nodes.label: probabilistic algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: probablAlgo

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines probabilistic algorithm as: Any algorithm that works for all practical purposes but has a theoretical chance of being wrong.

nodes.label: probabilistic Turing machine

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: probablturng

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines probabilistic Turing machine as: A Turing machine in which some transitions are random choices among finitely many alternatives.

nodes.label: probe sequence

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: probesequenc

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines probe sequence as: The list of locations which a method for open addressing produces as alternatives in case of a collision .

nodes.label: procedure

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: procedure

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines procedure as: A subroutine which does not return a value.

nodes.label: process algebra

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: processalgbr

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines process algebra as: An algebraic theory to formalize the notion of concurrent computation, best exemplified in CSP and CCS .

nodes.label: proper

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: proper

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines proper as: (1) A subunit of a unit is not equal to the unit itself. For instance, a proper substring is not the whole string , a proper subset is not the whole set , a proper subgraph is not the whole graph , etc. (2) According to a rule, as in proper coloring .

nodes.label: proper coloring

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: propercolor

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines proper coloring as: A vertex coloring or edge coloring of a graph in which no two adjacent vertices or edges have the same color.

nodes.label: proper subset

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: propersubset

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines proper subset as: A set S 2 is a proper subset of another set S 1 if every element in S 2 is in S 1 and S 1 has some elements which are not in S 2 .

nodes.label: prune and search

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: pruneNsearch

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines prune and search as: Find an optimal value by eliminating a constant fraction of remaining objects at each step. Eliminated objects are guaranteed not to affect the optimal value. A logarithmic number of steps reduces the number of objects to a constant, and a brute force approach can then solve it. Also known as decimation.

nodes.label: pseudo-random number generator

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: pseudorandomNumberGen

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines pseudo-random number generator as: A deterministic algorithm to generate a sequence of numbers with little or no discernible pattern in the numbers, except for broad statistical properties. Also known as PRNG, deterministic random bit generator, DRBG.

nodes.label: P-tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: ptree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines P-tree as: (1) A spatial access method that defines hyperplanes, in addition to the orthogonal dimensions, which node boundaries may parallel. Space is split by hierarchically nested polytopes (multidimensional boxes with nonrectangular sides). The R-tree is a special case that has no additional hyperplanes. (2) A spatial access method that splits space by hierarchically nested polytopes. The R-tree is a special case in which all polytopes are boxes.

nodes.label: purely functional language

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: purelyfnctnl

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines purely functional language as: A language that does not allow any destructive operation---one which overwrites data---such as the assignment operation. Purely functional languages are free of side effects, i.e., invoking a function has no effect other than computing the value returned by the function.

nodes.label: pushdown automaton

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: pushdownautm

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines pushdown automaton as: A restricted Turing machine where the tape acts as a pushdown store (or stack , where only the latest element can be read), with an extra one-way read-only input tape. Also known as PDA.

nodes.label: q sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: qsort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines q sort as: The sort function in many libraries. It is generally a combination of quicksort, for many items, and insertion sort , for a few items.

nodes.label: quadratic probing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: quadraticprb

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines quadratic probing as: A method of open addressing for a hash table in which a collision is resolved by putting the item in the next empty place given by a probe sequence . The space between places in the sequence increases quadratically.

nodes.label: quad trie

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: quadtrie

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines quad trie as: A tree in which each node is split according to some subset of the key , typically a character.

nodes.label: quantum computation

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: quantumComputation

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines quantum computation as: Computation based on quantum mechanical effects, such as superposition and entanglement, in addition to classical digital manipulations.

nodes.label: quick search

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: quicksearch

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines quick search as: A string matching algorithm that compares characters from the end of the search string to its beginning. When a character doesn't match, the next character in the text beyond the search string determines where the next possible match begins.

nodes.label: ragged matrix

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: raggedmatrix

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ragged matrix as: A matrix having irregular numbers of items in each row.

nodes.label: random search

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: randomSearch

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines random search as: Repeatedly check items in an array at random until successful.

nodes.label: random access machine

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: randomaccess

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines random access machine as: A model of computation whose memory consists of an unbounded sequence of registers, each of which may hold an integer. In this model, arithmetic operations are allowed to compute the address of a memory register.

nodes.label: randomized rounding

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: randomizdrnd

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines randomized rounding as: A probabilistic method to convert a solution of a relaxed problem into an approximate solution to the original problem.

nodes.label: randomized algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: randomizedAlgo

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines randomized algorithm as: An algorithm that makes random (or pseudorandom) choices.

nodes.label: randomized binary search tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: randomizedBinarySearchTree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines randomized binary search tree as: A binary search tree in which nodes have a randomly assigned priority. Updates keep priorities in heap order instead of keeping balance information and doing rebalance operations. Also known as cartesian tree, RBST.

nodes.label: randomized complexity

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: randomizedComplexity

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines randomized complexity as: The expected running time of the best possible randomized algorithm over the worst input.

nodes.label: random sampling

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: randomsampl

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines random sampling as: Using a randomly selected sample of the data to help solve a problem on the whole data.

nodes.label: range

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: range

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines range as: The possible results of a function or relation . For instance, the range of cosine is [-1,+1].

nodes.label: range sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rangesort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines range sort as: A bucket sort where the function to determine the bucket is based on the range of possible keys .

nodes.label: rank

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rank

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rank as: For a given match, this is the number of matches in a longest chain terminating with that match, inclusive.

nodes.label: rapid sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rapidSort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rapid sort as: A 2-pass sort algorithm that is efficient when the range of keys is approximately equal to the number of items and only keys are sorted. The first pass counts the occurrences of each key in an auxiliary array . The second pass goes over the auxiliary array writing the counted number of keys to the destination.

nodes.label: Ratcliff/Obershelp pattern recognition

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: ratcliffObershelp

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Ratcliff/Obershelp pattern recognition as: Compute the similarity of two strings as the number of matching characters divided by the total number of characters in the two strings. Matching characters are those in the longest common substring plus, recursively, matching characters in the unmatched region on either side of the longest common substring.

nodes.label: reachable

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: reachable

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines reachable as: A vertex v is reachable from another vertex u if there is a path of any length from u to v. Also known as reachability.

nodes.label: rebalance

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rebalance

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rebalance as: Restore balance to a tree .

nodes.label: recognizer

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: recognizer

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines recognizer as: A finite state machine with one or more states designated as accepting states . An input string is accepted if there is a path from the start state to an accepting state.

nodes.label: rectangular matrix

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rectangmatrx

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rectangular matrix as: An n × m matrix , or, one whose size may not be the same in both dimensions.

nodes.label: rectilinear

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rectilinear

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rectilinear as: Distance, paths, lines, etc. which are always parallel to axes at right angles. For example, a path along the streets of Salt Lake City or the moves of a rook in chess.

nodes.label: rectilinear Steiner tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rectilinearSteinertree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rectilinear Steiner tree as: A minimum-length rectilinear tree connecting a set of points, called terminals , in the plane. This tree may include points other than the terminals, which are called Steiner points .

nodes.label: recurrence relation

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: recurrence

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines recurrence relation as: The specification of a sequence of values in terms of earlier values in the sequence and base values. Also known as recurrence equations.

nodes.label: recursion tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: recursionTree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines recursion tree as: A method to analyze the complexity of an algorithm by diagramming the recursive function calls. Formal Definition: A recursion tree T(p) of degree p is either (i) null or (ii) has p children which are recursion trees.

nodes.label: recursion termination

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: recursiontrm

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines recursion termination as: The point when conditions are met and a recursive algorithm ceases calling itself and begins to return values.

nodes.label: recursive

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: recursive

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines recursive as: (1) A data structure that is partially composed of other instances of the data structure. For instance, a tree is composed of smaller trees ( subtrees ) and leaf nodes , and a list may have other lists as elements. (2) An algorithm in which functions might call themselves. For instance, quicksort or heapify .

nodes.label: recursively enumerable language

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: recursivelyEnumerableLang

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines recursively enumerable language as: A language accepted by a Turing machine .

nodes.label: recursive data structure

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: recursivstrc

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines recursive data structure as: A data structure that is partially composed of smaller or simpler instances of the same data structure. For instance, a tree is composed of smaller trees ( subtrees ) and leaf nodes , and a list may have other lists as elements.

nodes.label: reduced basis

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: reducedbasis

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines reduced basis as: A basis for a lattice that is nearly orthogonal.

nodes.label: reduction

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: reduction

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines reduction as: A computable transformation of one problem into another.

nodes.label: reflexive

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: reflexive

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines reflexive as: A binary relation R for which a R a for all a.

nodes.label: regular decomposition

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: regular

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines regular decomposition as: A space decomposition method that partitions the underlying space by recursively halving it across the various dimensions instead of permitting the partitioning lines to vary.

nodes.label: relation

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: relation

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines relation as: A computation which takes some inputs and yields an output. Any particular input may yield different outputs at different times. Formally, a mapping from each element in the domain to one or more elements in the range .

nodes.label: relational structure

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: relational

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines relational structure as: The counterpart in formal logic of a data structure or class instance in the object-oriented sense. Examples are strings , directed graphs , and undirected graphs . Sets of relational structures generalize the notion of languages as sets of strings.

nodes.label: relative performance guarantee

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: relativePerformGuar

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines relative performance guarantee as: The maximum ratio by which the result of a ρ-approximation algorithm may depart from the optimal solution . Also known as performance ratio.

nodes.label: relaxation

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: relaxation

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines relaxation as: An optimization problem with an enlarged feasible region (and extended objective function ) compared with an original optimization problem. Typically, the relaxation is considerably easier to solve than the original.

nodes.label: relaxed balance

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: relaxedBalance

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines relaxed balance as: When rebalancing a search tree is independent of updating the tree.

nodes.label: repeated squaring

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: repeatedSquaring

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines repeated squaring as: Compute the n th power of an expression in Θ(log n) steps by repeatedly squaring an intermediate result and multiplying an accumulating value by the intermediate result when appropriate.

nodes.label: rescalable

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rescalable

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rescalable as: An optimization for which given any instance of the problem and integer λ >0, there is an easily computed second instance that is the same except that the objective function for the second instance is (element-wise) λ times the objective function of the first instance. For such problems, the best one can hope for is a relative performance guarantee , not an absolute performance guarantee .

nodes.label: reservoir sampling

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: reservoirSampling

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines reservoir sampling as: Randomly select k items from a stream of items of unknown length. Save the first k items in an array of size k. For each item j, j > k, choose a random integer M from 1 to j (inclusive). If M ≤ k, replace item M of the array with item j.

nodes.label: restricted universe sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: restricted

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines restricted universe sort as: A sort algorithm that operates on the basis that the keys are members of a restricted set of values. They may not require comparisons of keys to perform the sorting.

nodes.label: R-file

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rfile

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines R-file as: A spatial access method which divides space into a hierarchically of nested boxes. Objects are indexed in the lowest cell which completely contains them.

nodes.label: ρ-approximation algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rhoapproxmtn

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ρ-approximation algorithm as: An approximation algorithm guaranteed to find a solution at most (or at least, as appropriate) ρ times the optimum. The ratio ρ is the performance ratio or relative performance guarantee of the algorithm.

nodes.label: Rice's method

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: ricesmethod

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Rice's method as: A method of complex asymptotics that can handle certain alternating sums arising in the analysis of algorithms.

nodes.label: right-threaded tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rightThreadedTree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines right-threaded tree as: A variant of a threaded tree in which only the right thread, i.e. link to the successor, of each node is maintained.

nodes.label: right rotation

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rightrotatn

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines right rotation as: (1) In a binary search tree , pushing a node N down and to the right to balance the tree. N's left child replaces N, and the left child's right child becomes N's left child. (2) In an array , moving all items to the next higher location. The last item is moved to the first location, which is now vacant. (3) In a list , removing the tail and inserting it at the head . Also known as rotate right.

nodes.label: Robin Hood hashing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: robinHoodHashing

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Robin Hood hashing as: In case of collision , the item with the longer probe sequence stays in the position. The other item is moved. This tends to equalize the length of probe sequences.

nodes.label: rooted tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rootedtree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rooted tree as: A tree in which one node is designated as the root . Also known as oriented tree.

nodes.label: rotation

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rotation

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rotation as: To switch children and parents among two or three adjacent nodes to restore balance to a tree .

nodes.label: RP

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rp

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines RP as: The class of languages for which membership can be determined in polynomial time by a probabilistic Turing machine with no false acceptances and less than half false rejections. "RP" means " R andomized P olynomial" time. Formal Definition: For a language, S, there exists a probabilistic Turing machine , M, that accepts or rejects any string in polynomial time . If w ∉ S, M rejects w. If w ∈ S, M accepts w with a probability at least 1/2. Also known as randomized polynomial time.

nodes.label: R-tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rtree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines R-tree as: (1) A spatial access method that splits space with hierarchically nested, and possibly overlapping, boxes. The tree is height-balanced. (2) A recursion tree .

nodes.label: run time

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: runtime

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines run time as: (1) The amount of time needed to execute an algorithm . (2) The time when a compiled program is executing, versus compile time.

nodes.label: saturated edge

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: saturatedEdge

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines saturated edge as: An edge in a flow network which has the maximum possible flow.

nodes.label: SBB tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sbbtree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines SBB tree as: A symmetric binary B-tree. Now known as a red-black tree .

nodes.label: scan

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: scan

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines scan as: A parallel operation in which each element in an array or linked list receives the sum of all previous elements. Also known as prefix sums.

nodes.label: scapegoat tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: scapegoatTree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines scapegoat tree as: A binary search tree that needs no balance information. Search time is logarithmic , and the amortized cost of update is logarithmic .

nodes.label: search tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: searchtree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines search tree as: A tree where every subtree of a node has keys less than any other subtree of the node to its right. The keys in a node are conceptually between subtrees and are greater than any keys in subtrees to its left and less than any keys in subtrees to its right.

nodes.label: search tree property

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: searchtrprop

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines search tree property as: When the key of every node of a binary tree is larger than the key of its left child and smaller than its right child.

nodes.label: secant search

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: secantSearch

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines secant search as: Search a sorted array by estimating the next position to check based on the values at the two previous positions checked.

nodes.label: secondary clustering

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: secondaryClustering

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines secondary clustering as: The tendency for some collision resolution schemes to create long run of filled slots away from a key hash position, e.g., along the probe sequence .

nodes.label: segment

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: segment

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines segment as: (1) The substring of a pattern delimited by two don't cares or one don't care and beginning or end of the pattern. (2) A substring .

nodes.label: Select

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: select

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Select as: A four-part algorithm to select the k th smallest element of an array . Part 1) Consider the array as groups of 5 elements; sort and find the median of each group. 2) Use Select recursively to find x , the median of the medians. 3) Next partition the array around x . 4) Let i be the number of elements in the low side of the partition. If k ≤ i, use Select recursively to find the k th element of the low side. Otherwise Select the k-i th element of the high side.

nodes.label: select and partition

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: selectAndPartition

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines select and partition as: Given an array A of n elements and a positive integer k ≤ n, find the k th smallest element of A and partition the array such that A[1], …, A[k-1] ≤ A[k] ≤ A[k+1], …, A[n].

nodes.label: select mode

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: selectmode

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines select mode as: An algorithm to find the mode, or most frequently occurring value, in a group of elements.

nodes.label: self-organizing list

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: selfOrganizingList

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines self-organizing list as: A list that reorders the elements based on some self-organizing heuristic [Wikipedia] to improve average access time.

nodes.label: self-loop

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: selfloop

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines self-loop as: An edge of a graph which starts and ends at the same vertex .

nodes.label: semidefinite programming

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: semidefinite

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines semidefinite programming as: A generalization of a linear program in which any subset of the variables may be constrained to form a semidefinite matrix.

nodes.label: separate chaining

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: separateChaining

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines separate chaining as: A scheme in which each position in the hash table has a list to handle collisions . Each position may be just a link to the list ( direct chaining ) or may be an item and a link, essentially, the head of a list. In the latter, one item is in the table, and other colliding items are in the list. Also known as external chaining.

nodes.label: separation theorem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: separatnthrm

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines separation theorem as: A theorem showing that two complexity classes are distinct. Most separation theorems have been proved by diagonalization .

nodes.label: set packing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: setpacking

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines set packing as: An optimization problem to find the largest number of mutually disjoint subsets that cover a given set of sets .

nodes.label: shadow heap

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shadowheap

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shadow heap as: A heap , implemented in an array , adjacent to an unordered table. The shadow is the table nodes and all their (recursive) parents , by array index, in the heap.

nodes.label: shadow merge

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shadowmerge

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shadow merge as: An algorithm to merge two heaps by concatenating the smaller heap to the larger, then reordering just the concatenated nodes and their parents to restore the heap property.

nodes.label: shadow merge insert

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shadowmrgins

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shadow merge insert as: An algorithm to insert a new node into a shadow heap . The new node is placed in the unordered table. When the table grows beyond some threshold size, table nodes and all their parents are reordered so everything is a heap.

nodes.label: Shannon-Fano coding

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shannonFano

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Shannon-Fano coding as: A variable-length coding based on the frequency of occurrence of each character. Divide the characters into two sets with the frequency of each set as close to half as possible, and assign the sets either 0 or 1 coding. Repeatedly divide the sets until each character has a unique coding.

nodes.label: shared memory

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sharedmemory

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shared memory as: All processors have the same global image of (and access to) all of the memory.

nodes.label: Shift-Or

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shiftOr

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Shift-Or as: A string matching algorithm which keeps an array of bits, R, showing if prefixes of the pattern don't match at the current place. Before searching, mismatch arrays are computed for each character in the alphabet and saved in an array, S. For the next position, with the character c, R = shift(R) or S[c]. If the last bit of R is 0, the pattern matches.

nodes.label: shortest common supersequence

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shortestCommonSuperseq

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shortest common supersequence as: Find the shortest string that contains two or more strings as subsequences .

nodes.label: shortest common superstring

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shortestCommonSuperstring

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shortest common superstring as: Find the shortest string that contains two or more strings as substrings .

nodes.label: shuffle sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shuffleSort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shuffle sort as: A distribution sort algorithm that begins by removing the first 1/8 of the n items, sorting them (recursively), and putting them in an array. This creates n/8 buckets to which the remaining 7/8 of the items are distributed. Each bucket is then sorted, and the buckets are concatenated.

nodes.label: sibling

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sibling

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sibling as: A node in a tree that has the same parent as another node is its sibling.

nodes.label: sieve of Eratosthenes

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sieve

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sieve of Eratosthenes as: An algorithm to find all prime numbers up to a certain N. Begin with an (unmarked) array of integers from 2 to N. The first unmarked integer, 2, is the first prime. Mark every multiple of this prime. Repeatedly take the next unmarked integer as the next prime and mark every multiple of the prime.

nodes.label: sift up

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: siftup

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sift up as: Restoring the heap property by swapping a node with its parent , and repeating the process on the parent until the root is reached or the heap property is satisfied.

nodes.label: signature

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: signature

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines signature as: The types or domains , and order, in some representations, of inputs to and outputs from a function .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sim

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ∼ as: (1) Proportional to. (2) Asymptotically equal to. A theoretical measure of the execution of an algorithm , usually the time or memory needed, given the problem size n, which is usually the number of items. Informally, saying some equation f(n) ∼ g(n) means it grows at the same rate as g(n). More formally, it means lim x → ∞ f(x)/g(x) = 1.

nodes.label: simple uniform hashing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simpleUniformHashing

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines simple uniform hashing as: The assumption or goal that items are equally likely to hash to any value.

nodes.label: simple merge

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simplemerge

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines simple merge as: Merge n sorted streams into one output stream. All the stream heads are compared, and the head with the least key is removed and written to the output. This is repeated until all streams are empty.

nodes.label: simple path

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simplepath

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines simple path as: A path that repeats no vertex , except that the first and last may be the same vertex.

nodes.label: simplex

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simplex

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines simplex as: The simplest N-dimensional polytope . The generalization of a triangle (2D) or tetrahedron (3D).

nodes.label: simulated annealing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simulatedAnnealing

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines simulated annealing as: A technique to find a good solution to an optimization problem by trying random variations of the current solution. A worse variation is accepted as the new solution with a probability that decreases as the computation proceeds. The slower the cooling schedule , or rate of decrease, the more likely the algorithm is to find an optimal or near- optimal solution .

nodes.label: simulation theorem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simulatnthrm

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines simulation theorem as: One kind of computation can be simulated by another kind within stated complexity bounds. Most known containment or equality relationships between complexity classes were proved this way.

nodes.label: single-destination shortest-path problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: singleDestShortestPath

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines single-destination shortest-path problem as: Find the shortest path from each vertex in a weighted, directed graph to a specific destination vertex.

nodes.label: single-source shortest-path problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: singleSourceShortestPath

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines single-source shortest-path problem as: Find the shortest paths from a specific source vertex to every other vertex in a weighted, directed graph . Dijkstra's algorithm solves this if all weights are nonnegative. The Bellman-Ford algorithm handles any weights.

nodes.label: single program multiple data

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: singleprogrm

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines single program multiple data as: The dominant style of parallel programming, where all processors use the same program, though each has its own data. Also known as SPMD.

nodes.label: singularity analysis

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: singularity

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines singularity analysis as: A complex asymptotic technique for determining the asymptotics of certain algebraic functions.

nodes.label: sink

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sink

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sink as: A vertex of a directed graph with no outgoing edges . More formally, a vertex with with out-degree 0.

nodes.label: skd-tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: skdtree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines skd-tree as: The spatial k-d tree is a spatial access method where successive levels are split along different dimensions. Objects are indexed by their centroid , and the minimum bounding box of objects in a node are stored in the node.

nodes.label: skew symmetry

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: skewsymmetry

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines skew symmetry as: The property that the flow is the same amount, but reversed direction, starting from either vertex of every edge of a flow network . More formally, for an edge e=(v,w), f(v,w) = -f(w,v), where f(a,b) is the flow from a to b.

nodes.label: skip list

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: skiplist

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines skip list as: A randomized variant of an ordered linked list with additional, parallel lists. Parallel lists at higher levels skip geometrically more items. Searching begins at the highest level, to quickly get to the right part of the list, then uses progressively lower level lists. A new item is added by randomly selecting a level, then inserting it in order in the lists for that and all lower levels. With enough levels, searching is O(log n) .

nodes.label: Smith algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: smithAlgorithm

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Smith algorithm as: A string matching algorithm which computes the shift value for both the rightmost character of the window and the character preceding it, then uses the maximum of the two values.

nodes.label: Smith-Waterman algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: smithWaterman

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Smith-Waterman algorithm as: A means of searching protein databases to find those with the best alignment.

nodes.label: smoothsort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: smoothsort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines smoothsort as: A variant of heapsort that takes advantage of a partially ordered table. Performance is O(n) when input is sorted and O(n log n) performance for worst case .

nodes.label: solvable

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: solvable

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines solvable as: A computational problem that can be solved by a Turing machine . The problem may have a nonbinary output.

nodes.label: sorted array

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sortedarray

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sorted array as: An array whose items are kept sorted, often so searching is faster.

nodes.label: sorted list

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sortedlist

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sorted list as: A list whose items are kept sorted.

nodes.label: soundex

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: soundex

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines soundex as: An algorithm to code surnames phonetically by reducing them to the first letter and up to three digits, where each digit is one of six consonant sounds. This reduces matching problems from different spellings.

nodes.label: source

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: source

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines source as: (1) A vertex of a directed graph with no incoming edges . More formally, a vertex with in-degree 0. (2) The vertex from which an edge of a directed graph leaves.

nodes.label: space-constructible function

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: space

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines space-constructible function as: A function s(n) that gives the actual space used by some Turing machine on all inputs of length n.

nodes.label: space ordering method

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: spaceOrderingMethod

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines space ordering method as: A mapping from a discrete k-dimensional space into a linear order.

nodes.label: spanning tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: spanningtree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines spanning tree as: A connected , acyclic subgraph containing all the vertices of a graph .

nodes.label: sparse graph

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sparsegraph

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sparse graph as: A graph in which the number of edges is much less than the possible number of edges.

nodes.label: sparse matrix

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sparsematrix

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sparse matrix as: A matrix that has relatively few non-zero (or "interesting") entries. It may be represented in much less than n × m space.

nodes.label: sparsification

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sparsificatn

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sparsification as: Technique for designing dynamic graph algorithms , which when applicable transform a time bound of T(n,m) onto O(T(n,n)), where m is the number of edges and n is the number of vertices of the given graph.

nodes.label: sparsity

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sparsity

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sparsity as: Instances of the longest common subsequence problem in which the number of matches is small compared to the product of the lengths of the input strings.

nodes.label: spatial access method

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: spatialAccessMethod

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines spatial access method as: A data structure to search for lines, polygons, etc. Also known as SAM.

nodes.label: square matrix

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: squarematrix

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines square matrix as: A n × n matrix , i.e., one whose size is the same in both dimensions.

nodes.label: stable

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stable

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines stable as: An algorithm where the relative order upon input of items with equal keys is always preserved in the output. Usually a sort algorithm.

nodes.label: stack tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stacktree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines stack tree as: A binary tree where no node , except the root , has more than one non- leaf child .

nodes.label: star encoding

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: starEncoding

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines star encoding as: Using a fixed dictionary , encode words in text with strings having many repeated characters, typically an asterisk or "star" (*).

nodes.label: star-shaped polygon

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: starshaped

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines star-shaped polygon as: A polygon P in which there exists an interior point p such that all the boundary points of P are visible from p.

nodes.label: start state

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: startstate

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines start state as: An initial state or condition of a finite state machine or Turing machine . Informally, how the memory is initially set.

nodes.label: state

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: state

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines state as: The condition of a finite state machine or Turing machine at a certain time. Informally, the content of memory.

nodes.label: state machine

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: statemachine

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines state machine as: A model of computation consisting of a (possibly infinite) set of states , a set of start states , an input alphabet , and a transition function which maps input symbols and current states to a next state . Usually understood to be a finite state machine .

nodes.label: static

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: static

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines static as: When the problem domain does not change.

nodes.label: s-t cut

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stcut

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines s-t cut as: A partitioning of the vertices of a flow network into S and T such that the source is in S and the sink is in T.

nodes.label: st-digraph

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stdigraph

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines st-digraph as: A directed acyclic graph with two specially marked nodes, the source s and the sink t.

nodes.label: Steiner point

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: steinerpoint

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Steiner point as: (1) A point that is not part of the input set of points, for instance, a point computed to construct a Steiner tree . (2) A point with a particular geometric relation to a triangle.

nodes.label: Steiner ratio

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: steinerratio

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Steiner ratio as: For a given variant of the Steiner tree problem, the maximum possible ratio of the length of a minimum spanning tree of a set of terminals to the length of an optimal Steiner tree of the same set of terminals. Usually written ρ (rho).

nodes.label: Steiner tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: steinertree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Steiner tree as: A minimum-weight tree connecting a designated set of vertices , called terminals , in an undirected , weighted graph or points in a space. The tree may include non-terminals, which are called Steiner vertices or Steiner points .

nodes.label: Steiner vertex

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: steinervertx

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Steiner vertex as: A point that is not part of the input set of points, for instance, a point computed to construct a Steiner tree .

nodes.label: stooge sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stoogesort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines stooge sort as: A terribly inefficient sort algorithm that swaps the top and bottom items if needed, then ( recursively ) sorts the bottom two-thirds, then the top two-thirds, then the bottom two-thirds again.

nodes.label: straight-line drawing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: straightline

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines straight-line drawing as: A graph drawing in which each edge is represented by a straight line segment.

nodes.label: strand sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: strandSort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strand sort as: A sort algorithm that works well if many items are in order. First, begin a sublist by moving the first item from the original list to the sublist. For each subsequent item in the original list, if it is greater than the last item of the sublist, remove it from the original list and append it to the sublist. Merge the sublist into a final, sorted list. Repeatedly extract and merge sublists until all items are sorted. Handle two or fewer items as special cases.

nodes.label: strictly decreasing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: strictlyDecreasing

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strictly decreasing as: A function from a partially ordered domain to a partially ordered range such that x < y implies f(x) > f(y).

nodes.label: strictly increasing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: strictlyIncreasing

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strictly increasing as: A function from a partially ordered domain to a partially ordered range such that x < y implies f(x) < f(y).

nodes.label: strictly lower triangular matrix

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: strictlyLowerTriangMat

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strictly lower triangular matrix as: A matrix that is only defined at (i,j) when i > j.

nodes.label: strictly upper triangular matrix

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: strictlyUpperTriangMat

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strictly upper triangular matrix as: A matrix that is only defined at (i,j) when i < j.

nodes.label: string

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: string

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines string as: A list of characters, usually implemented as an array . Informally a word, phrase, sentence, etc. Since text processing is so common, a special type with substring operations is often available.

nodes.label: string matching with errors

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stringMatchwError

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines string matching with errors as: Searching for approximate (e.g., up to a predefined number of symbol mismatches, insertions, and deletions) occurrences of a pattern string in a text string. Preprocessing, e.g., building an index, may or may not be allowed. Also known as approximate string matching.

nodes.label: string matching with mismatches

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stringMatchwMismatch

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines string matching with mismatches as: The special case of string matching with errors where mismatches are the only type of error allowed.

nodes.label: string editing problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stringedit

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines string editing problem as: The problem of finding an edit script of minimum cost which transforms a given string into another given string.

nodes.label: strip packing

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: strippacking

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strip packing as: Pack a set of rectangles into a strip of width 1 to minimize the height used. Rectangles may not overlap or be rotated. Without loss of generality, the height of rectangles is at most 1. This is NP-hard .

nodes.label: strongly connected component

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stronglyConnectedCompo

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strongly connected component as: A strongly connected subgraph , S, of a directed graph , D, such that no vertex of D can be added to S and it still be strongly connected. Informally, a maximal subgraph in which every vertex is reachable from every other vertex.

nodes.label: strongly connected graph

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stronglyConnectedGraph

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strongly connected graph as: A directed graph that has a path from each vertex to every other vertex. Formal Definition: A directed graph D=(V, E) such that for all pairs of vertices u, v ∈ V, there is a path from u to v and from v to u.

nodes.label: strongly NP-hard

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stronglyNP

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strongly NP-hard as: The complexity class of decision problems which are still NP-hard even when all numbers in the input are bounded by some polynomial in the length of the input.

nodes.label: strsrch

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: strsrch

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strsrch as: Find occurrences of a substring in a target string by trying the substring at each possible location in the string. Execution time is Θ(mn), where m is length of the target string and n is the length of the substring.

nodes.label: stupid sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stupidSort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines stupid sort as: (1) The original name of gnome sort . (2) An alternate name for bogosort .

nodes.label: subadditive ergodic theorem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: subadditive

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines subadditive ergodic theorem as: If a stationary and ergodic process satisfies the subadditive inequality, it grows almost surely linearly in time.

nodes.label: subgraph

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: subgraph

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines subgraph as: A graph whose vertices and edges are subsets of another graph . Formal Definition: A graph G'=(V', E') is a subgraph of another graph G=(V, E) iff V'⊆ V, and E'⊆ E ∧ ( (v 1 , v 2 )∈ E' → v 1 , v 2 ∈ V').

nodes.label: subgraph isomorphism

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: subgraphiso

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines subgraph isomorphism as: Decide if there is a subgraph of one graph which is isomorphic to another graph.

nodes.label: sublinear time algorithm

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sublinearTimeAlgo

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sublinear time algorithm as: A algorithm whose execution time, f(n), grows slower than the size of the problem, n, but only gives an approximate or probably correct answer.

nodes.label: subsequence

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: subsequence

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines subsequence as: Any string that can be obtained by deleting zero or more symbols from a given string.

nodes.label: subset

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: subset

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines subset as: A set S 1 is a subset of another set S 2 if every element in S 1 is in S 2 . S 2 may have exactly the same elements as S 1 . Formal Definition: S 1 ⊆ S 2 iff ∀ s, s ∈ S 1 → s ∈ S 2 .

nodes.label: substring

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: substring

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines substring as: A string v is a substring of a string u if u=u′ vu″ for some prefix u′ and suffix u″. Also known as factor.

nodes.label: subtree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: subtree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines subtree as: The tree which is a child of a node .

nodes.label: suffix

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: suffix

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines suffix as: The end characters of a string . More formally a string v is a suffix of a string u if u=u'v for some string u'.

nodes.label: suffix automaton

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: suffixautmtn

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines suffix automaton as: The smallest automaton accepting all suffixes of a string . The states form a directed acyclic word graph or DAWG.

nodes.label: superimposed code

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: superimposedCode

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines superimposed code as: A set of bit vectors such that no vector is a subset of a bitwise or of a small number of others.

nodes.label: superset

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: superset

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines superset as: A set S 1 is a superset of another set S 2 if every element in S 2 is in S 1 . S 1 may have elements which are not in S 2 .

nodes.label: supersink

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: supersink

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines supersink as: A vertex of a directed graph which is reachable from all other vertices.

nodes.label: supersource

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: supersource

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines supersource as: A vertex of a directed graph from which all other vertices are reachable .

nodes.label: symmetric

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: symmetric

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines symmetric as: A binary relation R for which a R b implies b R a.

nodes.label: symmetric set difference

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: symmetricSetDiff

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines symmetric set difference as: Members which are in either set , but not in both. That is, for sets A and B, it is (A - B) ∪ (B - A).

nodes.label: symmetry breaking

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: symmetrybrek

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines symmetry breaking as: To differentiate parts of a structure, such as a graph , which locally look the same to all vertices . Usually implemented with randomization .

nodes.label: tail

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: tail

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines tail as: (1) The last item of a list . (2) All but the first item of a list; the list following the head.

nodes.label: tail recursion

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: tailRecursion

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines tail recursion as: A special form of recursion where the last operation of a function is a recursive call. The recursion may be optimized away by executing the call in the current stack frame and returning its result rather than creating a new stack frame.

nodes.label: target

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: target

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines target as: The vertex which an edge of a directed graph enters.

nodes.label: temporal logic

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: temporllogic

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines temporal logic as: A logic with a notion of time included. The formulas can express facts about past, present, and future states. The formulas are interpreted over Kripke structures, which can model computation; hence temporal logic is very useful in formal verification .

nodes.label: terminal

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: terminal

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines terminal as: The set of points in a plane or vertices in a graph defining endpoints of a Steiner tree .

nodes.label: ternary search tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: ternarySearchTree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ternary search tree as: A 3-way tree where every node's left subtree has keys less than the node's key, every middle subtree has keys equal to the node's key, and every right subtree has keys greater than the node's key. If the key is a multikey ( string , array, list, etc.), the middle subtree organizes by the next subkey (character, array or list item, etc.) Also known as TST.

nodes.label: text

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: text

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines text as: A list of characters, usually thought of as a list of words separated by spaces.

nodes.label: threaded tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: threadedtree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines threaded tree as: A binary search tree in which each node uses an otherwise-empty left child link to refer to the node's in-order predecessor and an empty right child link to refer to its in-order successor.

nodes.label: three-dimensional

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: threedimnsnl

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines three-dimensional as: Dealing with or restricted to a space in which location can be completely described with exactly three orthogonal axes.

nodes.label: three-way merge sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: threewaymsrt

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines three-way merge sort as: A k-way merge sort which uses three input and three output streams.

nodes.label: time-constructible function

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: time

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines time-constructible function as: A function t(n) that gives the actual running time of some Turing machine on all inputs of length n.

nodes.label: time/space complexity

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: timespace

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines time/space complexity as: The maximum time or space required by a Turing machine on any input of length n.

nodes.label: top-down radix sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: topdownRadixSort

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines top-down radix sort as: A recursive bucket sort where elements are distributed based on succeeding pieces (characters) of the key .

nodes.label: topological order

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: topologicalOrder

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines topological order as: A numbering of the vertices of a directed acyclic graph such that every edge from a vertex numbered i to a vertex numbered j satisfies i<j.

nodes.label: topology tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: topologytree

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines topology tree as: Tree that describes a balanced decomposition of another tree, according to its topology. More precisely, given a restricted multilevel partition for a tree T, a topology tree satisfies the following: (1) A topology tree node at level l represents a vertex cluster at level l in the restricted multilevel partition, and (2) A node at level l ≥ 1 has at most two children , representing the vertex clusters at level l-1 whose union gives the vertex cluster the node represents.

nodes.label: total function

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: totalfunc

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines total function as: A function which is defined for all inputs of the right type, that is, for all of a domain .

nodes.label: totally undecidable problem

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: totallyUndecidableProb

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines totally undecidable problem as: A problem that cannot be solved by a Turing machine .

nodes.label: total order

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: totalorder

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines total order as: An order defined for all pairs of items of a set.
