nodes.label: Haptic Technology
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Haptic Technology as: The study of the use of touch and KINESTHESIS in order to produce HAPTIC COMPUTER INTERFACES that will allow users to interact with digital objects by kinesthetic feedback, force feedback, and tactile feedback.

nodes.label: Inventions
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Inventions as: A novel composition, device, or process, independently conceived de novo or derived from a pre-existing model.

nodes.label: Man-Machine Systems
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Man-Machine Systems as: A system in which the functions of the man and the machine are interrelated and necessary for the operation of the system.

nodes.label: Materials Science
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Materials Science as: An interdisciplinary study of the microstructure and composition of various materials such as metals, semiconductors, ceramics, and polymers, in relation to their macromolecular physical and chemical properties. Materials science enables the custom creation of new materials with specific properties and uses.

nodes.label: Medical Laboratory Science
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Medical Laboratory Science as: The specialty related to the performance of techniques in clinical pathology such as those in hematology, microbiology, and other general clinical laboratory applications.

nodes.label: Miniaturization
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Miniaturization as: The design or construction of objects greatly reduced in scale.

nodes.label: Printing, Three-Dimensional
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Printing, Three-Dimensional as: Process for making, building or constructing a physical object from a three-dimensional digital model by laying down many successive thin layers of building material.

nodes.label: Quality Control
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Quality Control as: A system for verifying and maintaining a desired level of quality in a product or process by careful planning, use of proper equipment, continued inspection, and corrective action as required. (Random House Unabridged Dictionary, 2d ed)

nodes.label: Technology, Dental
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Technology, Dental as: The field of dentistry involved in procedures for designing and constructing dental appliances. It includes also the application of any technology to the field of dentistry.

nodes.label: Technology, Pharmaceutical
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Technology, Pharmaceutical as: The application of scientific knowledge or technology to pharmacy and the pharmaceutical industry. It includes methods, techniques, and instrumentation in the manufacture, preparation, compounding, dispensing, packaging, and storing of drugs and other preparations used in diagnostic and determinative procedures, and in the treatment of patients.

nodes.label: Technology, Radiologic
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Technology, Radiologic as: The application of scientific knowledge or technology to the field of radiology. The applications center mostly around x-ray or radioisotopes for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes but the technological applications of any radiation or radiologic procedure is within the scope of radiologic technology.

nodes.label: Technology Transfer
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Technology Transfer as: Spread and adoption of inventions and techniques from one geographic area to another, from one discipline to another, or from one sector of the economy to another. For example, improvements in medical equipment may be transferred from industrial countries to developing countries, advances arising from aerospace engineering may be applied to equipment for persons with disabilities, and innovations in science arising from government research are made available to private enterprise.

nodes.label: Bioprinting
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Bioprinting as: A material transfer technique used for assembling biological material or cells into a prescribed organization to create functional structures such as MICROCHIP ANALYTICAL DEVICES , cell microarrays, or three dimensional anatomical structures.

nodes.label: Cell Engineering
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Cell Engineering as: Methods and techniques used to modify or select cells and develop conditions for growing cells for biosynthetic production of molecules ( METABOLIC ENGINEERING ), for generation of tissue structures and organs in vitro ( TISSUE ENGINEERING ), or for other BIOENGINEERING research objectives.

nodes.label: Synthetic Biology
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Synthetic Biology as: A field of biological research combining engineering in the formulation, design, and building (synthesis) of novel biological structures, functions, and systems.

nodes.label: Eye-Tracking Technology
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Eye-Tracking Technology as: Technology used for EYE MOVEMENT MEASUREMENTS , which capture and measure a persons EYE MOVEMENT and/or EYE GAZE

nodes.label: Water Supply
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Water Supply as: Means or process of supplying water (as for a community) usually including reservoirs, tunnels, and pipelines and often the watershed from which the water is ultimately drawn. (Webster, 3d ed)

nodes.label: User-Centered Design
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes User-Centered Design as: Design process using input from users regarding systems, devices, or software.

nodes.label: Automation, Laboratory
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Automation, Laboratory as: Controlled operations of analytic or diagnostic processes, or systems by mechanical or electronic devices.

nodes.label: Multiple-Instance Learning Algorithms
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Multiple-Instance Learning Algorithms as: Weakly supervised learning algorithms where training set is arranged in a labeled bag of instances, and a single class label is assigned to a bag.

nodes.label: Robotics
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Robotics as: The application of electronic, computerized control systems to mechanical devices designed to perform human functions. Formerly restricted to industry, but nowadays applied to artificial organs controlled by bionic (bioelectronic) devices, like automated insulin pumps and other prostheses.

nodes.label: Biomedical Technology
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Biomedical Technology as: The application of technology to the solution of medical problems.

nodes.label: Biomimetics
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Biomimetics as: An interdisciplinary field in materials science, ENGINEERING , and BIOLOGY , studying the use of biological principles for synthesis or fabrication of BIOMIMETIC MATERIALS .

nodes.label: Bioreactors
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Bioreactors as: Tools or devices for generating products using the synthetic or chemical conversion capacity of a biological system. They can be classical fermentors, cell culture perfusion systems, or enzyme bioreactors. For production of proteins or enzymes, recombinant microorganisms such as bacteria, mammalian cells, or insect or plant cells are usually chosen.

nodes.label: Industrial Microbiology
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Industrial Microbiology as: The study, utilization, and manipulation of those microorganisms capable of economically producing desirable substances or changes in substances, and the control of undesirable microorganisms.

nodes.label: Audiovisual Aids
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Audiovisual Aids as: Auditory and visual instructional materials.

nodes.label: Hot Melt Extrusion Technology
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Hot Melt Extrusion Technology as: Solvent-free method for preparing numerous types of drug delivery systems and dosage forms for active pharmaceutical ingredients that have solubility issues. It involves pumping polymeric materials at temperatures above their glass transition temperature to mix in active pharmaceutical ingredients with or without binders thus forming an amorphous product with an increase in the dissolution profile for the active pharmaceutical ingredients.

nodes.label: Microtechnology
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Microtechnology as: Manufacturing technology for making microscopic devices in the micrometer range (typically 1-100 micrometers), such as integrated circuits or MEMS . The process usually involves replication and parallel fabrication of hundreds or millions of identical structures using various thin film deposition techniques and carried out in environmentally-controlled clean rooms.

nodes.label: Stereolithography
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Stereolithography as: A 3D printing technology where a computer-controlled moving laser beam is used to build up the required structure, layer by layer, from liquid POLYMERS that harden on contact with laser light (photopolymerization).

nodes.label: Laboratory Proficiency Testing
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Laboratory Proficiency Testing as: Assessments aimed at determining agreement in diagnostic test results among laboratories. Identical survey samples are distributed to participating laboratories, with results stratified according to testing methodologies.

nodes.label: Chemistry Techniques, Synthetic
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Chemistry Techniques, Synthetic as: Methods used for the chemical synthesis of compounds. Included under this heading are laboratory methods used to synthesize a variety of chemicals and drugs.

nodes.label: Molecular Farming
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Molecular Farming as: The large scale production of pharmaceutically important and commercially valuable RECOMBINANT PROTEINS .

nodes.label: Metabolic Engineering
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Metabolic Engineering as: Methods and techniques used to genetically modify cells' biosynthetic product output and develop conditions for growing the cells as BIOREACTORS .

nodes.label: Water Wells
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Water Wells as: Constructions built to access underground water.

nodes.label: Autonomous Robots
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Autonomous Robots as: Machines that are engineered to learn about their environment and make decisions to complete tasks with little to no human intervention. These robots may be designed to complete tasks such as patient intervention, remote monitoring, inventory transportation, among many others.

nodes.label: Robotic Surgical Procedures
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Robotic Surgical Procedures as: Surgical procedures performed remotely using a computer that controls surgical instruments attached to mechanical arms designed to perform the tasks of the surgeon.

nodes.label: Biomedical Enhancement
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Biomedical Enhancement as: The use of technology-based interventions to improve functional capacities rather than to treat disease.

nodes.label: Nanomedicine
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Nanomedicine as: The branch of medicine concerned with the application of NANOTECHNOLOGY to the prevention and treatment of disease. It involves the monitoring, repair, construction, and control of human biological systems at the molecular level, using engineered nanodevices and NANOSTRUCTURES . (From Freitas Jr., Nanomedicine, vol 1, 1999).

nodes.label: Photobioreactors
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Photobioreactors as: Devices for generating biological products that use light as the energy source. They are used for controlled BIOMASS production such as growing cyanobacteria, mosses, or algae.

nodes.label: Books, Illustrated
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Books, Illustrated as: Books containing photographs, prints, drawings, portraits, plates, diagrams, facsimiles, maps, tables, or other representations or systematic arrangement of data designed to elucidate or decorate its contents. (From The ALA Glossary of Library and Information Science, 1983, p114)

nodes.label: Models, Structural
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Models, Structural as: A representation, generally small in scale, to show the structure, construction, or appearance of something. (From Random House Unabridged Dictionary, 2d ed)

nodes.label: Motion Pictures
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Motion Pictures as: The art, technique, or business of producing motion pictures for entertainment, propaganda, or instruction.

nodes.label: Multimedia
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Multimedia as: Materials, frequently computer applications, that combine some or all of text, sound, graphics, animation, and video into integrated packages. (Thesaurus of ERIC Descriptors, 1994)

nodes.label: Optical Storage Devices
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Optical Storage Devices as: A computer disk read by a laser beam, containing data prerecorded by a vendor. The buyer cannot enter or modify data in any way but the advantages lie in the speed of accessibility, relative immunity to damage, and relatively low cost of purchase.

nodes.label: Radio
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Radio as: The transmission and reception of electric impulses or signals by means of electric waves without a connecting wire, or the use of these waves for the wireless transmission of electric impulses into which sound is converted. (From Webster's 3d)

nodes.label: Sound Recordings
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Sound Recordings as: The storing of sound signals on various media such as cylinders, analog discs, digital discs, tapes, and wires.[LCSH, 10/27/2020]

nodes.label: Tape Recording
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Tape Recording as: Recording of information on magnetic or punched paper tape.

nodes.label: Television
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Television as: The transmission and reproduction of transient images of fixed or moving objects. An electronic system of transmitting such images together with sound over a wire or through space by apparatus that converts light and sound into electrical waves and reconverts them into visible light rays and audible sound. (From Webster, 3rd ed)

nodes.label: Microfluidics
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Microfluidics as: The study of fluid channels and chambers of tiny dimensions of tens to hundreds of micrometers and volumes of nanoliters or picoliters. This is of interest in biological MICROCIRCULATION and used in MICROCHEMISTRY and INVESTIGATIVE TECHNIQUES .

nodes.label: Click Chemistry
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Click Chemistry as: Organic chemistry methodology that mimics the modular nature of various biosynthetic processes. It uses highly reliable and selective reactions designed to click i.e., rapidly join small modular units together in high yield, without offensive byproducts. In combination with COMBINATORIAL CHEMISTRY TECHNIQUES , it is used for the synthesis of new compounds and combinatorial libraries.

nodes.label: Combinatorial Chemistry Techniques
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Combinatorial Chemistry Techniques as: A technology, in which sets of reactions for solution or solid-phase synthesis, is used to create molecular libraries for analysis of compounds on a large scale.

nodes.label: Cycloaddition Reaction
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Cycloaddition Reaction as: Synthetic organic reactions that use reactions between unsaturated molecules to form cyclical products.

nodes.label: Molecular Imprinting
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Molecular Imprinting as: A methodology for chemically synthesizing polymer molds of specific molecules or recognition sites of specific molecules. Applications for MOLECULARLY IMPRINTED POLYMERS (MIPs) include separations, assays and biosensors, and catalysis.

nodes.label: Solid-Phase Synthesis Techniques
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Solid-Phase Synthesis Techniques as: Techniques used to synthesize chemicals using molecular substrates that are bound to a solid surface. Typically a series of reactions are conducted on the bound substrate that results in either the covalent attachment of specific moieties or the modification of existing function groups. These techniques offer an advantage to those involving solution reactions in that the substrate compound does not have to be isolated and purified between the reaction steps.

nodes.label: Genetic Enhancement
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Genetic Enhancement as: The use of genetic methodologies to improve functional capacities of an organism rather than to treat disease.

nodes.label: Models, Anatomic
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Models, Anatomic as: Three-dimensional representation to show anatomic structures. Models may be used in place of intact animals or organisms for teaching, practice, and study.

nodes.label: Videodisc Recording
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Videodisc Recording as: The storing of visual and usually sound signals on discs for later reproduction on a television screen or monitor.

nodes.label: Videotape Recording
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Videotape Recording as: Recording of visual and sometimes sound signals on magnetic tape.

nodes.label: Microscopy, Video
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Microscopy, Video as: Microscopy in which television cameras are used to brighten magnified images that are otherwise too dark to be seen with the naked eye. It is used frequently in TELEPATHOLOGY .

nodes.label: SELEX Aptamer Technique
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes SELEX Aptamer Technique as: A method of generating a large library of randomized nucleotides and selecting NUCLEOTIDE APTAMERS by iterative rounds of in vitro selection. A modified procedure substitutes AMINO ACIDS in place of NUCLEOTIDES to make PEPTIDE APTAMERS .

nodes.label: Causality
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Causality as: The relating of causes to the effects they produce. Causes are termed necessary when they must always precede an effect and sufficient when they initiate or produce an effect. Any of several factors may be associated with the potential disease causation or outcome, including predisposing factors, enabling factors, precipitating factors, reinforcing factors, and risk factors.

nodes.label: Research Design
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Research Design as: A plan for collecting and utilizing data so that desired information can be obtained with sufficient precision or so that an hypothesis can be tested properly.

nodes.label: Science
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Science as: The study of natural phenomena by observation, measurement, and experimentation.

nodes.label: Precipitating Factors
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Precipitating Factors as: Factors associated with the definitive onset of a disease, illness, accident, behavioral response, or course of action. Usually one factor is more important or more obviously recognizable than others, if several are involved, and one may often be regarded as necessary. Examples include exposure to specific disease; amount or level of an infectious organism, drug, or noxious agent, etc.

nodes.label: Protective Factors
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Protective Factors as: An aspect of personal behavior or lifestyle, environmental exposure, or inborn or inherited characteristic, which, on the basis of epidemiologic evidence, is known to be associated with prevention or mitigation of a health-related condition considered important to prevent.

nodes.label: Risk Factors
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Risk Factors as: An aspect of personal behavior or lifestyle, environmental exposure, inborn or inherited characteristic, which, based on epidemiological evidence, is known to be associated with a health-related condition considered important to prevent.

nodes.label: Control Groups
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Control Groups as: Groups that serve as a standard for comparison in experimental studies. They are similar in relevant characteristics to the experimental group but do not receive the experimental intervention.

nodes.label: Double-Blind Method
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Double-Blind Method as: A method of studying a drug or procedure in which both the subjects and investigators are kept unaware of who is actually getting which specific treatment.

nodes.label: Random Allocation
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Random Allocation as: A process involving chance used in therapeutic trials or other research endeavor for allocating experimental subjects, human or animal, between treatment and control groups, or among treatment groups. It may also apply to experiments on inanimate objects.

nodes.label: Sample Size
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Sample Size as: The number of units (persons, animals, patients, specified circumstances, etc.) in a population to be studied. The sample size should be big enough to have a high likelihood of detecting a true difference between two groups. (From Wassertheil-Smoller, Biostatistics and Epidemiology, 1990, p95)

nodes.label: Research
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Research as: Critical and exhaustive investigation or experimentation, having for its aim the discovery of new facts and their correct interpretation, the revision of accepted conclusions, theories, or laws in the light of newly discovered facts, or the practical application of such new or revised conclusions, theories, or laws. (Webster, 3d ed)

nodes.label: Systems Integration
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Systems Integration as: The procedures involved in combining separately developed modules, components, or subsystems so that they work together as a complete system. (From McGraw-Hill Dictionary of Scientific and Technical Terms, 4th ed)

nodes.label: Systems Theory
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Systems Theory as: Principles, models, and laws that apply to complex interrelationships and interdependencies of sets of linked components which form a functioning whole, a system. Any system may be composed of components which are systems in their own right (sub-systems), such as several organs within an individual organism.

nodes.label: Artificial Life
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Artificial Life as: Research involving the synthesis of life and life-like phenomena and the application of such techniques toward the enhancement of our theoretical understanding of life and life-like phenomena, studied through the use of computer programs.

nodes.label: Behavioral Research
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Behavioral Research as: Research that involves the application of the behavioral and social sciences to the study of the actions or reactions of persons or animals in response to external or internal stimuli. (from American Heritage Dictionary, 4th ed)

nodes.label: Biomedical Research
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Biomedical Research as: Research that involves the application of the natural sciences, especially biology and physiology, to medicine.

nodes.label: Community-Based Participatory Research
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Community-Based Participatory Research as: Collaborative process of research involving researchers and community representatives.

nodes.label: Empirical Research
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Empirical Research as: The study, based on direct observation, use of statistical records, interviews, or experimental methods, of actual practices or the actual impact of practices or policies.

nodes.label: Evidence Gaps
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Evidence Gaps as: Areas where little or no evidence from impact evaluations and SYSTEMATIC REVIEWS is available and where future research should be focused (from https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/16941).

nodes.label: Interdisciplinary Research
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Interdisciplinary Research as: Research combining mastery in distinct fields or disciplines that apply and exchange tools, concepts, ideas, data methods, or results around a common project.

nodes.label: Knowledge Discovery
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Knowledge Discovery as: A process that searches for hidden and important connections among information or results.

nodes.label: Operations Research
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Operations Research as: A group of techniques developed to apply scientific methods and tools to solve the problems of DECISION MAKING in complex organizations and systems. Operations research searches for optimal solutions in situations of conflicting GOALS and makes use of mathematical models from which solutions for actual problems may be derived. (From Psychiatric Dictionary, 6th ed)

nodes.label: Peer Review, Research
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Peer Review, Research as: The evaluation by experts of the quality and pertinence of research or research proposals of other experts in the same field. Peer review is used by editors in deciding which submissions warrant publication, by granting agencies to determine which proposals should be funded, and by academic institutions in tenure decisions.

nodes.label: Proof of Concept Study
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Proof of Concept Study as: An empirical investigation which pertains to the development of prototypes or models that demonstrate the feasibility of novel concepts, ideas, principles, schema or their practical application.

nodes.label: Research Report
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Research Report as: Detailed account or statement or formal record of data resulting from empirical inquiry.

nodes.label: Social Validity, Research
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Social Validity, Research as: Evaluation of the degree of acceptance for the immediate variables associated with a procedure or program designed to change behavior. This includes the social significance of the goals of treatment, the social appropriateness of the treatment procedures, and the social importance of the effects of treatments.

nodes.label: Biobehavioral Sciences
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Biobehavioral Sciences as: An interdisciplinary scientific approach to the study of complex interactions among biological, social, behavioral and environmental factors.

nodes.label: Embryo Research
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Embryo Research as: Experimentation on, or using the organs or tissues from, a human or other mammalian conceptus during the prenatal stage of development that is characterized by rapid morphological changes and the differentiation of basic structures. In humans, this includes the period from the time of fertilization to the end of the eighth week after fertilization.

nodes.label: Fetal Research
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Fetal Research as: Experimentation on, or using the organs or tissues from, a human or other mammalian conceptus in the postembryonic period, after the major structures have been outlined. In humans, this corresponds to the period from the third month after fertilization until birth.

nodes.label: Genetic Research
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Genetic Research as: Research into the cause, transmission, amelioration, elimination, or enhancement of inherited disorders and traits.

nodes.label: Health Services Research
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Health Services Research as: The integration of epidemiologic, sociological, economic, and other analytic sciences in the study of health services. Health services research is usually concerned with relationships between need, demand, supply, use, and outcome of health services. The aim of the research is evaluation, particularly in terms of structure, process, output, and outcome. (From Last, Dictionary of Epidemiology, 2d ed)

nodes.label: Human Experimentation
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Human Experimentation as: The use of humans as investigational subjects.

nodes.label: Outcome Assessment, Health Care
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Outcome Assessment, Health Care as: Research aimed at assessing the quality and effectiveness of health care as measured by the attainment of a specified end result or outcome. Measures include parameters such as improved health, lowered morbidity or mortality, and improvement of abnormal states (such as elevated blood pressure).

nodes.label: Pharmaceutical Research
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Pharmaceutical Research as: RESEARCH activity focused on pharmaceutical products and services.

nodes.label: Pharmacy Research
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Pharmacy Research as: RESEARCH activity focused on PHARMACY .

nodes.label: Rehabilitation Research
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Rehabilitation Research as: Studies and research concerning the psychological, educational, social, vocational, industrial, and economic aspects of REHABILITATION .

nodes.label: Stem Cell Research
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Stem Cell Research as: Experimentation on STEM CELLS and on the use of stem cells.

nodes.label: Translational Research, Biomedical
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Translational Research, Biomedical as: The endeavour to traverse a specific step of the translation process of turning an observation in the laboratory, clinic, or community into an intervention that will improve the health of individuals and the public. (from Nat Rev Drug Discov. 2018 July ; 17(7): 455–456.)

nodes.label: Citizen Science
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Citizen Science as: Voluntary public participation in the scientific process, addressing real-world problems in ways that may include formulating research questions, conducting scientific experiments, collecting and analyzing data, interpreting results, making new discoveries, developing technologies and applications, for solving complex problems. (From https://www.citizenscience.gov/)

nodes.label: Grounded Theory
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Grounded Theory as: The generation of theories from analysis of empirical data.

nodes.label: Qualitative Research
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Qualitative Research as: Any type of research that employs nonnumeric information to explore individual or group characteristics, producing findings not arrived at by statistical procedures or other quantitative means. (Qualitative Inquiry: A Dictionary of Terms Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage Publications, 1997)

nodes.label: Mathematics
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Mathematics as: The deductive study of shape, quantity, and dependence. (From McGraw-Hill Dictionary of Scientific and Technical Terms, 6th ed)

nodes.label: Probability
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Probability as: The study of chance processes or the relative frequency characterizing a chance process.

nodes.label: Models, Statistical
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Models, Statistical as: Statistical formulations or analyses which, when applied to data and found to fit the data, are then used to verify the assumptions and parameters used in the analysis. Examples of statistical models are the linear model, binomial model, polynomial model, two-parameter model, etc.

nodes.label: Data Analysis
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Data Analysis as: Process of systematically applying statistical and/or logical techniques to describe and illustrate, condense and recap, and evaluate data (https://ori.hhs.gov/education).

nodes.label: Nonlinear Dynamics
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Nonlinear Dynamics as: The study of systems which respond disproportionately (nonlinearly) to initial conditions or perturbing stimuli. Nonlinear systems may exhibit chaos which is classically characterized as sensitive dependence on initial conditions. Chaotic systems, while distinguished from more ordered periodic systems, are not random. When their behavior over time is appropriately displayed (in phase space), constraints are evident which are described by strange attractors. Phase space representations of chaotic systems, or strange attractors, usually reveal fractal ( FRACTALS ) self-similarity across time scales. Natural, including biological, systems often display nonlinear dynamics and chaos.

nodes.label: Bayes Theorem
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Bayes Theorem as: A theorem in probability theory named for Thomas Bayes (1702-1761). In epidemiology, it is used to obtain the probability of disease in a group of people with some characteristic on the basis of the overall rate of that disease and of the likelihood of that characteristic in healthy and diseased individuals. The most familiar application is in clinical decision analysis where it is used for estimating the probability of a particular diagnosis given the appearance of some symptoms or test result.

nodes.label: Likelihood Functions
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Likelihood Functions as: Functions constructed from a statistical model and a set of observed data which give the probability of that data for various values of the unknown model parameters. Those parameter values that maximize the probability are the maximum likelihood estimates of the parameters.

nodes.label: Risk
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Risk as: The probability that an event will occur. It encompasses a variety of measures of the probability of a generally unfavorable outcome.

nodes.label: Uncertainty
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Uncertainty as: The condition in which reasonable knowledge regarding risks, benefits, or the future is not available.

nodes.label: Linear Models
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Linear Models as: Statistical models in which the value of a parameter for a given value of a factor is assumed to be equal to a + bx, where a and b are constants. The models predict a linear regression.

nodes.label: Logistic Models
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Logistic Models as: Statistical models which describe the relationship between a qualitative dependent variable (that is, one which can take only certain discrete values, such as the presence or absence of a disease) and an independent variable. A common application is in epidemiology for estimating an individual's risk (probability of a disease) as a function of a given risk factor.

nodes.label: Models, Spatial Interaction
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Models, Spatial Interaction as: Estimates of the flow of people, material or information between locations in geographic space.

nodes.label: Autoencoder
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Autoencoder as: An unsupervised learning technique where the machine learns patterns in unlabeled data sets, makes compressed representations and reconstructs the input as output at minimum loss of features from the input. Autoencoders are useful in denoising images, DIMENSIONALITY REDUCTION and feature extraction.

nodes.label: Backtracking Algorithms
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Backtracking Algorithms as: A general algorithmic technique that considers solutions one option at a time backtracking to get the desired solution. This allows searching every possible option recursively.

nodes.label: Boosting Machine Learning Algorithms
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Boosting Machine Learning Algorithms as: A form of ensemble learning methods which combines weak learners to create strong ones, which reduces training errors and bias in the training models. There are different types of boosting such as gradient boosting, XGBoost, and Adaboost.

nodes.label: Clustering Algorithms
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Clustering Algorithms as: Algorithms designed to find groups of similar data points (called clusters) in the dataset. Clustering is often used for feature engineering or pattern discovery in unsupervised machine learning.

nodes.label: Compression Algorithms
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Compression Algorithms as: A class of algorithms which both reduces and restores the size of files to increase their portability. Compression algorithms can be lossy or lossless.

nodes.label: Detection Algorithms
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Detection Algorithms as: Algorithms designed to find or localize the objects in images and assign the objects (affordances).

nodes.label: Dimensionality Reduction
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Dimensionality Reduction as: A machine learning process used to reduce the number of attributes or features of data (called dimensionality) thereby simplifying understanding of the dataset without a loss in data integrity.

nodes.label: Genetic Algorithms
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Genetic Algorithms as: Heuristic search algorithms which direct the random searches to the area of better performance or fitness function by computationally creating the conditions inspired by NATURAL SELECTION . They are commonly used to generate solutions for optimization problems.

nodes.label: Latent Class Analysis
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Latent Class Analysis as: A statistical algorithm used to analyze clusters of observed variables by constructing categorical unobserved or latent segment based on weighted analysis and the average probabilities. Such latent classes are used to infer variables whose relationships are not directly observed. In biomedical research, it is often used to categorize data that allows the determination of symptom clusters.

nodes.label: Machine Learning Algorithms
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Machine Learning Algorithms as: A class of algorithms which enables a computer to learn as it goes, thereby accomplishing its goal without being explicitly programmed to do so.

nodes.label: Parallel Algorithms
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Parallel Algorithms as: Algorithms that can execute several instructions simultaneously on different processing devices and then combine all the individual outputs to produce the final result.

nodes.label: Particle Swarm Optimization
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Particle Swarm Optimization as: A heuristic computational algorithm designed to find optimal solutions in a random search space. Particle swarm optimization measures swarm intelligence which is a computation measurement inspired by behaviors of self-organized swarming animals.

nodes.label: Prediction Algorithms
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Prediction Algorithms as: A class of algorithms which are designed to forecast unseen data. Prediction Algorithms can discover patterns, perform classification tasks, and identify trends.

nodes.label: Cellular Automata
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Cellular Automata as: Space-oriented dynamic modeling ALGORITHMS acting in an array of cells, whose temporal states evolve based on the rules (algorithms) of the automata. They are used to model complex dynamic systems for study and analysis in a variety of scientific fields.

nodes.label: Correlation of Data
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Correlation of Data as: Determination of whether or not two variables are correlated. This means to study whether an increase or decrease in one variable corresponds to an increase or decrease in the other variable.

nodes.label: Intelligent Systems
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Intelligent Systems as: Technological systems that perform automated tasks within specific environments enabled by artificial intelligence.

nodes.label: Machine Learning
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Machine Learning as: A type of ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE that enable COMPUTERS to independently initiate and execute LEARNING when exposed to new data.

nodes.label: Pattern Analysis, Machine
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Pattern Analysis, Machine as: The process of recognizing and extracting meaningful information from patterns in data. Pattern analysis in machine learning is often used for predictions and forecasting.

nodes.label: Prediction Methods, Machine
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Prediction Methods, Machine as: Methods of making prediction about a new measurement based on calculations of previous data.

nodes.label: Sentiment Analysis
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Sentiment Analysis as: A data mining technique in which subjective information such as sentiments, OPINIONS , and attitudes are extracted and analyzed from data.

nodes.label: Multifactor Dimensionality Reduction
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Multifactor Dimensionality Reduction as: A statistical tool for detecting and modeling gene-gene interactions. It is a non-parametric and model-free approach.

nodes.label: Adaptive Algorithms
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Adaptive Algorithms as: Algorithms designed to solve a problem by modifying their behaviors when faced with an unseen task with limited data during training.

nodes.label: Classification Algorithms
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Classification Algorithms as: A class of algorithms that predicts into which category an observation belongs based on training data.

nodes.label: Generative Adversarial Networks
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Generative Adversarial Networks as: An unsupervised learning network which is composed of two separate networks, a generator which produces content and a discriminator which works to identify real content from the generated content. Over time, generative adversarial networks create data that increasingly resembles the input data.

nodes.label: Adverse Outcome Pathways
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Adverse Outcome Pathways as: Models connecting initiating events at the cellular and molecular level to population-wide impacts. Computational models may be at levels relating toxicology to adverse effects.

nodes.label: Healthcare Failure Mode and Effect Analysis
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Healthcare Failure Mode and Effect Analysis as: Prospective risk assessment tool aimed at identifying potential risks and their impact in healthcare settings.

nodes.label: Genetic Risk Score
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Genetic Risk Score as: Estimate of an individual's genetic liability to a trait or disease, calculated according to their genotype profile and relevant genome-wide association study data. (from Tutorial: a guide to performing polygenic risk score analyses. Nat Protoc. 2020 Sep;15(9):2759.)

nodes.label: Heart Disease Risk Factors
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Heart Disease Risk Factors as: Aspects of personal behavior or lifestyle, environmental exposure, inherited conditions and characteristics, which are determined to be associated with HEART DISEASES .

nodes.label: Deep Learning
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Deep Learning as: Supervised or unsupervised machine learning methods that use multiple layers of data representations generated by nonlinear transformations, instead of individual task-specific ALGORITHMS , to build and train neural network models.

nodes.label: Ensemble Learning
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Ensemble Learning as: A method in machine learning where several base learners are combined to create an optimal learning model. This can be used for a variety of models including forecasting, classification, or function approximation.

nodes.label: Federated Learning
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Federated Learning as: A method of training machine learning models whereby multiple devices train their own copy of the artificial intelligence model using decentralized local data. These locally trained model results are then aggregated by a central server to update the global model without accessing local data.

nodes.label: Reinforcement Machine Learning
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Reinforcement Machine Learning as: A machine learning training method in which an agent in an uncertain environment is rewarded for optimal behaviors and punished for undesired behaviors, allowing the agent to learn from trial-and-error.

nodes.label: Representation Machine Learning
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Representation Machine Learning as: A class of machine learning approaches that allow a system to discover the representations required for feature detection or classification from raw data. The requirement for manual feature engineering is reduced by allowing a machine to learn the features and apply them to a given activity.

nodes.label: Supervised Machine Learning
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Supervised Machine Learning as: A MACHINE LEARNING paradigm used to make predictions about future instances based on a given set of labeled paired input-output training (sample) data.

nodes.label: Transfer Machine Learning
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Transfer Machine Learning as: Process of training a new learning network by beginning with previously trained for a related problem, leading to less time and energy required for training the new learning network.

nodes.label: Unsupervised Machine Learning
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Unsupervised Machine Learning as: A MACHINE LEARNING paradigm used to make predictions about future instances based on a given set of unlabeled paired input-output training (sample) data.

nodes.label: Predictive Learning Models
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Predictive Learning Models as: Machine learning models which are trained to analyze historical data to find patterns and trends, allowing it to predict future outcomes.

nodes.label: Cardiometabolic Risk Factors
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Cardiometabolic Risk Factors as: A cluster of personal behavior or lifestyle, environmental exposure, inborn or inherited conditions and characteristics, which, on the basis of epidemiological evidence, is known to be associated with CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASES and TYPE 2 DIABETES MELLITUS .

nodes.label: Obesity Paradox
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Obesity Paradox as: An observation that high BODY MASS INDEX is sometimes associated with lower CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE mortality in certain population, e.g., ELDERLY .

nodes.label: Large Language Models
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Large Language Models as: Computational designs that apply DEEP LEARNING methods on extremely large data sets as a basis for predicting and constructing natural-sounding text.

nodes.label: Support Vector Machine
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Support Vector Machine as: SUPERVISED MACHINE LEARNING algorithm which learns to assign labels to objects from a set of training examples. Examples are learning to recognize fraudulent credit card activity by examining hundreds or thousands of fraudulent and non-fraudulent credit card activity, or learning to make disease diagnosis or prognosis based on automatic classification of microarray gene expression profiles drawn from hundreds or thousands of samples.

nodes.label: Adjustable speed drives
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Adjustable speed drives as: Drives that save energy by ensuring the motor's speed is properly matched to the load placed on the motor. Terms used to describe this category include polyphase motors, motor oversizing, and motor rewinding.

nodes.label: Adjusted electricity
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Adjusted electricity as: A measurement of electricity that includes the approximate amount of energy used to generate electricity. To approximate the adjusted amount of electricity, the site-value of the electricity is multiplied by a factor of 3. This conversion factor of 3 is a rough approximation of the Btu value of raw fuels used to generate electricity in a steam-generation power plant.

nodes.label: Aftermarket converted vehicle
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Aftermarket converted vehicle as: A standard conventionally fueled, factory-produced vehicle to which equipment has been added that enables the vehicle to operate on alternative fuel.

nodes.label: Agglomerating character
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Agglomerating character as: Agglomeration describes the caking properties of coal. Agglomerating character is determined by examination and testing of the residue when a small powdered sample is heated to 950 degrees Centigrade under specific conditions. If the sample is "agglomerating," the residue will be coherent, show swelling or cell structure, and be capable of supporting a 500-gram weight without pulverizing.

nodes.label: Air cleaner
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Air cleaner as: A device using filters or electrostatic precipitators to remove indoor-air pollutants such as tobacco smoke, dust, and pollen. Most portable units are 40 watts when operated on low speed and 100 watts on high speed.

nodes.label: Air collector
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Air collector as: A medium-temperature collector used predominantly in space heating, utilizing pumped air as the heat-transfer medium.

nodes.label: Air conditioning
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Air conditioning as: Cooling and dehumidifying the air in an enclosed space by use of a refrigeration unit powered by electricity or natural gas. Note: Fans, blowers, and evaporative cooling systems ("swamp coolers") that are not connected to a refrigeration unit are excluded.

nodes.label: Air pollution abatement equipment
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Air pollution abatement equipment as: Equipment used to reduce or eliminate airborne pollutants, including particulate matter (dust, smoke, fly, ash, dirt, etc.), sulfur oxides,nitrogen oxides (NOx), carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons, odors, and other pollutants. Examples of air pollution abatement structures and equipment include flue-gas particulate collectors, flue-gas desulfurization units and nitrogen oxide control devices.

nodes.label: Alkylation
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Alkylation as: A refining process for chemically combining isobutane with olefin hydrocarbons (e.g., propylene, butylene) through the control of temperature and pressure in the presence of anacid catalyst, usually sulfuric acid or hydrofluoric acid. The product alkylate, an isoparaffin, has high octane value and is blended with motor and aviation gasoline to improve the antiknock value of the fuel.

nodes.label: Alternating current (AC)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Alternating current (AC) as: An electric current that reverses its direction at regularly recurring intervals.

nodes.label: Alternative fuel vehicle (AFV)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Alternative fuel vehicle (AFV) as: A vehicle designed to operate on an alternative fuel (for example, compressed natural gas, liquefied propane gas, or electricity). The vehicle could be either a dedicated vehicle designed to operate exclusively on alternative fuel or a nondedicated vehicle designed to operate on alternative fuel and/or a gasoline or diesel fuel.

nodes.label: Amorphous silicon
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Amorphous silicon as: An alloy of silica and hydrogen, with a disordered, noncrystalline internal atomic arrangement, that can be deposited in thin-film layers (a few micrometers in thickness) by a number of deposition methods to produce thin-film photovoltaic cells on glass, metal, or plastic substrates.

nodes.label: Ampere
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Ampere as: The unit of measurement of electrical current produced in a circuit by 1 volt acting through a resistance of 1 Ohm.

nodes.label: Apparent power
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Apparent power as: The product of the voltage (in volts) and the current (in amperes). It comprises both active and reactive power. It is measured in "volt-amperes" and often expressed in "kilovolt-amperes" (kVA) or "megavolt-amperes" (MVA). See

nodes.label: Appliance
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Appliance as: A piece of equipment, commonly powered by electricity, used to perform a particular energy-driven function. Examples of common appliances are refrigerators, clothes washers and dishwashers, conventional ranges/ovens and microwave ovens, humidifiers and dehumidifiers, toasters, radios, and televisions. Note: Appliances are ordinarily self-contained with respect to their function. Thus, equipment such as central heating and air conditioning systems and water heaters, which are connected to distribution systems inherent to their purposes, are not considered appliances.

nodes.label: Asphalt
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Asphalt as: A dark brown-to-black cement-like material obtained by petroleum processing and containing bitumens as the predominant component; used primarily for road construction. It includes crude asphalt as well as the following finished products: cements, fluxes, the asphalt content of emulsions (exclusive of water), and petroleum distillates blended with asphalt to make cutback asphalts. Note: The conversion factor for asphalt is 5.5 barrels per short ton.

nodes.label: Atmospheric crude oil distillation
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Atmospheric crude oil distillation as: The refining process of separating crude oil components at atmospheric pressure by heating to temperatures of about 600 degrees to 750 degrees Fahrenheit (depending on the nature of the crude oil and desired products) and subsequent condensing of the fractions by cooling.

nodes.label: Auger mine
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Auger mine as: A surface mine in which the coal bed is removed by means of a large diameter drill. Usually operated only when the overburden becomes too thick for economical strip mining.

nodes.label: Automatic set-back or clock thermostat
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Automatic set-back or clock thermostat as: A thermostat that can be set to turn the heating/cooling system off and on at certain predetermined times.

nodes.label: Auxiliary generator
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Auxiliary generator as: A generator at the electric plant site that provides power for the operation of the electrical generating equipment itself, including related demands such as plant lighting, during periods when the electric plant is not operating and power is unavailable from the grid. A black start generator used to start main central station generators is considered to be an auxiliary generator.

nodes.label: Azimuth angle
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Azimuth angle as: The orientation angle relative to north that a solar panel tilts toward: 0° is north, 90° is east, 180° is south, and 270° is west.

nodes.label: Backup fuel
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Backup fuel as: In a central heat pump system, the fuel used in the furnace that takes over the space heating when the outdoor temperature drops below that which is feasible to operate a heat pump.

nodes.label: Backup power
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Backup power as: Electric energy supplied by a utility to replace power and energy lost during an unscheduled equipment outage.

nodes.label: Barrel
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Barrel as: A unit of volume equal to 42 U.S. gallons.

nodes.label: Barrels per calendar day
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Barrels per calendar day as: The amount of input that a distillation facility can process under usual operating conditions. The amount is expressed in terms of capacity during a 24-hour period and reduces the maximum processing capability of all units at the facility under continuous operation (see

nodes.label: Barrels per stream day
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Barrels per stream day as: The maximum number of barrels of input that a distillation facility can process within a 24-hour period when running at full capacity under optimal crude and product slate conditions with no allowance for downtime.

nodes.label: Base load capacity
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Base load capacity as: The generating equipment normally operated to serve loads on an around-the-clock basis.

nodes.label: Baseboard heater
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Baseboard heater as: As a type of heating equipment, a system in which either electric resistance coils or finned tubes carrying steam or hot water are mounted behind shallow panels along baseboards. Baseboards rely on passive convection to distribute heated air in the space. Electric baseboards are an example of an "Individual Space Heater."

nodes.label: Battery electric vehicle (BEV)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Battery electric vehicle (BEV) as: An all-electric vehicle that receives power by plugging into an electric power source and storing the power in a battery pack. BEVs do not use any petroleum-based or other liquid- or gas-based fuel during operation and do not produce tailpipe emissions.

nodes.label: Bi-fuel vehicle
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Bi-fuel vehicle as: A motor vehicle that operates on two different fuels, but not on a mixture of the fuels. Each fuel is stored in a separate tank.

nodes.label: Bituminous coal
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Bituminous coal as: A dense coal, usually black, sometimes dark brown, often with well-defined bands of bright and dull material, used primarily as fuel in steam-electric power generation, with substantial quantities also used for heat and power applications in manufacturing and to make coke. Bituminous coal is the most abundant coal in active U.S. mining regions. Its moisture content usually is less than 20 percent. The heat content of bituminous coal ranges from 21 to 30 million Btu per ton on a moist, mineral-matter-free basis. The heat content of bituminous coal consumed in the United States averages 24 million Btu per ton, on the as-received basis (i.e., containing both inherent moisture and mineral matter).

nodes.label: Black liquor
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Black liquor as: A by product of the paper production process, alkaline spent liquor, that can be used as a source of energy. Alkaline spent liquor is removed from the digesters in the process of chemically pulping wood. After evaporation, the residual "black" liquor is burned as a fuel in a recovery furnace that permits the recovery of certain basic chemicals.

nodes.label: Blast furnace
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Blast furnace as: A furnace in which solid fuel (coke) is burned with an air blast to smelt ore.

nodes.label: Blast-furnace gas
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Blast-furnace gas as: The waste combustible gas generated in a blast furnace when iron ore is being reduced with coke to metallic iron. It is commonly used as a fuel within steel works.

nodes.label: Blending plant
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Blending plant as: A facility that has no refining capability but is either capable of producing finished motor gasoline through mechanical blending or blends oxygenates with motor gasoline.

nodes.label: Boiler
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Boiler as: A device for generating steam for power, processing, or heating purposes; or hot water for heating purposes or hot water supply. Heat from an external combustion source is transmitted to a fluid contained within the tubes found in the boiler shell. This fluid is delivered to an end-use at a desired pressure, temperature, and quality.

nodes.label: Boiler fuel
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Boiler fuel as: An energy source to produce heat that is transferred to the boiler vessel in order to generate steam orhot water. Fossil fuel is the primary energy source used to produce heat for boilers.

nodes.label: Boiling-water reactor (BWR)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Boiling-water reactor (BWR) as: A light-water reactor in which water, used as both coolant and moderator, is allowed to boil in the core. The resulting steam can be used directly to drive a turbine.

nodes.label: Bottled gas, LPG, or propane
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Bottled gas, LPG, or propane as: Any fuel gas supplied to a building in liquid form, such as liquefied petroleum gas, propane, or butane. It is usually delivered by tank truck and stored near the building in a tank or cylinder until used.

nodes.label: Bottom ash
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Bottom ash as: Residue mainly from the coal burning process that falls to the bottom of the boiler for removal and disposal.

nodes.label: Bottoming cycle
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Bottoming cycle as: A waste-heat recovery boiler recaptures the unused energy and uses it to produce steam to drive a steam turbine generator to produce electricity.

nodes.label: Breeder reactor
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Breeder reactor as: A reactor that both produces and consumes fissionable fuel, especially one that creates more fuel than it consumes. The new fissionable material is created by a process known as breeding, in which neutrons from fission are captured in fertile materials.

nodes.label: British thermal unit
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines British thermal unit as: The quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 pound of liquid water by 1 degree Fahrenheit at the temperature at which water has its greatest density (approximately 39 degrees Fahrenheit).

nodes.label: Btu conversion factor
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Btu conversion factor as: A factor for converting energy data between one unit of measurement and British thermal units (Btu). Btu conversion factors are generally used to convert energy data from physical units of measure (such as barrels, cubic feet, or short tons) into the energy-equivalent measure of Btu. (See

nodes.label: Built-in electric units
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Built-in electric units as: An individual-resistance electric-heating unit that is permanently installed in the floors, walls, ceilings, or baseboards and is part of the electrical installation of the building. Electric-heating devices that are plugged into an electric socket or outlet are not considered built in. (Also see

nodes.label: Bulk station
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Bulk station as: A facility used primarily for the storage and/or marketing of petroleum products, which has a total bulk storage capacity of less than 50,000 barrels and receives its petroleum products by tank car or truck.

nodes.label: Bulk terminal
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Bulk terminal as: A facility used primarily for the storage and/or marketing of petroleum products, which has a total bulk storage capacity of 50,000 barrels or more and/or receives petroleum products by tanker, barge, or pipeline.

nodes.label: Bundled utility service (electric)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Bundled utility service (electric) as: A means of operation whereby energy, transmission, and distribution services, as well as ancillary and retail services, are provided by one entity.

nodes.label: Burnup
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Burnup as: Amount of thermal energy generated per unit mass of fuel, expressed as Gigawatt-Days Thermal per Metric Ton of Initial Heavy Metal (GWDT/MTIHM), rounded to the nearest gigawatt day.

nodes.label: Bus
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Bus as: An electrical conductor that serves as a common connection for two or more electrical circuits.

nodes.label: Calcination
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Calcination as: A process in which a material is heated to a high temperature without fusing, so that hydrates, carbonates, or other compounds are decomposed and the volatile material is expelled.

nodes.label: Calcium sulfite
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Calcium sulfite as: A white powder, soluble in diluted sulfuric acid. Used in the sulfite process for the manufacture of wood pulp.

nodes.label: Canadian deuterium uranium reactor (CANDU)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Canadian deuterium uranium reactor (CANDU) as: Uses heavy water or deuterium oxide (D

nodes.label: Capacity (purchased)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Capacity (purchased) as: The amount of energy and capacity available for purchase from outside the system.

nodes.label: Carbon intensity
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Carbon intensity as: The amount of carbon by weight emitted per unit of energy consumed. A common measure of carbon intensity is weight of carbon per British thermal unit (Btu) of energy. When there is only one fossil fuel under consideration, the carbon intensity and the emissions coefficient are identical. When there are several fuels, carbon intensity is based on their combined emissions coefficients weighted by their energy consumption levels. Also see

nodes.label: Carburetor
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Carburetor as: A fuel delivery device for producing a proper mixture of gasoline vapor and air and for delivering it to the intake manifold of an internal combustion engine. Gasoline is gravity-fed from a reservoir bowl into a throttle bore, where it is allowed to evaporate into the stream of air being inducted by the engine. Also see

nodes.label: Casinghead gas (or oil well gas)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Casinghead gas (or oil well gas) as: Natural gas produced along with crude oil from oil wells. It contains either dissolved or associated gas or both.

nodes.label: Cast silicon
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Cast silicon as: Crystalline silicon obtained by pouring pure molten silicon into a vertical mold and adjusting the temperature gradient along the mold volume during cooling to obtain slow, vertically advancing crystallization of the silicon. The polycrystalline ingot thus formed is composed of large, relatively parallel, interlocking crystals. The cast ingots are sawed into wafers for further fabrication into photovoltaic cells. Cast silicon wafers and ribbon silicon sheets fabricated into cells are usually referred to aspolycrystalline photovoltaic cells.

nodes.label: Catalytic converter
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Catalytic converter as: A device containing a catalyst for converting automobile exhaust into mostly harmless products.

nodes.label: Catalytic cracking
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Catalytic cracking as: The refining process of breaking down the larger, heavier, and more complex hydrocarbon molecules into simpler and lighter molecules. Catalytic cracking is accomplished by the use of a catalytic agent and is an effective process for increasing the yield of gasoline from crude oil. Catalytic cracking processes fresh feeds and recycled feeds.

nodes.label: Catalytic hydrotreating
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Catalytic hydrotreating as: A refining process for treating petroleum fractions from atmospheric or vacuum distillation units (e.g., naphthas, middle distillates, reformer feeds, residual fuel oil, and heavy gas oil) and other petroleum (e.g., cat cracked naphtha,coker naphtha, gas oil, etc.) in the presence of catalysts and substantial quantities of hydrogen. Hydrotreating includes desulfurization, removal of substances (e.g., nitrogen compounds) that deactivate catalysts, conversion of olefins to paraffins to reduce gum formation in gasoline, and other processes to upgrade the quality of the fractions.

nodes.label: Cells to OEM (non-PV)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Cells to OEM (non-PV) as: Cells shipped to non-photovoltaic original equipment manufacturers such as boat manufacturers, car manufacturers, etc.

nodes.label: Central chiller
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Central chiller as: Any centrally located air conditioning system that produces chilled water in order to cool air. The chilled water or cold air is then distributed throughout the building, using pipes or air ducts or both. These systems are also commonly known as "chillers," "centrifugal chillers," "reciprocating chillers," or "absorption chillers." Chillers are generally located in or just outside the building they serve. Buildings receiving district chilled water are served by chillers located at central physical plants.

nodes.label: Central cooling
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Central cooling as: Cooling of an entire building with a refrigeration unit to condition the air. Typically central chillers and duct work are present in the centrally cooled building.

nodes.label: Central physical plant
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Central physical plant as: A plant owned by, and on the grounds of, a multibuilding facility that provides district heating, district cooling, or electricity to other buildings on the same facility. To qualify as a central plant it must provide district heat, district chilled water, or electricity to at least one other building. The central physical plant may be by itself in a separate building or may be located in a building where other activities occur.

nodes.label: Central warm air furnace
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Central warm air furnace as: A type of space heating equipment where a central combustor or resistance unit generally using gas, fuel oil, or electricity provides warm air through ducts leading to the various rooms. Heat pumps are not included in this category. A forced air furnace is one in which a fan is used to force the air through the ducts. In a gravity furnace, air is circulated by gravity, relying on the natural flow of warm air up and cold air down; the warm air rises through ducts and the cold air falls through ducts that return it to the furnace to be reheated and this completes the circulation cycle.

nodes.label: Centralized water heating system
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Centralized water heating system as: Equipment, to heat and store water for other than space heating purposes, which provides hot water from a single location for distribution throughout a building. A residential type tank water heater is a good example of a centralized water heater.

nodes.label: Chemical separation
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Chemical separation as: A process for extracting uranium and plutonium from dissolved spent nuclear fuel and irradiated targets. The fission products that are left behind are high-level waste. Chemical separation is also known as reprocessing.

nodes.label: Christmas tree
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Christmas tree as: The valves and fittings installed at the top of a gas or oil well to control and direct the flow of well fluids.

nodes.label: Circuit-mile
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Circuit-mile as: The total length in miles of separate circuits regardless of the number of conductors used per circuit.

nodes.label: Clinker
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Clinker as: Powdered cement, produced by heating a properly proportioned mixture of finely ground raw materials (calciumcarbonate, silica, alumina, and iron oxide) in a kiln to a temperature of about 2,700 degrees Fahrenheit.

nodes.label: Coal
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Coal as: A readily combustible black or brownish-black rock whose composition, including inherent moisture, consists of more than 50 percent by weight and more than 70 percent by volume of carbonaceous material. It is formed from plant remains that have been compacted, hardened, chemically altered, and metamorphosed by heat and pressure over geologic time.

nodes.label: Coal Blending
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Coal Blending as: The process of combining two or more coals with different characteristics to obtain coal with a certain quality, such as low sulfur content.

nodes.label: Coal briquets
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Coal briquets as: Anthracite, bituminous, and lignite briquets comprise the secondary solid fuels manufactured from coal by a process in which the coal is partly dried, warmed to expel excess moisture, and then compressed into briquets, usually without the use of a binding substance. In the reduction of briquets to coal equivalent, different conversion factors are applied according to their origin from hard coal, peat, brown coal, or lignite.

nodes.label: Coal gasification
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Coal gasification as: The process of converting coal into gas. The basic process involves crushing coal to a powder, which is then heated in the presence of steam and oxygen to produce a gas. The gas is then refined to reduce sulfur and other impurities. The gas can be used as a fuel or processed further and concentrated into chemical or liquid fuel.

nodes.label: Coal liquefaction
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Coal liquefaction as: A chemical process that converts coal into clean-burning liquid hydrocarbons, such as synthetic crude oil and methanol.

nodes.label: Coal mine
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Coal mine as: An industrial operation for extracting coal from the ground. Mines include earth-moving and excavating operations and usually incorporate activities related to the processing (cleaning and crushing or sizing) and transporting of coal (such as loading the coal into a rail car) to the end user.

nodes.label: Coal synfuel
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Coal synfuel as: Coal-based solid fuel that has been processed by a coal synfuel plant; and coal-based fuels such as briquettes, pellets, or extrusions, which are formed from fresh or recycled coal and binding materials.

nodes.label: Coalbed Methane Well Gas
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Coalbed Methane Well Gas as: Methane produced from coal seams. Coalbed methane is formed during coalification, which is the geologic process that transforms organic material into coal.

nodes.label: Cofiring
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Cofiring as: The process of burning natural gas in conjunction with another fuel to reduce air pollutants.

nodes.label: Cogeneration system
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Cogeneration system as: A system using a common energy source to produce both electricity and steam for other uses, resulting in increased fuel efficiency.

nodes.label: Coke (coal)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Coke (coal) as: A solid carbonaceous residue derived from low-ash, low-sulfur bituminous coal from which the volatile constituents are driven off by baking in an oven at temperatures as high as 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit so that the fixed carbon and residual ash are fused together. Coke is used as a fuel and as a reducing agent in smelting iron ore in a blast furnace. Coke from coal is grey, hard, and porous and has a heating value of 24.8 million Btu per ton.

nodes.label: Coke Battery
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Coke Battery as: A series of coke ovens stacked in rows into which coal is loaded and processed into coke.

nodes.label: Coke Oven
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Coke Oven as: A chamber of brick or other heat-resistant material in which coal is heated to separate the coal gas, coal water, and tar. The coal gas and coal water fuse together with carbon and the remaining ash, forming a hard residue commonly referred to as coke. Coke is primarily used in steel production. There are two types of coke ovens: (1) beehive ovens, which were originally built round with a spherical top like an old-fashioned beehive, and have an opening in the top and various small openings for draft at the base. The ovens were developed into banks (rows) of joining cubicles. During the heating process of the coal, tar, gas, and other byproducts are lost. (2) Byproduct ovens, which were built in rectangular form with the front and back removable, and which are arranged so that all volatile byproducts can be pumped out.

nodes.label: Combined cycle
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Combined cycle as: An electric generating technology in which electricity is produced from otherwise lost waste heat exiting from one or more gas (combustion) turbines. The exiting heat is routed to a conventional boiler or to a heat recovery steam generator for utilization by a steam turbine in the production of electricity. This process increases the efficiency of the electric generating unit.

nodes.label: Combined cycle unit
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Combined cycle unit as: An electric generating unit that consists of one or more combustion turbines and one or more boilers with a portion of the required energy input to the boiler(s) provided by the exhaust gas of the combustion turbine(s).

nodes.label: Combined hydroelectric plant
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Combined hydroelectric plant as: A hydroelectric plant that uses both pumped water and natural streamflow for the production of power.

nodes.label: Combined pumped-storage plant
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Combined pumped-storage plant as: A pumped-storage hydroelectric power plant that uses both pumped water and natural stream flow to produce electricity.

nodes.label: Combined-heat-and-power (CHP) plant
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Combined-heat-and-power (CHP) plant as: A plant designed to produce both heat and electricity from a single heat source. Note: This term is being used in place of the term "cogenerator" that was used by EIA in the past.
