CHP better describes the facilities because some of the plants included do not produce heat and power in a sequential fashion and, as a result, do not meet the legal definition of cogeneration specified in the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act (PURPA).

nodes.label: Combustion chamber
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Combustion chamber as: An enclosed vessel in which chemical oxidation of fuel occurs.

nodes.label: Commercial facility
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Commercial facility as: An economic unit that is owned or operated by one person or organization and that occupies two or more commercial buildings at a single location. A university and a large hospital complex are examples of a commercial multi-building facility.

nodes.label: Commercial operation (nuclear)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Commercial operation (nuclear) as: The phase of reactor operation that begins when power ascension ends and the operating utility formally declares the nuclear power plant to be available for the regular production of electricity. This declaration is usually related to the satisfactory completion of qualification tests on critical components of the unit.

nodes.label: Completion (oil/gas production)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Completion (oil/gas production) as: The term refers to the installation of permanent equipment for the production of oil or gas. If a well is equipped to produce only oil or gas from one zone or reservoir, the definition of a "well" (classified as an oil well or gas well) and the definition of a "completion" are identical. However, if a well is equipped to produce oil and/or gas separately from more than one reservoir, a "well" is not synonymous with a "completion." (See

nodes.label: Compressor station
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Compressor station as: Any combination of facilities that supply the energy to move gas in transmission or distribution lines or into storage by increasing the pressure.

nodes.label: Concentrating solar power or solar thermal power system
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Concentrating solar power or solar thermal power system as: A solar energy conversion system characterized by the optical concentration of solar rays through an arrangement of mirrors to generate a high temperature working fluid. Also see

nodes.label: Concentrator
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Concentrator as: A reflective or refractive device that focuses incident insolation onto an area smaller than the reflective or refractive surface, resulting in increased insolation at the point of focus.

nodes.label: Condenser cooling water
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Condenser cooling water as: A source of water external to a boiler's feed system is passed through the steam leaving the turbine in order to cool and condense the steam. This reduces the steam's exit pressure and recaptures its heat, which is then used to preheat fluid entering the boiler, thereby increasing the plant's thermodynamic efficiency.

nodes.label: Conductor
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Conductor as: Metal wires, cables, and bus-bar used for carrying electric current. Conductors may be solid or stranded, that is,built up by a assembly of smaller solid conductors.

nodes.label: Construction pipeline (of a nuclear reactor)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Construction pipeline (of a nuclear reactor) as: The various stages involved in the acquisition of a nuclear reactor by a utility. The events that define these stages are the ordering of a reactor, the licensing process, and the physical construction of the nuclear generating unit. A reactor is said to be "in the pipeline" when the reactor is ordered and "out of the pipeline" when it completes low power testing and begins operation toward full power.

nodes.label: Construction work in progress (CWIP)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Construction work in progress (CWIP) as: The balance shown on a utility's balance sheet for construction work not yet completed butin process. This balance line item may or may not be included in the rate base.

nodes.label: Continuous mining
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Continuous mining as: A form of room pillar mining in which a continuous mining machine extracts and removes coal from the working face in one operation; no blasting is required.

nodes.label: Conventional blendstock for oxygenate blending (CBOB)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Conventional blendstock for oxygenate blending (CBOB) as: Motor gasoline blending components intended for blending with oxygenates to produce finished conventional motor gasoline.

nodes.label: Conventional fuel ethanol
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Conventional fuel ethanol as: Fuel ethanol produced by fermenting cornstarch. Fuel ethanol is typically blended with motor gasoline as an oxygenate or

nodes.label: Conventional gasoline
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Conventional gasoline as: Finished motor gasoline not included in the oxygenated or reformulated gasoline categories. Note: This category excludes reformulated gasoline blendstock for oxygenate blending (RBOB) as well as other blendstock.

nodes.label: Conventional hydroelectric plant
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Conventional hydroelectric plant as: A plant in which all of the power is produced from natural streamflow as regulated by available storage.

nodes.label: Conventional mill (uranium)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Conventional mill (uranium) as: A facility engineered and built principally for processing of uraniferous ore materials mined from the earth and the recovery, by chemical treatment in the mill's circuits, of uranium and/or other valued coproduct components from the processed one.

nodes.label: Conventional oil and natural gas production
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Conventional oil and natural gas production as: Crude oil and natural gas that is produced by a well drilled into a geologic formation in which the reservoir and fluid characteristics permit the oil and natural gas to readily flow to the wellbore.

nodes.label: Conversion factor
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Conversion factor as: A factor for converting data between one unit of measurement and another (such as between short tons and British thermal units, or between barrels and gallons). (See

nodes.label: Converted (alternative-fuel) vehicle
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Converted (alternative-fuel) vehicle as: A vehicle originally designed to operate on gasoline/diesel that was modified or altered to run on an alternative fuel after its initial delivery to an end-user.

nodes.label: Cooling system
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Cooling system as: An equipment system that provides water to the condensers and includes water intakes and outlets; cooling towers; and ponds, pumps, and pipes.

nodes.label: Crude oil input
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Crude oil input as: The total crude oil put into processing units at refineries.

nodes.label: Crude oil qualities
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Crude oil qualities as: Refers to two properties of crude oil, the sulfur content, and API gravity, which affect processing complexity and product characteristics.

nodes.label: Crude oil refinery input
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Crude oil refinery input as: The total crude oil put into processing units at refineries.

nodes.label: Current (electric)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Current (electric) as: A flow of electrons in an electrical conductor. The strength or rate of movement of the electricity is measured in amperes.

nodes.label: Cycle/reactor history
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Cycle/reactor history as: A group of assemblies that have been irradiated in the same cycles in an individual reactor and are said to have the same cycle/reactor history.

nodes.label: Daylighting controls
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Daylighting controls as: A system of sensors that assesses the amount of daylight and controls lighting or shading devices to maintain a specified lighting level. The sensors are sometimes referred to as "photocells."

nodes.label: Decontamination
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Decontamination as: Removal of unwanted radioactive or hazardous contamination by a chemical or mechanical process.

nodes.label: Dedicated vehicle
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Dedicated vehicle as: A vehicle that operates only on an alternative fuel, as when a vehicle is configured to operate on compressed natural gas. Note: A vehicle powered by an electric motor is not to be treated as dedicated.

nodes.label: Deepest total depth
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Deepest total depth as: The deepest total depth of a given well is the distance from a surface reference point (usually the Kelly bushing) to the point of deepest penetration measured along the well bore. If a well is drilled from a platform or barge over water, the depth of the water is included in the total length of the well bore.

nodes.label: Degasification system
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Degasification system as: The methods employed for removing methane from a coal seam that could not otherwise be removed by standard ventilation fans and thus would pose a substantial hazard to coal miners. These systems may be used prior to mining or during mining activities.

nodes.label: Delayed coking
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Delayed coking as: A process by which heavier crude oil fractions can be thermally decomposed under conditions of elevated temperatures and pressure to produce a mixture of lighter oils and petroleum coke. The light oils can be processed further in other refinery units to meet product specifications. The coke can be used either as a fuel or in other applications such as the manufacturing of steel or aluminum.

nodes.label: Deliveries (electric)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Deliveries (electric) as: Energy generated by one system and delivered to another system through one or more transmission lines.

nodes.label: Denaturant
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Denaturant as: Petroleum, typically pentanes plus or conventional motor gasoline, added to fuel ethanol to make it unfit for human consumption. Fuel ethanol is denatured, usually prior to transport from the ethanol production facility, by adding 2 to 5 volume percent denaturant. See

nodes.label: Denatured
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Denatured as: Fuel ethanol that is rendered unfit for human consumption by the addition of a petroleum denaturant, typically pentanes plus or conventional motor gasoline. Fuel ethanol is usually denatured prior to transport from the ethanol production facility, by adding 2- to 5-volume-percent

nodes.label: Dependable capacity
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Dependable capacity as: The load-carrying ability of a station or system under adverse conditions for a specified period of time.

nodes.label: Depleted storage field
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Depleted storage field as: A sub-surface natural geological reservoir, usually a depleted gas or oil field, used for storing natural gas.

nodes.label: Depth of deepest production
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Depth of deepest production as: The depth of the deepest production is the length of the well bore measured (in feet) from the surface reference point to the bottom of the open hole or the deepest perforation in the casing of a producing well.

nodes.label: Design electrical rating (capacity) net
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Design electrical rating (capacity) net as: The nominal net electrical output of a nuclear unit, as specified by the utility for the purpose of plant design.

nodes.label: Design head
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Design head as: The achieved river, pondage, or reservoir surface height (forebay elevation) that provides the water level to produce the full flow at the gate of the turbine in order to attain the manufacturer's installed nameplate rating for generation capacity.

nodes.label: Development well
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Development well as: A well drilled within the proved area of an oil or gas reservoir to the depth of a stratigraphic horizon known to be productive. Also see Well.

nodes.label: Diesel fuel
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Diesel fuel as: A fuel composed of distillates obtained in petroleum refining operation or blends of such distillates with residual oil used in motor vehicles. The boiling point and specific gravity are higher for diesel fuels than for gasoline.

nodes.label: Diesel fuel system
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Diesel fuel system as: Diesel engines are internal combustion engines that burn diesel oil rather than gasoline. Injectors are used to spray droplets of diesel oil into the combustion chambers, at or near the top of the compression stroke. Ignition follows due to the very high temperature of the compressed intake air, or to the use of "glow plugs," which retain heat from previous ignitions (spark plugs are not used). Diesel engines are generally more fuel-efficient than gasoline engines but must be stronger and heavier because of high compression ratios.

nodes.label: Diesel-electric plant
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Diesel-electric plant as: A generating station that uses diesel engines to drive its electric generators.

nodes.label: Diffusive transport
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Diffusive transport as: The process by which particles of liquids or gases move from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.

nodes.label: Direct electricity load control
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Direct electricity load control as: The utility installs a radio-controlled device on the HVAC equipment. During periods of particularly heavy use of electricity, the utility will send a radio signal to the building in its service territory with this device and turn off the HVAC for a certain period.

nodes.label: Direct load control
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Direct load control as: This Demand-Side Management category represents the consumer load that can be interrupted at the time of annual peak load by direct control of the utility system operator. Direct Load Control does not include Interruptible Load. This type of control usually involves residential consumers.

nodes.label: Directional (deviated) well
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Directional (deviated) well as: A well purposely deviated from the vertical, using controlled angles to reach an objective location other than directly below the surface location.

nodes.label: Discharged fuel
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Discharged fuel as: Irradiated fuel removed from a nuclear reactor during refueling. Also see

nodes.label: Distillate fuel oil
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Distillate fuel oil as: A general classification for one of the petroleum fractions produced in conventional distillation operations. It includes diesel fuels and fuel oils. Products known as No. 1, No. 2, and No. 4 diesel fuel are used in on-highway diesel engines, such as those in trucks and automobiles, as well as off-highway engines, such as those in railroad locomotives and agricultural machinery. Products known as No. 1, No. 2, and No. 4 fuel oils are used primarily for space heating and electric power generation.

nodes.label: Distillation unit (atmospheric)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Distillation unit (atmospheric) as: The primary distillation unit that processes crude oil (including mixtures of other hydrocarbons) at approximately atmospheric conditions. It includes a pipe still for vaporizing the crude oil and a fractionation tower for separating the vaporized hydrocarbon components in the crude oil into fractions with different boiling ranges. This is done by continuously vaporizing and condensing the components to separate higher oiling point material. The selected boiling ranges are set by the processing scheme, the properties of the crude oil, and the product specifications.

nodes.label: Distributed generator
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Distributed generator as: A generator that is located close to the particular load that it is intended to serve. General, but non-exclusive, characteristics of these generators include: an operating strategy that supports the served load; and interconnection to a distribution or sub-transmission system (138 kV or less).

nodes.label: Distributed/point-of-use water-heating system
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Distributed/point-of-use water-heating system as: A system for heating hot water, for other than space heating purposes, which is located at more than one space within a building. A point-of-use water heater is located at the faucet and heats water only as required for immediate use. Because water is not heated until it is required, this equipment is more energy-efficient.

nodes.label: Distribution system
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Distribution system as: The portion of the transmission and facilities of an electric system that is dedicated to delivering electric energy to an end-user.

nodes.label: District chilled water
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines District chilled water as: Chilled water from an outside source used as an energy source for cooling in a building. The water is chilled in a central plant and piped into the building. Chilled water may be purchased from a utility or provided by a central physical plant in a separate building that is part of the same multibuilding facility (for example, a hospital complex or university).

nodes.label: District energy
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines District energy as: Energy produced in a centralized plant, other than in an electric power plant, that is consumed or stored as steam, hot water, or chilled water. This energy is distributed through a network of pipes to meet demand for process steam, heat, or cooling within a commercial or residential building, multibuilding facility, group of buildings, or an industrial facility.

nodes.label: District heat
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines District heat as: Steam or hot water from an outside source used as an energy source in a building. The steam or hot water is produced in a central plant and piped into the building. The district heat may be purchased from a utility or provided by a physical plant in a separate building that is part of the same facility (for example, a hospital complex or university).

nodes.label: Double circuit line
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Double circuit line as: A transmission line having two separate circuits. Because each carries three-phase power, at least six conductors, three per circuit, are required.

nodes.label: Dry bottom boiler
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Dry bottom boiler as: No slag tanks at furnace throat area. The throat area is clear. Bottom ash drops through the throat to the bottom ash water hoppers. This design is used where the ash melting temperature is greater than the temperature on the furnace wall, allowing for relatively dry furnace wall conditions.

nodes.label: Dry hole
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Dry hole as: An exploratory or development well found to be incapable of producing either oil or gas in sufficient quantities to justify completion as an oil or gas well. Also see

nodes.label: Dual fuel vehicle (1)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Dual fuel vehicle (1) as: A motor vehicle that is capable of operating on an alternative fuel and on gasoline or diesel fuel. These vehicles have at least two separate fuel systems which inject each fuel simultaneously into the engine combustion chamber.

nodes.label: Dual fuel vehicle (2)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Dual fuel vehicle (2) as: A motor vehicle that is capable of operating on an alternative fuel and on gasoline or diesel fuel. This term is meant to represent all such vehicles whether they operate on the alternative fuel and gasoline/diesel simultaneously (e.g., flexible-fuel vehicles) or can be switched to operate on gasoline/diesel or an alternative fuel (e.g., bi-fuel vehicles).

nodes.label: Dual-fired unit
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Dual-fired unit as: A generating unit that can produce electricity using two or more input fuels. In some of these units, only the primary fuel can be used continuously; the alternate fuel(s) can be used only as a start-up fuel or in emergencies.

nodes.label: Dump energy
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Dump energy as: Energy generated in a hydroelectric plant by water that cannot be stored or conserved and which energy is in excess of the needs of the system producing the energy.

nodes.label: Electric energy
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Electric energy as: The ability of an electric current to produce work, heat, light, or other forms of energy. It is measured in kilowatthours.

nodes.label: Electric plant (physical)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Electric plant (physical) as: A facility containing prime movers, electric generators, and auxiliary equipment for converting mechanical, chemical, and/or fission energy into electric energy.

nodes.label: Electric power plant
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Electric power plant as: A station containing prime movers, electric generators, and auxiliary equipment for converting mechanical, chemical, and/or fission energy into electric energy.

nodes.label: Electric pump for well water
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Electric pump for well water as: This pump forces the water from a well below ground level up into the water pipes that circulate through the house. When this pump is not working, there is a limited supply of running water in the house.

nodes.label: Electric system loss
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Electric system loss as: Total energy loss from all causes for an electric utility.

nodes.label: Electric system reliability
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Electric system reliability as: The degree to which the performance of the elements of the electrical system results in power being delivered to consumers within accepted standards and in the amount desired. Reliability encompasses two concepts, adequacy and security. Adequacy implies that there are sufficient generation and transmission resources installed and available to meet projected electrical demand plus reserves for contingencies. Security implies that the system will remain intact operationally (i.e., will have sufficient available operating capacity) even after outages or other equipment failure. The degree of reliability may be measured by the frequency, duration, and magnitude of adverse effects on consumer service.

nodes.label: Electric vehicle (EV)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Electric vehicle (EV) as: A general term for any on-road licensed vehicle that can plug into an electric power source and uses electric power to move. EVs plug into a source of electricity and store power in a battery pack for all or part of their power needs. Includes Battery Electric Vehicles (BEVs) and Plug-in Hybrid Vehicles (PHEVs). Can also be referred to as Plug-in Electric Vehicles (PEV).

nodes.label: Electric zone
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Electric zone as: A portion of the grid controlled by the independent system operator.

nodes.label: Electrical system energy losses
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Electrical system energy losses as: The amount of energy lost during generation, transmission, and distribution of electricity, including plant and unaccounted for use.

nodes.label: Electricity generation
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Electricity generation as: The process of producing electric energy or the amount of electric energy produced by transforming other forms of energy, commonly expressed in kilowatthours(kWh) or megawatthours (MWh).

nodes.label: Electricity-only plant
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Electricity-only plant as: A plant designed to produce electricity only. See also Combined heat and power (CHP) plant.

nodes.label: Elution
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Elution as: The process of using a solvent (eluent) to remove select ions (e.g., uranium) from an adsorbent such as ion-exchange resins.

nodes.label: Emissions coefficient
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Emissions coefficient as: A unique value for scaling emissions to activity data in terms of a standard rate of emissions per unit of activity (e.g., pounds of carbon dioxide emitted per Btu of fossil fuel consumed).

nodes.label: Energy consumption
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Energy consumption as: The use of energy as a source of heat or power or as a raw material input to a manufacturing process.

nodes.label: Energy deliveries
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Energy deliveries as: Energy generated by one electric utility system and delivered to another system through one or more transmission lines.

nodes.label: Energy management and control system(EMCS)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Energy management and control system(EMCS) as: An energy conservation feature that uses mini/microcomputers, instrumentation, control equipment, and software to manage a building's use of energy for heating, ventilation, air conditioning, lighting, and/or business-related processes. These systems can also manage fire control, safety, and security. Not included as EMCS are time-clock thermostats.

nodes.label: Engine size
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Engine size as: The total volume within all cylinders of an engine when pistons are at their lowest positions. The engine is usually measured in "liters" or "cubic inches of displacement (CID)." Generally, larger engines result in greater engine power, but less fuel efficiency. There are 61.024 cubic inches in a liter.

nodes.label: Enrichment tails assay
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Enrichment tails assay as: A measure of the amount of fissile uranium (U-235) remaining in the waste stream from the uranium enrichment process. The natural uranium "feed" that enters the enrichment process generally contains 0.711 percent (by weight) U-235. The "product stream" contains enriched uranium (more than 0.711 percentU-235) and the "waste" or "tails" stream contains depleted uranium (less than 0.711 percent U-235). At the historical enrichment tails assay of 0.2 percent, the waste stream would contain 0.2 percent U-235. A higher enrichment tails assay requires more uranium feed (thus permitting natural uranium stockpiles to be decreased), while increasing the output of enriched material for the same energy expenditure.

nodes.label: Environmental restoration
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Environmental restoration as: Although usually described as "cleanup," this function encompasses a wide range of activities, such as stabilizing contaminated soil; treating groundwater; decommissioning process buildings, nuclear reactors, chemical separations plants, and many other facilities; and exhuming sludge and buried drums of waste.

nodes.label: EPA certification
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines EPA certification as: A permanent label on fireplace inserts and freestanding wood stoves manufactured after July1, 1988, indicating that the equipment meets EPA standards for clean burning.

nodes.label: Equilibrium cycle
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Equilibrium cycle as: An analytical term that refers to fuel cycles that occur after the initial one or two cycles of a reactor's operation. For a given type of reactor, equilibrium cycles have similar fuel characteristics.

nodes.label: Evacuated-tube collector
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Evacuated-tube collector as: A collector in which solar thermal heat is captured by use of a collector fluid that flows through an absorber tube contained inside an evacuated glass tube.

nodes.label: Evaporative cooler (swamp cooler)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Evaporative cooler (swamp cooler) as: An air-cooling unit that turns air into moist, cool air by saturating the air with water vapor. It does not cool air by use of a refrigeration unit.

nodes.label: Exploratory well
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Exploratory well as: A hole drilled a) to find and produce oil or gas in an area previously considered unproductive area; b) to find a new reservoir in a known field, i.e., one previously producing oil and gas from another reservoir, or c) to extend the limit of a known oil or gas reservoir.

nodes.label: Extraction loss
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Extraction loss as: The extraction of gas plant liquids constituents such as

nodes.label: Fast breeder reactor (FBR)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Fast breeder reactor (FBR) as: A reactor in which the fission chain reaction is sustained primarily by fast neutrons rather than by thermal or intermediate neutrons. Fast reactors require little or no moderator to slow down the neutrons from the speeds at which they are ejected from fissioning nuclei. This type of reactor produces more fissile material than it consumes.

nodes.label: Fission
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Fission as: The process whereby an atomic nucleus of appropriate type, after capturing a neutron, splits into (generally) two nuclei of lighter elements, with the release of substantial amounts of energy and two or more neutrons.

nodes.label: Fixed carbon
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Fixed carbon as: The nonvolatile matter in coal minus the ash. Fixed carbon is the solid residue other than ash obtained by prescribed methods of destructive distillation of a coal. Fixed carbon is the part of the total carbon that remains when coal is heated in a closed vessel until all matter is driven off.

nodes.label: Flat plate pumped
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Flat plate pumped as: A medium-temperature solar thermal collector that typically consists of a metal frame, glazing, absorbers (usually metal), and insulation and that uses a pumped liquid as the heat-transfer medium predominant use is in water-heating applications.

nodes.label: Floating Storage Regasification Unit (FSRU)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Floating Storage Regasification Unit (FSRU) as: A floating vessel that can transport, store, and regasify liquefied natural gas (LNG) onboard, usually for the purpose of delivering natural gas to destinations that do not have a regasification terminal onshore.

nodes.label: Floor, wall, or pipeless furnace
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Floor, wall, or pipeless furnace as: Space-heating equipment consisting of a ductless combustor or resistance unit, having an enclosed chamber where fuel is burned or where electrical-resistance heat is generated to warm the rooms of a building. A floor furnace is located below the floor and delivers heated air to the room immediately above or (if under a partition) to the room on each side. A wall furnace is installed in a partition or in an outside wall and delivers heated air to the rooms on one or both sides of the wall. A pipeless furnace is installed in a basement and delivers heated air through a large register in the floor of the room or hallway immediately above.

nodes.label: Flue gas desulfurization
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Flue gas desulfurization as: Equipment used to remove sulfur oxides from the combustion gases of a boiler plant before discharge to the atmosphere. Also referred to as scrubbers. Chemicals such as lime are used as scrubbing media.

nodes.label: Flue-gas desulfurization unit (scrubber)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Flue-gas desulfurization unit (scrubber) as: Equipment used to remove sulfur oxides from the combustion gases of a boiler plant before discharge to the atmosphere. Chemicals such as lime are used as the scrubbing media.

nodes.label: Flue-gas particulate collector
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Flue-gas particulate collector as: Equipment used to remove fly ash from the combustion gases of a boiler plant before discharge to the atmosphere. Particulate collectors include electrostatic precipitators, mechanical collectors (cyclones), fabric filters (baghouses), and wet scrubbers.

nodes.label: Fluid catalytic cracking
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Fluid catalytic cracking as: The refining process of breaking down the larger, heavier, and more complex hydrocarbon molecules into simpler and lighter molecules. Catalytic cracking is accomplished by the use of a catalytic agent and is an effective process for increasing the yield of gasoline from crude oil. Catalytic cracking processes fresh feeds and recycled feeds.

nodes.label: Fluid coking
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Fluid coking as: A thermal cracking process utilizing the fluidized-solids technique to remove carbon (coke) for continuous conversion of heavy, low-grade oils into lighter products.

nodes.label: Fly ash
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Fly ash as: Particulate matter mainly from coal ash in which the particle diameter is less than 1 x 104 meter. This ash is removed from the flue gas using flue gas particulate collectors such as fabric filters and electrostatic precipitators.

nodes.label: Forced outage
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Forced outage as: The shutdown of a generating unit, transmission line, or other facility for emergency reasons or a condition in which the generating equipment is unavailable for load due to unanticipated breakdown.

nodes.label: Fossil fuel plant
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Fossil fuel plant as: A plant using coal, petroleum, or gas as its source of energy.

nodes.label: Fossil fuel steam-electric power plant
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Fossil fuel steam-electric power plant as: An electricity generation plant in which the

nodes.label: Foundry coke
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Foundry coke as: This is a special coke that is used in furnaces to produce cast and ductile iron products. It is a source of heat and also helps maintain the required carbon content of the metal product. Foundry coke production requires lower temperatures and longer times than blast furnace coke.

nodes.label: Fractionation
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Fractionation as: The process by which saturated hydrocarbons are removed from natural gas and separated into distinct products, or "fractions," such as propane, butane, and ethane.

nodes.label: Fresh feed input
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Fresh feed input as: Represents input of material (crude oil, unfinished oils, natural gas liquids, other hydrocarbons and oxygenates or finished products) to processing units at a refinery that is being processed (input) into a particular unit for the first time.

nodes.label: Fresh feeds
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Fresh feeds as: Crude oil or petroleum distillates that are being fed to processing units for the first time.

nodes.label: Fuel cell
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Fuel cell as: A device capable of generating an electrical current by converting the chemical energy of a fuel (e.g.,

nodes.label: Fuel cell electric vehicle (FCEV)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Fuel cell electric vehicle (FCEV) as: An electric vehicle that generates on-board electricity with a fuel cell powered by hydrogen rather than relying on electricity from a high capacity battery.

nodes.label: Fuel injection
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Fuel injection as: A fuel delivery system whereby gasoline is pumped to one or more fuel injectors under high pressure. The fuel injectors are valves that, at the appropriate times, open to allow fuel to be sprayed or atomized into a throttle bore or into the intake manifold ports. The fuel injectors are usually solenoid operated valves under the control of the vehicle's on-board computer (thus the term "electronic fuel injection"). The fuel efficiency of fuel injection systems is less temperature-dependent than carburetor systems. Diesel engines always use injectors.

nodes.label: Fuels solvent deasphalting
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Fuels solvent deasphalting as: A refining process for removing asphalt compounds from petroleum fractions, such as reduced crude oil. The recovered stream from this process is used to produce fuel products.

nodes.label: Fugitive emissions
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Fugitive emissions as: Unintended leaks of gas from the processing, transmission, and/or transportation of fossil fuels.

nodes.label: Full power day
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Full power day as: The equivalent of 24 hours of full power operation by a reactor. The number of full power days in a specific cycle is the product of the reactor's capacity factor and the length of the cycle.

nodes.label: Full power operation
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Full power operation as: Operation of a unit at 100 percent of its design capacity. Full-power operation precedes commercial operation.

nodes.label: Furnace
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Furnace as: The part of a boiler or warm-air space-heating plant in which combustion takes place.

nodes.label: Gas cooled fast breeder reactor (GCFB)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Gas cooled fast breeder reactor (GCFB) as: A fast breeder reactor that is cooled by a gas (usually helium) under pressure.

nodes.label: Gas to liquids (GTL)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Gas to liquids (GTL) as: A process that combines the carbon and hydrogen elements in natural gas molecules to make synthetic liquid petroleum products, such as diesel fuel.

nodes.label: Gas turbine plant
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Gas turbine plant as: A plant in which the prime mover is a gas turbine. A gas turbine consists typically of an axial-flow air compressor and one or more combustion chambers where liquid or gaseous fuel is burned and the hot gases are passed to the turbine and where the hot gases expand drive the generator and are then used to run the compressor.

nodes.label: Gas well
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Gas well as: A well completed for production of natural gas from one or more gas zones or reservoirs. Such wells contain no completions for the production of crude oil.

nodes.label: Gas well productivity
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Gas well productivity as: Derived annually by dividing gross natural gas withdrawals from gas wells by the number of producing gas wells on December 31 and then dividing the quotient by the number of days in the year.

nodes.label: Gasohol
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Gasohol as: A blend of finished motor gasoline containing alcohol (generally ethanol but sometimes methanol) at a concentration between 5.7 percent and 10 percent by volume. Also see

nodes.label: Gasoline blending components
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Gasoline blending components as: Naphthas which will be used for blending or compounding into finished aviation or motor gasoline (e.g., straight-run gasoline, alkylate, reformate, benzene, toluene, andxylene). Excludes oxygenates (alcohols, ethers), butane, and pentanes plus.

nodes.label: Gasoline motor, (leaded)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Gasoline motor, (leaded) as: Contains more than 0.05 grams of lead per gallon or more than 0.005 grams of phosphorus per gallon. The actual lead content of any given gallon may vary. Premium and regular grades are included, depending on the octane rating. Includes leaded gasohol. Blendstock is excluded until blending has been completed. Alcohol that is to be used in the blending of gasohol is also excluded.

nodes.label: Gate station
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Gate station as: Location where the pressure of natural gas being transferred from the transmission system to the distribution system is lowered for transport through small diameter, low pressure pipelines.

nodes.label: Generating station
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Generating station as: A station that consists of electric generators and auxiliary equipment for converting mechanical, chemical, or nuclear energy into electric energy.

nodes.label: Generating unit
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Generating unit as: Any combination of physically connected generators, reactors, boilers, combustion turbines, and other prime movers operated together to produce electric power.

nodes.label: Generator capacity
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Generator capacity as: The maximum output, commonly expressed in megawatts (MW), that generating equipment can supply to system load, adjusted for ambient conditions.

nodes.label: Generator nameplate capacity (installed)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Generator nameplate capacity (installed) as: The maximum rated output of a generator, prime mover, or other electric power production equipment under specific conditions designated by the manufacturer. Installed generator nameplate capacity is commonly expressed in megawatts (MW) and is usually indicated on a nameplate physically attached to the generator.

nodes.label: Geologic sequestration
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Geologic sequestration as: A type of engineered sequestration, where captured carbon dioxide is injected for permanent storage into underground geologic reservoirs, such as oil and natural gas fields, saline aquifers, or abandoned coal mines.

nodes.label: Geothermal plant
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Geothermal plant as: A plant in which the prime mover is a steam turbine. The turbine is driven either by steam produced from hot water or by natural steam that derives its energy from heat found in rock.

nodes.label: Gross additions to construction work in progress for the month
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Gross additions to construction work in progress for the month as: This amount should include the monthly gross additions for an electric plant in the process of construction.

nodes.label: Gross gas withdrawal
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Gross gas withdrawal as: The full-volume of compounds extracted at the wellhead, including nonhydrocarbon gases and natural gas plant liquids.

nodes.label: Gross inputs
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Gross inputs as: The crude oil, unfinished oils, and natural gas plant liquids put into atmospheric crude oil distillation units.

nodes.label: Gross vehicle weight rating (GVWR)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Gross vehicle weight rating (GVWR) as: Vehicle weight plus carrying capacity.

nodes.label: Heat content
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Heat content as: The amount of heat energy available to be released by the transformation or use of a specified physical unit of an energy form (e.g., a ton of coal, a barrel of oil, a kilowatthour of electricity, a cubic foot of natural gas, or a pound of steam). The amount of heat energy is commonly expressed in British thermal units (Btu). Note: Heat content of combustible energy forms can be expressed in terms of either gross heat content (higher or upper heating value) or net heat content (lower heating value), depending upon whether or not the available heat energy includes or excludes the energy used to vaporize water (contained in the original energy form or created during the combustion process). The Energy Information Administration typically uses gross heat content values.

nodes.label: Heat pump
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Heat pump as: Heating and/or cooling equipment that, during the heating season, draws heat into a building from outside and, during the cooling season, ejects heat from the building to the outside. Heat pumps are vapor-compression refrigeration systems whose indoor/outdoor coils are used reversibly as condensers or evaporators, depending on the need for heating or cooling.

nodes.label: Heat pump (air source)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Heat pump (air source) as: An air-source heat pump is the most common type of heat pump. The heat pump absorbs heat from the outside air and transfers the heat to the space to be heated in the heating mode. In the cooling mode the heat pump absorbs heat from the space to be cooled and rejects the heat to the outside air. In the heating mode when the outside air approaches 32o F or less, air-source heat pumps loose efficiency and generally require a back-up (resistance) heating system.

nodes.label: Heat pump (geothermal)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Heat pump (geothermal) as: A heat pump in which the refrigerant exchanges heat (in a heat exchanger) with a fluid circulating through an earth connection medium (ground or ground water). The fluid is contained in a variety of loop (pipe) configurations depending on the temperature of the ground and the ground area available. Loops may be installed horizontally or vertically in the ground or submersed in a body of water.

nodes.label: Heating value
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Heating value as: Heating value: A measure of the energy content of the physical unit of any combustible fuel. For a fuller discussion of

nodes.label: Heavy-water-moderated reactor
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Heavy-water-moderated reactor as: A reactor that uses heavy water as its moderator. Heavy water is an excellent moderator and thus permits the use of in expensive natural (unenriched) uranium as fuel.

nodes.label: Heliostat
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Heliostat as: A mirror that reflects solar rays onto a central receiver. A heliostat automatically adjusts its position to track daily or seasonal changes in the sun's position. The arrangement of heliostats around a central receiver is also called a solar collector field.

nodes.label: High efficiency ballast
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines High efficiency ballast as: A lighting conservation feature consisting of an energy-efficient version of a conventional electromagnetic ballast. The ballast is the transformer for fluorescent and high-intensity discharge (HID) lamps, which provides the necessary current, voltage, and wave-form conditions to operate the lamp. A high-efficiency ballast requires lower power input than a conventional ballast to operate HID and fluorescent lamps.

nodes.label: High-temperature collector
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines High-temperature collector as: A solar thermal collector designed to operate at a temperature of 180 degrees Fahrenheit or higher.

nodes.label: Horizontal axis wind turbine
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Horizontal axis wind turbine as: The most common type of wind turbine where the axis of rotation is oriented horizontally. Also see

nodes.label: Horsepower
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Horsepower as: A unit for measuring the rate of work (or power) equivalent to 33,000 foot-pounds per minute or 746 watts.

nodes.label: Hours under load
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Hours under load as: The hours the boiler is operating to drive the generator producing electricity.

nodes.label: HTGR
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines HTGR as: High Temperature Gas-cooled Reactor

nodes.label: Hub height
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Hub height as: In a horizontal-axis wind turbine, the distance from the turbine platform to the rotor shaft.

nodes.label: Humidifier
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Humidifier as: A humidifier adds moisture to the air(often needed in winter when indoor air is very dry). It may be a portable unit or attached to the heating system.

nodes.label: HVAC
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines HVAC as: An abbreviation for the heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning system; the system or systems that condition air in a building.

nodes.label: HVAC conservation feature
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines HVAC conservation feature as: A building feature designed to reduce the amount of energy consumed by the heating, cooling, and ventilating equipment.

nodes.label: Hybrid transmission line
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Hybrid transmission line as: A double-circuit line that has one alternating current and one direct circuit. The AC circuit usually serves local loads along the line.

nodes.label: Hydraulic fracturing
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Hydraulic fracturing as: A process that stimulates or increases production and ultimate recovery from a well by pumping a fluid and a proppant (sand or similar material) at high pressure into a well to create fractures in the reservoir that the proppant holds open. Hydraulic fracturing increases the surface of the formation available for oil and natural gas to flow into the wellbore (the hole drilled into the earth to extract oil and natural gas). Water is the most commonly used fluid, but carbon dioxide and nitrogen are sometimes used. The proppant is usually sand, but resin-coated sand, ceramics, and sintered bauxite are sometimes used. Hydraulic fracturing is common in low-permeability formations.

nodes.label: Hydraulic head
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Hydraulic head as: The distance between the respective elevations of the upstream water surface (headwater) above and the downstream surface water (tailwater) below a hydroelectric power plant.

nodes.label: Improved recovery
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Improved recovery as: Extraction of crude oil or natural gas by any method other than those that rely primarily on natural reservoir pressure, gas lift, or a system of pumps.

nodes.label: Incandescent lamp
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Incandescent lamp as: A glass enclosure in which light is produced when a tungsten filament is electrically heated so that it glows. Much of the energy is converted into heat; therefore, this class of lamp is a relatively inefficient source of light. Included in this category are the familiar screw-in light bulbs, as well as somewhat more efficient lamps, such as tungsten halogen lamps, reflector or r-lamps, parabolic aluminized reflector (PAR) lamps, and ellipsoidal reflector(ER) lamps.

nodes.label: Incandescent light bulbs, including regular or energy-efficient light bulbs
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Incandescent light bulbs, including regular or energy-efficient light bulbs as: An incandescent bulb is a type of electric light in which light is produced by a filament heated by electric current. The most common example is the type you find in most table and floor lamps. In commercial buildings, incandescent lights are used for display lights in retail stores, hotels and motels. This includes the very small, high-intensity track lights used to display merchandise or provide spot illumination in restaurants. Energy efficient light bulbs, known as "watt-savers," use less energy than a standard incandescent bulb. "Long-life" bulbs, bulbs that last longer than standard incandescent but produce considerably less light, are not considered energy-efficient bulbs. This category also includes halogen lamps. Halogen lamps are a special type of incandescent lamp containing halogen gas to produce a brighter, whiter light than standard incandescent. Halogen lamps come in three styles bulbs, models with reflectors, and infrared models with reflectors. Halogen lamps are especially suited to recessed or "canned fixtures," track lights, and outdoor lights.

nodes.label: Independent system operator (ISO)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Independent system operator (ISO) as: An independent, federally regulated entity established to coordinate regional transmission in a non-discriminatory manner and ensure the safety and reliability of the electric system.

nodes.label: Initial operation
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Initial operation as: First availability of a newly constructed unit to provide power to the grid. For a nuclear unit, this time is when the Full Power Operating License for the unit is received.

nodes.label: Insulator
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Insulator as: A material that is a very poor conductor of electricity. The insulating material is usually a ceramic or fiberglass when used in the transmission line and is designed to support a conductor physically and to separate it electrically from other conductors and supporting material.

nodes.label: Integral collector storage (ICS)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Integral collector storage (ICS) as: A solar thermal collector in which incident solar radiation is absorbed directly by the storage medium.

nodes.label: Integrated demand
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Integrated demand as: The summation of the continuously varying instantaneous demand averaged over a specified interval of time. The information is usually determined by examining a demand meter.

nodes.label: Integrated gasification-combined cycle technology
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Integrated gasification-combined cycle technology as: Coal, water, and oxygen are fed to gasifier, which produces syngas. This medium-Btu gas is cleaned (particulates and sulfur compounds removed) and is fed to a gas turbine. The hot exhaust of the gas turbine and heat recovered from the gasification process are routed through a heat-recovery routed through a heat-recovery generator to produce steam, which drives a steam turbine to produce electricity.

nodes.label: Interconnected system
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Interconnected system as: A system consisting of two or more individual power systems normally operating with connecting tie lines.

nodes.label: Intermediate grade gasoline
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Intermediate grade gasoline as: A grade of unleaded gasoline with an octane rating intermediate between "regular" and "premium." Octane boosters are added to gasolines to control engine pre-ignition or "knocking" by slowing combustion rates.

nodes.label: Intermediate load (electric system)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Intermediate load (electric system) as: The range from base load to a point between base load and peak. This point may be the midpoint, a percent of the peak load, or the load over a specified time period.

nodes.label: Intermittent electric generator or intermittent resource
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Intermittent electric generator or intermittent resource as: An electric generating plant with output controlled by the natural variability of the energy resource rather than dispatched based on system requirements. Intermittent output usually results from the direct, non-stored conversion of naturally occurring energy fluxes such as solar energy, wind energy, or the energy of free-flowing rivers (that is, run-of-river hydroelectricity).

nodes.label: Internal Collector Storage (ICS)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Internal Collector Storage (ICS) as: A solar thermal collector in which incident solar radiation is absorbed by the storage medium.

nodes.label: Internal combustion engine (ICE)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Internal combustion engine (ICE) as: Generates mechanical power by burning a liquid, such as gasoline, diesel, or biofuels, or a gaseous fuel, such as compressed natural gas.

nodes.label: Internal combustion plant
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Internal combustion plant as: A plant in which the prime mover is an internal combustion engine. An internal combustion engine has one or more cylinders in which the process of combustion takes place, converting energy released from the rapid burning of a fuel-air mixture into mechanical energy. Diesel or gas-fired engines are the principal types used in electric plants. The plant is usually operated during periods of high demand for electricity.

nodes.label: Interruptible load
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Interruptible load as: This Demand-Side Management category represents the consumer load that, in accordance with contractual arrangements, can be interrupted at the time of annual peak load by the action of the consumer at the direct request of the system operator. This type of control usually involves large-volume commercial and industrial consumers. Interruptible Load does not include Direct Load Control.

nodes.label: Interstate pipeline
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Interstate pipeline as: Any person engaged in natural gas transportation subject to the jurisdiction of Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) under the Natural Gas Act.

nodes.label: Intrastate pipeline
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Intrastate pipeline as: Any person engaged in natural gas transportation (not including gathering) that is not subject to the jurisdiction of the Commission under the Natural Gas Act (other than any such pipeline that is not subject to the jurisdiction of the Commission solely by reason of Section 1(c) of the Natural Gas Act).

nodes.label: Ion exchange
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Ion exchange as: Reversible exchange of ions adsorbed on a mineral or synthetic polymer surface with ions in solution in contact with the surface. A chemical process used for recovery of uranium from solution by the interchange of ions between a solution and a solid, commonly a resin.

nodes.label: Irradiated nuclear fuel
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Irradiated nuclear fuel as: Nuclear fuel that has been exposed to radiation in the reactor core at any power level.

nodes.label: Isomerization
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Isomerization as: A refining process that alters the fundamental arrangement of atoms in the molecule without adding or removing anything from the original material. Used to convert normal butane into isobutane (C

nodes.label: Isopach
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Isopach as: A line on a map drawn through points of equal thickness of a designated unit (such as a coal bed).

nodes.label: Jacket
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Jacket as: The enclosure on a water heater, furnace, or boiler.

nodes.label: Joint-use facility
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Joint-use facility as: A multiple-purpose hydroelectric plant. An example is a dam that stores water for both flood control and power production.

nodes.label: Joule (J)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Joule (J) as: The meter-kilogram-second unit of work or energy, equal to the work done by a force of one newton when its point of application moves through a distance of one meter in the direction of the force; equivalent to 107 ergs and one watt-second.

nodes.label: Kaplan turbine
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Kaplan turbine as: A type of turbine that that has two blades whose pitch is adjustable. The turbine may have gates to control the angle of the fluid flow into the blades.

nodes.label: Kerogen
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Kerogen as: Naturally occurring solid organic matter in sedimentary rock that is insoluble in organic solvents. Kerogen originates from algae, plankton, and plant material from aquatic and terrestrial environments. Under the right conditions of pressure, temperature, and time, kerogen can form oil and natural gas.

nodes.label: Kerosene
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Kerosene as: A light petroleum distillate that is used in space heaters, cook stoves, and water heaters and is suitable for use as a light source when burned in wick-fed lamps. Kerosene has a maximum distillation temperature of 400 degrees Fahrenheit at the 10-percent recovery point, a final boiling point of 572 degrees Fahrenheit, and a minimum flash point of 100 degrees Fahrenheit. Included are No. 1-K and No. 2-K, the two grades recognized by ASTM Specification D 3699 as well as all other grades of kerosene called range or stove oil, which have properties similar to those of No. 1 fuel oil. Also see Kerosene-type jet fuel.

nodes.label: Kilovolt-Ampere (kVa)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Kilovolt-Ampere (kVa) as: A unit of apparent power, equal to 1,000 volt-amperes; the mathematical product of the volts and amperes in an electrical circuit.

nodes.label: Kilowatthour (kWh)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Kilowatthour (kWh) as: A measure of electricity defined as a unit of work or energy, measured as 1 kilowatt (1,000watts) of power expended for 1 hour. One kWh is equivalent to 3,412 Btu.

nodes.label: Landfill gas
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Landfill gas as: Gas that is generated by decomposition of organic material at landfill disposal sites. The average composition of landfill gas is approximately 50 percent methane and 50 percent carbon dioxide and water vapor by volume. The methane percentage, however, can vary from 40 to 60 percent, depending on several factors including waste composition (e.g. carbohydrate and cellulose content). The methane in landfill gas may be vented, flared, combusted to generate electricity or useful thermal energy on-site, or injected into a pipeline for combustion off-site.

nodes.label: Large-scale solar
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Large-scale solar as: Solar thermal and photovoltaic generating units at power plants larger than or equal to one megawatt.

nodes.label: Lead acid battery
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Lead acid battery as: An electrochemical battery that uses lead and lead oxide for electrodes and sulfuric acid for the electrolyte.

nodes.label: Leading edge
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Leading edge as: In reference to a wind energy conversion system, the area of a turbine blade surface that first comes into contact with the wind.

nodes.label: Life extension
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Life extension as: Restoration or refurbishment of a plant to its original performance without the installation of new combustion technologies. Life extension results in 10 to 20 years of plant life beyond the anticipated retirement date, but usually does not result in larger capacity.

nodes.label: Lift
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Lift as: The force that pulls a wind turbine blade, as opposed to drag.

nodes.label: Light water reactor (LWR)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Light water reactor (LWR) as: A nuclear reactor that uses water as the primary coolant and moderator, with slightly enriched uranium as fuel.

nodes.label: Lighting conservation feature
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Lighting conservation feature as: A building feature or practice designed to reduce the amount of energy consumed by the lighting system.

nodes.label: Lighting equipment
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Lighting equipment as: These are light bulbs used to light the building's interior, such as incandescent light bulbs, fluorescent light bulbs, compact fluorescent light bulbs, and high-intensity discharge (HID) lights.

nodes.label: Liquid collector
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Liquid collector as: A medium-temperature solar thermal collector, employed predominantly in water heating, which uses pumped liquid as the heat-transfer medium.

nodes.label: Liquid metal fast breeder reactor
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Liquid metal fast breeder reactor as: A nuclear breeder reactor, cooled by molten sodium, in which fission is caused by fast neutrons.

nodes.label: Load loss (3 hours)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Load loss (3 hours) as: Any significant incident on an electric utility system that results in a continuous outage of 3 hours or longer to more than 50,000 customers or more than one half of the total customers being served immediately prior to the incident, whichever is less.

nodes.label: Load management technique
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Load management technique as: Utility demand management practices directed at reducing the maximum kilowatt demand on an electric system and/or modifying the coincident peak demand of one or more classes of service to better meet the utility system capability for a given hour, day, week, season, or year.

nodes.label: Load on equipment
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Load on equipment as: One hundred percent load is the maximum continuous net output of the unit at normal operating conditions during the annual peak load month. For example, if the equipment is capable of operating at 5% over pressure continuously, use this condition for 100% load.

nodes.label: Longwall mining
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Longwall mining as: An automated form of underground coal mining characterized by high recovery and extraction rates, feasible only in relatively flat-lying, thick, and uniform coalbeds. A high-powered cutting machine is passed across the exposed face of coal, shearing away broken coal, which is continuously hauled away by a floor-level conveyor system. Longwall mining extracts all machine-minable coal between the floor and ceiling within a contiguous block of coal, known as a panel, leaving no support pillars within the panel area. Panel dimensions vary over time and with mining conditions but currently average about 900 feet wide (coal face width) and more than 8,000 feet long (the minable extent of the panel, measured indirection of mining). Longwall mining is done under movable roof supports that are advanced as the bed is cut. The roof in the mined-out area is allowed to fall as the mining advances.

nodes.label: Low power testing
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Low power testing as: The period of time between a plant's nuclear generating unit's initial fuel loading date and the issuance of its operating (full-power) license. The maximum level of operation during this period is 5 percent of the unit's thermal rating.

nodes.label: Lubricants
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Lubricants as: Substances used to reduce friction between bearing surfaces, or incorporated into other materials used as processing aids in the manufacture of other products, or used as carriers of other materials. Petroleum lubricants may be produced either from distillates or residues. Lubricants include all grades of lubricating oils, from spindle oil to cylinder oil to those used in greases.

nodes.label: Lumens/Watt (lpw)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Lumens/Watt (lpw) as: A measure of the efficacy (efficiency) of lamps. It indicates the amount of light (lumens) emitted by the lamp for each unit of electrical power (Watts) used.

nodes.label: Machine drive (motors)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Machine drive (motors) as: The direct process end use in which thermal or electric energy is converted into mechanical energy. Motors are found in almost every process in manufacturing. Therefore, when motors are found in equipment that is wholly contained in another end use (such as process cooling and refrigeration), the energy is classified there rather than in machine drive.

nodes.label: Main heating fuel
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Main heating fuel as: The form of energy used most frequently to heat the largest portion of the floorspace of a structure. The energy source designated as the main heating fuel is the source delivered to the site for that purpose, not any subsequent form into which it is transformed on site to deliver the heat energy (e.g., for buildings heated by a steam boiler, the main heating fuel is the main input fuel to the boiler, not the steam or hot water circulated through the building.) Note: In commercial buildings, the heating must be to at least 50 degrees Fahrenheit.

nodes.label: Mains
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Mains as: A system of pipes for transporting gas within a distributing gas utility's retail service area to points of connection with consumer service pipes.

nodes.label: Manufactured gas
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Manufactured gas as: A gas obtained by destructive distillation of coal or by the thermal decomposition of oil, or by the reaction of steam passing through a bed of heated coal or coke. Examples are coal gases, coke oven gases, producer gas, blast furnace gas, blue (water) gas, carbureted water gas. Btu content varies widely.

nodes.label: Marketed production
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Marketed production as: Gross withdrawals less gas used for repressuring, quantities vented and flared, and nonhydrocarbon gases removed in treating or processing operations. Includes all quantities of gas used in field and processing plant operations.

nodes.label: Maximum dependable capacity, net
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Maximum dependable capacity, net as: The gross electrical output measured at the output terminals of the turbine generator(s) during the most restrictive seasonal conditions, less the station service load.

nodes.label: Maximum generator nameplate capacity
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Maximum generator nameplate capacity as: The maximum rated output of a generator, prime mover, or other electric power production equipment under specific conditions designated by the manufacturer.

nodes.label: Mean power output (of a wind turbine)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Mean power output (of a wind turbine) as: The average power output of a wind energy conversion system at a given mean wind speed based on a Raleigh frequency distribution.

nodes.label: Medium-temperature collector
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Medium-temperature collector as: A collector designed to operate in the temperature range of 140 degrees to 180 degrees Fahrenheit, but that can also operate at a temperature as low as 110 degrees Fahrenheit. The collector typically consists of a metal frame, metal absorption panels with integral flow channels (attached tubing for liquid collectors or integral ducting for air collectors), and glazing and insulation on the sides and back.

nodes.label: Microgroove
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Microgroove as: A small groove scribed into the surface of a solar photovoltaic cell which is filled with metal for contacts.

nodes.label: Micrometer (or Micron)
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Micrometer (or Micron) as: One-millionth of a meter. It can also be expressed as 10-6 meter.

nodes.label: Mill feed
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Mill feed as: Uranium ore supplied to a crusher or grinding mill in an ore-dressing process.

nodes.label: Milling of uranium
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Milling of uranium as: The processing of uranium from ore mined by conventional methods, such as underground or open-pit methods, to separate the uranium from the undesired material in the ore.

nodes.label: Mineral-matter-free basis
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Mineral-matter-free basis as: Mineral matter in coal is the parent material in coal from which ash is derived and which comes from minerals present in the original plant materials that formed the coal, or from extraneous sources such as sediments and precipitates from mineralized water. Mineral matter in coal cannot be analytically determined and is commonly calculated using data on ash and ash-forming constituents. Coal analyses are calculated to the mineral matter free basis by adjusting formulas used in calculations in order to deduct the weight of mineral matter from the total coal.

nodes.label: Minority carrier
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Minority carrier as: A current carrier, either an electron or a hole, that is in the minority in a specific layer of a semiconductor material; the diffusion of minority carriers under the action of the cell junction voltage is the current in a photovoltaic device.

nodes.label: Moderator
