nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral genome replication as: Any process involved directly in viral genome replication, including viral nucleotide metabolism.

nodes.label: viral tropism switching
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral tropism switching as: A process by which the range of hosts which a virus can bind and infect is changed. Examples include phages that switch between types of fibers via the action of a virally encoded invertase.

nodes.label: viral mRNA export from host cell nucleus
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral mRNA export from host cell nucleus as: The directed movement of intronless viral mRNA from the host nucleus to the cytoplasm for translation.

nodes.label: virus maturation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines virus maturation as: The refolding and structural rearrangements of virion parts to transition from the intermediate virion to the more mature virion. Maturation usually involves proteolysis events and changes in the folding of the virion proteins. Can occur inside the host cell or after release.

nodes.label: IRES-dependent viral translational initiation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines IRES-dependent viral translational initiation as: Process by which viral mRNA translation is initiated, where a domain in the 5' untranslated region (UTR) of the viral mRNA called an internal ribosome entry site (IRES) binds the host 43S preinitiation complex, circumventing regular cap-dependent translation initiation.

nodes.label: viral capsid secondary envelopment
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral capsid secondary envelopment as: The process in which a capsid acquires another membrane envelope, subsequent to acquiring an initial membrane envelope.

nodes.label: viral translation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral translation as: A process by which viral mRNA is translated into viral protein, using the host cellular machinery.

nodes.label: ribosomal skipping
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines ribosomal skipping as: A translation process in which a specific viral peptide prevents the ribosome from covalently linking a new inserted amino acid, and lets it continue translation, thereby cleaving the nascent protein while allowing translation to continue.

nodes.label: viral tail assembly
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral tail assembly as: The aggregation, arrangement and bonding together of a set of components to form a virus tail.

nodes.label: viral head-tail joining
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral head-tail joining as: Process by which virus heads and tails are attached to each other.

nodes.label: cap snatching
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cap snatching as: A transcription initiation process during which a nucleotide sequence between 10 and 20 nucleotides in size is cleaved from the 5' end of host mRNAs by a viral RNA-dependent polymerase. The capped leader sequence obtained is subsequently used to prime transcription on the viral genome, which ultimately leads to the synthesis of capped, translatable viral mRNAs.

nodes.label: symbiont genome ejection through host cell envelope
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines symbiont genome ejection through host cell envelope as: Entry of a symbiont's genome into the host cell through the host cell envelope. Occurs in non-enveloped prokaryotic viruses. Caudovirales carry an ejection apparatus that can be long and contractile, long and noncontractile, or short, and is able to penetrate the host cell envelope to deliver the viral genome into the host cell cytoplasm.

nodes.label: exit of virus from host cell nucleus
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines exit of virus from host cell nucleus as: The directed movement of the viral genome or a viral particle out of the host cell nucleus.

nodes.label: transport of virus
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines transport of virus as: The directed movement of a virus, or part of a virus, into, out of, or within a host cell.

nodes.label: superinfection exclusion
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines superinfection exclusion as: The process by which a preexisting viral infection prevents a secondary infection with the same or a closely related virus. Typically some aspect of viral entry is inhibited, but post entry mechanisms have also been documented.

nodes.label: latent virus replication
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines latent virus replication as: Any process required for latent viral replication in a cell.

nodes.label: virion assembly
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines virion assembly as: A late phase of the viral life cycle during which all the components necessary for the formation of a mature virion collect at a particular site in the cell and the basic structure of the virus particle is formed.

nodes.label: viral scaffold assembly and maintenance
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral scaffold assembly and maintenance as: The assembly and maintenance of the viral scaffold around which the viral capsid is constructed.

nodes.label: viral transcription
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral transcription as: The process by which a viral genome, or part of a viral genome, is transcribed within the host cell.

nodes.label: viral genome maturation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral genome maturation as: The processes involved in creating a mature, stable viral genome. Begins after genome replication with a newly synthesized nucleic acid and ends when the genome is ready to be packaged. Includes the addition of proteins to the newly synthesized genome, and DNA repair processes.

nodes.label: viral budding
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral budding as: A viral process by which enveloped viruses acquire a host-derived membrane enriched in viral proteins to form their external envelope. The process starts when nucleocapsids, assembled or in the process of being built, induce formation of a membrane curvature in the host plasma or organelle membrane and wrap up in the forming bud. The process ends when the bud is eventually pinched off by membrane scission to release the enveloped particle into the lumenal or extracellular space.

nodes.label: reorganization of host cellular membranes to establish sites of replication
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines reorganization of host cellular membranes to establish sites of replication as: A process in which a virus triggers host intracellular membranes to be reorganized, forming membranous webs, which are thought to be the site of replication or certain viruses, for example the HPV virus.

nodes.label: lysis of host organelle involved in viral entry into host cell
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines lysis of host organelle involved in viral entry into host cell as: The viral-induced lysis of an organelle (endosome, lysosome, or caveosome) that is involved in the uptake of a virus into a host cell. Occurs once the virus is within the organelle, and results in transfer of the viral contents from the organelle compartment into the cytoplasm.

nodes.label: virus baseplate assembly
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines virus baseplate assembly as: The aggregation, arrangement and bonding together of a set of components to form a virus baseplate.

nodes.label: viral release from host cell
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral release from host cell as: The dissemination of mature viral particles from a host cell, e.g. by cell lysis or the budding of virus particles from the cell membrane.

nodes.label: virion maturation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines virion maturation as: Maturation of a virion after separation from the host cell. Not all viruses mature after separation. In those that do, maturation typically involves rearangement and/or cleavage of viral proteins, resulting in the virion becoming competent for reinfection.

nodes.label: viral genome packaging
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral genome packaging as: The encapsulation of the viral genome within the capsid.

nodes.label: viral translational frameshifting
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral translational frameshifting as: A process which occurs during viral translation, which involves a translational recoding mechanism called programmed ribosomal frameshifting. This causes the ribosome to alter its reading of the mRNA to an a different open reading frame to produce alternate viral proteins.

nodes.label: viral protein processing
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral protein processing as: Any protein maturation process achieved by the cleavage of a peptide bond or bonds within a viral protein.

nodes.label: viral translational termination-reinitiation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral translational termination-reinitiation as: A process which occurs as part of viral mRNA translation which allows expression of a downstream open reading frame (ORF) in a dicistronic mRNA. In this process, ribosomes translate the upstream ORF but following termination, a proportion of 40S subunits remain tethered to the mRNA and go on to re-initiate translation at the start codon of the downstream ORF.

nodes.label: viral gene expression
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral gene expression as: A process by which a viral gene is converted into a mature gene product or products (proteins or RNA). This includes viral transcription, processing to produce a mature RNA product, and viral translation.

nodes.label: viral replication complex formation and maintenance
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral replication complex formation and maintenance as: The process of organizing and assembling viral replication proteins in preparation for viral replication.

nodes.label: virus tail fiber assembly
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines virus tail fiber assembly as: The aggregation, arrangement and bonding together of a set of components to form a virus tail fiber.

nodes.label: viral RNA editing
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral RNA editing as: The process by which bases in viral mRNA are chemically altered during viral transcription. This is usually the incorporation of 1 - 6 additional nucleotides, which shifts the reading frame, allowing the generation of different protein products or through a specific nucleotide change that eliminates the termination codon.

nodes.label: viral capsid assembly
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral capsid assembly as: The assembly of a virus capsid from its protein subunits.

nodes.label: viral genome circularization
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral genome circularization as: The circularization of a viral genome following infection of a host cell. This is common amongst bacterial viruses to protect the viral genome ends from nucleases, to convert the linear genome to an integrative precursor or to give rise to the replicative form of the genome. It can be mediated by covalent closure of the DNA sticky ends, recombinaison between redundant terminal sequences or via the binding of a protein at the viral DNA extremities.

nodes.label: release from viral latency
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines release from viral latency as: The process by which a virus begins to replicate following a latency replication decision (switch).

nodes.label: uncoating of virus
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines uncoating of virus as: The process by which an incoming virus is disassembled in the host cell to release a replication-competent viral genome.

nodes.label: viral latency
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral latency as: The process by which, after initial infection, a virus lies dormant within a cell and viral production ceases. The process ends when the virus switches from latency and starts to replicate.

nodes.label: multicellular organismal reproductive process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines multicellular organismal reproductive process as: The process, occurring above the cellular level, that is pertinent to the reproductive function of a multicellular organism. This includes the integrated processes at the level of tissues and organs.

nodes.label: fertilization
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines fertilization as: The union of gametes of opposite sexes during the process of sexual reproduction to form a zygote. It involves the fusion of the gametic nuclei (karyogamy) and cytoplasm (plasmogamy).

nodes.label: reproductive process in single-celled organism
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines reproductive process in single-celled organism as: A process, occurring at the cellular level, that is involved in the reproductive function of a single-celled organism.

nodes.label: premature acrosome loss
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines premature acrosome loss as: The discharge, by sperm, of a single, anterior secretory granule before the sperm reaches to the zona pellucida of the oocyte. The process begins with the fusion of the outer acrosomal membrane with the sperm plasma membrane and ends with the exocytosis of the acrosomal contents.

nodes.label: mating plug formation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines mating plug formation as: The deposition of a plug of sperm or other gelatinous material into the opening of the vulva by a male at the termination of copulation. Probably acts to prevent subsequent matings by other males.

nodes.label: sexual reproduction
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines sexual reproduction as: A type of reproduction that combines the genetic material of two gametes (such as a sperm or egg cell or fungal spores). The gametes have an haploid genome (with a single set of chromosomes, the product of a meiotic division) and combines with one another to produce a zygote (diploid).

nodes.label: ovulation cycle process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines ovulation cycle process as: A process involved in the sexual cycle seen in females, often with physiologic changes in the endometrium that recur at regular intervals during the reproductive years.

nodes.label: embryo implantation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines embryo implantation as: Attachment of the blastocyst to the uterine lining.

nodes.label: multi-organism reproductive process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines multi-organism reproductive process as: A biological process that directly contributes to the process of producing new individuals, involving another organism.

nodes.label: sperm motility
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines sperm motility as: Any process involved in the controlled movement of a sperm cell.

nodes.label: meiotic drive
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines meiotic drive as: A biological process that results in the unequal transmission of alleles, haplotypes, or chromosomes from a parental genome to gametes. In the absence of meiotic drive, the two copies of each gene or chromosome in a diploid organism are transmitted to offspring with equal probability, whereas meiotic drive results in overrepresentation of the driving allele among the surviving products of meiosis.

nodes.label: acrosome reaction
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines acrosome reaction as: The discharge, by sperm, of a single, anterior secretory granule following the sperm's attachment to the zona pellucida of the oocyte. The process begins with the fusion of the outer acrosomal membrane with the sperm plasma membrane and ends with the exocytosis of the acrosomal contents into the zona pellucida.

nodes.label: meiotic cell cycle
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines meiotic cell cycle as: Progression through the phases of the meiotic cell cycle, in which canonically a cell replicates to produce four offspring with half the chromosomal content of the progenitor cell via two nuclear divisions.

nodes.label: meiotic cell cycle process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines meiotic cell cycle process as: A process that is part of the meiotic cell cycle.

nodes.label: developmental process involved in reproduction
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines developmental process involved in reproduction as: A developmental process in which a progressive change in the state of some part of an organism, germline or somatic, specifically contributes to its ability to form offspring.

nodes.label: asexual reproduction
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines asexual reproduction as: A type of reproduction in which new individuals are produced from a single organism, either from an unfertilized egg or from a single cell or group of cells.

nodes.label: spore dispersal
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines spore dispersal as: Any process in which an organism disseminates its spores.

nodes.label: parasexual reproduction with cellular fusion
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines parasexual reproduction with cellular fusion as: A type of reproduction in which new individuals are produced from two individuals, with the fusion of two somatic cells.

nodes.label: antigen sampling in mucosal-associated lymphoid tissue
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines antigen sampling in mucosal-associated lymphoid tissue as: The process of apical-to-basolateral delivery of soluble and particulate antigens to underlying mucosal-associated lymphoid tissue.

nodes.label: antigen processing and presentation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines antigen processing and presentation as: The process in which an antigen-presenting cell expresses antigen (peptide or lipid) on its cell surface in association with an MHC protein complex.

nodes.label: leukocyte homeostasis
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines leukocyte homeostasis as: The process of regulating the proliferation and elimination of cells of the immune system such that the total number of cells of a particular cell type within a whole or part of an organism is stable over time in the absence of an outside stimulus.

nodes.label: tolerance induction
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines tolerance induction as: A process that directly activates any of the steps required for tolerance, a physiologic state in which the immune system does not react destructively against the components of an organism that harbors it or against antigens that are introduced to it.

nodes.label: B cell selection
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines B cell selection as: The process dependent upon B cell antigen receptor signaling in response to self or foreign antigen through which B cells are selected for survival.

nodes.label: activation of immune response
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines activation of immune response as: Any process that initiates an immune response.

nodes.label: leukocyte activation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines leukocyte activation as: A change in morphology and behavior of a leukocyte resulting from exposure to a specific antigen, mitogen, cytokine, cellular ligand, or soluble factor.

nodes.label: immune effector process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines immune effector process as: Any process of the immune system that executes a component of an immune response. An effector immune process takes place after its activation.

nodes.label: immunological memory process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines immunological memory process as: Any process of the immune system that can contribute to the formation of immunological memory or an immune response based upon activation of immunological memory.

nodes.label: lymphocyte costimulation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines lymphocyte costimulation as: The process of providing, via surface-bound receptor-ligand pairs, a second, antigen-independent, signal in addition to that provided by the B- or T cell receptor to augment B- or T cell activation.

nodes.label: production of molecular mediator of immune response
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines production of molecular mediator of immune response as: The synthesis or release of any molecular mediator of the immune response, resulting in an increase in its intracellular or extracellular levels.

nodes.label: somatic diversification of immune receptors
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines somatic diversification of immune receptors as: The somatic process allowing for the production of immune receptors whose specificity is not encoded in the germline genomic sequences.

nodes.label: myeloid cell homeostasis
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines myeloid cell homeostasis as: The process of regulating the proliferation and elimination of myeloid cells such that the total number of myeloid cells within a whole or part of an organism is stable over time in the absence of an outside stimulus.

nodes.label: immune system development
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines immune system development as: The process whose specific outcome is the progression of an organismal system whose objective is to provide calibrated responses by an organism to a potential internal or invasive threat, over time, from its formation to the mature structure. A system is a regularly interacting or interdependent group of organs or tissues that work together to carry out a given biological process.

nodes.label: hemocyte differentiation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines hemocyte differentiation as: The process in which a relatively unspecialized cell acquires the characteristics of a mature hemocyte. Hemocytes are blood cells associated with a hemocoel (the cavity containing most of the major organs of the arthropod body) which are involved in defense and clotting of hemolymph, but not involved in transport of oxygen.

nodes.label: hemocyte proliferation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines hemocyte proliferation as: The multiplication or reproduction of hemocytes, resulting in the expansion of the cell population. Hemocytes are blood cells associated with a hemocoel (the cavity containing most of the major organs of the arthropod body) which are involved in defense and clotting of hemolymph, but not involved in transport of oxygen.

nodes.label: T cell selection
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines T cell selection as: The process in which T cells that express T cell receptors that are restricted by self MHC protein complexes and tolerant to self antigens are selected for further maturation.

nodes.label: leukocyte migration
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines leukocyte migration as: The movement of a leukocyte within or between different tissues and organs of the body.

nodes.label: cell division
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cell division as: The process resulting in division and partitioning of components of a cell to form more cells; may or may not be accompanied by the physical separation of a cell into distinct, individually membrane-bounded daughter cells.

nodes.label: synaptic vesicle transport
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines synaptic vesicle transport as: The directed movement of synaptic vesicles.

nodes.label: cellular developmental process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cellular developmental process as: A biological process whose specific outcome is the progression of a cell over time from an initial condition to a later condition.

nodes.label: cell adhesion molecule production
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cell adhesion molecule production as: The appearance of a cell adhesion molecule due to biosynthesis or secretion.

nodes.label: cell cycle process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cell cycle process as: The cellular process that ensures successive accurate and complete genome replication and chromosome segregation.

nodes.label: process utilizing autophagic mechanism
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines process utilizing autophagic mechanism as: A cellular process involving delivery of a portion of the cytoplasm to lysosomes or to the plant or fungal vacuole that does not involve direct transport through the endocytic or vacuolar protein sorting (Vps) pathways. This process typically leads to degradation of the cargo; however, it can also be used to deliver resident proteins, such as in the cytoplasm-to-vacuole targeting (Cvt) pathway.

nodes.label: signal transduction
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines signal transduction as: The cellular process in which a signal is conveyed to trigger a change in the activity or state of a cell. Signal transduction begins with reception of a signal (e.g. a ligand binding to a receptor or receptor activation by a stimulus such as light), or for signal transduction in the absence of ligand, signal-withdrawal or the activity of a constitutively active receptor. Signal transduction ends with regulation of a downstream cellular process, e.g. regulation of transcription or regulation of a metabolic process. Signal transduction covers signaling from receptors located on the surface of the cell and signaling via molecules located within the cell. For signaling between cells, signal transduction is restricted to events at and within the receiving cell.

nodes.label: stomatal movement
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines stomatal movement as: The process of opening or closing of stomata, which is directly related to the stomatal conductance (measuring rate of passage of either water vapor or carbon dioxide (CO2) through stomata).

nodes.label: cell aggregation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cell aggregation as: The clustering together and adhesion of initially separate cells to form an aggregate. Examples include the clustering of unicellular organisms or blood cells in suspension and the condensation of mesenchymal cells during cartilage formation.

nodes.label: protein unfolding
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines protein unfolding as: The process of assisting in the disassembly of non-covalent linkages in a protein or protein aggregate, often where the proteins are in a non-functional or denatured state.

nodes.label: cell death
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cell death as: Any biological process that results in permanent cessation of all vital functions of a cell. A cell should be considered dead when any one of the following molecular or morphological criteria is met: (1) the cell has lost the integrity of its plasma membrane; (2) the cell, including its nucleus, has undergone complete fragmentation into discrete bodies (frequently referred to as apoptotic bodies). The cell corpse (or its fragments) may be engulfed by an adjacent cell in vivo, but engulfment of whole cells should not be considered a strict criteria to define cell death as, under some circumstances, live engulfed cells can be released from phagosomes (see PMID:18045538).

nodes.label: protein quality control
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines protein quality control as: The chemical reactions and pathways resulting in the breakdown or refolding of proteins recognized as aberrant, including misfolded, dysfunctional, or incompletely synthesized proteins, and orphan subunits that fail to assemble into their cognate protein complex.

nodes.label: protein folding
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines protein folding as: The process of assisting in the covalent and noncovalent assembly of single chain polypeptides or multisubunit complexes into the correct tertiary structure.

nodes.label: cell motility
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cell motility as: Any process involved in the controlled self-propelled movement of a cell that results in translocation of the cell from one place to another.

nodes.label: RNA folding
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines RNA folding as: The process of assisting in the covalent and noncovalent assembly of single or multimeric RNAs into the correct tertiary structure.

nodes.label: microtubule organizing center localization
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines microtubule organizing center localization as: Any process in which the microtubule organizing center is transported to, and/or maintained in, a specific location within the cell.

nodes.label: execution phase of necroptosis
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines execution phase of necroptosis as: A stage of the necroptotic process that starts after a necroptotic signal has been relayed to the execution machinery. Key steps of the execution phase are swelling of organelles, minor ultrastructural modifications of the nucleus (specifically, dilatation of the nuclear membrane and condensation of chromatin into small, irregular, circumscribed patches) and increased cell volume (oncosis), culminating in the disruption of the plasma membrane and subsequent loss of intracellular contents. The execution phase ends when the cell has died.

nodes.label: membrane docking
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines membrane docking as: The initial attachment of a membrane or protein to a target membrane. Docking requires only that the proteins come close enough to interact and adhere.

nodes.label: cell communication
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cell communication as: Any process that mediates interactions between a cell and its surroundings. Encompasses interactions such as signaling or attachment between one cell and another cell, between a cell and an extracellular matrix, or between a cell and any other aspect of its environment.

nodes.label: phenotypic switching
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines phenotypic switching as: A reversible switch of a cell from one cell type or form to another, at a frequency above the expected frequency for somatic mutations. Phenotypic switching involves changes in cell morphology and altered gene expression patterns. For example, Candida albicans switches from white cells to opaque cells for sexual mating. Phenotypic switching also occurs in multicellular organisms; smooth muscle cells (SMCs) exhibit phenotypic transitions to allow rapid adaption to fluctuating environmental cues.

nodes.label: septum digestion after cytokinesis
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines septum digestion after cytokinesis as: The process of physically separating the septal cell wall material by enzymatic digestion, that occurs after daughter cells are separated by cytokinesis.

nodes.label: microtubule-based process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines microtubule-based process as: Any cellular process that depends upon or alters the microtubule cytoskeleton, that part of the cytoskeleton comprising microtubules and their associated proteins.

nodes.label: cellular detoxification
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cellular detoxification as: Any process carried out at the cellular level that reduces or removes the toxicity of a toxic substance. These may include transport of the toxic substance away from sensitive areas and to compartments or complexes whose purpose is sequestration of the toxic substance.

nodes.label: plasmid maintenance
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines plasmid maintenance as: The maintenance of the integrity of extrachromosomal plasmid DNA; includes processes that ensure plasmids are retained in the daughter cells after cell division.

nodes.label: cytolysis
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cytolysis as: The rupture of cell membranes and the loss of cytoplasm.

nodes.label: cell wall organization or biogenesis
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cell wall organization or biogenesis as: A process that results in the biosynthesis of constituent macromolecules, assembly, arrangement of constituent parts, or disassembly of a cell wall.

nodes.label: cell killing
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cell killing as: Any process in an organism that results in the killing of its own cells or those of another organism, including in some cases the death of the other organism. Killing here refers to the induction of death in one cell by another cell, not cell-autonomous death due to internal or other environmental conditions.

nodes.label: export from cell
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines export from cell as: The directed movement of some substance from a cell, into the extracellular region. This may occur via transport across the plasma membrane or via exocytosis.

nodes.label: cellular localization
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cellular localization as: A cellular localization process whereby a substance or cellular entity, such as a protein complex or organelle, is transported to, and/or maintained in, a specific location within a cell including the localization of substances or cellular entities to the cell membrane.

nodes.label: horizontal gene transfer
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines horizontal gene transfer as: The introduction of genetic information into a cell to create a genetically different individual, without production of new individuals.

nodes.label: cellular component organization or biogenesis
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cellular component organization or biogenesis as: A process that results in the biosynthesis of constituent macromolecules, assembly, arrangement of constituent parts, or disassembly of a cellular component.

nodes.label: transmembrane transport
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines transmembrane transport as: The process in which a solute is transported across a lipid bilayer, from one side of a membrane to the other.

nodes.label: exocytic process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines exocytic process as: The cellular processes that contribute to exocytosis.

nodes.label: cell-cell fusion
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cell-cell fusion as: A cellular process in which two or more cells combine together, their plasma membrane fusing, producing a single cell. In some cases, nuclei fuse, producing a polyploid cell, while in other cases, nuclei remain separate, producing a syncytium.

nodes.label: cell cycle
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cell cycle as: The progression of biochemical and morphological phases and events that occur in a cell during successive cell replication or nuclear replication events. Canonically, the cell cycle comprises the replication and segregation of genetic material followed by the division of the cell, but in endocycles or syncytial cells nuclear replication or nuclear division may not be followed by cell division.

nodes.label: cell activation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cell activation as: A multicellular organismal process by which exposure to an activating factor such as a cellular or soluble ligand results in a change in the morphology or behavior of a cell.

nodes.label: cell competition in a multicellular organism
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cell competition in a multicellular organism as: Competitive interactions within multicellular organisms between cell populations that differ in growth rates, leading to the elimination of the slowest-growing cells.

nodes.label: cell population proliferation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cell population proliferation as: The multiplication or reproduction of cells, resulting in the expansion of a cell population.

nodes.label: ciliary basal body segregation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines ciliary basal body segregation as: The process in which the duplicated basal bodies migrate in pairs to the mitotic poles of the nucleus and results in equal distribution in the daughter cells. Ciliary basal body segregation ensures inheritance of the duplicated mitochondrial DNA to the two daughter cells in the Trypanosoma parasites.

nodes.label: nutrient storage
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines nutrient storage as: The accumulation and maintenance in cells or tissues of a nutrient, a substance that is used by an organism to survive, to grow, and to reproduce; such as proteins, vitamins, and minerals. Nutrient reserves can be accumulated for mobilization and utilization when needed.

nodes.label: intermediate filament-based process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines intermediate filament-based process as: Any cellular process that depends upon or alters the intermediate filament cytoskeleton, that part of the cytoskeleton comprising intermediate filaments and their associated proteins.

nodes.label: execution phase of apoptosis
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines execution phase of apoptosis as: A stage of the apoptotic process that starts with the controlled breakdown of the cell through the action of effector caspases or other effector molecules (e.g. cathepsins, calpains etc.). Key steps of the execution phase are rounding-up of the cell, retraction of pseudopodes, reduction of cellular volume (pyknosis), chromatin condensation, nuclear fragmentation (karyorrhexis), plasma membrane blebbing and fragmentation of the cell into apoptotic bodies. When the execution phase is completed, the cell has died.

nodes.label: cellular senescence
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cellular senescence as: A cell aging process stimulated in response to cellular stress, whereby normal cells lose the ability to divide through irreversible cell cycle arrest.

nodes.label: cellular process involved in reproduction in multicellular organism
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cellular process involved in reproduction in multicellular organism as: A process, occurring at the cellular level, that is involved in the reproductive function of a multicellular organism.

nodes.label: light absorption
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines light absorption as: The reception of a photon by a cell.

nodes.label: localization of cell
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines localization of cell as: Any process in which a cell is transported to, and/or maintained in, a specific location.

nodes.label: actin filament-based process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines actin filament-based process as: Any cellular process that depends upon or alters the actin cytoskeleton, that part of the cytoskeleton comprising actin filaments and their associated proteins.

nodes.label: vesicle-mediated transport
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines vesicle-mediated transport as: A cellular transport process in which transported substances are moved in membrane-bounded vesicles; transported substances are enclosed in the vesicle lumen or located in the vesicle membrane. The process begins with a step that directs a substance to the forming vesicle, and includes vesicle budding and coating. Vesicles are then targeted to, and fuse with, an acceptor membrane.

nodes.label: cell adhesion
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cell adhesion as: The attachment of a cell, either to another cell or to an underlying substrate such as the extracellular matrix, via cell adhesion molecules.

nodes.label: metabolic process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines metabolic process as: A cellular process consisting of the biochemical pathways by which a living organism transforms chemical substances. This includes including anabolism (biosynthetic process) and catabolism (catabolic process). Metabolic processes includes the transformation of small molecules, as well macromolecular processes such as DNA repair and replication, protein synthesis and degradation.

nodes.label: ensheathment of neurons
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines ensheathment of neurons as: The process in which glial cells envelop neuronal cell bodies and/or axons to form an insulating layer. This can take the form of myelinating or non-myelinating ensheathment.

nodes.label: cell recognition
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cell recognition as: The process in which a cell in an organism interprets its surroundings.

nodes.label: locomotion involved in locomotory behavior
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines locomotion involved in locomotory behavior as: Self-propelled movement of a cell or organism from one location to another in a behavioral context; the aspect of locomotory behavior having to do with movement.

nodes.label: directional locomotion
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines directional locomotion as: Self-propelled movement of a cell or organism from one location to another along an axis.

nodes.label: flight
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines flight as: Self-propelled movement of an organism from one location to another through the air, usually by means of active wing movement.

nodes.label: taxis
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines taxis as: The directed movement of a motile cell or organism in response to an external stimulus.

nodes.label: multicellular organismal locomotion
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines multicellular organismal locomotion as: Locomotion in a multicellular organism, i.e. self-propelled movement of a multicellular organism from one location to another.

nodes.label: swimming
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines swimming as: Self-propelled movement of an organism from one location to another through water, often by means of active fin movement.

nodes.label: ultradian rhythm
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines ultradian rhythm as: The specific actions or reactions of an organism that recur with a regularity more frequent than every 24 hours.

nodes.label: circadian rhythm
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines circadian rhythm as: Any biological process in an organism that recurs with a regularity of approximately 24 hours.

nodes.label: ovulation cycle
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines ovulation cycle as: The type of sexual cycle seen in females, often with physiologic changes in the endometrium that recur at regular intervals during the reproductive years.

nodes.label: pollen tube reception
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines pollen tube reception as: An interaction between the pollen tube, part of the male gametophyte, and the female gametophyte (typically the synergid cells), that results in the arrest of pollen tube growth, rupture of the pollen tube and the release of the sperm cells.

nodes.label: agglutination involved in conjugation with cellular fusion
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines agglutination involved in conjugation with cellular fusion as: The aggregation or adhesion of compatible mating types via complementary cell-cell interactions during conjugation with cellular fusion of a unicellular organism. An example of this process is agglutination in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

nodes.label: socially cooperative development
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines socially cooperative development as: The process whose specific outcome is the progression of a non-reproductive fruiting body over time, from its formation to the mature structure. A non-reproductive fruiting body is a colonial multicellular structure consisting of co-operating unicellular organisms, some of which are spores. An example of such a process is found in Dictyostelium discoideum and Myxococcus xanthus colonies.

nodes.label: olfactory sociosexual communication
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines olfactory sociosexual communication as: The use of external chemical cues called pheromones to send social and sexual information between members of the same species, leading to specific behavioral responses. Pheromones may be detected by two olfactory sensory circuits, the main olfactory pathway and the vomeronasal system.

nodes.label: flocculation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines flocculation as: The reversible, non-sexual aggregation of single-celled organisms in suspension to form aggregates of many cells known as flocs.

nodes.label: single-species biofilm formation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines single-species biofilm formation as: A process in which planktonically growing microorganisms of the same species grow at a liquid-air interface or on a solid substrate under the flow of a liquid and produce extracellular polymers that facilitate matrix formation, resulting in a change in the organisms' growth rate and gene transcription.

nodes.label: pollen tube adhesion
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines pollen tube adhesion as: The process in which the pollen tube adheres to cells of the stigma and style.

nodes.label: anatomical structure formation involved in morphogenesis
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines anatomical structure formation involved in morphogenesis as: The developmental process pertaining to the initial formation of an anatomical structure from unspecified parts. This process begins with the specific processes that contribute to the appearance of the discrete structure and ends when the structural rudiment is recognizable. An anatomical structure is any biological entity that occupies space and is distinguished from its surroundings. Anatomical structures can be macroscopic such as a carpel, or microscopic such as an acrosome.

nodes.label: anatomical structure morphogenesis
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines anatomical structure morphogenesis as: The process in which anatomical structures are generated and organized. Morphogenesis pertains to the creation of form.

nodes.label: myxococcal fruiting body development
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines myxococcal fruiting body development as: The process whose specific outcome is the progression of the myxococcal fruiting body over time, from its formation to the mature structure. The process begins when myxococci respond to a lack of nutrients in the environment and ends when the myxococcal fruiting body is a mature structure.

nodes.label: anatomical structure arrangement
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines anatomical structure arrangement as: The process that gives rise to the configuration of the constituent parts of an anatomical structure. This process pertains to the physical shaping of a rudimentary structure. Anatomical structures can be macroscopic such as a carpel, or microscopic such as an acrosome.

nodes.label: developmental induction
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines developmental induction as: A developmental process involving two tissues in which one tissue (the inducer) produces a signal that directs cell fate commitment of cells in the second tissue (the responder).

nodes.label: sporulation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines sporulation as: The process whose specific outcome is the progression of a spore over time, from its initiation to the mature structure. A spore is a structure that can be used for dissemination, for survival of adverse conditions because of its heat and desiccation resistance, and/or for reproduction.

nodes.label: meristem initiation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines meristem initiation as: Initiation of a region of tissue in a plant that is composed of one or more undifferentiated cells capable of undergoing mitosis and differentiation, thereby effecting growth and development of a plant by giving rise to more meristem or specialized tissue.

nodes.label: dormancy process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines dormancy process as: A developmental process in which dormancy (sometimes called a dormant state) is induced, maintained or broken. Dormancy is a suspension of most physiological activity and growth that can be reactivated.

nodes.label: age-related resistance
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines age-related resistance as: An innate immune response that is positively correlated with host plant development. As a plant develops, its innate resistance to pathogenic infections increases. The mechanisms involved in age-related resistance differ in nature or in aspects of regulation from the hypersensitive response (HR), systemic acquired resistance (SAR), or induced systemic resistance (ISR).

nodes.label: plant organ senescence
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines plant organ senescence as: A plant organ developmental process during which a plant dismantles cellular components to reclaim the cellular building blocks and nutrients that have been deposited in the plant organs during growth.

nodes.label: anatomical structure regression
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines anatomical structure regression as: The developmental process in which an anatomical structure is destroyed as a part of its normal progression.

nodes.label: acquisition of mycelium reproductive competence
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines acquisition of mycelium reproductive competence as: A maturation process by which an organism acquires the ability to reproduce. In fungi, reproductive competence only occurs in a population of filamentous cells that form a mycelium.

nodes.label: developmental maturation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines developmental maturation as: A developmental process, independent of morphogenetic (shape) change, that is required for an anatomical structure, cell or cellular component to attain its fully functional state.

nodes.label: abscission
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines abscission as: The controlled shedding of a body part.

nodes.label: anatomical structure development
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines anatomical structure development as: The biological process whose specific outcome is the progression of an anatomical structure from an initial condition to its mature state. This process begins with the formation of the structure and ends with the mature structure, whatever form that may be including its natural destruction. An anatomical structure is any biological entity that occupies space and is distinguished from its surroundings. Anatomical structures can be macroscopic such as a carpel, or microscopic such as an acrosome.

nodes.label: spore-bearing structure formation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines spore-bearing structure formation as: The process of generating a spore-bearing structure. A spore-bearing structure is an anatomical structure that produces new spores.

nodes.label: dedifferentiation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines dedifferentiation as: The process in which a specialized structure (cell, tissue or organ) loses structural or functional features that characterize it in the mature organism, or some other relatively stable phase of the organism's life history. Under certain conditions, these structures can revert back to the features of their ancestors.

nodes.label: acquisition of seed longevity
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines acquisition of seed longevity as: The acquisition of seed longevity is the ordered series of events during seed development, that prevent embryo deterioration and ROS damage and thus contribute to seed viability over time or in response to adverse environmental conditions. These events include protective (e.g. production of glassy cytoplasm ) and repair (e.g. oxidative stress responses) processes.

nodes.label: innervation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines innervation as: The process in which a nerve invades a tissue and makes functional synaptic connection within the tissue.

nodes.label: megagametogenesis
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines megagametogenesis as: The process whose specific outcome is the progression of the embryo sac over time, from its formation as the megaspore to the mature structure. The process begins when three of the four haploid megaspores disintegrate, and the fourth undergoes mitosis giving rise to a binucleate syncytial embryo sac. The two haploid nuclei migrate to the opposite poles of the embryo sac and then undergo two rounds of mitosis generating four haploid nuclei at each pole. One nucleus from each set of four migrates to the center of the cell. Cellularization occurs, resulting in an eight-nucleate seven-celled structure. This structure contains two synergid cells and an egg cell at the micropylar end, and three antipodal cells at the other end. A binucleate endosperm mother cell is formed at the center.

nodes.label: multicellular organismal-level extracellular fluid acidification
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines multicellular organismal-level extracellular fluid acidification as: Any process that reduces the pH of an extracellular fluid of a multicellular organism, corresponding to an increase in hydrogen ion concentration.

nodes.label: ossification
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines ossification as: The formation of bone or of a bony substance, or the conversion of fibrous tissue or of cartilage into bone or a bony substance.

nodes.label: amyloid-beta clearance
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines amyloid-beta clearance as: The process in which amyloid-beta is removed from extracellular brain regions by mechanisms involving cell surface receptors.

nodes.label: otolith tethering
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines otolith tethering as: The attachment of a developing otolith to the kinocilia of tether cells in the inner ear.

nodes.label: pigment accumulation in tissues
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines pigment accumulation in tissues as: The aggregation of coloring matter in a particular location in a tissue, occurring in response to an external stimulus.

nodes.label: vibrational conductance of sound to the inner ear
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines vibrational conductance of sound to the inner ear as: The transmission of vibrations via ossicles to the inner ear.

nodes.label: midbrain-hindbrain boundary maturation during brain development
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines midbrain-hindbrain boundary maturation during brain development as: A developmental process occurring after the brain has been specified along the neural axis that is required for the midbrain-hindbrain boundary to attain its fully functional state. The midbrain-hindbrain domain of the embryonic brain is comprised of the mesencephalic vesicle and the first rhombencephalic vesicle at early somitogenesis stages. An organizing center at the boundary patterns the midbrain and hindbrain primordia of the neural plate.

nodes.label: muscle attachment
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines muscle attachment as: The developmental process in which a skeletal muscle attaches to its target (such as bone or body wall).

nodes.label: plasma lipoprotein particle organization
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines plasma lipoprotein particle organization as: A protein-lipid complex subunit organization process that results in the formation, disassembly, or alteration of a plasma lipoprotein particle. A plasma lipoprotein particle is a spherical particle with a hydrophobic core of triglycerides and/or cholesterol esters, surrounded by an amphipathic monolayer of phospholipids, cholesterol and apolipoproteins.

nodes.label: coagulation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines coagulation as: The process in which a fluid solution, or part of it, changes into a solid or semisolid mass.

nodes.label: system process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines system process as: A multicellular organismal process carried out by any of the organs or tissues in an organ system. An organ system is a regularly interacting or interdependent group of organs or tissues that work together to carry out a biological objective.

nodes.label: pupariation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines pupariation as: The onset of prepupal development when the larval stops crawling, everts its spiracles and the larval cuticle becomes the puparium or pupal case that surrounds the organism for the duration of metamorphosis.

nodes.label: meristem determinacy
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines meristem determinacy as: The process in which a meristem becomes determinate (i.e. ceases to produce lateral organs and may or may not terminally differentiate).

nodes.label: microgametogenesis
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines microgametogenesis as: The process whose specific outcome is the progression of the pollen grain over time, from its formation as the microspore to the mature structure.

nodes.label: neurotrophin production
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines neurotrophin production as: The appearance of a neurotrophin due to biosynthesis or secretion by cells in a neuron's target field, resulting in an increase in its intracellular or extracellular levels. A neurotrophin is any of a family of growth factors that prevent apoptosis in neurons and promote nerve growth.

nodes.label: multicellular organism growth
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines multicellular organism growth as: The increase in size or mass of an entire multicellular organism, as opposed to cell growth.

nodes.label: post-embryonic development
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines post-embryonic development as: The process whose specific outcome is the progression of the organism over time, from the completion of embryonic development to the mature structure. See embryonic development.

nodes.label: pollen germination
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines pollen germination as: The physiological and developmental changes that occur in a heterosporous plant pollen grain, beginning with hydration and terminating with the emergence of the pollen tube through the aperture.

nodes.label: seed dormancy process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines seed dormancy process as: A dormancy process in which dormancy (sometimes called a dormant state) is induced, maintained or broken in a seed. Seed dormancy is a suspension of most physiological activity and growth in a seed, including the embryo contained therein, that can be reactivated. It often requires special conditions for reactivation, such as specific temperature, scarification, or leaching of inhibitors.

nodes.label: callus formation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines callus formation as: The process by which a callus is formed at a wound site. A plant callus is a portion of plant tissue that consists of mass of undifferentiated plant cells. It consists primarily of parenchyma cells but possibly contains other cell types as the callus begins to differentiate.

nodes.label: stem cell population maintenance
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines stem cell population maintenance as: The process by which an organism or tissue maintains a population of stem cells of a single type. This can be achieved by a number of mechanisms: stem cell asymmetric division maintains stem cell numbers; stem cell symmetric division increases them; maintenance of a stem cell niche maintains the conditions for commitment to the stem cell fate for some types of stem cell; stem cells may arise de novo from other cell types.

nodes.label: multicellular organism development
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines multicellular organism development as: The biological process whose specific outcome is the progression of a multicellular organism over time from an initial condition (e.g. a zygote or a young adult) to a later condition (e.g. a multicellular animal or an aged adult).

nodes.label: polyphenic determination
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines polyphenic determination as: The process in which individuals that have the potential to develop any of several possible distinct developmental paths have their individual developmental fates determined in response to environmental and/or genetic cues.

nodes.label: determination of adult lifespan
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines determination of adult lifespan as: The pathways that regulate the duration of the adult phase of the life-cycle of an animal.

nodes.label: meristem maintenance
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines meristem maintenance as: Any process involved in maintaining the identity, size and shape of a meristem.

nodes.label: tissue remodeling
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines tissue remodeling as: The reorganization or renovation of existing tissues. This process can either change the characteristics of a tissue such as in blood vessel remodeling, or result in the dynamic equilibrium of a tissue such as in bone remodeling.

nodes.label: multicellular organismal movement
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines multicellular organismal movement as: Any physiological process involved in changing the position of a multicellular organism or an anatomical part of a multicellular organism.

nodes.label: tissue migration
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines tissue migration as: The process in which the population of cells that make up a tissue undergo directed movement.

nodes.label: digestion
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines digestion as: The whole of the physical, chemical, and biochemical processes carried out by multicellular organisms to break down ingested nutrients into components that may be easily absorbed and directed into metabolism.

nodes.label: photoreceptor cell maintenance
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines photoreceptor cell maintenance as: Any process preventing the degeneration of the photoreceptor, a specialized cell type that is sensitive to light.

nodes.label: multi-multicellular organism process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines multi-multicellular organism process as: A multicellular organism process which involves another multicellular organism of the same or different species.

nodes.label: bud dormancy process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines bud dormancy process as: A dormancy process in which dormancy (sometimes called a dormant state) is induced, maintained or broken in a bud. Bud dormancy is a suspension of most physiological activity and growth that can be reactivated. It may be a response to environmental conditions such as seasonality or extreme heat, drought, or cold. The exit from bud dormancy is marked by the resumed growth of the bud.

nodes.label: multicellular organism adhesion
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines multicellular organism adhesion as: The attachment of a multicellular organism to a substrate or other organism.

nodes.label: production of molecular mediator involved in inflammatory response
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines production of molecular mediator involved in inflammatory response as: The synthesis or release of any molecular mediator of the inflammatory response following an inflammatory stimulus, resulting in an increase in its intracellular or extracellular levels.

nodes.label: sleep
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines sleep as: Any process in which an organism enters and maintains a periodic, readily reversible state of reduced awareness and metabolic activity. Usually accompanied by physical relaxation, the onset of sleep in humans and other mammals is marked by a change in the electrical activity of the brain.

nodes.label: multicellular organismal-level homeostasis
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines multicellular organismal-level homeostasis as: Any process involved in the maintenance of an internal steady state at the level of the multicellular organism.

nodes.label: pseudocleavage
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines pseudocleavage as: Partial constriction of the cytoplasm of a cell to form a furrow that resembles a cleavage furrow but does not complete cytokinesis.

nodes.label: morphogenesis of a branching structure
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines morphogenesis of a branching structure as: The process in which the anatomical structures of branches are generated and organized. A branch is a division or offshoot from a main stem. Examples in animals would include blood vessels, nerves, lymphatics and other endothelial or epithelial tubes.

nodes.label: keratinization
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines keratinization as: The process in which the cytoplasm of the outermost cells of the vertebrate epidermis is replaced by keratin. Keratinization occurs in the stratum corneum, feathers, hair, claws, nails, hooves, and horns.

nodes.label: midbrain-hindbrain boundary maturation during neural plate development
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines midbrain-hindbrain boundary maturation during neural plate development as: A developmental process occurring before the brain has been specified along the neural axis that is required for the midbrain-hindbrain boundary to attain its fully functional state. The midbrain-hindbrain domain of the embryonic brain is comprised of the mesencephalic vesicle and the first rhombencephalic vesicle at early somitogenesis stages. An organizing center at the boundary patterns the midbrain and hindbrain primordia of the neural plate.

nodes.label: organism emergence from protective structure
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines organism emergence from protective structure as: The developmental process in which an organism emerges from a surrounding protective structure such as an egg or pupa case.

nodes.label: transcytosis
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines transcytosis as: The directed movement of endocytosed material through the cell and its exocytosis from the plasma membrane at the opposite side.

nodes.label: pattern specification process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines pattern specification process as: Any developmental process that results in the creation of defined areas or spaces within an organism to which cells respond and eventually are instructed to differentiate.

nodes.label: pupation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines pupation as: The act of becoming a pupa, a resting stage in the life cycle of organisms with complete metamorphosis. This event marks the end of the prepupal period and the beginning of the pupal period.

nodes.label: molting cycle
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines molting cycle as: The periodic casting off and regeneration of an outer covering of cuticle, feathers, hair, horns, skin, etc.

nodes.label: molting cycle process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines molting cycle process as: A multicellular organismal process involved in the periodic casting off and regeneration of an outer covering of cuticle, feathers, hair, horns, skin.

nodes.label: scab formation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines scab formation as: Formation of hardened covering (a scab) at a wound site. The scab has multiple functions including limiting blood loss, providing structural stability to the wound and guarding against infection.

nodes.label: organ growth
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines organ growth as: The increase in size or mass of an organ. Organs are commonly observed as visibly distinct structures, but may also exist as loosely associated clusters of cells that function together as to perform a specific function.

nodes.label: seed germination
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines seed germination as: The physiological and developmental changes that occur in a seed commencing with water uptake (imbibition) and terminating with the elongation of the embryonic axis.

nodes.label: plasma lipoprotein particle clearance
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines plasma lipoprotein particle clearance as: The process in which a lipoprotein particle is removed from the blood via receptor-mediated endocytosis and its constituent parts degraded.

nodes.label: cytokine production
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cytokine production as: The appearance of a cytokine due to biosynthesis or secretion following a cellular stimulus, resulting in an increase in its intracellular or extracellular levels.

nodes.label: biological process involved in symbiotic interaction
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines biological process involved in symbiotic interaction as: A process carried out by gene products in an organism that enable the organism to engage in a symbiotic relationship, a more or less intimate association, with another organism. The various forms of symbiosis include parasitism, in which the association is disadvantageous or destructive to one of the organisms; mutualism, in which the association is advantageous, or often necessary to one or both and not harmful to either; and commensalism, in which one member of the association benefits while the other is not affected. However, mutualism, parasitism, and commensalism are often not discrete categories of interactions and should rather be perceived as a continuum of interaction ranging from parasitism to mutualism. In fact, the direction of a symbiotic interaction can change during the lifetime of the symbionts due to developmental changes as well as changes in the biotic/abiotic environment in which the interaction occurs. Microscopic symbionts are often referred to as endosymbionts.

nodes.label: hematophagy
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines hematophagy as: A feeding behavior that involves the ingestion of blood. Hematophagous animals have mouth parts and chemical agents for penetrating vascular structures in the skin of hosts. To overcome natural hemostasis, vasoconstriction, inflammation, and pain sensation in the host, hematophagous animals pre-inject chemical substances with anesthetic and/or anticoagulant properties.

nodes.label: formation of structure involved in a symbiotic process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines formation of structure involved in a symbiotic process as: The progression of an organism from an initial condition to a later condition, occurring when the organism is in a symbiotic interaction.

nodes.label: disruption of anatomical structure in another organism
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines disruption of anatomical structure in another organism as: The disruption of an anatomical structure of another organism, leading to damage or temporary subversion of that structure.

nodes.label: modulation of process of another organism
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines modulation of process of another organism as: A process in which an organism effects a change in a biological process in another organism.

nodes.label: nitric oxide storage
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines nitric oxide storage as: The accumulation and maintenance in cells or tissues of nitric oxide (NO). Nitric oxide is stored in the form of dinitrosyl-iron complexes, which are stabilized, and possibly sequestered, by binding to glutathione S-transferase proteins.

nodes.label: organelle localization
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines organelle localization as: Any process in which an organelle is transported to, and/or maintained in, a specific location.

nodes.label: macromolecule localization
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines macromolecule localization as: Any process in which a macromolecule is transported to, or maintained in, a specific location.

nodes.label: receptor localization to synapse
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines receptor localization to synapse as: Any process in which a receptor is transported to, and/or maintained at the synapse, the junction between a nerve fiber of one neuron and another neuron or muscle fiber or glial cell.

nodes.label: chemical homeostasis
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines chemical homeostasis as: Any biological process involved in the maintenance of an internal steady state of a chemical.

nodes.label: cellular homeostasis
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cellular homeostasis as: Any process involved in the maintenance of an internal steady state at the level of the cell.

nodes.label: detoxification of free heme
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines detoxification of free heme as: Any process that reduces or removes the toxicity of free heme. These include transport of heme away from sensitive areas and to compartments or complexes whose purpose is sequestration of heme.

nodes.label: toxin catabolic process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines toxin catabolic process as: The chemical reactions and pathways resulting in the breakdown of toxin, a poisonous compound (typically a protein) that is produced by cells or organisms and that can cause disease when introduced into the body or tissues of an organism.

nodes.label: mycothiol-dependent detoxification
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines mycothiol-dependent detoxification as: The chemical reactions using mycothiol to convert an alkylating agent to an S-conjugate of mycothiol. The latter is cleaved to release mercapturic acid which is excreted from the cell.

nodes.label: detoxification of nitrogen compound
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines detoxification of nitrogen compound as: Any process that reduces or removes the toxicity of nitrogenous compounds which are dangerous or toxic. This includes the aerobic conversion of toxic compounds to harmless substances.

nodes.label: detoxification of inorganic compound
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines detoxification of inorganic compound as: Any process that reduces or removes the toxicity of inorganic compounds. These include transport of such compounds away from sensitive areas and to compartments or complexes whose purpose is sequestration of inorganic compounds.

nodes.label: detoxification of endogenously produced metabolite
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines detoxification of endogenously produced metabolite as: A process that reduces or removes the toxicity of an endogenously produced substance. Mechanisms of resistance to endogenously produced compounds include modification the compound, export, sequestration, or mutations in the target enzyme.

nodes.label: detoxification of arsenic-containing substance
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines detoxification of arsenic-containing substance as: Any process that reduces or removes the toxicity of compounds containing arsenic, including arsenates, arsenites, and arsenides. These include transport of such compounds away from sensitive areas and to compartments or complexes whose purpose is sequestration of arsenic or arsenic-containing compounds.

nodes.label: viral capsid
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral capsid as: The protein coat that surrounds the infective nucleic acid in some virus particles. It comprises numerous regularly arranged subunits, or capsomeres.

nodes.label: viral capsid, internal space
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral capsid, internal space as: The region of a virus contained within the capsid shell, and usually containing the viral genome and accessory proteins.

nodes.label: virion nucleoid
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines virion nucleoid as: The region of a virion in which the nucleic acid is confined.

nodes.label: virion membrane
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines virion membrane as: The lipid bilayer surrounding a virion.

nodes.label: viral nucleocapsid
