nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral nucleocapsid as: The complete protein-nucleic acid complex that is the packaged form of the genome in a virus particle.

nodes.label: viral inner capsid
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral inner capsid as: The inner layer of a double or triple concentric icosahedral capsid. Inner capsids are part of reoviridae and cystoviridae virions.

nodes.label: viral outer capsid
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral outer capsid as: The outer layer of a double or triple concentric icosahedral capsid. Outer capsids are part of reoviridae and cystoviridae virions.

nodes.label: viral intermediate capsid
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral intermediate capsid as: The intermediate layer of a triple concentric icosahedral capsid. Intermediate capsids are part of reoviridae virions.

nodes.label: virus tail, shaft
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines virus tail, shaft as: The tube of the non-contractile tails of some viruses.

nodes.label: virus tail, sheath
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines virus tail, sheath as: The external contractile envelope of the tail of some viruses. Its contraction ensures ejection of the virus DNA into the host cytoplasm.

nodes.label: icosahedral viral capsid, spike
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines icosahedral viral capsid, spike as: A short structure attached to an icosahedral virion capsid, and used for attachment to the host cell.

nodes.label: virus tail, fiber
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines virus tail, fiber as: The fibrous region of the virus tail used to scan, recognize and attach to the host cell.

nodes.label: viral procapsid
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral procapsid as: A stable empty viral capsid produced during the assembly of viruses.

nodes.label: virus tail, tip
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines virus tail, tip as: The basal end of the virus tail, which is used by the virus to attach to the host cell.

nodes.label: viral tegument
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral tegument as: A structure lying between the capsid and envelope of a virus, varying in thickness and often distributed asymmetrically.

nodes.label: capsomere
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines capsomere as: Any of the protein subunits that comprise the closed shell or coat (capsid) of certain viruses.

nodes.label: virus tail, tube
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines virus tail, tube as: The internal tube of the tail of some viruses. The virus tail tube is the channel for DNA ejection into the host cytoplasm.

nodes.label: virus tail
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines virus tail as: Part of the virion that may be used to recognize, attach and inject the viral genome and accessory proteins into the host cell.

nodes.label: virus tail, baseplate
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines virus tail, baseplate as: Multiprotein component at the distal (head) end of the virus tail to which fibers of tailed viruses may be attached.

nodes.label: icosahedral viral capsid, collar
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines icosahedral viral capsid, collar as: A small disk located at the base of some icosahedral virus capsids.

nodes.label: icosahedral viral capsid, neck
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines icosahedral viral capsid, neck as: A region of constriction located below the head and above the tail sheath of viruses with contractile tails (Myoviridae).

nodes.label: viral capsid, decoration
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral capsid, decoration as: Component of the virus capsid (head), located on the outer head surface. Involved in the stabilization of the head structure and usually non-essential.

nodes.label: viral membrane
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral membrane as: The lipid bilayer of a virion, a complete fully infectious extracellular virus particle.

nodes.label: bacterial-type flagellum filament
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines bacterial-type flagellum filament as: The long (approximately 20 nm), thin external structure of the bacterial-type flagellum, which acts as a propeller.

nodes.label: A band
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines A band as: The dark-staining region of a sarcomere, in which myosin thick filaments are present; the center is traversed by the paler H zone, which in turn contains the M line.

nodes.label: actin filament branch point
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines actin filament branch point as: The part of an actin filament where the structure forks.

nodes.label: apoplast
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines apoplast as: The cell membranes and intracellular regions in a plant are connected through plasmodesmata, and plants may be described as having two major compartments: the living symplast and the non-living apoplast. The apoplast is external to the plasma membrane and includes cell walls, intercellular spaces and the lumen of dead structures such as xylem vessels. Water and solutes pass freely through it.

nodes.label: etioplast prolamellar body
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines etioplast prolamellar body as: A three dimensional regular lattice found in etioplasts. It is composed of a continuous system of tubules but when exposed to light the symmetrical arrangement is rapidly lost as tubules become pinched off into two dimensional sections of lattice. These for perforated sheets of membrane that move apart, extend and increase, finally establishing the typical granal and intergranal lamellae of the mature chloroplast.

nodes.label: postsynaptic endocytic zone
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines postsynaptic endocytic zone as: A stably positioned site of clathrin adjacent and physically attached to the postsynaptic specialization, which is the site of endocytosis of post-synaptic proteins.

nodes.label: cytosol
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cytosol as: The part of the cytoplasm that does not contain organelles but which does contain other particulate matter, such as protein complexes.

nodes.label: intracellular immature spore
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines intracellular immature spore as: A cell or part of the cell that constitutes an early developmental stage of a spore, a small reproductive body that is highly resistant to desiccation and heat and is capable of growing into a new organism, produced especially by certain bacteria, fungi, algae, and nonflowering plants.

nodes.label: lysosomal glycocalyx
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines lysosomal glycocalyx as: The polysaccharide-based coating on the inner side of a lysosomal membrane. It may be involved in protecting the membrane from digestion by lysosomal enzymes.

nodes.label: bacterial-type flagellum basal body, MS ring
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines bacterial-type flagellum basal body, MS ring as: One of the rings of the bacterial-type flagellar basal body; a double-flanged ring that anchors the basal body to the cytoplasmic membrane.

nodes.label: distal axon
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines distal axon as: That part of an axon close to and including the growth cone or the axon terminus.

nodes.label: ciliary cap
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines ciliary cap as: An intracellular compartmentalized cilium structure found in insect spermatids which is bounded by a membrane derived from the invagination of the cell membrane that remains associated with the primary cilium as it is internalized. The ciliary cap is maintained at the end of the axoneme distal to the centriole and is separated from the cytosolic axoneme/cytoplasm by a putative transition zone, which may extend into the ciliary cap, and include a structure at the base of the ciliary cap termed the ring centriole.

nodes.label: dense nuclear body
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines dense nuclear body as: A location in the host cell nucleus where viral proteins colocalize late in infection prior to the onset of viral DNA synthesis. More than one site can be present simultaneously.

nodes.label: M band
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines M band as: The midline of aligned thick filaments in a sarcomere; location of specific proteins that link thick filaments. Depending on muscle type the M band consists of different numbers of M lines.

nodes.label: photoreceptor inner segment
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines photoreceptor inner segment as: The inner segment of a vertebrate photoreceptor containing mitochondria, ribosomes and membranes where opsin molecules are assembled and passed to be part of the outer segment discs.

nodes.label: surface coat of collagen and cuticulin-based cuticle extracellular matrix
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines surface coat of collagen and cuticulin-based cuticle extracellular matrix as: An electron dense, amorphous envelope that comprises the outermost layer of the cuticle. The surface coat is loosely apposed to the epicuticle, has distinct biochemical properties, is synthesized by cells other than the underlying hypodermis, and is labile. In addition to serving as a lubricant to protect against abrasion and dehydration, the surface coat may also play important roles in infection and immune evasion. An example of this component is found in Caenorhabditis elegans.

nodes.label: bacterial-type flagellum secretion apparatus
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines bacterial-type flagellum secretion apparatus as: A part of the bacterial-type flagellum that is located at the cytoplasmic side of the MS ring and composed of six membrane proteins (FlhA, FlhB, FliP, FliQ, FliR, and FliO, or orthologs thereof) and three soluble proteins (FliI, FliH, and FliJ, or orthologs thereof) in the cytoplasm. It is responsible for secretion of flagellar type III protein substrates, including the proteins of the flagellar rod, hook, and filament.

nodes.label: neuron projection branch point
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines neuron projection branch point as: The location where a secondary projection arises from a neuron projection.

nodes.label: photoreceptor outer segment
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines photoreceptor outer segment as: The outer segment of a vertebrate photoreceptor that contains a stack of membrane discs embedded with photoreceptor proteins.

nodes.label: germ tube
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines germ tube as: The slender tubular outgrowth first produced by most spores in germination.

nodes.label: mating projection base
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines mating projection base as: The region where the mating projection meets the bulk of the cell, in unicellular fungi exposed to mating pheromone.

nodes.label: lateral plasma membrane
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines lateral plasma membrane as: The portion of the plasma membrane at the lateral side of the cell. In epithelial cells, lateral plasma membranes are on the sides of cells which lie at the interface of adjacent cells.

nodes.label: nexine
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines nexine as: The inner, non-sculptured part of the exine which lies below the sexine.

nodes.label: mitochondrial membrane scission site
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines mitochondrial membrane scission site as: The site on the mitochondrial membrane where the separation of a single continuous mitochondrial membrane into two membranes occurs as a final step in mitochondrial fission.

nodes.label: ventral disc crossbridge
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines ventral disc crossbridge as: Structure horizontally linking adjacent microribbons of the ventral disc in Giardia species (trophozoite stage). The composition of crossbridges is not fully known yet.

nodes.label: extracellular region
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines extracellular region as: The space external to the outermost structure of a cell. For cells without external protective or external encapsulating structures this refers to space outside of the plasma membrane. This term covers the host cell environment outside an intracellular parasite.

nodes.label: cortical dynamic polarity patch
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cortical dynamic polarity patch as: A region of the cell cortex that contains a higher concentration of growth polarity factors than the surrounding cortex and that changes position over time. An example is found in fission yeast cells during early mating, in which the GTPase Cdc42 dynamically to discrete zones within the cortex prior to shmoo formation.

nodes.label: cell trailing edge membrane
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cell trailing edge membrane as: The portion of the plasma membrane surrounding the trailing edge of a motile cell.

nodes.label: granular component
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines granular component as: A structure found in the nucleolus, which contains nearly completed preribosomal particles destined for the cytoplasm.

nodes.label: distal portion of axoneme
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines distal portion of axoneme as: The portion of the axoneme that is close to the tip of the cilium.

nodes.label: mitochondrial crista
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines mitochondrial crista as: Any of the inward folds of the mitochondrial inner membrane. Their number, extent, and shape differ in mitochondria from different tissues and organisms. They appear to be devices for increasing the surface area of the mitochondrial inner membrane, where the enzymes of electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation are found. Their shape can vary with the respiratory state of the mitochondria.

nodes.label: dinoflagellate apex
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines dinoflagellate apex as: The anterior most point of a dinoflagellate epicone.

nodes.label: extrahaustorial matrix
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines extrahaustorial matrix as: The space between the symbiont plasma membrane and the extrahaustorial membrane of the host.

nodes.label: nuclear envelope adjacent to nuclear pore complex
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines nuclear envelope adjacent to nuclear pore complex as: The region of the nuclear envelope situated in close proximity to a nuclear pore complex.

nodes.label: preprophase band
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines preprophase band as: A dense band of microtubules, 1-3 pm wide, that appears just beneath the cell membrane before the start of cell division in the cells of higher plants. It precedes the onset of prophase and then disappears as mitosis begins, yet it somehow determines the plane of orientation of the new cell plate forming in late telophase and marks the zone of the parental cell wall where fusion with the growing cell plate ultimately occurs.

nodes.label: left lateral basal body pair
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines left lateral basal body pair as: Set of two basal bodies found in Giardia species (trophozoite stage). It comprises the anterior and ventral basal bodies located to the right of the left nucleus of the trophozoite when viewed dorsally.

nodes.label: C zone
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines C zone as: A region of the A band in which myosin-binding protein C is located and that can be seen by electron microscopy. This is a functional zone that also includes myosin.

nodes.label: ascus epiplasm
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines ascus epiplasm as: Ascus cytoplasm that is not packaged into ascospores.

nodes.label: mitochondrial inner boundary membrane
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines mitochondrial inner boundary membrane as: The portion of the mitochondrial inner membrane that is not invaginated to form cristae. The inner boundary membrane lies parallel to the outer membrane.

nodes.label: spindle matrix
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines spindle matrix as: A proteinaceous, nuclear-derived structure that embeds the microtubule spindle apparatus from pole to pole in a microtubule-independent manner during mitosis.

nodes.label: prospore membrane spindle pole body attachment site
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines prospore membrane spindle pole body attachment site as: The region of the prospore membrane to which the spindle pole body (SPB) is anchored; the prospore membrane extends from the SPB attachment site to surround the spore nucleus.

nodes.label: cytosolic region
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cytosolic region as: Any (proper) part of the cytosol of a single cell of sufficient size to still be considered cytosol.

nodes.label: epicuticle of collagen and cuticulin-based cuticle extracellular matrix
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines epicuticle of collagen and cuticulin-based cuticle extracellular matrix as: A lipid-containing layer of cuticle that lies between the cortical layer and the surface coat. An example of this component is found in Caenorhabditis elegans.

nodes.label: immunological synapse
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines immunological synapse as: An area of close contact between a lymphocyte (T-, B-, or natural killer cell) and a target cell formed through the clustering of particular signaling and adhesion molecules and their associated membrane rafts on both the lymphocyte and the target cell and facilitating activation of the lymphocyte, transfer of membrane from the target cell to the lymphocyte, and in some situations killing of the target cell through release of secretory granules and/or death-pathway ligand-receptor interaction.

nodes.label: nuclear lamina
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines nuclear lamina as: The fibrous, electron-dense layer lying on the nucleoplasmic side of the inner membrane of a cell nucleus, composed of lamin filaments. The polypeptides of the lamina are thought to be concerned in the dissolution of the nuclear envelope and its re-formation during mitosis. The lamina is composed of lamin A and lamin C filaments cross-linked into an orthogonal lattice, which is attached via lamin B to the inner nuclear membrane through interactions with a lamin B receptor, an IFAP, in the membrane.

nodes.label: endexine
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines endexine as: The inner part of the exine, which stains.

nodes.label: kinetoplast
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines kinetoplast as: A sub-structure within the large single mitochondrion of kinetoplastid parasites and which is closely associated with the flagellar pocket and basal body of the flagellum.

nodes.label: medial membrane band
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines medial membrane band as: A sterol-rich region of the plasma membrane which forms at the cell surface overlying the contractile ring and spreads into the invaginating plasma membrane surrounding the septum.

nodes.label: ventral disc supernumerary microtubule array
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines ventral disc supernumerary microtubule array as: A partial left-handed spiral array of microtubules that lies generally dorsal to the main ventral disc microtubule array in Giardia species (trophozoite stage).

nodes.label: T-tubule
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines T-tubule as: Invagination of the plasma membrane of a muscle cell that extends inward from the cell surface around each myofibril. The ends of T-tubules make contact with the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane.

nodes.label: myelin sheath adaxonal region
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines myelin sheath adaxonal region as: The region of the myelin sheath nearest to the axon.

nodes.label: spermatid residual body
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines spermatid residual body as: A membrane-bounded, anucleate mass of cytoplasm that is separated from one or more developing male germ cells during spermatogenesis and discarded. The residual body receives most of the cytoplasm and organelles not required by the spermatid or spermatozoon, such as ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi, and excess cytoskeletal components, and is subsequently degraded, typically by phagocytosis by somatic cells of the gonad (e.g. Sertoli cells in vertebrates, gonadal sheath cells in nematodes) or by extrusion into the reproductive tract.

nodes.label: leading edge membrane
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines leading edge membrane as: The portion of the plasma membrane surrounding the leading edge of a motile cell.

nodes.label: mitotic nuclear bridge midzone membrane domain
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines mitotic nuclear bridge midzone membrane domain as: A nuclear membrane part at the midzone of the mitotic nuclear bridge. The midzone forms a bulge that is enriched in nuclear pores that lack baskets.

nodes.label: dense fibrillar component
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines dense fibrillar component as: A structure found in the nucleolus, which contains newly synthesized preribosomal RNA (pre-rRNA) and a collection of proteins.

nodes.label: bacterial-type flagellum hook-filament junction
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines bacterial-type flagellum hook-filament junction as: The region of the bacterial-type flagellum where the hook and filament meet.

nodes.label: inner dense plaque of desmosome
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines inner dense plaque of desmosome as: The desmosomal part containing the C-termini of desmoplakins which interact with the keratin intermediate filaments, serving to tether the intermediate filaments to the plasma membrane.

nodes.label: I band
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines I band as: A region of a sarcomere that appears as a light band on each side of the Z disc, comprising a region of the sarcomere where thin (actin) filaments are not overlapped by thick (myosin) filaments; contains actin, troponin, and tropomyosin; each sarcomere includes half of an I band at each end.

nodes.label: virus-like capsid
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines virus-like capsid as: A protein coat that surrounds nucleic acid to form a structure similar to a virus capsid. Virus-like capsids are non-infectious and are encoded by endogenous (non-viral) genes. Fly and tetrapod Arc (ancestrally-related to retrotransposon Gag) are examples of proteins that can self-assemble into capsid-like structures which encapsulate Arc mRNA and mediate the intercellular transmission of RNA.

nodes.label: endomembrane system
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines endomembrane system as: A collection of membranous structures involved in transport within the cell. The main components of the endomembrane system are endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi bodies, vesicles, cell membrane and nuclear envelope. Members of the endomembrane system pass materials through each other or though the use of vesicles.

nodes.label: organelle
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines organelle as: Organized structure of distinctive morphology and function. Includes the nucleus, mitochondria, plastids, vacuoles, vesicles, ribosomes and the cytoskeleton, and prokaryotic structures such as anammoxosomes and pirellulosomes. Excludes the plasma membrane.

nodes.label: axon hillock
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines axon hillock as: Portion of the neuronal cell soma from which the axon originates.

nodes.label: longitudinal sarcoplasmic reticulum
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines longitudinal sarcoplasmic reticulum as: The portion of the free sarcoplasmic reticulum consisting of longitudinal tubules that connect terminal cisternae.

nodes.label: DNA replication termination region
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines DNA replication termination region as: A chromosomal region that contains fork pausing elements influencing the progression and merging of DNA replication forks.

nodes.label: cell projection
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cell projection as: A prolongation or process extending from a cell, e.g. a flagellum or axon.

nodes.label: bacterial-type flagellum basal body, C ring
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines bacterial-type flagellum basal body, C ring as: Cytoplasmic ring located at the base of the bacterial-type flagellar basal body; acts as a rotor; includes three switch proteins, which generate torque and can change their conformational state in a bimodal fashion, so that the motor direction can switch between clockwise and counterclockwise.

nodes.label: mitotic actomyosin contractile ring, proximal layer
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines mitotic actomyosin contractile ring, proximal layer as: The region of the mitotic actomyosin ring adjacent to the plasma membrane where membrane bound scaffolds are located.

nodes.label: dityrosine layer of spore wall
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines dityrosine layer of spore wall as: The outermost layer of the spore wall, as described in Saccharomyces.

nodes.label: fibrillar center
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines fibrillar center as: A structure found most metazoan nucleoli, but not usually found in lower eukaryotes; surrounded by the dense fibrillar component; the zone of transcription from multiple copies of the pre-rRNA genes is in the border region between these two structures.

nodes.label: lysosomal matrix
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines lysosomal matrix as: A matrix composed of supramolecular assemblies of lysosomal enzymes and lipids which forms at a pH of 5.0 within the lysosome.

nodes.label: ventral disc microtubule array
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines ventral disc microtubule array as: A part of the ventral disc of Giardia species (trophozoite stage) consisting of a spiral array of microtubules linked to the ventral membrane. These microtubules form the base of the ventral disc dorsal microribbons that extend nearly perpendicular from the membrane.

nodes.label: foot layer
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines foot layer as: The inner layer of the ectexine.

nodes.label: reservosome membrane
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines reservosome membrane as: The lipid bilayer surrounding a reservosome.

nodes.label: central region of growth cone
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines central region of growth cone as: The center of the migrating motile tip of a growing nerve cell axon or dendrite.

nodes.label: smooth endoplasmic reticulum cisterna
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines smooth endoplasmic reticulum cisterna as: A subcompartment of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum consisting of lumenal expansion into a flattened, disc-shaped cavity.

nodes.label: sperm head-tail coupling apparatus
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines sperm head-tail coupling apparatus as: A centrosome-based structure consisting of two cylindrical microtubule-based centrioles and associated components which anchors the flagellum to the sperm head.

nodes.label: ventral surface of cell
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines ventral surface of cell as: The surface of a migrating cell that is in contact with the substratum or cell layer.

nodes.label: satellite fibril
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines satellite fibril as: An axoneme part that is found in the flagella of mammalian sperm and is located in the middle piece between the outer dense fibers (on the concave side of outer dense fibers as seen in cross-section).

nodes.label: bacterial-type flagellum filament cap
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines bacterial-type flagellum filament cap as: The proteinaceous structure at the distal tip of the bacterial-type flagellar filament.

nodes.label: H zone
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines H zone as: A relatively pale zone traversing the center of the A band of a sarcomere, visible in relaxed muscle fibers; consists of the central portion of thick (myosin) filaments that are not overlapped by thin (actin) filaments.

nodes.label: basal labyrinth
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines basal labyrinth as: A region in the lower half of some cells formed from extensive infoldings of the basal plasma membrane; includes cytoplasm adjacent to the infolded membrane.

nodes.label: granum
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines granum as: Distinct stack of lamellae seen within chloroplasts. Grana contain the pigments, electron transfer compounds, and enzymes essential to the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.

nodes.label: perikaryon
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines perikaryon as: The portion of the cell soma (neuronal cell body) that excludes the nucleus.

nodes.label: phagocytic cup
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines phagocytic cup as: An invagination of the cell membrane formed by an actin dependent process during phagocytosis. Following internalization it is converted into a phagosome.

nodes.label: organelle membrane contact site
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines organelle membrane contact site as: A zone of apposition between the membranes of an organelle with another membrane, either another membrane of the same organelle, a membrane of another organelle, or the plasma membrane. Membrane contact sites (MCSs) are structured by bridging complexes. They are specialized for communication, including the efficient traffic of small molecules such as Ca2+ ions and lipids, as well as enzyme-substrate interactions.

nodes.label: ring centriole
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines ring centriole as: A ring-like structure observed at the base of the ciliary cap of insect spermatids. This structure may anchor the axoneme to the ciliary cap membrane and/or act as a diffusion barrier, proposed to be analogous to the annulus of mammalian sperm flagellum.

nodes.label: site of polarized growth
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines site of polarized growth as: Any part of a cell where non-isotropic growth takes place.

nodes.label: synaptic cleft
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines synaptic cleft as: The narrow gap that separates the presynaptic and postsynaptic membranes, into which neurotransmitter is released.

nodes.label: perinuclear region of cytoplasm
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines perinuclear region of cytoplasm as: Cytoplasm situated near, or occurring around, the nucleus.

nodes.label: synaptonemal structure
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines synaptonemal structure as: A proteinaceous scaffold found between homologous chromosomes during meiosis.

nodes.label: actomyosin
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines actomyosin as: Any complex of actin, myosin, and accessory proteins.

nodes.label: nucleoplasm
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines nucleoplasm as: That part of the nuclear content other than the chromosomes or the nucleolus.

nodes.label: mucus layer
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines mucus layer as: An extracellular region part that consists of a protective layer of mucus secreted by epithelial cells lining tubular organs of the body such as the colon or secreted into fluids such as saliva. Mucus is a viscous slimy secretion consisting of mucins (i.e. highly glycosylated mucin proteins) and various inorganic salts dissolved in water, with suspended epithelial cells and leukocytes.

nodes.label: chitosan layer of spore wall
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines chitosan layer of spore wall as: The second outermost layer of the spore wall, as described in Saccharomyces.

nodes.label: ventral disc dorsal microribbon
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines ventral disc dorsal microribbon as: Trilaminar structure extending perpendicularly into the cytoplasm along the length of ventral disc microtubules in Giardia species (trophozoite stage). Constituents of dorsal microribbons (also called dorsal ribbons or microribbons) include alpha-coiled-helix proteins approximately 29 to 38 kDa in size. These proteins line the edges of the microribbons but are not found in microtubules. Tubulins are not found in microribbons.

nodes.label: reservosome matrix
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines reservosome matrix as: A matrix composed of planar membranes, vesicles and lipid inclusions within the reservosome.

nodes.label: peripheral region of growth cone
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines peripheral region of growth cone as: The non-central region or periphery of the migrating motile tip of a growing nerve cell axon or dendrite.

nodes.label: centrosomal core
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines centrosomal core as: The core region of the centrosome, a layered structure containing proteins, surrounded by the centrosomal corona. The core duplicates once per cell cycle at the G2/M transition when two outer layers form the mitotic spindle poles.

nodes.label: cell division site
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cell division site as: The eventual plane of cell division (also known as cell cleavage or cytokinesis) in a dividing cell. In Eukaryotes, the cleavage apparatus, composed of septin structures and the actomyosin contractile ring, forms along this plane, and the mitotic, or meiotic, spindle is aligned perpendicular to the division plane. In bacteria, the cell division site is generally located at mid-cell and is the site at which the cytoskeletal structure, the Z-ring, assembles.

nodes.label: extracellular core region of desmosome
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines extracellular core region of desmosome as: The desmosomal part containing the desmosomal cadherins, desmogleins and desmocollins, that establish contact and adhere to neighboring cells in a Ca2+-dependent manner.

nodes.label: unicellular trichome branch
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines unicellular trichome branch as: A cell projection part that is a branch of a unicellular trichome.

nodes.label: mitotic nuclear bridge stalk
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines mitotic nuclear bridge stalk as: Either of the regions of a mitotic nuclear bridge proximal to the main portion of each daughter nucleus. The nuclear envelope in the stalk regions is depleted of nuclear pore complexes.

nodes.label: cone matrix sheath
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cone matrix sheath as: A biochemically and structurally distinct domain of the retinal interphotoreceptor matrix that is specifically associated with cone photoreceptor cell inner and outer segments.

nodes.label: bacterial-type flagellum hook
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines bacterial-type flagellum hook as: The portion of the bacterial-type flagellum that connects the filament to the basal body.

nodes.label: actin body
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines actin body as: An amorphous cytoskeletal structure consisting of aggregated actin filaments and associated proteins (including fibrin and capping protein) in which there is little or no actin filament turnover. In yeast (S. pombe and S. cerevisiae) these are found only in quiescent cells and are thought to serve as a reserve store of actin.

nodes.label: sarcomere
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines sarcomere as: The repeating unit of a myofibril in a muscle cell, composed of an array of overlapping thick and thin filaments between two adjacent Z discs.

nodes.label: starch grain
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines starch grain as: Plant storage body for amylose and amylopectin, 1-100um in diameter. Also contains small amounts of enzymes, amino acids, lipids and nucleic acids. The shape of the grain varies widely amongst species, but is often spherical or disk-shaped.

nodes.label: nucleoplasmic periphery of the nuclear pore complex
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines nucleoplasmic periphery of the nuclear pore complex as: Nucleoplasm situated in close proximity and peripheral to a nuclear pore complex.

nodes.label: cluster of actin-based cell projections
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cluster of actin-based cell projections as: A cell part consisting of multiple, closely packed actin-based cell projections.

nodes.label: sperm fibrous sheath
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines sperm fibrous sheath as: A cytoskeletal structure surrounding the axoneme and outer dense fibers of the sperm flagellum. Consists of two longitudinal columns connected by closely arrayed semicircular ribs that assemble from distal to proximal throughout spermiogenesis. The fibrous sheath probably influences the degree of flexibility, plane of flagellar motion, and the shape of the flagellar beat.

nodes.label: Schmidt-Lanterman incisure
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines Schmidt-Lanterman incisure as: Regions within compact myelin in which the cytoplasmic faces of the enveloping myelin sheath are not tightly juxtaposed, and include cytoplasm from the cell responsible for making the myelin. Schmidt-Lanterman incisures occur in the compact myelin internode, while lateral loops are analogous structures found in the paranodal region adjacent to the nodes of Ranvier.

nodes.label: subpellicular network
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines subpellicular network as: A mechanically stable cytoskeletal structure associated with the cytoplasmic face of the pellicle and surrounding the microtubule-based cytoskeleton.

nodes.label: dinoflagellate hypocone
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines dinoflagellate hypocone as: The part of a dinoflagellate cell below the cingulum; also referred to as the posterior portion of a dinoflagellate cell. It is separated from the epicone by the cingulum.

nodes.label: chromatin
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines chromatin as: The ordered and organized complex of DNA, protein, and sometimes RNA, that forms the chromosome.

nodes.label: intercellular bridge
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines intercellular bridge as: A direct connection between the cytoplasm of two cells that is formed following the completion of cleavage furrow ingression during cell division. They are usually present only briefly prior to completion of cytokinesis. However, in some cases, such as the bridges between germ cells during their development, they become stabilised.

nodes.label: ciliary pocket collar
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines ciliary pocket collar as: A constriction site at the junction of the plasma, flagellar and flagellar pocket membranes where the flagellum emerges from the cell body. Observed in some unicellular eukaryotic species such as Chlamydomonas, Giardia and Trypanosoma.

nodes.label: axonemal central bridge
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines axonemal central bridge as: Part of the 9+2 axoneme, that occurs in most motile cilia, consisting of the two bridges which connect the central pair of single microtubules.

nodes.label: annular furrow extracellular matrix
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines annular furrow extracellular matrix as: The extracellular matrix part that is a regularly spaced indentation in the outer cortical layer of the cuticle. The pattern of annular furrows corresponds to sites of invaginations in hypodermal cell membranes that, in turn, correspond to submembranous regions where actin microfilament bundles assemble early in lethargus, the first phase of the molting cycle in which activity and feeding decline.

nodes.label: half bridge of spindle pole body
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines half bridge of spindle pole body as: Structure adjacent to the plaques of the spindle pole body.

nodes.label: religious concepts
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines religious concepts as: Ideas and notions that are fundamentally religious.

nodes.label: philosophical concepts
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines philosophical concepts as: Concepts related to knowledge, learning, and scholarship.

nodes.label: Styles and Periods Facet
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Styles and Periods Facet as: Includes the names of art and architecture styles, historical periods, art movements, cultures, and ethnicities. Names of people and sites are included if they designate distinct styles or periods. Examples: Yoruba, Louis XIV, Aztec, German, Neolithic.

nodes.label: book history
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines book history as: Research into the evolution of the book and its variants (pamphlets, newspapers, broadsheets) in all aspects of its production, dissemination and consumption in relation to literary, political, economical, social and religious history. The history of the book includes subjects such as the production of manuscripts in medieval scriptoria, authorship, printing techniques, economic aspects of printing and publishing, design, printshops and publishing houses, trade, ownership and reading culture, typography, typesetting and printing techniques, and book collecting and connoisseurship. Use " literary history" Use “literary history” for the study of literary trends and movements.

nodes.label: literary studies
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines literary studies as: Discipline dealing with the written and oral verbal works of a nation, region, period, or language, of a particular group or individual, of a particular form or genre, on a particular subject, or for a particular audience. For written works on a particular subject, use "literature (documents)." For the written works of a particular individual or group of individuals, use "writings (documents)." For the genre of liturature rather than the discipline that studies it, use "literature (genre)." Use "book history" for the study of the trade, production, and consumption of books as physical objects.

nodes.label: museology
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines museology as: The theory and practice of the organization, administration, functions, and technical processes of museums, including documentation and collections management, as well as their history, philosophy, and purposes.

nodes.label: paper history
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines paper history as: Study of the origin and evolution of paper as a product and material: paper production, paper trade, the management of papermills and paper factories, raw materials, and the cultural importance of paper as an information carrier.

nodes.label: auspicia
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines auspicia as: In ancient Roman religion, the signs of the gods that were inscribed in nature and meant to be deciphered. Auspicia were seen as affirmative or negative answers to proposed courses of action. Auspicia often came from the sky as thunder, lightning, and different kinds of birds although there were other kinds as well. Public auspicia were taken by magistrates or augurs in the sacred space of the templum.

nodes.label: biblical
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines biblical as: Of, relating to, or contained in the Bible, which contains the sacred scriptures of Judaism or Christianity.

nodes.label: blasphemy
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines blasphemy as: An irreverent or impious act, attitude, or utterance regarding something considered inviolable or sacrosanct, particularly something concerning God.

nodes.label: cultism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines cultism as: Having to do with the formation or following of a cult, which is a religious group having beliefs that differ significantly from dominant or orthodox religions or society.

nodes.label: divine judgment
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines divine judgment as: Actions and status of a dvinity's retributive justice by which the destiny of people or other creatures is decided, typically according to their merits and demerits.

nodes.label: doctrinal concepts
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines doctrinal concepts as: Religious concepts related to doctrine.

nodes.label: Dreaming, the
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Dreaming, the as: A fundamental concept of Australian aboriginal religion that refers to a mythological period of time before living memory when the world was shaped and humanized by the actions of mythic ancestral beings. Some of these beings were in human or animal (totemic) form while others changed their form. They were responsible for creating the different types of plants and animals, including humans, as well as for establishing local social order and laws to live by. In aboriginal belief, these ancestors are spiritually as much alive today as they ever were. As a belief system, the Dreaming includes totemism: man is regarded as part of nature, not fundamentally different from his mythic ancestors or from animals, all of which share a common life force. This connection is often made visible through the use of totem figures.

nodes.label: heresy
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines heresy as: Theological or religious opinion or doctrine maintained in opposition to the official or orthodox doctrine of a given church, creed, or religious system.

nodes.label: monasticism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines monasticism as: A form of religious life that emphasizes the perfection of the individual through immersion in a consecrated community or, more rarely, through a solitary and ascetic existence. Monasticism is found in both Buddhism and Christianity, particularly in the Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches. Although it began as a lay movement in Christianity, clergy soon came to dominate and it began to involve voluntary poverty and a life devoted to worship. The rule of Benedict was the most important early monastic legislation and it became the standard of Western Christian monasticism. The mendicant orders, which combined monastic life with missionary work and preaching, were created in the 13th century. Scholarship was emphasized in some medieval monastic systems, which led to important religious research and manuscripts.

nodes.label: private devotion
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines private devotion as: The psychological process of experiencing devotional feelings in a private sphere, whether or not encouraged by the church authorities, often with the aid of texts, figurines or images.

nodes.label: rabbinical
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines rabbinical as: Of, relating to, or characteristic of the teachings of rabbis that constitute the Talmud.

nodes.label: religious ideologies
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines religious ideologies as: Organized bodies of ideas and attitudes having to do with religion, which is broadly defined as belief systems that encompass various personal and institutional relationships between human beings and what they regard as holy, sacred, or divine, usually but not always a deity, or a spiritual or occult force.

nodes.label: worship
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines worship as: The reverent love and allegiance accorded a deity, idol, or sacred object, often expressed through ceremonies, prayers, or other religious rituals.

nodes.label: aesthetic concepts
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines aesthetic concepts as: Concepts related to perception of what is ideal or beautiful.

nodes.label: betrayal
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines betrayal as: Violation of trust or confidence or an abandonment of something committed to one's charge, such as a revelation or divulging of something which it is desirable to keep secret or a treacherous giving up to an enemy.

nodes.label: cosmos
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines cosmos as: An ordered and harmonious system that comprises the world or universe.

nodes.label: evil
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines evil as: The state of a person or situation of being morally depraved, bad, wicked, or vicious. The antithesis of "good."

nodes.label: fate
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines fate as: The principle, power, or agency by which, according to certain philosophical and popular systems of belief, all events, or some events in particular, are unalterably predetermined from eternity.

nodes.label: fortitude
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines fortitude as: Moral strength or courage, unyielding courage, endurance of pain or adversity.

nodes.label: fortune
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines fortune as: Chance or luck, when regarded as a cause of events and changes in human affairs.

nodes.label: hope
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines hope as: The expectation of something desired.

nodes.label: hózhó
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines hózhó as: Philosophical concept central to Navajo aesthetics and culture. Advocates for individuals to be balanced and in harmony with other spiritual and material aspects of Navajo life (landscape, community, etc.) In Navajo material culture and art, beauty is achieved through this balance. This concept can be seen expressed in textiles and pottery through their balanced compositions and in sandpainting in its illustrations of interconnected, harmonious relationships between people, animals, spirits, and the land. Also is applied to contemporary art made by Navajo artists.

nodes.label: ideology
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines ideology as: Any organized body of ideas and attitudes, especially about the structure and working of human society, that comprehends a program of practical political and social action and is more or less institutionalized or shared with others. Originally used for a branch of knowledge dealing with the history and nature of ideas.

nodes.label: ignorance
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines ignorance as: The fact or condition of lacking knowledge or awareness, either generally or about a particular thing.

nodes.label: immortality
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines immortality as: In philosophical and religious traditions, the concept of or belief in the continued existence of a material thing into infinity, or of the existance of an immaterial soul or mind beyond the physical death of the body.

nodes.label: inventiveness
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines inventiveness as: The quality, faculty, or aptitude for creating unique solutions to problems, or of inventng new things, language, art, etc.

nodes.label: metaphysical concepts
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines metaphysical concepts as: Philosophical concepts that deal with the nature of reality.

nodes.label: morality
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines morality as: Ethical wisdom, knowledge, or qualities, as evidenced in behavior conforming to moral law or accepted moral standards, particularly in relation to sexual matters or personal qualities judged to be good.

nodes.label: prudence
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines prudence as: Concept concerning the ability to recognize and follow the most suitable or sensible course of action, utilizing good sense, discretion, circumspection, caution.

nodes.label: survival
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines survival as: The state or fact of the continuance of anything after the end of other like things within the same context, as after some event. The persistence of a living thing, custom, or observance, after the circumstances or conditions in which it originated or which gave significance to it have ceased.

nodes.label: truth
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines truth as: A property of beliefs, propositions, and linguistic statements, being that they conform with fact or agree with reality.

nodes.label: vengeance
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines vengeance as: The act or condition of inflicting retributive injury or punishment in retaliation for an injury or offense.

nodes.label: wisdom
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines wisdom as: Accumulated learning and soundness of judgment in the choice of means and ends.

nodes.label: world
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines world as: The state or realm of existence, particularly of the physical.

nodes.label: theater arts
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines theater arts as: Broad discipline concerning drama, dance, critical studies, and theater design/technology; a professionally-oriented study of theater, that involves training, practice, and study in the processes of doing theater.

nodes.label: electronic music
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines electronic music as: Music in which sound is generated, transferred, triggered, or amplified by electronic devices. The creation of electronic music may involve the use of magnetic tape or digital technology and whose reproduction involves the use of loudspeakers. For works created with only natural sound sources recorded and manipulated via discs or magnetic tape use "musique concrète." For music created entirely through the use of a computer, in which the sound is initiated purely through digital means, use "computer music."

nodes.label: jazz
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines jazz as: Music, often improvisational, originally developed around the turn of the 20th century by African Americans from elements of blues and ragtime, with syncopated rhythms and a European harmonic structure. Jazz consistently evolved throughout the 20th century with numerous phases, from a New Orleans style or swing, to "free jazz," for example, which emerged in the late 1950s. Therefore, jazz itself has no precise definition, however it has rarely been a completely composed music.

nodes.label: musical theater
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines musical theater as: Genre of theatrical performance that combines songs, spoken dialogue, acting, and dance.

nodes.label: rhythm and blues
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines rhythm and blues as: Any of various kinds of popular music typically having a strong rhythm and featuring a horn section. Originally and principally associated with African-American performers, particularly a style prominent during the late 1940s and 1950s derived from or influenced by the blues and jazz.

nodes.label: serial music
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines serial music as: A structural principle for musical composition used since the early 20th century in which a series or set of elements are used repeatedly.

nodes.label: myths
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines myths as: Individual stories derived from a mythology; distinguished from historical accounts in that they are considered by current scholars to lack a determinable basis of fact or natural explanation; typically concerning a being, hero, deity, or event and explains some practice, rite, or phenomenon of nature.

nodes.label: arts-related disciplines
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines arts-related disciplines as: Branches of learning devoted to the arts.

nodes.label: linguistics
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines linguistics as: Scientific study of language as a system, covering the structure, sounds, and meaning, as well as the history of the relations of languages to each other and the cultural place of language in human behavior.

nodes.label: linguistics-related disciplines
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines linguistics-related disciplines as: Branches of learning and professions related to linguistics.

nodes.label: comparative literature
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines comparative literature as: The study of similar literary works from two or more nations, periods, or languages in relation to each other, or the study of any literary phenomenon from the perspective of at least two literatures.

nodes.label: literary criticism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines literary criticism as: The discipline of describing, interpreting, and evaluating literary works, including the exposition of principles, methods, and theories for the analysis of such works.

nodes.label: literary history
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines literary history as: Study of literary trends and movements over time, as well as the development of various branches or genres of literature.

nodes.label: poetics
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines poetics as: The theory, art, or study of the nature and function of poetry and with identifying and describing its types, forms, and techniques.

nodes.label: museography
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines museography as: Refers to museum methods of classification, description and display of objects; the practical application of the body of theory known as museology.

nodes.label: museum administration
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines museum administration as: The study and practice of the administration of museums.

nodes.label: aesthetics
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines aesthetics as: Appreciation or criticism of the beautiful. The term refers to a branch of Western philosophy concerned primarily with the fine arts, although it may also be used in the context of the appreciation of natural beauty. Usage of the term dates from the 18th century, although historical discussions regarding issues now called "aesthetics" date from Antiquity.

nodes.label: axiology
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines axiology as: Study of values, primarily of intrinsic values (as those in ethics, aesthetics, and religion), but also of instrumental values (as those in economics), particularly with reference to the manner in which they can be known or experienced, their nature and kinds, and their ontological status.

nodes.label: epistemology
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines epistemology as: Branch of philosophy that studies the nature, origin, limits, and validity of human knowledge.

nodes.label: phenomenology
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines phenomenology as: Branch of modern philosophy dealing with the description and classification of phenomena.

nodes.label: philosophy of art
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines philosophy of art as: The study of the nature of art, including interpretation, representation, expression, and form. It is closely related to "aesthetics," which is the philosophical study of beauty.

nodes.label: teleology
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines teleology as: Philosophical study of finality, especially as it pertains to design or purposes in the processes of nature.

nodes.label: religion-related disciplines
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines religion-related disciplines as: Branches of learning devoted to religion.

nodes.label: absolution
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines absolution as: A declaration of forgiveness of sins. In Christianity it refers specifically to the formal remission of sin imparted by a priest or minister either in private after confession or as part of the liturgy in public worship. In Catholicism it is part of the sacrament of penance.

nodes.label: afterlife
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines afterlife as: The idea of survival of a person in some form after physical death. This notion is present in a wide variety of forms in different religions.

nodes.label: apotheosis
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines apotheosis as: Doctrinal concept concerning the spiritual departure from earthly life or the deification of a person.

nodes.label: ascension
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines ascension as: The act or process of rising from the earthly to the heavenly sphere. One example is Christ's ascension witnessed by the apostles forty days after his resurrection. Another prime example is the ascent of the Prophet Muhammad to heaven.

nodes.label: Buddhist doctrinal concepts
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Buddhist doctrinal concepts as: Concepts related to the doctrine of Buddhism.

nodes.label: Christian doctrinal concepts
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Christian doctrinal concepts as: Concepts related to the doctrine of Christianity.

nodes.label: Cihuatlampan
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Cihuatlampan as: Place of women, referring to the western horizon where the Cihuateteoh carry the sun as it sets into Mictlan (the land of the dead).

nodes.label: divine light
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines divine light as: Light emanating from a holy personage or visions of supernatural light in general. Usually associated with Christ or the Virgin, and specifically the Transfiguration and the Ascension. For motifs based on the concept of divine light, use "glories."

nodes.label: eternity
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines eternity as: Infinite time, which has neither beginning nor end.

nodes.label: faith
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines faith as: Act or state of wholeheartedly and steadfastly believing in the existence, power and benevolence of a supreme being.

nodes.label: gates of hell
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines gates of hell as: Entrances to the underworld as known in any of various religions and belief systems. The gates of hell may be either apprehended in a material sense to correspond to caves or other places on earth, or conceived of in only an abstract or spiritual sense.

nodes.label: heaven
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines heaven as: Place or state of eternal bliss and ideal relationship with God or the gods, usually accorded as the reward for virtue and true religious faith.

nodes.label: Hindu doctrinal concepts
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Hindu doctrinal concepts as: Concepts related to the doctrine of Hinduism.

nodes.label: Jain doctrinal concepts
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Jain doctrinal concepts as: Concepts related to the doctrine of Jainism.

nodes.label: Mazahuahcan
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Mazahuahcan as: Refers to the conception of the west.

nodes.label: Mictlampan
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Mictlampan as: Reference to the North. In the context of Aztec mythology, Mictlampan is associated with Mictlantecuhtli, the god of the dead.

nodes.label: purgatory
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines purgatory as: State or place of spiritual cleansing and purification, allowing a purging of sins. A notable example is in the doctrine of the Roman Catholic Church, where it is defined as a state where the souls of those who die in grace undergo such punishment as necessary to expiate their unforgiven venial sins before entering heaven.

nodes.label: redemption
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines redemption as: Expiation or atonement for a crime, sin, or offence, including a release from punishment. In theology, deliverance from sin and damnation by atonement or, in Christianity, by the salvation of Christ.

nodes.label: reincarnation
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines reincarnation as: The doctrinal concept that some aspect of the self or soul can be reborn any number of times in a new body (animal or human) after death. Fundamental to a number of Eastern religions such as Hinduism and Buddhism, this belief is also found in some modern Western belief systems such as theosophy.

nodes.label: salvation
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines salvation as: The doctrinal concept of the deliverance of man or his soul from evil or sin by religious means, the restoration of people to their true state, and the attainment of eternal and blessed life. God's intervention is responsible for salvation in theistic religions while in Buddhism salvation comes from escaping the cycle of birth and rebirth, thereby reaching nirvana.

nodes.label: theophany
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines theophany as: The doctrinal concept of divine manifestation, especially the appearance of a god to a human.

nodes.label: Tlalocan
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Tlalocan as: In Nahuatl, Tlalocan used as a reference to the East, refers mainly to a place of Tlalocs.

nodes.label: Adoptionism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Adoptionism as: Christian doctrine that Jesus of Nazareth became the son of God by exaltation that was not his at birth.

nodes.label: agnosticism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines agnosticism as: Doctrine affirming that the existence of God is possible, but denying that there are any sufficient reasons for holding either that God does or does not exist.

nodes.label: animism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines animism as: Refers to the belief in spiritual beings capable of influencing human events, based on the idea that animals, plants and even inanimate objects have souls like humans. The 19th-century anthropologist Edward Tylor thought it to be the earliest form of religion, a view not accepted by modern anthropologists.

nodes.label: asceticism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines asceticism as: Refers to the practice of self-control and self-denial as an act of religious devotion and a means of achieving greater spiritual awareness; it is found in different forms and to different extents in all religions. Ascetic practices include fasting, a solitary life, meditation, celibacy, the renunciation of possessions, and the mortification of flesh.

nodes.label: atheism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines atheism as: Doctrine that there is neither God nor any other deity.

nodes.label: Deism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Deism as: Refers most often to the ideas of a heterogeneous religious movement of the late 17th and 18th centuries that flourished mainly in Britain. Deism also became very popular in 18th-century Germany. The movement was concerned with defending the rationality of religion and belief in God in the face of rising skepticism, especially as a consequence of Newton's laws. According to Deist writers, there exists a supreme being who initiated creation and is thus the basis of reality, but who does not intervene in the world and its natural laws (i.e. does not answer prayers or perform miracles). Nevertheless, Deism holds that religion is natural to humanity, and emphasizes natural religion as opposed to revealed religion or the teachings of churches. Natural religion comes from a certain body of religious knowledge that is inborn in everyone or that can be acquired through reason. Important Deist writings include Matthew Tindal's 'Christianity as Old as the Creation' (1730), the so-called 'Deist Bible.' Other important English Deists were Lord Herbert of Cherbury and Anthony Ashley Cooper.

nodes.label: Gnosticism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Gnosticism as: Refers to a religious ideology popular in the 4th-century Christian world although it may have had earlier, non-Christian roots stemming from a break from Judaism. The believers in Gnosticism felt that they alone would attain full salvation because they possessed the teachings of Christ regarding the cosmic origins and spiritual destiny of people. It was considered heretic because of its low view of God as Creator, its secret traditions, and its belief that Christ was not really human and that his crucifixion was simply an attempt to fool evil forces.

nodes.label: Hasidism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Hasidism as: Refers to a type of Jewish mysticism characterized by an ascetic lifestyle, strict observance of the commandments, and ecstatic forms of worship and prayer. Its origins are usually traced back to Poland in the late 18th century and it was developed in opposition to rabbinic authority and certain Jewish traditions. Hasidism emphasizes prayer as a means of communicating with God as opposed to study of the Torah. As Hasidism spread throughout the world, it was eventually accepted as part of Orthodox Judaism.

nodes.label: millenarianism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines millenarianism as: Refers to a Christian religious ideology usually based on an interpretation of Revelation 20. 1-7 which holds that there will be a thousand-year reign of the saints, either right before or after Christ's return. Millenarianism has had its followers since the early days of Christianity, but it became particularly popular in the 19th century, when groups such as the Plymouth Brethren and the Adventists embraced apocalyptic and millennial ideas. Recently the term has also been applied by social scientists to any religious group waiting for a sudden transformation of the world; such groups tend to become popular during times of social change or crisis.

nodes.label: monolatry
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines monolatry as: The worship of one god, particularly when it is recognized that other deities exist. In such a system, one god has a central and dominating position, although the principle of polytheism is not abandoned.

nodes.label: monotheism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines monotheism as: The religious ideology that there is only one god, as opposed to polytheism and pantheism. Whereas facets of earlier cultures, such as the Egyptians, worshipped one god, a full long-term doctrine of monotheism developed first within Judaism and it remains a central part of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. Muslims and Jews think that Christianity's belief in the three aspects of God, the Holy Trinity, denies monotheism.

nodes.label: Monothelitism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Monothelitism as: Religious doctrine proposed in 622 and adopted by Byzantine Emperor Heraclius which declared that Jesus Christ had one will but two natures, the divine and the human. This ideology was developed under Patriarch Sergius I of Constantinople in attempt to bridge the gap between Monophysites and Chalcedonians, although neither group accepted it. In 680, the Third Council of Constantinople declared Monothelitism as heretical.

nodes.label: paganism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines paganism as: Refers to the religious beliefs and practices of religions outside of the so-called 'major' religions. Pagans are sometimes defined as those who are not Christian, Jewish, or Muslim; occasionally the term is more narrowly used to described any non-Christian, sometimes even Jews.

nodes.label: pantheism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines pantheism as: Religious ideology based on the belief that God and the universe are ultimately identical, and therefore only the divine is real and sense experience is not. Pantheism is an important element of Hinduism and some schools of Buddhism.

nodes.label: Pietism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Pietism as: A religious ideology originally developed within Lutheranism in the 17th and 18th centuries as a reform movement and reaction against rigid Protestant dogmatism. Pietism emphasizes good works, study of the Bible, and devotion. It came to influence other movements and ideologies such as evangelicalism, Methodism, and Moravian Brethren.

nodes.label: polytheism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines polytheism as: The religious ideology that there are many gods, as opposed to monotheism. Polytheism is characteristic of primitive religions as well as the religions of ancient Greece and Rome.

nodes.label: quietism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines quietism as: Refers generally to the belief that God only works in a person who is completely quiet and passive; religious followers should therefore withdraw from the everyday world and suppress their will. It also refers more specifically to forms of Christian mysticism, particularly to trends in the Middle Ages and 17th-century controversies in Spain and France.

nodes.label: shamanism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines shamanism as: Refers generally to the religious practices of some northern Asian peoples who believe that good and evil spirits inhabit the world and can be summoned or heard through inspired priests acting as mediums. Shamanism is also found amongst the pre-Chrisitian Lapps, the Inuit, the Plains Indians of North America, some Australian Aborigines, and some other peoples. The term was originally used by the Tungus people of Siberia.

nodes.label: theosophy
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines theosophy as: Any religious or philosophic ideology based on mystical insight into the nature of God or divine truth. This insight is attained only through direct experience of the divine.

nodes.label: totemism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines totemism as: Complex of religious and social beliefs and practices whereby individuals or groups of people identify with or consider themselves to be in close kinship or spiritual affinity with a specific natural object or plant or animal species.

nodes.label: hagiolatry
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines hagiolatry as: The reverence, worship, or allegiance accorded individuals identified as saints, often expressed through ceremonies, prayers, or other religious rituals.

nodes.label: liturgy
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines liturgy as: Refers generally to the prescribed rites of formal and public worship, typically including words, music, symbolic aids, and ritual actions. The diverse forms of liturgy reflect the needs and attitudes of different religious communities. The term can also refer more specifically to the Christian rite of the Eucharist.

nodes.label: dian jing
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines dian jing as: Used in a garden context, this term refers to accentuating scenic spots. At key scenic points, steps are taken to augment their remarkable appearance. The surrounding structures often are given names related to details of the natural environs, or inscribed with poetry describing the essence of the scenery, thereby contributing details that enhance the aesthetic appeal of the location.

nodes.label: empathy
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines empathy as: The capacity for participating in, or a vicarious experiencing of, another's feelings, volitions, or ideas.

nodes.label: grandeur
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines grandeur as: The quality of being majestic, magnificent, splendid, stately, or imposing in an awe-inspiring way.

nodes.label: Ideal, the
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Ideal, the as: The aesthetic quality of the permanent, essential, or eternal character of appearances or other phenomena, which is rooted in an idea of perfection or archetype. It is ultimately derived from from Plato's "Theory of Ideas," which holds that perfection is a concept that is only mirrored imperfectly in real life. This perfection was the ideal to which artists sought to strive in certain periods, styles, or contexts. The concept was particularly evident in various periods of antique art, the Renaissance, and in the 17th- and 18th-century art academies throughout Europe.

nodes.label: imperfection
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines imperfection as: The state, quality, or condition of being inaccurate, incomplete, defective and/or displeasing in some way.

nodes.label: mimesis
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines mimesis as: Aesthetic concept that takes imitation as the primary operative aspect in the creation of a work.

nodes.label: perfection
