nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines perfection as: The state, quality, or condition of being accurate, complete, without defect and/or delightful.

nodes.label: Picturesque, the
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Picturesque, the as: Aesthetic concept or expression, arising in Europe first in painting of the 18th century and later in architecture of the 19th century, characterized by rough, curious, or irregular forms; it applies particularly to rustic landscapes and crumbling buildings having neither the awe-inspiring grandeur of the Sublime nor the order and regularity of beauty.

nodes.label: quality
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines quality as: Use in the context of aesthetic judgment for the concept of inherent merit, worthiness, or excellence in something. For the function of selecting quality standards for a project and monitoring the finished work to assure compliance with those standards, use "quality control."

nodes.label: sabi
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines sabi as: Aesthetic and poetic ideal particularly important in the Japanese tea ceremony and haiku poetry which advocates taking pleasure and finding tranquility in the old, tarnished and imperfect for their own sake. It is sometimes used synonymously or in conjunction with the concept of "wabi".

nodes.label: significant form
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines significant form as: Certain combinations of lines, colors, and spatial elements that excite pure aesthetic emotion; term coined by art critic Clive Bell.

nodes.label: Sublime, the
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Sublime, the as: The conception or expression of awe-inspiring grandeur in a work of art.

nodes.label: ugliness
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines ugliness as: That which evokes an awareness or feeling of deep revulsion or painfully disturbs a previously accepted aesthetic ideal. Can be considered as culturally defined or as an individual reaction.

nodes.label: wabi
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines wabi as: An aesthetic ideal advocating for the appreciation of austerity, simplicity, and humility that has deeply influenced Japanese culture. This ideal finds surpassing beauty and deep significance in what is humble or commonplace and appears natural or artless. It expressed in the aesthetic of the tea ceremony, particularly in its ceramics. Its influence can also be seen in the practice of collecting older paintings and works of calligraphy and, more recently, in the rough and natural style of contemporary grass style ink painting. Wabi became a part of a poetic ideal only when it was absorbed into the concept of "sabi".

nodes.label: social ethics
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines social ethics as: Ethics that have as their utilitarian end the well-being and fair treatment of the entire community.

nodes.label: bad luck
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines bad luck as: A combination of adverse circumstances or events occurring by chance; a person's apparent tendency to have ill fortune; misfortune.

nodes.label: good luck
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines good luck as: A combination of favorable circumstances or events occurring by chance; success, prosperity, or advantage apparently brought about by chance rather than through one's own actions or abilities.

nodes.label: chaos
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines chaos as: The state of utter confusion and disorder, where everything exists as an undifferentiated, formless mass or mixture. Derived from the original concept in ancient Greek cosmology, meaning the primevil emptiness of the universe before distinct entities came into being.

nodes.label: dialectic
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines dialectic as: Originally in ancient Greece, a form of logical argumentation proceeding by question and answer. In modern times it is the idea that internal contradictions are transcended, but then give rise to new contradictions that themselves must be resolved. As a concept of evolution, it applies to diverse fields including philosophy, nature, and history.

nodes.label: identity
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines identity as: Those characteristics or conditions of a thing, person, or group that remain the same amid change or that distinguish a thing, person, or group from another.

nodes.label: presence
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines presence as: Concept regarding the condition of being present in front of, or in the same place with a person or thing.

nodes.label: supernatural
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines supernatural as: Beyond or outside of the natural order. The term is typically used to refer to events or phenomena that are not explicable given the existing characterizations of nature. Occult phenomena and extrasensory perception are examples.

nodes.label: absurdism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines absurdism as: A philosophical movement or attitude associated with Albert Camus that posits that humanity's search for meaning is futile in a chaotic, senseless universe.

nodes.label: anthropomorphism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines anthropomorphism as: Interpretation of what is not human in terms of human characteristics.

nodes.label: Aristotelianism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Aristotelianism as: Philosophy incorporating essential features of the thinking of Aristotle.

nodes.label: Augustinianism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Augustinianism as: Refers to the philosophical and theological ideas and doctrines derived from the work of Augustine (354-430), bishop of Hippo, and associated with the Augustinian orders. The intellectual tradition of Augustinianism has been influential since the Middle Ages, when it developed. Augustine offered an optimistic ontology and an escape from skepticism. He also formulated a cosmic theory to account for the plurality of form in the world and to reconcile it with the uniqueness of God's creative act. Augustine also described the ultimate goal of human life as a life of beatitude combined with ethical-political concern. Primacy of faith, knowledge of the soul, divine illumination, and grace are all essential aspects of Augustinianism. Augustine believed that truth resided in man's soul and it was this truth alone that instructs man. This truth, the greatest proof of God's existence, confers joy and happiness. Augustine's speculation on the Trinity and predestination were also highly influential.

nodes.label: determinism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines determinism as: Doctrine that all acts of will result from causes which determine them either in such a manner that people have no alternative course of action, or that the will is still free in the sense of being uncompelled. Determinism holds that all behaviors and events are determined by God or by the laws of the universe before they occur. Determinism takes different forms in religions, but the basic issue is how to reconcile the omnipotence of God or the inevitable effects of karma with the freedom and resposibility of a individual person.

nodes.label: dualism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines dualism as: Doctrine that the universe is under the dominion of two opposing principles, one of which is good and the other evil.

nodes.label: globalism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines globalism as: The approach to social, cultural, scientific, ecological, or humanistic questions involving an orientation to the world as a single interacting system, and the placing of its interests above those of individual regions or nations. For the similar theory or belief discussed or applied specifically in the context of politics and political science, use "internationalism."

nodes.label: holism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines holism as: Theory according to which a whole cannot be analyzed without residue into the sum of its parts or reduced to discrete elements.

nodes.label: individualism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines individualism as: The ethical doctrine or principle that the interests of the individual are or ought to be paramount in determination of conduct.

nodes.label: nihilism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines nihilism as: Extreme form of skepticism that denies the objective reality of all values, beliefs, and truths.

nodes.label: nominalism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines nominalism as: Theory that there are no universal essences in reality, that the mind can frame no single concept or image corresponding to any universal or general term, and that only individual concrete entities have existence.

nodes.label: Platonism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Platonism as: Refers to the philosophy of Plato or to any philosophy inspired by Plato, especially to Plato's idea that the phenomena perceived by the senses are an imperfect and transitory reflection of the ideal forms of an unchanging and eternal reality. This absolute reality (or realities) gives value and meaning to everything's existence, particularly to human life.

nodes.label: pluralism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines pluralism as: Philosophical theory that recognizes more than one ultimate reality or value, each capable of rational support and all appropriately included as options for individual choice. For the cultural movement promoting the full participation of diverse ethnic, racial, religious, or social groups within the larger community, use "multiculturalism."

nodes.label: positivism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines positivism as: The philosophical doctrine of Auguste Comte and his successors. It asserts that knowledge of reality can be achieved only through the particular sciences and ordinary observation.

nodes.label: pragmatism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines pragmatism as: Philosophical movement, dominant in the United States during the first quarter of the 20th century, based on the principle that the usefulness, workability, and practicality of ideas, policies, and proposals are the criteria of their merit. It stresses the priority of action over doctrine, of experience over fixed principles, and it holds that ideas borrow their meanings from their consequences and their truths from their verification.

nodes.label: rasquachismo
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines rasquachismo as: Perspective, or sensibility of the underdog, or the view of the downtrodden. The term is used specifically within the Chicano and Chicano artist community, specifically for purposes of defining identity.

nodes.label: scholasticism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines scholasticism as: The philosophical systems and speculative tendencies of various Medieval Christian thinkers, who, working against a background of fixed religious dogma, sought to solve anew general philosophical problems (as of faith and reason, will and intellect, and the provability of the existence of God), initially under the influence of the mystical and intuitional tradition of patristic philosophy, and especially Augustinianism, and later under that of Aristotle.

nodes.label: stoicism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines stoicism as: A philosophical movement that flourished in Greek and Roman antiquity. Stoics have always believed that the goal of all inquiry is to provide humanity with a mode of conduct characterized by tranquility of mind and certainty of moral worth, and urged participation in the affairs of humankind. Thus, moral worth, duty, and justice are singularly Stoic emphases, together with a certain sternness of mind.

nodes.label: syncretism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines syncretism as: Reconciliation or union of conflicting (as religious) beliefs or an effort intending such.

nodes.label: transcendentalism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines transcendentalism as: A philosophic movement based on an idealistic belief in the essential unity of all things, the innate goodness of man, and the supremacy of insight over logic and experience in understanding reality and ascertaining truths. It is considered to be a part of the Romantic movement and had a powerful impact on the arts, particularly literature. The term generally refers to 19th-century transcendentalism in New England although the movement was found in other countries including Germany and England.

nodes.label: utilitarianism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines utilitarianism as: Doctrine that usefulness is the highest good and that the determining characteristic of right conduct should be the usefulness of its consequence.

nodes.label: choreography
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines choreography as: The aspect of the discipline of dance that involves inventing or arranging and putting together steps, gestures, and patterns to form dances, and separate dances to form a dance composition.

nodes.label: music theory
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines music theory as: Discipline involving the study of the theoretical aspects of music and its notation, typically as opposed to actual performance.

nodes.label: vocal arts
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines vocal arts as: Discipline involving the study of singing and other vocal expressions, including performance.

nodes.label: dramaturgy
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines dramaturgy as: Describes the discipline of theatrical or dramatic composition, representation, and research. English dramaturgy is derived from German Dramaturgie, a concept developed by the German dramatist and critic Gotthold Lessing in a series of essays entitled 'Hamburgische Dramaturgie,' published 1767 to 1769. The discipline includes researching, selection, adaptation, or development of texts, scripts, plays, operas, or films for a theater or other production company.

nodes.label: computer music
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines computer music as: Musical works not in a specific form or of a specific type in which sound is generated or composed solely by computers or other electronic data-processing machinery via software or other means.

nodes.label: granular synthesis
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines granular synthesis as: A method for generating sound involving the combination of tiny waveform fragments to create larger acoustic events. This is generally achieved with the use of digital computers.

nodes.label: musique concrète
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines musique concrète as: Musical works created by recording natural sounds and subsequently altering and rearranging them into a composition. The word "concrète" refers to the method of working directly with sound rather than a system of abstract musical notation. Originally recorded onto discs, these works were later realized with magnetic tape as the technology became available. Developed by the French composer Pierre Schaeffer and colleagues, including Pierre Henry, in the Club d'Essai and Groupe de Recherches Musicales at the Office de Radio-diffusion et Télévision Française ca. 1948. The term "musique concrète" is reserved for works created solely with naturally occurring sounds recorded onto disc or magnetic tape. For works created from sounds generated primarily by electronic synthesis, or using combinations of natural and synthesized sound, use "electronic music."

nodes.label: Noh
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Noh as: Important form of classical Japanese dance drama that has been performed since the 14th century. It is often based on stories from traditional literature with a supernatural being transformed into human form as a hero telling a story. Noh integrates masks, costumes and various props into a dance-based performance, Emotions are mainly conveyed through stylized conventional gestures.

nodes.label: twelve-tone music
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines twelve-tone music as: A body of musical compositions created since the early part of the 20th century created using the twelve-tone system attributed to Arnold Schoenberg. Generally twelve-tone music is considered a subset of serial music, but there is some disagreement on this.

nodes.label: architectural criticism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines architectural criticism as: The study or practice of the analytical description, interpretation, and evaluation of architectural works.

nodes.label: architectural history
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines architectural history as: Study of the development over time of the human built environment.

nodes.label: art criticism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines art criticism as: The study or practice of the analytical description, interpretation, and evaluation of visual art works and exhibitions.

nodes.label: art history
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines art history as: Study of the visual arts within a historical framework, from from prehistory to the present, including stylistic development, use of art in communication and decoration, and the aesthetic and intellectual value of art. It first became a dedicated field of study in the 19th century Western world.

nodes.label: art therapy
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines art therapy as: Study and practice of the therapeutic use of images and objects, to foster nonverbal communication, creativity, and physical interaction, and to uncover verbal associations and interpretations, helping to identify and understand patients' emotional, motor, and perceptual dysfunctions.

nodes.label: musicology
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines musicology as: Scientific and orderly investigation and study of music and related areas, including history, theory, music education, acoustics, psychology, and social and cultural aspects.

nodes.label: applied linguistics
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines applied linguistics as: Branch of linguistics where the primary concern is the application of linguistic theories, methods, and findings to practical language problems, such as language teaching, lexicography, translation, stylistics, and speech therapy.

nodes.label: theoretical linguistics
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines theoretical linguistics as: Branch of linguistics where the primary aim is to establish universal principles for the study of language and languages, and to determine the underlying structure and other characteristics of human language.

nodes.label: cryptography
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines cryptography as: The practice of writing in code or symbols.

nodes.label: cryptology
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines cryptology as: The discipline concerned with data communication and storage in secure and usually secret form, including the science, study, or practice of encrypting and decrypting information.

nodes.label: etymology
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines etymology as: Study of the history of a particular word or element of a word, or of historical linguistic change.

nodes.label: semiotics
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines semiotics as: Theory and study of signs and symbols dealing especially with their function in languages, including syntax, semantics, and pragmatics.

nodes.label: process philosophy
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines process philosophy as: Refers to the theistic philosophy that views creative becoming as the universal form of reality and emphasizes the relational nature of all being.

nodes.label: anthropology of religion
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines anthropology of religion as: Study of religion using the methods and theories of anthropology.

nodes.label: comparative religion
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines comparative religion as: Comparative study of the characteristics of religious systems in different societies that focuses on the origin and evolution of religious beliefs and practices from earlier or less urbanized societies to modern ones, aims to develop a universal evolutionary continuum of religions, and stresses a scientific methodology. For the comparative study of religions that largely disregards evolutionary schemes and features a primarily historical methodology, use "religious history."

nodes.label: philosophy of religion
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines philosophy of religion as: The philosophical study of religion, especially concerning the rationality of religious beliefs, and the descriptive analysis and elucidation of religious language, belief, and practice.

nodes.label: psychology of religion
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines psychology of religion as: Branch of religious study in which religious thought, experience, and behavior are studied using the concepts and methodology of psychology.

nodes.label: sociology of religion
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines sociology of religion as: Study of religion using the sociological method of approach.

nodes.label: biblical studies
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines biblical studies as: Critical study of the Bible and biblical writings, including such approaches as textual analysis, historical study, exegesis, hermeneutics, and literary and linguistic criticism.

nodes.label: church history
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines church history as: Study of the history of the Christian Church and its sects and branches.

nodes.label: ecclesiology
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines ecclesiology as: Study of the doctrines of the church, including the study of ecclesiastical art, antiquities, and the adornment and equipment of churches.

nodes.label: eschatology
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines eschatology as: The science or teachings concerned with last things, such as the end of history or of the present world, the fate of the soul after death, the final judgment of individuals, and the creation or restoration of a perfect world.

nodes.label: religious ethics
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines religious ethics as: Study of ethics inspired and informed by religious doctrine, faith, and experience, also the study of religious doctrine and commitment with reference to ethics.

nodes.label: religious history
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines religious history as: Refers to the comparative historical study of the nature and structure of the world's religions and their diverse manifestations over time in different societies and cultures. For the comparative study of the characteristics of religious systems in different societies that aims to develop a universal evolutionary continuum of religions and stresses a scientific methodology, see "comparative religion."

nodes.label: arhats
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines arhats as: Buddhist saints, the most accomplished of the four types of who have defeated all afflictions and will enter nirvana upon death. Typically depicted as 16 in number, who vowed to remain alive to preserve his teachings.

nodes.label: bardo
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines bardo as: In Tibetan Buddhism, the intermediate state between death and rebirth. Bardo, which can last up to 49 days, follows a vision of a beam of clear light by the dying person.

nodes.label: bhūmi
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines bhūmi as: The earth, floor, or foundation, symbolically stages of enlightenment in Buddhist practice.

nodes.label: buddha field
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines buddha field as: In Buddhism, realms of individual bodhisattvas who have attained awakening; may have varying spiritual climates or degrees of perfection, either pure or mixed.

nodes.label: dharma
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines dharma as: Refers to a key concept with multiple meanings in Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism. In Hinduism, dharma is the religious and moral law governing and enabling society and individual conduct. It is found in the early religious manuals called the dharmasutras and has been expanded into larger compilations of law called the dharmashastra. Dharma in Buddhism retains the Hindu sense of cosmic law and order but it also came to be applied to the teachings of the Buddha who is seen as a manifestation of the universal truth that is dharma. Thus, dharma is the practice of this truth in Buddhism. The triratna ("three jewels") is a fundamental aspect of Buddhism and consists of the Buddha, dharma, and the sangha (community of believers). In the context of Buddhist metaphysics, the term in the plural (dharmas) refers to the interrelated elements that make up the empirical world. In addition to being commonly understood as moral virtue in Jaina philosophy, dharma also refers to an eternal "substance" (dravya) that is the medium that allows living beings to move. It is a meaning unique to Jainism. The term may simply refer to the teachings of the Jinas. For the Jains, dharma has its opposite in adharma which is error and immorality as well as the ability to rest or pause.

nodes.label: dhyana
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines dhyana as: In Hinduism and Buddhism, a type of profound meditation; the penultimate (seventh) stage of yoga.

nodes.label: karma
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines karma as: The chain of causation that drives all phenomena, in which virtuous actions lead to future happiness and evil acts the opposite. The sum of a person's actions in one of his successive states of existence, regarded as determining his fate in the next. Among symbols for karma is the endless knot. Karma is a key concept in Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, Sikhism, and Taoism.

nodes.label: mappō
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines mappō as: The clearest expression of apocalyptic thought in Japanese Buddhism, this third and final age of Buddhism was believed to have begun in 1052. During this end of the Buddhist Law, Buddhism is thought to degenerate to the point where the teaching still exists, but there is no true practice of it. This religious pessimism and preparation for the end times caused a flurry of art commissions during the late Heian period in areas such as sculpture, calligraphy, painting and temple building by wealthy aristocrats who hoped to gain salvation by honoring Amida Buddha.

nodes.label: nirvana
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines nirvana as: Concept of state of deep inner freedom and peace, the supreme goal of Hinduism and Buddhism. Reaching nirvana means liberation from samsara, the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth. In Buddhism, nirvana represents freedom from attachments and individual consciousness and the attainment of tranquility and purity. Nirvana is conceived somewhat differently within the various schools of Buddhism. In Hinduism it furthermore means that union with God or the Absolute is possible.

nodes.label: pure land
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines pure land as: In Mahayana Buddhism, pure abodes or celestial realms of a buddha or bodhisattva; used for East Asian Buddhism, Taoism, and Bon. For realms both pure and mixed, use "buddha fields."

nodes.label: satori
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines satori as: In Zen Buddhism, satori refers to a sudden personal enlightenment analagous to the original moment of spiritual rebirth experienced by the Gautama Buddha.

nodes.label: uṣṇīsạ
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines uṣṇīsạ as: Physical mark identifying a buddha, conventionally depicted as a cranial bump and said to possess magical properties.

nodes.label: consubstantiation
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines consubstantiation as: The doctrine according to which the substances of both the body and blood of Christ and of the bread and wine coexist in the eucharistic elements after being consecrated. The concept is attributed to Luther, who was opposed to the doctrine of transubstantiation. Luther illustrated the concept with the analogy of an iron in a fire: the fire and the iron are united in the red-hot iron yet both are still present.

nodes.label: immaculate conception
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines immaculate conception as: The Christian doctrinal concept that the Virgin Mary was free from original sin from the moment of conception, unlike all other humans after Adam and Eve. Although this belief was promulgated as Roman Catholic dogma by Pope Pius IX in 1854, it has been rejected by Protestants and the Orthodox Church.

nodes.label: stigmatization
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines stigmatization as: The appearance of wounds on the hands, feet, and side corresponding to those received by Christ upon crucifixion, which have appeared, inexplicably, on some people who intensely contemplate the Passion of Christ.

nodes.label: avatara
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines avatara as: Refers to the descent to earth of a Hindu deity in a visible form. The word comes from the Sanskrit meaning 'descent.' The concept comes from the tradition associated with the deity Vishnu who periodically appeared on earth in human or animal form in order to save it from severe danger or destruction. Vishnu's most famous manifestations have been as Krishna and Rama. The deity is expected to return in the last of his forms to destroy and subsequently recreate the world at a time when it is completely depraved. In more recent times the concept has been challenged by reformers, particularly in regards to manifestations in animal forms. At the same time, others have put forward the idea that humans, even non-Hindus such as Jesus or Muhammad, can become avataras by a divine infilling.

nodes.label: bhakti
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines bhakti as: In Hinduism, loving and adoring devotion to God or to one's chosen manifestation of the divine that leads to a close personal relationship with God. By surrendering to God, one can receive grace, however low one's station. In most religious texts of popular Hinduism, bhakti is recommended as the most effective path to the divine. This concept is behind some of the world's most moving theistic poetry.

nodes.label: moksha
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines moksha as: In Hinduism, liberation from samsara, the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth. This liberation would mean a state of bliss (ananda), freedom from sorrow and higher awareness. It is the fourth and ultimate artha (goal) for Hindus, attained when ignorance, desire, and all attachments are overcome. There are various interpretations of moksha, especially in regard to how it is attained, whether by personal effort, by grace of a personal god, or a combination of the two. In Jainism, moksha lies beyond enlightenment and is freedom from the impediment of karma; enlightenment provides the means for rooting out all remaining karma.

nodes.label: pañcadēvōpāsanā
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines pañcadēvōpāsanā as: Worship of five divinities: Viṣṇu, Śiva, Sūrya, Gaṇapati, and Śakti.

nodes.label: samsara
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines samsara as: The cycle of death and rebirth experienced by all unawakened beingsover potentially infinite eons consisting often of six destinies: (1) divinity, (2) demigod, (3) human, (4) animal, (5) ghost, and (6) hell dweller in Buddhism, Hinduism and Jainism. Although debated, the concept is probably of non-Vedic or heterodox origin.

nodes.label: trimurti
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines trimurti as: Hindu concept of the collapse of the three main Hindu gods, Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva, into a single form with three faces. Some scholars consider the trimurti as a way to reconcile different monotheistic approaches with one another and with the concept of ultimate reality (Brahman) since the trimurti manifests the cosmic functions of the Supreme Being. The trimurti was classically expressed in the poem 'Kumarasambhava' by Kalidasa (ca. 4th-5th century).

nodes.label: ahimsa
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines ahimsa as: Refers to the principle of respect for all life and the practice of non-injury to all living beings; it is found in Buddhism, some Hindu sects, and especially Jainism. Ahimsa is based on the belief that all living creatures are sacred and that violence has negative effects on those who commit it, for example, harming a living thing may result in an unfavorable reincarnation. The term comes from the Sanskrit meaning 'not-harming.'

nodes.label: cāraṇa
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines cāraṇa as: In Jainism, cāraṇa refers to the 'capability to move in the sky,' one of the eight extraordinary powers of mythical flying ascetics.

nodes.label: image quality
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines image quality as: Use with reference to photographic and electronic images, usually pertaining to the clarity of details, often relating to the degree of resolution.

nodes.label: group identity
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines group identity as: An individual person's conscious sharing of some kind of essential character with one or more groups of other people, such as a race, nation, social class, profession, or body of people organized into a group at some particular time for some particular purpose.

nodes.label: Neo-Platonism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Neo-Platonism as: Refers to a philosophy developed by Plotinus in Alexandria in the 3rd century CE that consists of a modified version of Platonism combined with aspects of Judaic and Christian thought and possibly Oriental mysticism. Neo-Platonism holds that there is one source from which all existence comes from and with which an individual soul can be mystically united; it also emphasizes the plurality of levels of being, with the physical universe perceptible to the senses being the lowest. Neo-Platonism developed in a variety of forms over many centuries and it has enjoyed numerous revivals and modifications throughout history.

nodes.label: amalgam style
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines amalgam style as: Style that combines recognizable elements of two or more defined styles.

nodes.label: ancient
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines ancient as: In the discipline of art and architectural history, typically refers to the period in Europe, Asia Minor, and north Africa, prior to the fall of the western Roman Empire. The term is also sometimes applied more generally to prehistory and to early cultures in other areas of the world.

nodes.label: Archaeological Style
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Archaeological Style as: Style of visual arts that intentionally imitates ancient objects or style. Most often used to refer to jewelry design, but may also be applied to paintings, sculpture, and occasionally to architecture.

nodes.label: geologic time scale
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines geologic time scale as: An internationally recognized time scale of Earth's history since the planet's formative period subdivided into eons, eras, periods, and epochs.

nodes.label: Late Glacial
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Late Glacial as: Designating the latter part of the last Quaternary glacial period, immediately preceding the current postglacial period, marked predominantly by the retreat of glaciers.

nodes.label: Post-Colonial
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Post-Colonial as: Basic reference to 'after the colonial" condition, periods, and cultures of peoples, states, and societies that have been through a process of formal decolonization. Since the 1980s the term is used to also refer to the trend to question Western knowledge, categories, and assumptions.

nodes.label: prehistoric
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines prehistoric as: Refers to the period antecedent to the first contemporary written accounts of a people. The time span for this period varies according to specific local habitation patterns and in different scholarly disciplines.

nodes.label: protohistoric
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines protohistoric as: Periods and cultures between prehistory and history, during which a culture or civilization has not yet developed writing, but other cultures have provided written historical records for this people in a given area.

nodes.label: three-age system
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines three-age system as: Division of human prehistory into three ages: the Stone Age, the Bronze Age, and the Iron Age.

nodes.label: Antarctic
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Antarctic as: Having to do with the style or culture of the south polar region of the earth, which comprises the continent of Antarctica together with the seas and islands of the Southern Ocean. Also refers to the flora, fauna, geography, oceanography, or climate of the region.

nodes.label: Asian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Asian as: Refers to the cultures of the continent of Asia, which is in the eastern hemisphere, and is bounded by the Pacific Ocean, the Indian Ocean, the Arctic Ocean, and is generally considered to be delimited on the west by the Ural Mountains. It also refers to the numerous islands off the coast of Asia.

nodes.label: Early Western World
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Early Western World as: Refers to a style region encompassing the Mediterranean and the Occident.

nodes.label: European
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines European as: Styles, periods, and cultures of the continent of Europe, which is in the northern hemisphere, is bounded by the Arctic Ocean, the Atlantic Ocean, and the Mediterranean Sea, and is generally considered to be delimited on the east by the Ural Mountains.

nodes.label: Global
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Global as: Styles, periods, and cultures that cross boundaries of multiple nations and regions.

nodes.label: Islamic World, The
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Islamic World, The as: Refers to a style region encompassing the regions where Islam is prevalent.

nodes.label: Middle Eastern
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Middle Eastern as: Styles and cultures existing in the extensive area that includes the nations of southwest Asia and northeastern Africa. The term was formerly used to also include Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, and Burma.

nodes.label: Oceanic
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Oceanic as: Cultures and styles of various regions in Oceania, comprising islands scattered throughout the Pacific Ocean (generally excluding Japan, Indonesia, and the Philippines), but including Australia.

nodes.label: The Americas
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines The Americas as: Refers to a style region encompassing North, Central and South America.

nodes.label: bungalow style
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines bungalow style as: Style of domestic architecture with a one- to one-and-a-half-story building having a low-pitched gable or hipped roof, with widely projecting, often bracketed eaves, dormers, and conspicuous front porches.

nodes.label: military style
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines military style as: Style of fashion, decorative arts, and architecture that invoke elements of miliary design and architecture.

nodes.label: old-fashioned
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines old-fashioned as: A style that belongs to or resembles a style or fashion of an earlier time. The term refers not to an absolute time frame, but is relative to the period being discussed, not to the present. For example, a style popular in 1710 may in 2010 be said to have been "old fashioned" in 1750. "Old fashioned" differs from "retro" in implying that a style or object is antiquated, outdated, and sometimes unfashionable in form or character, while "retro" implies reference to a previous style (usually from the mid-20th century) that is still considered desirable and popular for its nostalgic value.

nodes.label: period style
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines period style as: Term referring to any generic style, particularly in the context of interior design, characterized by the incorporation of antiques or replicas of antiques of one particular named style, usually styles from 18th and 19th-century Europe and the United States (e.g., American Colonial, Louis XIV, Hepplewhite, etc.).

nodes.label: plantation house style
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines plantation house style as: Style of architecture, interior design, or other works that evokes elements of plantation houses of the American south or of Hawaii or other island colonial settlements. Particulary appropriate when the work is not affiliated with a plantation, but only the style is appropriated.

nodes.label: pre-colonial
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines pre-colonial as: General term designating a culture, style, or period occurring or existing before the colonial period of a country. Often used in reference to indigenous cultures prior to European colonization.

nodes.label: ranch style
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines ranch style as: Style of domestic architecture, particularly in North American 1940s-1950s. Characterized by having one-story and low-pitched roofs.

nodes.label: shabby chic
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines shabby chic as: A style, particularly in the context of interior design, characterized by European or American antiques or replicas of antiques that that show evidence of wear and age, such as layers of paint that are worn and chipped and faded or muted fabrics. The style first developed in Britain. The term was coined in the "World of Interiors" magazine in the 1980s and has become a registered trademark for a US company.

nodes.label: plastic arts
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines plastic arts as: In general, refers to the visual arts as opposed to literature, poetry, or other writing. In a narrower sense, it sometimes refers to all visual arts concerned with three-dimensional objects, but not two-dimensional visual arts. For works made of the material plastic, use "plastic (organic material)."

nodes.label: technical art history
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines technical art history as: Refers to an emerging interdisciplinary field which seeks to integrate scientific study of art into the practice of art history; and the interpretative methods of the art historian into the conservation lab. An outgrowth of the subdiscipline of art history once known as Technical Studies, the field has recently established itself within graduate program curricula.

nodes.label: automotive design
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines automotive design as: Practice and discipline of designing the appearance, ergonomics, complex systems, and other aspects of motor vehicles, usually road vehicles such as automobiles, motorcycles, trucks, buses, coaches, and vans.

nodes.label: communication design
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines communication design as: Discipline that focuses on the presentation of information using visual and written elements. Communication design is a broad concept covering various disciplines, such as advertising, branding, web design, user interface design, information design, and social media. Communication designers focus on the strategy, content, and context of their messages, and how they can influence the behavior, attitude, and perception of their audience. Communication design uses research, analysis, storytelling, and user testing to create effective and engaging visual solutions that meet the needs and goals of clients and users.

nodes.label: costume design
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines costume design as: Designing clothing, accessories, and ensembles intended to create an appearance characteristic of a particular period, person, place, or thing, especially (but not exclusively) for theatrical performances. For the design of clothing and accessories for personal wear, use "fashion design."

nodes.label: fashion design
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines fashion design as: Designing clothing, accessories, and ensembles for personal wear. For the design of clothing, accessories, and ensembles intended to create an appearance characteristic of a particular period, person, place, or thing, especially (but not exclusively) for theatrical performances, use "costume design." For the concept of a prevailing, usually short lived custom, usage, or style in clothing, cars, restaurants, and other personal possessions and services, use "fashion."

nodes.label: furniture design
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines furniture design as: Practice and discipline of designing furniture.

nodes.label: garden design
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines garden design as: Discipline specializing in garden projects that are most often sited at a residence. Garden design is generally of smaller scale than landscape design, and may have defined boundaries.The practice differs from landscape architecture in the level of accreditation of the practitioner. For the discipline that requires licensed architects to design the use of outdoor space and the land, and that may include site planning, urban planning, park and recreation planning, garden design and historic preservation, use 'landscape architecture.'

nodes.label: graphic design
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines graphic design as: The process of designing visual communications and text for commercial applications, usually to be printed or reproduced photographically, such as in advertisements, books, magazines, newspapers, leaflets, posters, diagrams, trademarks, corporate identities, sign systems, packaging, film, television graphics, etc.

nodes.label: industrial design
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines industrial design as: The design of functional objects that can be mass-produced, including machine-made consumer and commercial products.

nodes.label: interior decoration
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines interior decoration as: The discipline focused on selecting and organizing the surface coverings, draperies, furniture, and furnishings of architectural interiors, usually of existing spaces.

nodes.label: interior design
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines interior design as: Discipline specializing in the design of interiors of homes or other buildings, including placement of furniture, accessories, aesthetic or decorative schemes, and spatial arrangements, construction, building systems, acoustics, lighting, heating, and air conditioning of spaces. May refer to design for existing spaces or for spaces in the planning phases. For the discipline limited to the choices of color, texture, and superficial arrangement of furnishings of a space, prefer "interior decoration." For the discipline focusing more on the architecture of the interior, prefer "interior architecture (discipline)."

nodes.label: jewelry design
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines jewelry design as: Discipline and activity of designing ornaments such as bracelets, necklaces, and rings for personal adornment.

nodes.label: paper engineering
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines paper engineering as: Design of paper structures and mechanisms, such as pop-up elements in books and greeting cards, cut-and-assemble paper models, and various types of paper containers.

nodes.label: participatory design
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines participatory design as: Participation by workers and residents in the design of the spaces, structures, or communities which they use or inhabit.

nodes.label: set design
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines set design as: The discipline and practice of designing and creating the sets, that is the physical surroundings in which the action takes place, for films, television, or theater.

nodes.label: textile design
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines textile design as: Practice and discipline of designing textiles.

nodes.label: Web design
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Web design as: Refers to the practice of designing for Websites, including graphical functional, and structural considerations.

nodes.label: ethnomusicology
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines ethnomusicology as: Branch of musicology focusing on the study of music in its cultural context.

nodes.label: organology
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines organology as: Descriptive and analytical study of musical instruments.

nodes.label: architectural photography
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines architectural photography as: Specialization of photography focused on architecture as subject.

nodes.label: anthropological linguistics
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines anthropological linguistics as: Study of speech communities, particularly those with no writing system, by the application of anthropological and linguistic techniques.

nodes.label: computational linguistics
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines computational linguistics as: Branch of linguistics concerned with the use of computers for the analysis and synthesis of language data, as in translation, word frequency counts, and speech recognition and synthesis.

nodes.label: sociolinguistics
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines sociolinguistics as: The study of language as it functions in society, and of the interaction between linguistic and social variables.

nodes.label: graphemics
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines graphemics as: Study of writing systems and of their relation to speech.

nodes.label: historical linguistics
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines historical linguistics as: Study of the development of or changes in words, speech, and language or groups of languages over time.

nodes.label: metalinguistics
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines metalinguistics as: Branch of linguistics that deals with the relation of language to the rest of culture-determined behavior.

nodes.label: phonetics
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines phonetics as: Study of the production, transmission, perception, classification, and physical or acoustical properties of speech sounds and how they are organized in language. For the study of the sound patterns and systems of languages, use "phonology."

nodes.label: phonology
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines phonology as: Study of the systems and patterns of language, including how speech sounds are combined, organized, and convey meaning. For the study of the production, transmission, perception, and description of speech sounds, use "phonetics."

nodes.label: pragmatics
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines pragmatics as: Study of the aspects of meaning in language that are related to the use of language in a natural context.

nodes.label: semantics
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines semantics as: Study of meanings in language and of changes in those meanings.

nodes.label: toponymy
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines toponymy as: Etymological study of the place-names of a region or language.

nodes.label: parinirvāṇa
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines parinirvāṇa as: In Buddhism, the final nirvana or nirvana-after-death, which occurs upon the death of the body or ultimate departure from the conventional realm of a person who is an awakened being, having attained nirvana during his or her lifetime.

nodes.label: Stone Age
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Stone Age as: Refers to the period and culture associated with the first age of the Three Age system developed by Christian Jürgensen Thomsen in 1836. It is a stage in the development of hominids or of a prehistoric human culture characterized by the creation and use of stone tools and weapons, as distinguished from later stages of culture when bronze or iron were used for these purposes. The Stone Age is generally divided into three periods, Paleolithic, Mesolithic, and Neolithic, distinguished from each other by the degree of sophistication evident in the fashioning and use of tools.

nodes.label: transitional periods Stone Age to Bronze Age
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines transitional periods Stone Age to Bronze Age as: Transitional periods related to Stone Age to Bronze Age cultures.

nodes.label: Bronze Age
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Bronze Age as: Refers to the period and culture associated with the second age in the Three Age system developed by Christian Jürgensen Thomsen in 1836. It is characterized by the widespread use of bronze, which is an alloy of copper and tin, lead, antimony, or arsenic, in the manufacture of tools and weapons. It developed at different times in different parts of the world, from around 3,500 BCE in Greece and China to around 1,400 BCE in several areas of Europe. There was not a Bronze Age in the Americas, since the local Stone Age cultures were introduced directly to Iron Age technologies by European explorers.

nodes.label: Iron Age
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Iron Age as: Refers to the period and culture associated with the third age in the Three Age system developed by Christian Jürgensen Thomsen in 1836. Iron Age culture typically developed from the Bronze Age at the point when the qualities of iron were exploited, particularly through carburization, in the manufacture of tools, weapons, and implements. It developed at different times in various parts of the world, first appearing in the Middle East and southeastern Europe around 1,200 BCE, and in China around 600 BCE. In the Americas, it did not develop from the Bronze Age but was introduced to Stone Age cultures by European explorers.

nodes.label: prehistoric African
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines prehistoric African as: Cultures and styles from the prehistoric era in Africa.

nodes.label: Ancient African
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Ancient African as: Cultures and styles of Africa in ancient times.

nodes.label: Colonial African
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Colonial African as: Styles and cultures belonging to Africa under colonial, usually European, rule or influence.

nodes.label: modern African
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines modern African as: Styles and cultures belonging to modern Africa, generally from the 19th century and later.

nodes.label: African sculpture styles
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines African sculpture styles as: Sculpture styles belonging to African cultures.

nodes.label: African diaspora
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines African diaspora as: Culture of the body of people who were displaced from their African homeland, and their descendants. Examples include those who traveled in ancient migrations and those who were involuntarily transported due to enslavement.

nodes.label: Ancient Asian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Ancient Asian as: Cultures and styles of any nations or peoples of Asia in ancient times; the time frame generally includes centuries BCE, sometimes including periods up to around 1000 CE.

nodes.label: Southeast Asian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Southeast Asian as: Refers to the cultures of the region of Asia situated east of the Indian subcontinent and south of China, encompassing the long-historied and ethnically diverse cultures of a continental mainland and a series of archipelagoes 700 miles to the east and south of the continent. In general, the arts in the region predominantly reflect religion, particularly the personality and character of Buddha and the Hindu gods, and history, particularly glorified heroes of national and mythic pasts. The Buddha image remains the central motif in sculptural and painting styles, while other minor or native figures from Buddhist, Islamic, and Hindu scriptures are sometimes reflected in mural works. Art in the region features tribal geometric and spiral patterns, Indian floral designs, and animal imagery based on local mythologies. A general penchant for themes of fantasy, human and divine beauty, and celebratory sensuality pervades the art of this region.

nodes.label: West Asian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines West Asian as: Styles and cultures located in the highlands of Anatolia, the Caucasus, and the Armenian and Iranian highlands. Distinguished from the Middle East, which is sometimes known as "Western Asia."

nodes.label: Ancient European
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Ancient European as: Styles, periods, and cultures of ancient Europe.

nodes.label: Early Netherlandish
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Early Netherlandish as: The culture and the styles of art produced in the Southern Netherlands during the 15th and early 16th centuries.

nodes.label: European regions
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines European regions as: Used to describe styles of the regions of Europe.

nodes.label: Hellenic
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Hellenic as: The style or culture of the ancient Hellenes, including the Iron Age Greek culture to the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BCE, in Greece and all its colonies.

nodes.label: Holy Roman Imperial
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Holy Roman Imperial as: The culture or period of the Holy Roman Empire, a multi-ethnic complex of territories in central Europe during the medieval and early modern periods until its dissolution in 1806.

nodes.label: Hutsul
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Hutsul as: Culture and ethnicity of the Hutsul people of the Carpathian mountains, primarily in the Ukraine and Romania.

nodes.label: Dutch Colonial Revival
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Dutch Colonial Revival as: Architectural styles inspired by Dutch architecture, primarily in North America, Europe, and areas of Dutch colonization.

nodes.label: Late Modernism
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Late Modernism as: General term for the recent art made between the aftermath of World War II and the early years of the 21st century.

nodes.label: Neo-Symbolist
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Neo-Symbolist as: Style that refers back to the original Symbolist movement, characterized by a complex synthesis of psychology, mystical and occult practices, and linguistics used to challenge traditional relationships between representation and meaning.

nodes.label: hip-hop
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines hip-hop as: Cultural movement encompassing DJing, rap and rap music, dance and dance music, graffiti writing, and styles of dress. The movement began in the 1970s, in the South Bronx section of New York City, a depressed, predominantly African American neighborhood. The popularity of rap music in particular throughout the 1980s to the present, helped turn hip-hop into an international movement.

nodes.label: Minimal
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Minimal as: A style developed in the mid 20th century, characterized by simplicity and lack of decoration to the point of starkness. The movement advocated reducing art to the state of non-art by removing nature and culture, resulting in artwork in pure, simple forms and objects placed randomly. The term can be extended to all art, including literature, design, music, visual art, and performance. With specific reference to the visual arts, the term is used to describe an abstract art movement and style, predominantly of sculpture, that flourished in the mid- and late 1960s. With specific reference to music, it refers to a style that emerged in the United States in the 1960s featuring prolonged repetition of short passages and unvarying harmonies.

nodes.label: Postmodern
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Postmodern as: Refers to the style and period of art and architecture that developed in the 1960s and after, when there was a clear challenge to the dominance of Modernism. Generally speaking, it advocated a pluralistic approach to the arts and it stated that Modernism had failed because of a lack of a coded language of meaning to the viewer. The term was first used by Spanish poet Federico de Onis in 1934 and later by Arnold Toynbee's "A Study of History" in 1938, but it was in the 1970s when it came into wide use in connection with a trend in architecture that employed selective Eclecticism and Historicism. This resulted in structures that displayed a knowledge of Modernism, but also playful, whimsical, applications of Classical elements. In the other arts, such as painting, there was a return to a classical approach to the human figure, style, and composition, often resulting in Old Masters style works, but with updated imagery, such as the inclusion of current celebrities, or artists from the past. In photography, as well as painting, a narrative or story telling approach to work also became popular. By the early 1980s, many work dubbed Postmodern, were purchased by the corporate art market, where large sums were paid for the work of relatively new artists. By the 1990s, Postmodernism showed signs of slowing down in terms of popularity, when more traditional Modernist forms began to re-emerge.

nodes.label: space age
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines space age as: Refers to the period from the mid-1950s through the early 1970s when rocketry was first used to launch satellites and manned missions to extraterrestrial space. Generally applied to works that were inspired by new techniques, materials, and designs developed for space flight; or the images, experiences, or psychological states recorded by astronauts during space missions. The term has been applied to works of art, design, music, and architecture characteristic of this period.

nodes.label: Post-1945
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Post-1945 as: General term for styles and periods from post-1945.

nodes.label: pre-Islamic
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines pre-Islamic as: Very generally the term covers from late prehistory to the time when Islam became the dominant religion and way of life in those areas of the world where, at various times after the early seventh century CE, a majority of the population or a preponderance of the ruling classes converted to Islam. It covers a wide and varied range of cultures, artistic traditions, and time periods, varying with the different times when Islam came to different regions and influenced and was influenced by different traditions.

nodes.label: Saracenic
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Saracenic as: Historical term used by medieval Christian Europeans for the culture and style of Arab Muslims, and eventually all Muslims across the Middle East, North Africa, and Europe. Rather than referencing a specific ethnic group, the term was a sweeping religious and geopolitical label used throughout the Middle Ages, most notably during the Crusades. The meaning of the term has then shifted dramatically across different historical eras. For the style and culture of Muslim lands use "Islamic (style and culture)."

nodes.label: Kingdom of Jerusalem
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Kingdom of Jerusalem as: Culture of the Crusader state established in the Southern Levant by Godfrey of Bouillon in 1099 after the First Crusade.

nodes.label: Australian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Australian as: Describes the culture and style of Aboriginal Australians and current inhabitants of Australia, such as rock art, sculpture in wood, clay and sand, body decoration and bark painting, created both before and after European colonization.

nodes.label: Melanesian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Melanesian as: Describes the culture and style of the inhabitants of the Melanesian Islands. Melanesians are well known for creating sculptures utilizing a vast range of media, their traditional communal architecture, and body arts.

nodes.label: Polynesian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Polynesian as: Nationality, culture, and styles of the Polynesian Islands. Art forms include traditional wood-carving, barkcloth, mat-making, tattoo, and other body arts. Polynesian art was greatly developed, but little of what existed has survived to the modern day due to the perishability of the utilized material - bark cloth, basketry, and featherwork. Although architecture was developed everywhere in Polynesia, only the ruined stone structures of the eastern Polynesian islands remain proof of the Polynesians' exceptional architectural skill.

nodes.label: Oceanic sculpture styles
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Oceanic sculpture styles as: Sculpture styles belonging to Oceanic cultures.

nodes.label: Oceanic ceramic styles
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Oceanic ceramic styles as: Ceramic styles belonging to Oceanic cultures.

nodes.label: Australasian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Australasian as: The culture and peoples occupying the section of Oceania south of the equator and north of latitude 47.00 S.

nodes.label: Hispanic
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Hispanic as: Styles and cultures that developed in Spain and elsewhere under Spanish influence, especially those that developed under the influence of colonists from Spain and their descendants in the Americas.

nodes.label: American regions
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines American regions as: Used to describe styles of the regions of the Americas, including styles found in North, Central, and South America, as well as the Caribbean.

nodes.label: Native American
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Native American as: Whenever possible, use the specific tribal name. The collective term "Native American" is currently widely used in the United States for indigenous peoples. However, many groups increasingly prefer "American Indian" or "Indigenous American." For the indigenous peoples of Canada use the term "Indigenous peoples" which refers to the First Nations, Inuit, and Métis. For the broader concept of the cultures of any native peoples of Central America, South America, North America, or the West Indies, use "Indigenous people (culture)."

nodes.label: Latin American
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Latin American as: In the strictest sense, refers to the cultures of the countries of South America, North America, Central America, and the Caribbean that were originally colonized by Spain. It may also refer more broadly to all the cultures of this region, including those that were originally colonized by the French or Portuguese.

nodes.label: modern American
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines modern American as: Styles, periods, cultures, and movements of America in modern times.

nodes.label: Ancient American
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Ancient American as: General term for the styles and cultures of the Paleo-Indians of the Americas; also may refer generally to any of the cultures of Americas prior to the arrival of European colonists.

nodes.label: Hispanic-American
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Hispanic-American as: Refers to the cultures and styles of the countries and communities in South America, North America, Central America, and the Caribbean where Spanish is the official language. In the United States the term Hispanic American also refers to the culture of people from the United States with Latin American or Spanish heritage.

nodes.label: Pan-American
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Pan-American as: Pan-American broadly refers to the culture of North, Central, and South America. Rooted in the history of U.S.-Latin American relations, it also specifically refers to expressions developed during the first half of the 20th century. The term refers either to the art, architecture and political- economic agreements associated with a U.S. leadership and its hegemonic interests in Latin America and to the Latin American art expressions and movements of anti-imperialism that rejected unilateral agreements with the U.S. during this period.

nodes.label: Ibero-American
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Ibero-American as: It refers to the culture and expressions of Spanish and Portuguese-speaking nations across The Americas, distinguishing them from French and English speaking countries. The term is sometimes used to describe a broader community that includes the European nations of Spain and Portugal, emphasizing their shared Iberian heritage and linguistic connections betwing countries that were once part of the Spanish or Portuguese empires.

nodes.label: architectonics
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines architectonics as: The study of the scientific or technical aspects of architecture as distinguished from the purely artistic or historical aspect.

nodes.label: naval architecture
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines naval architecture as: Art or science of designing and building ships and other waterborne craft.

nodes.label: urban design
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines urban design as: The field of study and practice of designing the specific appearance, integration, and function of cities, towns, and villages. It is an interdisciplinary field that works with many built environment professions, including urban planning, architecture, landscape architecture, and civil engineering. For the field concerned with long-term planning for additions and improvements to the spatial organization and content of urban areas, use “urban planning.”

nodes.label: vāstuvidyā
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines vāstuvidyā as: In Indian architecture, a science of building, architecture.

nodes.label: syntax
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines syntax as: That branch of grammar that studies the formation of sentences, the relationships among their component words, clauses, and phrases, and the rules governing word order in a given language.

nodes.label: Neozoic
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Neozoic as: An era following the Palaeozoic era, comprising both the Mesozoic and Cenozoic (Cainozoic) eras.

nodes.label: Archean
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Archean as: On the geologic time scale, the period preceding the Proterozoic Eon, spanning about 1.5 billion years, in which the Earth's atmosphere was probably of methane, ammonia, and other gases, and the surface cooled enough that rocks and continental plates began to form.

nodes.label: Eolithic
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Eolithic as: The culture and period dating from the beginning of the Stone Age, preceding the Paleolithic and characterized by the earliest crude stone tools.

nodes.label: Paleolithic
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Paleolithic as: Refers to the period and culture associated with the first use of chipped stone tools in a given area. The time frame of this period may differ greatly in different parts of the world, but is first evident in hominids by 2,500,000 Before Present. The earliest surviving artistic output by a culture usually dates from the Paleolithic period, and may include small carved stone and bone figures, as well as large-scale paintings and incised designs in caves. Paleolithic artistic output in western art is evident from roughly 30,000 BCE to 10,000 BCE.

nodes.label: Mesolithic
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Mesolithic as: Usually refers specifically to a period of cultural development in Europe that began as early as 10,000 BCE, after the end of the Pleistocene Epoch when glaciation began to retreat, and lasted until about 2,700 BCE. The term is also sometimes used generally for a period associated with the transitional phase between Paleolithic and Neolithic cultures in any given area. Mesolithic culture overlaps with Paleolithic and Neolithic cultures, and is characterized by great environmental and cultural change and diverse local adaptations to special environments. The period is typically marked by the production of microliths that were mounted on shafts, bone, antler, wooden tools, and an occasional polished stone tool. Surviving artistic output includes carvings and cave paintings with relatively sophisticated depictions of human and animal forms.

nodes.label: Neolithic
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Neolithic as: Refers to the final stage of Stone Age development of a human culture, characterized by sophisticated stone tools created by polishing or grinding, wide-spread domestication of animals and plants, settlement in permanent villages, and the appearance of pottery and weaving. Neolithic cultures first appeared during the Holocene Epoch, around 9,000 BCE, and survived in certain remote areas of the world into the 19th century. Artistic products include wooden and stone houses, religious monuments, fortifications, carvings, paintings, textiles, and pottery.

nodes.label: Chalcolithic
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Chalcolithic as: Refers to the period and culture associated with the transitional phase between the Stone Age and the Bronze Age. It is characterized by the hammering, melting, and casting of copper for ornaments and tools, and is distinguished from Bronze Age technologies in that the copper was typically not or only seldomly combined with tin or other metal in an alloy, and stone tools were used at the same time as metal ones. Chalcolithic cultures developed at different times in different parts of the world, ranging from early sporadic use of copper around 7,000 BCE in the Near East to established use by around 1,900 BCE in Britain.

nodes.label: Eneolithic
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Eneolithic as: Refers to the period and culture associated with the transitional phase between the Stone Age and the Bronze Age. Some scholars distinguish this period from the Chalcolithic by classifying Eneolithic as late Neolithic, when copper and flint implements were used at the same time, while Chalcolithic would be the transitional phase when bronze and stone were used at the same time. Most literature does not make the distinction, and uses the term "Chalcolithic" to cover this entire phase. An exception is among Italian scholars, who tend to use the term "Eneolithic" instead.

nodes.label: Final Neolithic
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Final Neolithic as: Refers to the last stage of a Neolithic culture, which often partially overlaps with the Early Bronze Age. It is generally held to have occurred from around 4,000 BCE to around 3,000 BCE in Europe, lasting until around 2,000 BCE in parts of the British Isles.

nodes.label: Early Bronze Age
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Early Bronze Age as: Refers to the earliest phase of Bronze Age cultures, which developed differently in different regions, either from Chalcolithic or Neolithic technologies. It differs from the Middle and Late Bronze Age cultures primarily in metal assemblages and burial rites. It is characterized in part by the earliest experimentation with copper alloys to produce bronze, as well as the improvement of stone tools, and various other local cultural developments. Some scholars classify the Chalcolithic as the earliest phase of the Bronze Age.

nodes.label: Middle Bronze Age
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Middle Bronze Age as: Refers to a phase of the Bronze Age distinguished from the Early and Late Bronze Age cultures by differences in metal assemblages and burial rites. It is characterized in part by metalworking techniques and tool and weapon designs of increasing sophistication, including the utilization of valve molds, cire perdue, sheet work, structural ribs, rivets, and pommels on the end of the hilts of swords.

nodes.label: Late Bronze Age
