nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Late Bronze Age as: Refers to the final stage of Bronze Age cultures, distinguished from the Early and Middle Bronze Age cultures by differences in metal assemblages and burial rites. It is characterized in part by very sophisticated and elaborate metalworking techniques and tool and weapon designs. It is characterized by the development of mass-produced objects, hollow objects, armor, and large objects, such as caldrons and shields.

nodes.label: Early Iron Age
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Early Iron Age as: Refers to the earliest phase of the Iron Age, when the distinct functional properties of iron were first exploited, including the use of forging, and it began to supplant bronze in the production of tools and weapons.

nodes.label: Middle Iron Age
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Middle Iron Age as: Refers to a phase of Iron Age culture marked by technological and social developments, including carburized iron or steel.

nodes.label: Late Iron Age
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Late Iron Age as: Refers to a phase of Iron Age culture noted for particular technological and social developments, including the tempering of iron implements.

nodes.label: Abyssinian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Abyssinian as: Style and culture of the historical group that dwelled in the Horn of Africa from the 11th century, comprising mostly Christian, Semitic-speaking peoples in a territory including Eritrea, Tigray, Gonder, and parts of Gojam, Shewa, and Welo in the territory of the modern nation of Ethiopia.

nodes.label: Algerian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Algerian as: Style and culture of the people of Algeria or Algiers, in northern Africa.

nodes.label: Angolan
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Angolan as: Style and culture of the people of Angola, a republic (formerly a Portuguese colony) in southwestern Africa.

nodes.label: Beninese
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Beninese as: Style and culture of the people of Bénin, particularly of the modern inhabitants. For the style and culture of the more ancient people of southern Nigeria, use "Benin."

nodes.label: Burkina Faso
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Burkina Faso as: Style and culture of the people of Burkina Faso.

nodes.label: Burundi
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Burundi as: Style and culture of the people of Burundi.

nodes.label: Cameroonian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Cameroonian as: Style and culture of the nation of Cameroon, lying at the junction of western and central Africa.

nodes.label: Cape Verdean
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Cape Verdean as: Style and culture of the people of Cape Verde.

nodes.label: Chadian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Chadian as: Style or culture of the nation of Chad.

nodes.label: Djiboutian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Djiboutian as: Style and culture of the nation of Dijbouti.

nodes.label: Equatorial Guinean
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Equatorial Guinean as: Style and culture of the people of Equatorial Guinea.

nodes.label: Eritrean
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Eritrean as: Style and culture of the people of the modern nation of Eritrea, or to the ancient civilization that flourished in this region.

nodes.label: Gabonese
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Gabonese as: Style and culture of the inhabitants of the nation of Gabon.

nodes.label: Gambian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Gambian as: Style and culture of inhabitants of the nation of Gambia.

nodes.label: Ghanaian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Ghanaian as: Style and culture of the people of the nation of Ghana.

nodes.label: Guinea-Bissauan
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Guinea-Bissauan as: Style and culture of the people from Guinea-Bissau.

nodes.label: Guinean
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Guinean as: Style and culture of people of the modern nation of Guinée (Republic of Guinea) or of the historical people of the broader region of forest and coastal areas of western Africa between the tropic of Cancer and the equator known also as "Guinea."

nodes.label: Ivorian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Ivorian as: Style and culture of the Ivory Coast.

nodes.label: Kenyan
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Kenyan as: Style and culture of Kenya.

nodes.label: Lesotho
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Lesotho as: Style and culture of any of the ethnic groups of Lesotho, particularly the Sotho.

nodes.label: Libyan
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Libyan as: Style and culture of inhabitants of the large ancient country, Libya, in North Africa, or of the modern state of Libya.

nodes.label: Mahoran
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Mahoran as: Style and culture of the people of Mayotte, the southeasternmost island of the Comoros archipelago.

nodes.label: Malawian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Malawian as: Style and culture of people of the nation of Malawi.

nodes.label: Malian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Malian as: Style and culture of Mali in West Africa, either the ancient empire of the 13th and 14th centuries or of the modern republic founded in 1960.

nodes.label: Maure
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Maure as: Style and culture of a people of mixed Arab-Berber descent inhabiting the Western Sahara, neighboring parts of Morocco, Mali, Algeria, and the Islamic Republic of Mauritania. To refer to the products, style and culture of people living within the boundaries of Mauritania proper use "Mauritanian."

nodes.label: Mauritian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Mauritian as: The style and culture of the island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean.

nodes.label: Moroccan
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Moroccan as: Style and culture of the nation of Morocco or its historical counterparts.

nodes.label: Mozambican
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Mozambican as: Style and culture of the nation of Mozambique.

nodes.label: Namibian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Namibian as: Style and culture of the people of the nation of Namibia or of the Namib desert.

nodes.label: Reunionese
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Reunionese as: Nationality, styles, and culture of Réunion, Africa, located in the Indian Ocean, east of Madagascar.

nodes.label: Rhodesian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Rhodesian as: Nationality, culture, or styles of the historical area of Rhodesia, Africa. For the nationality of the modern nation, use "Zimbabwean."

nodes.label: Rwandan
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Rwandan as: Nationality, style, and culture of Rwanda, in central-eastern Africa.

nodes.label: Rwandese
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Rwandese as: The style and culture of the people speaking the Bantu Rwanda language of East Africa, or of any of the inhabitants of the country of Rwanda.

nodes.label: Sao Tomean
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Sao Tomean as: Style and culture of the nation of São Tomé and Príncipe.

nodes.label: Senegalese
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Senegalese as: Style and culture of the people of Senegal.

nodes.label: Seychellois
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Seychellois as: Style and culture of the nation of Seychelles, an island republic in the western Indian Ocean, comprising about 115 islands.

nodes.label: Sierra Leonean
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Sierra Leonean as: Style and culture of the nation of Sierra Leone.

nodes.label: Somalian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Somalian as: General national designation of the nation of Somalia, the Somali Democratic Republic.

nodes.label: South African
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines South African as: Style and culture of the people of South Africa.

nodes.label: Sudanese
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Sudanese as: Style and culture of the people of the Sudan.

nodes.label: Tanzanian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Tanzanian as: Style and culture of the East African state of Tanzania, formed in 1964 by the union of the republics of Tanganyika and Zanzibar.

nodes.label: Togolese
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Togolese as: Nationality, style, or culture of the West African state of Togo (formerly Togoland).

nodes.label: Ugandan
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Ugandan as: The style and culture of the central African State, Uganda.

nodes.label: Zambian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Zambian as: The style and culture of the south central African country, Zambia (formerly Northern Rhodesia).

nodes.label: Zimbabwean
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Zimbabwean as: The style and culture of Zimbabwe or of Black Rhodesians in the former Rhodesia.

nodes.label: prehistoric North African periods
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines prehistoric North African periods as: Periods related to prehistoric North African cultures.

nodes.label: prehistoric Sub-Saharan African periods
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines prehistoric Sub-Saharan African periods as: Periods related to prehistoric Sub-Saharan African cultures.

nodes.label: Ancient West African
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Ancient West African as: Cultures and styles of West Africa in ancient times.

nodes.label: Ancient Central African
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Ancient Central African as: Cultures and styles of Central Africa in ancient times.

nodes.label: Ancient Southern African
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Ancient Southern African as: Cultures and styles of southern Africa in ancient times.

nodes.label: ancient East African
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines ancient East African as: Cultures and styles of East Africa in ancient times.

nodes.label: Ancient North African
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Ancient North African as: Styles and cultures of North Africa in ancient times.

nodes.label: modern East African
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines modern East African as: Styles and culture belonging to modern East Africa.

nodes.label: Southern African
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Southern African as: Styles and cultures originating in the southernmost region of the African continent, comprising the modern countries of Angola, Botswana, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Swaziland, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. The island nation of Madagascar is excluded because of its distinct language and cultural heritage.

nodes.label: Eastern African
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Eastern African as: Styles and cultures of the eastern area of Africa, traditionally divided into two parts: East Africa (Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda) and the Horn of Africa (Somalia, Djibouti, Eritrea, and Ethiopia).

nodes.label: North African
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines North African as: Styles and cultures of the African peoples living in Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, and Mauritania.

nodes.label: Pole Style
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Pole Style as: Style of African sculpture, typically elongated, severe, and abstract-looking.

nodes.label: Round Style
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Round Style as: Style of African sculpture, characteristically naturalistic, gentle, and organic, featuring rounded shapes, and giving the impression of flesh over the bone structure.

nodes.label: Turkestani
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Turkestani as: Culture and styles of historic Turkestan, a region in Central Asia inhabited by Turkic and other peoples.

nodes.label: West Turkestani
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines West Turkestani as: Refers to the culture and styles of West Turkestan, which covered present-day Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and the southern part of Kazakhstan.

nodes.label: Taiwanese
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Taiwanese as: Nationality, styles, or culture of Taiwan, East Asia.

nodes.label: Afanasievo
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Afanasievo as: Refers to the Neolithic culture established in the slopes of the Afanasyevskaya Mountains from the 2nd millennium BCE. Sites have revealed tombs marked with stone circles symbolizing the Sun God, later ones took the form of barrows or large mounds. Pottery in earlier graves consisted of elongated, spherical vessels with herringbone patterns, while later pottery was flat-bottomed.

nodes.label: Altai
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Altai as: Style and culture of the mountain range running along border shared by China and Mongolia.

nodes.label: Andronovo
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Andronovo as: Refers to the Neolithic culture established in the steppes of the Minusinsk basin during the 2nd and 1st millennia BCE. Sites have revealed earth houses designed for permanent habitation, with hearths for heating purposes and cooking. Bronze objects were also numerous, and workshops existed for working copper.

nodes.label: Karasuk
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Karasuk as: Refers to the Iron Age culture established in the Minusinsk basin on the Yenisey River from about 1200 BCE to about 70 BCE. Sites have revealed elbow-shaped knifes related to those used between the 14th and 11th centuries BCE in China during the Shang Period. Also notable are pillars with stylized ram heads or human figures.

nodes.label: Okunev
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Okunev as: Refers to the Eneolithic culture established in the steppes of the Minusinsk basin by Mongoloid peoples probably of Northern Siberian descent, from the beginning of the 2nd millennium BCE. Tombs have revealed a variety of stone sculptures.

nodes.label: Siberian Arctic Native styles
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Siberian Arctic Native styles as: Styles belonging to Siberian Arctic Native cultures.

nodes.label: Tashtyk
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Tashtyk as: Refers to the Eneolithic culture established in the Minusinsk Basin between the 1st century BCE and the 5th century CE. Notable artifacts from the period include examples of the Scynthian-Siberian Animal style on bronze and gold, and clay funeral masks portraying faces with a two-color decoration.

nodes.label: Tungus
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Tungus as: Culture and style of the indigenous Tungusic people native to the vast subarctic boreal forests (taiga) of Siberia and the Russian Far East, as well as parts of northern China and Mongolia.

nodes.label: Assamese
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Assamese as: The Assamese are a major ethnic group of approximately 19.5 million people centered in the Indian state of Assam in northeastern India, speaking Assamese, the easternmost Indo-Aryan language with over 15 million native speakers. Their culture developed largely in isolation along the Brahmaputra River valley, shaped by centuries of interaction with neighboring Tibeto-Burman peoples, Tibetan influences, and the Ahom kingdom established by Tai invaders in 1229. Predominantly Hindu with animist traditions, the Assamese reflect a diverse heritage of Aryan, Ahom, and indigenous influences, and their language has historically served as a regional lingua franca across parts of northeastern India.

nodes.label: Bangladeshi
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Bangladeshi as: The nationality, style, or culture of Bangladesh, located at the northeast corner of the Indian subcontinent.

nodes.label: Indic
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Indic as: Culture and style of a diverse ethnolinguistic collection of peoples predominantly found in South Asia who speak languages belonging to the Indo-Aryan branch of the Indo-European family. As they settled the fertile Indus and Gangetic plains, their semi-nomadic pastoral lifestyle transitioned into intensive iron-age agriculture. They brought with them horses, spoked-wheel chariots, and a highly structured spiritual tradition.

nodes.label: Magars
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Magars as: The Magars are a Sino-Tibetan/Tibeto-Burman ethnic group native primarily to west-central Nepal, where they represent approximately 6.9% of the national population, with additional communities in northern India, Bhutan, Bangladesh, and diaspora populations worldwide. Their traditional homeland, historically known as Magarat, centered on the Palpa region west of the Gandaki River and was organized into confederations of twelve and eighteen Magar kingdoms during the medieval period. The Magars speak the Magar language (Magar Kura) in two major dialectal groups, practice a blend of Tibetan Buddhism, Hinduism, and shamanistic traditions, and are historically renowned for their service in Gurkha military regiments.

nodes.label: Pakistani
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Pakistani as: Refers to the style and culture of modern Pakistan.

nodes.label: Sri Lankan
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Sri Lankan as: Culture and style of an Indo-Aryan ethnic group native to the island country of Sri Lanka. They possess a 2,500-year written history characterized by grand ancient kingdoms, pioneering hydraulic engineering, and a foundational role in the preservation of Theravada Buddhism.

nodes.label: Akha
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Akha as: The Akha are an ethnic group inhabiting mountainous regions of Laos, Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam, and China's Yunnan Province, with approximately 80,000 now residing in northern Thailand following migrations that intensified during the 20th century due to civil conflicts. They speak Akha, a Loloish language within the Tibeto-Burman family that is closely related to Lisu. Historical evidence suggests the Akha may have ruled the Baoshan and Tengchong plains in Yunnan prior to the Ming dynasty invasion of 1644.

nodes.label: Batak
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Batak as: The Batak are a collective term for closely related Austronesian ethnic groups predominantly found in North Sumatra and adjacent provinces of Indonesia, who speak related Batak languages and share cultural traditions. The term encompasses six main subgroups—the Toba, Karo, Simalungun, Pakpak-Dairi, Angkola, and Mandailing—as well as other related ethnic groups with distinct languages and traditional customs (adat). With an estimated population of 6 million centered around Lake Toba, the Batak maintain indigenous writing systems (surat Batak) and diverse religious practices including Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, and syncretic traditions such as Malim.

nodes.label: Brao
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Brao as: The Brao are a Mon-Khmer language-speaking ethnic group of approximately 60,000 people divided into multiple subgroups, primarily residing in the southern Lao provinces of Champasak and Attapeu, the northeastern Cambodian provinces of Ratanakiri and Stung Treng, and a single village in Vietnam's Central Highlands. Historically inhabiting upland forested landscapes where they practiced swidden agriculture as their main livelihood, the Brao have experienced significant displacement as many communities in both Laos and Cambodia have been variously manipulated, coerced, or forced to resettle to lowland areas and adopt wet rice cultivation. This resettlement represents a major disruption to traditional Brao land use patterns and subsistence practices that were historically centered on upland forest environments.

nodes.label: Burmese
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Burmese as: Refers generally to the ethnic cultures of the region corresponding to modern Myanmar located in the western region of mainland Southeast Asia. Refers specifically to the style and period of the British colonial occupation from 1885 to 1948. Art in the region reveals bas-relief and monumental stone sculptures of Buddhist iconography and some British colonial influences.

nodes.label: Cambodian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Cambodian as: Nationality, culture, or style of Cambodia, located in the southern portion of the Indochina Peninsula in Southeast Asia. Arts and crafts of the region reveal Indian and other regional influences through various sculptures of wood and stone, lapidary pieces comprised of silver, gold, and ivory, and silk sheath pieces in various luxurious hues of red, blue, and gold.

nodes.label: Dayak
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Dayak as: The Dayak are indigenous Austronesian ethnic groups native to Borneo, comprising over 200 distinct riverine and hill-dwelling communities located principally in the central and southern interior of the island, each with its own dialect, customs, laws, territory, and culture. While these diverse groups share common distinguishing cultural traits, they maintain distinct identities and traditions. Historically practicing animist beliefs (Kaharingan and Folk Hinduism), the Dayak have undergone significant religious transformation since the 19th century, with mass conversions to Christianity and Islam.

nodes.label: Hmong
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Hmong as: Refers to the style and culture of the Hmong people centralized in scattered areas throughout China, Vietnam, Laos, and Thailand. Artistic production in this style features predominantly silver jewelry designs ranging from sliver chain necklaces with lock-shaped pendants attached to neck-rings, large collar necklaces covering the entire chest-area, heavy and narrow bracelets, to circle earrings that surround the ear, widening from narrow ends to a broad center, with pointed pendants hanging from tiny chains. Textile styles feature batik production characterized by geometric patterns on hemp and cotton, appliqué and reverse appliqué in bold colors, cold-dyed indigo, specific symbolic embroidery designs such as mustard blossom, cucumber seed, tiger teeth, and eye of the peacock, elaborate needlework, silk cocoon fibers, and flower and story cloth panel designs depicting village life, shaman's séances, legends and warfare.

nodes.label: Indochinese
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Indochinese as: Nationality and culture of the region between India and China, the areas of the current nations Burma, Kampuchea (Cambodia), Laos, Thailand, Vietnam and Malaysia.

nodes.label: Indonesian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Indonesian as: Refers to the cultures and styles of Indonesia, reflecting the blend of various regional cultures from the Southeast Asian mainland and Oceania. The style is generally driven by the philosophies of Buddhism, Hinduism, and Islam. Sculptural production in the region generally features megalithic monuments such as menhirs, dolmens, stone sarcophagi, terraced burial mounds, large stones carved into the shape of animals and humans, and stone skull troughs. Early styles of sculpture in the region feature smooth planes, convexity, impassive expressions, and lack of movement. Ornamental works from this region imitate Chinese Chou and pre-Han works and feature bronze drums with molded flanges and relief ornamentation consisting of stylized masks with ear piercings. Indian-influenced works feature intricate bronze Buddhas and bodhisattvas. In architecture, the style features temple complexes known as tjandis and candis.

nodes.label: Jarai
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Jarai as: The Jarai (or Dega) are an Austronesian indigenous people inhabiting Vietnam's Central Highlands and Cambodia's Ratanakiri Province, with diaspora communities in the United States following their collaboration with US forces during the Vietnam War. Speaking a Malayo-Polynesian language related to Cham and other Pacific Island languages, the approximately 332,558 Jarai constitute the largest Montagnard ethnic group and comprise 23% of Ratanakiri's population. While Cambodian and Vietnamese Jarai communities maintain shared cultural traditions and close interchange, their languages have diverged due to respective Khmer and Vietnamese linguistic influences, with only the Vietnamese Jarai possessing a standardized Latin script writing system.

nodes.label: Kachin
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Kachin as: Culture of the tribal Tibeto-Burman ethnic group inhabiting parts of northeastern Myanmar (Burma) and contiguous areas of India (Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland) and China (Yunnan).

nodes.label: African (general, continental cultures)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines African (general, continental cultures) as: Refers to the cultures of the continent of Africa, which is bounded by the Atlantic Ocean, the Indian Ocean, and the Mediterranean Sea.

nodes.label: Siberian (culture or style)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Siberian (culture or style) as: Style and culture of Siberia, particularly to that of any of the large number of small ethnic groups living in Siberia. Most engage either in reindeer herding or fishing, while some also hunt furbearing animals or farm and raise horses or cattle.

nodes.label: architecture (discipline)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines architecture (discipline) as: The art or science of designing and building structures, especially habitable structures, in accordance with principles determined by aesthetic and practical or material considerations. For a general term for the actual structures or parts of structures that were made by human beings, see "architecture (object genre)."

nodes.label: visual arts (discipline)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines visual arts (discipline) as: Discipline concerning physical objects that are meant to be perceived primarily through the sense of sight, were created by the use of skill and imagination, and possess an aesthetic that is valued and of a quality and type that would be collected by art museums or private collectors.

nodes.label: arts (broad discipline)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines arts (broad discipline) as: Refers broadly to the areas of activity that encompass both performing and visual arts. With reference more narrowly to the fine arts or the fine and decorative arts together, see "art."

nodes.label: design (discipline)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines design (discipline) as: Discipline comprising the creation of conceptual schemes for the organization or appearance of graphic works, objects, structures, or systems.

nodes.label: grammar (discipline)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines grammar (discipline) as: The study of the rules of a language governing the sounds, words, sentences, and other elements, including their structure, combination, and interpretation.

nodes.label: religion (discipline)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines religion (discipline) as: Study of religious beliefs and traditions in human life and culture from the perspective of the humanistic disciplines.

nodes.label: <religion and related disciplines>
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines <religion and related disciplines> as: The discipline of religion and closely related disciplines.

nodes.label: Associated Concepts
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Associated Concepts as: The Associated Concepts hierarchy contains terms for concepts and phenomena relating to a wide range of topics, including topics not directly related to art, for example philosophical concepts. Relation to other hierarchies: Terms for branches of learning and areas of specialization, as well as professions and professional specialties, (e.g., "history") are found in the Disciplines hierarchy, while concepts associated with these disciplines (e.g., "positivism ") appear here. Terms for styles and for art and architecture movements (e.g., "Neoclassical," "Impressionist") are found in the Styles and Periods hierarchy, while forms of expression (e.g., "abstraction") and broad categories of art and architecture that are not specific to a given people or period (e.g., "organic architecture," "street art") are here.

nodes.label: <linguistics and related disciplines>
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines <linguistics and related disciplines> as: The discipline of linguistics and other disciplines related to it.

nodes.label: <religions and religious concepts>
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines <religions and religious concepts> as: Religions and concepts related to religions.

nodes.label: music (performing arts genre)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines music (performing arts genre) as: Performing arts genre having to do with the combining of vocal or instrumental sounds in measured time to communicate emotions, ideas, or states of mind, usually according to cultural standards of rhythm, melody, and, in most Western music, harmony.

nodes.label: performing arts (discipline)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines performing arts (discipline) as: Disciplines concerning arts that depend upon performances presented to the attention of observers through the live or recorded actions of the artists, such as actors, musicians, poets, etc.

nodes.label: music (discipline)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines music (discipline) as: The discipline of combining vocal or instrumental sounds to produce beauty of form, harmony, melody, rhythm, expressive content, etc.; musical composition, performance, analysis, etc., as a subject of study; the occupation or profession of musicians.

nodes.label: ethics (philosophical concept)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines ethics (philosophical concept) as: System of moral principles or rules of conduct for voluntary human action. For the branch of philosophy that studies these principles and rules, with respect to the rightness or wrongness of certain human actions, and the goodness or badness of the motives and ends of such actions, use "ethics (philosophy)."

nodes.label: dance (discipline)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines dance (discipline) as: Discipline involving the study of dancing and movement, including performance.

nodes.label: photography (discipline)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines photography (discipline) as: The dedicated practice of making photographs as an applied art.
